0.title: The Son of God on the Move: The Gospel According to Mark
0.overview:
Mark's gospel is the sound of boots on cobblestones. No family tree, no angel’s announcement, no birth story: the very first sentence plants a flag and the rest of the book is a march: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.' Everything else is commentary on that title. Before a parable is told or a sermon delivered, demons have been cast out, fevers have broken, a leper has been made clean, and four fishermen have walked away from their nets to follow a man they have known for minutes. Mark writes at full sprint.

The tradition connecting this gospel to the apostle Peter is ancient and remarkably consistent. Papias, writing around 125 AD, records that Mark was Peter's 'interpreter' and wrote down accurately — though not in strict chronological order — what Peter preached about the Lord's words and deeds. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Eusebius all confirm the connection. The Gospel itself supports it: the gospel is saturated with the vivid, concrete, eyewitness detail of a man who was there — the green grass at the feeding (6:39), the look of anger on Jesus's face (3:5), the specific towns and houses and times of day. Peter's voice is everywhere. Mark's pen is the instrument by which that voice was preserved. The gospel was almost certainly written for a Roman audience — Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4), translates Aramaic phrases (3:17; 5:41; 7:34; 14:36; 15:22, 34), and uses Latin words that Roman readers knew (centurion, legion, denarius, praetorium). Scholars place the composition in the late 50s to mid-60s AD, either during Peter's lifetime or in the immediate aftermath of his death.

Which Mark? The Gospel itself names no author, but the early church agreed that it was John Mark, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first believers (Acts 12:12). He set out with Paul and Barnabas and turned back (Acts 13:13), was the cause of their parting (Acts 15:37–39), was later restored to Paul’s confidence, he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Tim 4:11), and was with Peter in Rome, who calls him Mark, my son (1 Pet 5:13). That is the man the tradition makes Peter’s interpreter.

Why is it so much shorter than Matthew and Luke, with no birth story? Mark gives mostly what Jesus did, and gives a large share of the book to his last week, rather than long blocks of teaching. He begins where the apostles’ preaching began, with John the Baptist and the public ministry (cf. Acts 10:37–38), and leaves the birth to Matthew and Luke. Shorter is not lesser; what Mark gives is the most vivid of the four.

The word that unlocks Mark is euthys — immediately, at once, straightway. It appears some forty-one times. This is not careless repetition; it tells us what the kingdom is like. When the King arrives, things happen. The blind see, the lame walk, the demons flee — and they do not do so on a leisurely timetable. The gospel's organizing question is not 'Who teaches about God?' but 'Who has authority over everything?' — over disease, over death, over the demonic, over the sea, over sin, over the law, over the grave. The answer Mark gives is Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God. The theological heart of the entire book is found in 10:45: 'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.' Everything before that verse is the demonstration of who he is; everything after it is the unfolding of what that service costs. Mark is the story of Jesus’ suffering and death with a long introduction, and the introduction is glorious.

1.title: The Kingdom Breaks In
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. <sup>2</sup>As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, “Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, <sup>3</sup>the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight”— <sup>4</sup>John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>5</sup>And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>6</sup>Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. <sup>7</sup>And he preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. <sup>8</sup>I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>9</sup>In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. <sup>10</sup>And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. <sup>11</sup>And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>12</sup>The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. <sup>13</sup>And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him. <sup>14</sup>Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, <sup>15</sup>and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” <sup>16</sup>Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>19</sup>And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. <sup>22</sup>And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. <sup>23</sup>And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, <sup>24</sup>“What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>25</sup>But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” <sup>26</sup>And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. <sup>27</sup>And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.” <sup>28</sup>And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee. <sup>29</sup>And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. <sup>30</sup>Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. <sup>31</sup>And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them. <sup>32</sup>That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. <sup>33</sup>And the whole city was gathered together at the door. <sup>34</sup>And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. <sup>35</sup>And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. <sup>36</sup>And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, <sup>37</sup>and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out.” <sup>39</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. <sup>40</sup>And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>41</sup>Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, “I will; be clean.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean. <sup>43</sup>And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, <sup>44</sup>and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>45</sup>But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
1.overview:
Mark 1 moves fast. In forty-five verses we go from the wilderness prophet to a leper made clean, by way of a baptism with the Spirit descending and the Father speaking, forty days facing Satan, four fishermen leaving their boats, a demon cast out in a synagogue, a fever healed with a touch, a whole town at a door after dark, and a prayer before dawn. Mark is not writing a full biography; he is showing who this man is by what he does when he arrives.

The chapter falls into four movements: the prologue (vv. 1–13), the kingdom announcement and the first calling (vv. 14–20), the day in Capernaum (vv. 21–34), and the morning prayer and preaching tour, ending with the cleansing of a leper (vv. 35–45).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Prologue: The Son Announced, Baptized, and Tested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first thirteen verses tell the reader three things before the public ministry starts: who Jesus is, which voices announce him, and that he has already met the enemy and stood firm.

Mark’s account of the temptation (vv. 12–13) is the shortest of the three: no dialogue, only the Spirit driving him out, Satan, the wild animals and the angels. Mark does not explain the victory; the reader will see its evidence as demons flee before him.
verseByVerse.theology:
At the baptism (vv. 9–11) the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks: the three persons of the one God revealed together. The Father’s words draw on Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm of David’s king, and Isaiah 42:1, the Servant on whom God’s Spirit rests, so that the King and the suffering Servant meet in one person.

Why was the sinless Jesus baptised with a baptism of repentance? Because he came to stand where sinners stand: God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). What begins at the Jordan is finished at the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: John wore camel’s hair and a leather belt, the dress of Elijah (2 Kings 1:8): a prophet’s uniform and a visible claim. He preached in the desert, not in Jerusalem, and the city of priests and scribes largely missed the moment. God’s preparing voice does not always come from where we expect it.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark’s first line names Jesus the Messiah and the Son of God, and every scene after it shows his authority over demons, disease and men’s lives, and shows him using it for the unclean: he comes near them, and by the end of the chapter he has taken the leper’s place outside the towns.

The setting. Mark is probably the earliest Gospel, written in the AD 50s or 60s. Early church writers from Papias (early second century) onwards say that John Mark wrote down the preaching of the apostle Peter, and later writers place it in Rome, for Gentile Christians facing persecution under Nero. Mark was the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10) and travelled with Paul and later with Peter (1 Peter 5:13). His Gospel gives about a third of its length to Jesus’ last week: a passion story with a long introduction.

A title, not an introduction. Verse 1 works the way In the beginning, God created works in Genesis 1:1: it announces what the whole document is about, something new and as large as creation. It may also mean that the whole story of Jesus’ life is only the beginning of the gospel, which continues to run on through the church to the ends of the earth, and has reached you.

Of the gospel. Euangelion means good news, and in the first century it was not chiefly a religious word. When a battle was won, a herald ran back with the gospel of victory, and an inscription from Priene in 9 BC calls the birthday of Caesar Augustus the beginning of the good news for the world. Mark takes Caesar’s word and gives it to a crucified Galilean. In Isaiah the good news is that God reigns and comes himself to save his people (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7), and Mark is announcing that the decisive battle has been joined and won, and that the one who won it is Jesus of Nazareth. The world had heralds for its emperors, and they are dust; their gospels are inscriptions in museums. But the good news of this King has outlived every empire that tried to silence it, because it is not the news of a man who seized a throne but of the Son of God who came down from one.

Of Jesus Christ. Jesus means the LORD saves. Christ is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed One, the King God promised to send. It is not a surname but a title, and to say it in Rome was to name a king other than Caesar.

The Son of God. The title that frames the whole Gospel. It stands here at the start; at the baptism the Father calls him his beloved Son (1:11); on the mountain of transfiguration he says it again (9:7); and at the cross, when the body hangs dead and there is nobody left to impress, a Roman centurion says it aloud: Truly this man was the Son of God (15:39). The great question of this Gospel is who Jesus is, and Mark tells the reader the answer in the first sentence. The disciples will take eight chapters to see half of it.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts omit the Son of God, including the original hand of the great fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus. Most, including Codex Vaticanus and very early and diverse witnesses and translations, include it. The likeliest explanation is mechanical rather than theological. Ancient copies wrote the sacred names as abbreviations, two letters with a stroke above, and in this phrase four such contractions fall one after another, of Jesus Christ, Son of God, a row of nearly identical short forms. That is exactly where a copyist’s eye slips and a phrase drops out. This commentary’s view: probably original; it fits the shape of the whole Gospel. And nothing depends on it. Strike it out and Mark is still about what verse 1 says, because he spends sixteen chapters proving it from every direction. The title does not rest on a disputed line in the first sentence. It rests on the book.

Who was Mark, and can his account be trusted if he was not one of the Twelve? Mark is very probably the young man who left Paul and Barnabas halfway through their first journey (Acts 13:13), so badly that Paul refused to take him again (Acts 15:37–39). Years later Paul writes that Mark is very useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). So what is probably the earliest Gospel was written by a man who had once failed and been restored, which is a gospel in itself. His account rests on Peter, an eyewitness from the first day at the lake to the empty tomb, and the ancient church received it on that basis. The vivid details, the cushion in the boat, the green grass, the hired servants, are just what Peter’s memory would supply on Mark’s page. Vividness alone cannot prove an eyewitness, but it fits what the early church reported about Mark’s source.
verseByVerse.note: “Gospel” means good news. “Christ” is the Greek form of the Hebrew “Messiah” — the anointed one, the promised king. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: John’s opening: the Word who was God

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written. Mark combines three Old Testament texts: Exodus 23:20, where God sends an angel before Israel on the road; Malachi 3:1, behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and Isaiah 40:3, a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the LORD. He names Isaiah, the most prominent prophet and the source of the main theme, as Jewish writers sometimes did when they combined texts. The claim is simple and enormous: the voice has cried, the way is being prepared, and the Lord himself is coming.

My messenger. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: the messenger goes ahead of the LORD, and the next line says that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. The one being prepared for is God. In Mark the words are spoken to Jesus: “before me” has become “your way”. The way of the LORD is the way of Jesus.

The voice. In Isaiah 40 this voice announces comfort to God’s people in exile: their warfare is ended, their iniquity is pardoned, and God himself is coming to lead them home through the desert in a new exodus. Mark begins his Gospel inside that comfort.

Prepare the way. Before a king visited a province, roads were repaired and straightened, valleys filled and hills levelled. John prepares hearts by calling them to repent. And LORD in Isaiah, in small capitals in your Bible, is the divine name itself. Mark applies two passages about clearing a road for the arrival of God, without argument or apology, to the arrival of a Galilean carpenter: two sentences in, he has identified Jesus with the God of Israel. The God of the burning bush, whose name the prophets wrote in trembling, did not send a deputy. He came himself, by the road Isaiah promised, on the feet of a man from Nazareth.

The terms for everything that follows. When this man forgives sins in chapter 2, the scribes will ask who can forgive sins but God alone, and they will be asking the right question. When he tells the sea to be still in chapter 4, the disciples will ask who this is, that even the wind and the sea obey him, and they will be asking the right question too. Mark answered both in his second verse, before either was raised.

Isaiah or the prophets. Later scribes, puzzled that words partly from Malachi are credited to Isaiah, changed it to the prophets in some manuscripts, and the KJV and NKJV follow them; the earliest manuscripts read Isaiah, as most modern Bibles do.

Why does Mark start with old prophecies instead of with Jesus himself? Because the good news is not a new idea that turned up in the first century. It is the keeping of a promise. Mark wants his Gentile readers in Rome to know that Jesus is not a religious novelty but the arrival of the God whom Israel’s prophets had promised for centuries. It also tells you how to read your Old Testament: not as a different religion that the New Testament replaced, but as the road on which the Lord was always coming. When you read Isaiah or Malachi, you are reading about Jesus before he arrived.

In everyday life. A road is prepared by taking out what is in the way: the hill of pride, the hollow of discouragement, the crooked place where you have learned to go round a sin instead of dealing with it. Name one such thing to Christ today; Isaiah’s call came wrapped in comfort, and he does not wait for the road to be perfect before he walks it.
verseByVerse.note: Mark names Isaiah, the better-known prophet, though the first line comes from Malachi.

verseByVerse.quote: John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the wilderness. After a long age in which Israel had felt that the voice of prophecy was silent, a prophet stands up. And the place is chosen: the wilderness is where Israel was born as a nation, and where the prophets said the restoration would begin (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). To go out there was to go back to the beginning, past the temple and the whole apparatus of religion in Jerusalem, and start again.

A baptism of repentance. Baptism means washing, immersion. Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism, but something you did to yourself, repeatedly. Later Jewish sources describe a once-for-all washing for Gentile converts, though how early it began is disputed. If it was already practised, John is giving the washing meant for outsiders to the descendants of Abraham, telling them that their ancestry will not save them. Repentance (metanoia) means a change of mind and heart, turning from sin to God, and the baptism expressed it.

For the forgiveness of sins. John’s baptism pointed to the forgiveness God would give through the one coming after him (v. 8). Paul says John told the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus (Acts 19:4).

All Jerusalem. All is a natural exaggeration, but the movement was huge, and it tells us the country knew something was wrong. People do not walk into a river and confess their sins in public because a preacher is eloquent. They do it because he has said out loud what they already suspected about themselves.

Confessing their sins. They confess at the Jordan, where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). John brings them back to the edge of the land, as if Israel had to cross in again. Most were the ordinary religious population of a religious country, and what John got them to admit was that religion had not dealt with their sin. That is still one of the hardest admissions a churchgoer ever makes, and there is no way to the rest of this book that goes round it.

The one who came down into the same river. John could wash bodies and name sins; he could not carry them away. Within a few verses the one who would carry them walks down into the same water, the only man in Israel with nothing to confess, and takes his place in the line. Jesus bears Joshua’s name, the LORD saves, and he goes down into the Jordan ahead of his people to lead them into a rest Joshua never gave (Hebrews 4:8–10).

What it does not mean. Not that water baptism itself forgives sins. Forgiveness comes from God to those who repent and believe; baptism is the outward sign. No rite can take away sin by itself (Hebrews 10:4).

How is John’s baptism different from Christian baptism, and what does that mean for me? John’s baptism looked forward to a Saviour who had not yet died and risen; Christian baptism looks back to one who has, and is into his name. What carries across is the order. People came to John repenting and confessing, and then were baptised. That is why this commentary holds to believer’s baptism, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession does: baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. Many faithful brothers and sisters baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the covenant sign for Christian families as circumcision was for Israel’s, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Christ. If you have repented and trusted Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your church about it. It is the ordinary first step of obedience, not a reward for advanced Christians.
verseByVerse.note: The Jordan runs south from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. John’s baptism was a public washing that marked a turning from sin; confession came with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now John was clothed with camel's hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. And he preached, saying, "After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Camel’s hair. This is not simply practical desert clothing. It copies Elijah, who wore a garment of hair with a belt of leather about his waist (2 Kings 1:8). John is dressed like Elijah, deliberately, in public, and Malachi closes by promising that Elijah would come before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Jesus later confirms it: Elijah has come (9:11–13).

Locusts and wild honey. The food of the desert, permitted by the law (Leviticus 11:22). It is not penance but a life stripped to what God supplies, outside the religious system he was sent to confront.

If John was Elijah, why did he deny it? When the priests asked him, Are you Elijah? he said, I am not (John 1:21). He was denying that he was Elijah returned in person, which is what they meant. He was not the old prophet come back from heaven. He was the one who came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), fulfilling Malachi’s promise. Scripture knows nothing of reincarnation: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). John was a new man, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, sent in Elijah’s role. The costume was telling the truth before John ever opened his mouth.

Not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task, so lowly that a saying recorded in later rabbinic writings allowed a disciple to do every service for his teacher except this one. John places himself below that. The greatest of the prophets (Matthew 11:11) sees himself as less than a slave before Jesus. This is genuine preparation: not building a movement around yourself, but pointing away from yourself so insistently that when the one you announce arrives, people recognise him.

The stronger one. Mightier simply means stronger, from the ordinary Greek word for strong (ischyros), and Jesus picks up that word himself when he is accused of casting out demons by Satan: no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (3:27). John is announcing the stronger one, who walks into the enemy’s house and takes back what was stolen. Soon Jesus is facing that strong man in the wilderness, and demons are crying out in a synagogue at the sight of him.

With the Holy Spirit. Jesus would do what only God can: pour out the Holy Spirit, as the prophets promised for the last days (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27). This happened at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:33). To be baptised with the Spirit is to be brought into new life by the Spirit, cleansed and indwelt: God the Holy Spirit comes to live in you, not as a visitor but as a resident. Your body becomes his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), and he does not leave (John 14:16–17). Every believer receives this (1 Corinthians 12:13).

What it does not mean. Not that Spirit baptism is a second experience after conversion for some believers only, as some Pentecostal traditions teach. Paul says all believers were baptised in one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Many who use that language love Christ deeply and have known real seasons of fresh blessing; the difference is over what to call them, and later fillings with the Spirit are real and to be sought. This commentary’s view: Spirit baptism happens at conversion; believers are then filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).

How do I know I have the Spirit if I have never had a dramatic experience? By what he does, not by how it felt. The Spirit makes you call God Father with real trust (Romans 8:15–16). He makes Jesus precious to you and teaches you to confess him as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes you hate the sin you once loved and fight it. He produces, slowly, love, joy, patience and kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ, you have the Spirit, whether or not you can name the day (Romans 8:9). Ask him to fill you afresh, and keep in step with him.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

parallels.desc: Elijah’s dress: hair and a leather belt

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days. One sentence is Mark’s entire account of the first thirty years of the Lord’s life. No genealogy, no manger, no shepherds; Jesus is simply standing there, a grown man of about thirty (Luke 3:23) walking into a river. Mark is not writing a biography but making a case for who Jesus is, and it begins the moment Jesus steps into public view.

From Nazareth of Galilee. Both words were a problem. Galilee was looked down on by Jerusalem, and its accent gave Peter away in a courtyard (14:70). Nazareth was a village of perhaps a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament: Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46). This man arrives on foot from a village nobody could place, at the wrong end of the country. The Lord whose way was prepared comes from nowhere important.

The walk itself. If John was at the crossings near Jericho, the road from Nazareth is three or four days, walked with the deliberate intention of joining a queue of people confessing their sins.

Baptized by John. A surprise. John’s baptism was for repentance and confession of sins, and Jesus had no sin to confess (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Why was he baptised? Matthew records his answer: to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:15). He identified himself with sinners, standing in the water with them, as he would later take their place on the cross (10:45). He obeyed every command of God on our behalf, so that his perfect obedience could be counted to people who have none. What he finishes at Golgotha he starts here, waist-deep in the Jordan.

Why do the Gospels differ so much in what they include? Each writer selected from far more than he could record (John 21:25) and arranged it for his purpose and his readers. Matthew, writing probably for Jewish believers, opens with the genealogy from Abraham; Luke, the careful historian, gives the birth; John begins before creation. Mark, writing for persecuted believers in Rome who needed to know who Jesus is and what following him costs, goes straight to the action. The four do not compete. They are four witnesses to one Lord, and together they give a fuller portrait than any one could alone.

In everyday life. If you have ever thought that the important things happen elsewhere, among people with better names and better postcodes, remember where the Son of God grew up. And if your sin puts you at the back of the queue, remember who chose to stand in it.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament.

parallels.desc: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately. Mark’s favourite word, here for the first time. It beats through this chapter like footsteps and gives his Gospel its urgency.

Torn open. Matthew and Luke say the heavens were opened; Mark says they were ripped. Isaiah had prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now God has done it. Mark uses the same word only once more: when the temple curtain is torn in two from top to bottom at Jesus’ death (15:38). The tearing at his baptism and the tearing at his death frame the whole Gospel. Heaven was torn open, and what came through was not thunder but love: the eternal Father looked on his eternal Son, standing in the river with sinners, and said, my beloved, my delight.

Like a dove. The Spirit anoints Jesus, marking him out and equipping him for his work as Messiah, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation, or the dove that came back to Noah with peace after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12).

My beloved Son. Matthew records the words as an announcement, this is my beloved Son; Mark gives them as the Father addressed them to the Son himself, an intimate word of identity spoken before the battle begins. The words join three Scriptures and lay them on one man. You are my Son comes from Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm. Beloved recalls Genesis 22:2, your son, your only son, whom you love, spoken of Isaac, who was to be offered. With you I am well pleased echoes Isaiah 42:1, the Servant who will later bear the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Israel had not expected these figures to meet in one person. The Father lays all of them on Jesus: the royal Son, the beloved Son who will be offered, and the Servant who will suffer.

Before he has done anything. The Father says it before a single miracle or sermon: he affirms before the Son serves. And this becomes the pattern of the Christian life, because those who are in Christ are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6): we serve from the security of the Father’s voice, not in search of it. God’s welcome does not rise and fall with your performance. On your best day and your worst he regards you as he regards his Son, because you are joined to his Son by faith and clothed with him (Galatians 3:26–27).

The Trinity. The Father speaks from the torn heaven, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends upon him: the three persons of the one God, revealed together, in the open, at the start.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism, as the early heresy called adoptionism taught. Mark’s first verse already calls him the Son of God. The baptism reveals and anoints who he already is.

Does God still speak from heaven like this? Not with new words to be added to Scripture. The voice at the Jordan was part of God’s once-for-all revelation of his Son, and it was written down so that we could hear it. God now speaks to us by his Son through the Scriptures, which are complete and sufficient (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Christians who say God spoke to them usually mean that he pressed a truth or a prompting on their heart; such impressions are to be tested by Scripture and never carry its authority. That is not a smaller gift. When you open your Bible to this verse, you are hearing the same Father say the same thing about the same Son, and, if you are in Christ, you are hearing how he regards you for his Son’s sake.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.note: “Torn open” (schizō) is the word Mark uses again when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus’ death (15:38).

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drove him out. It is a strong word, the one Mark uses again and again for casting out demons. The same Spirit who descended at the baptism thrusts Jesus into the desert. The test was not an accident but God’s purpose: from the voice of the Father straight into the face of the enemy.

Forty days. The number is never decorative in Scripture. Israel was forty years in the wilderness, tested and failed (Deuteronomy 8:2). Moses was forty days on the mountain (Exodus 34:28). Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus relives Israel’s story and succeeds where Israel failed. Israel was called God’s son (Exodus 4:22), was tested in the desert with hunger, and grumbled and turned to idols. Jesus, the true Son, is tested in the desert and stays faithful; Matthew and Luke show him answering Satan each time from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel’s wilderness years (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). He is the faithful Israel God always looked for, and his obedience is counted to those joined to him by faith.

Being tempted by Satan. Satan means adversary. He is a real, personal enemy who tempted the first Adam and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts Jesus, whom Paul calls the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (1 Corinthians 15:45). And this settles a comfort people badly need: being tempted is not sinning. Jesus was tempted, genuinely, and remained without sin: we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). So the arrival of a foul thought is not evidence that you are a fraud, only that you are being tempted, as the sinless Son of God was. What matters is what you do next, and the one who did not give way is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

With the wild animals. Only Mark mentions this. Some hear menace, the danger and loneliness of the place; others hear Eden and the peaceable kingdom where the wolf shall dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9). It may hold both: a man in real danger, and a sign of the creation that is coming. And Mark’s first readers in Rome, whose fellow believers Nero had dressed in the skins of animals to be torn to death by dogs, as Tacitus records, would take comfort that Jesus too had been among wild beasts and was kept.

The angels were ministering. Serving him, perhaps with food, as an angel fed the exhausted Elijah in the desert (1 Kings 19:5–8). Satan is there, the wild animals are there, and heaven is feeding him in the middle of it. That is a fair picture of the Christian life: real opposition, real exposure and real provision, all in the same wilderness at the same time.

Two men tested. Adam was tested in a garden, full and safe and in company, and he fell. The Son of God was tested in a desert, hungry and alone, and he did not. Everything that follows in this Gospel, every demon that flees, every disease that lifts, the tomb that empties, rests on the fact that the enemy came at him with everything and could not move him. He did it for us, in our name and in our flesh, and his victory in the desert is the first battle of the war he finished at the cross.

Named, tested, sent. The Son is named (1:11), then tested, then sent (1:14–15). Before he preaches the kingdom he has met the enemy on the enemy’s ground, so when demons start crying out at him, the reader knows why they are afraid (1:24; 3:27).

If the Spirit led Jesus into temptation, why do we pray, lead us not into temptation? Because God and Satan had different purposes in the same wilderness. Satan meant it as a trap; God meant it as a test, to prove his Son and to begin his victory. God himself tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people through testing for their good (James 1:2–4). Jesus went in our place into the full strength of the enemy’s attack, so we pray humbly, as he taught us, not to be brought into it, and to be delivered from evil. And when testing comes, we are not alone in it. He has been there, and won, and God provides the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Luke record the three temptations; Mark gives only the fact.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Kingdom Announced and the First Disciples Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John’s arrest marks the handover: the forerunner’s work is done, and the one he announced steps forward. Verses 14–15 give the gospel in four phrases: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand, repent, believe. It is an announcement that calls for an answer, not an offer to think about.

Then Jesus walks by the lake, speaks, and two pairs of brothers leave their work and their father to follow him. Mark does not explain it; he shows what happens when people meet someone with this authority.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 is the thesis of Mark’s Gospel. The time is fulfilled: the moment God appointed has arrived. The kingdom is at hand: God’s rule is present in the person of the King. Repent: turn round. Believe in the gospel: stake everything on the news that the King has come. The kingdom is not a programme or an idea but a Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Simon, Andrew, James and John left their nets, and Zebedee was left in the boat with the hired servants, not abandoned, but Jesus’ claim on his sons was greater than their father’s. The call of Jesus still comes before every other claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After John was arrested. Literally handed over. Herod Antipas imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to his brother’s wife (6:17–18), and Mark will tell it in full in chapter 6. The same word is later used of Jesus being handed over to death (9:31; 10:33; 15:1): the forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s.

Into Galilee. The northern region around the lake, with a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles. The public ministry of the Son of God begins among the farms and fishing villages of the north, far from every institution with the authority to certify him. He will get to Jerusalem, and it will kill him; but the years of teaching and healing happen out where ordinary people live.

The gospel of God. In verse 1 it was the gospel of Jesus Christ; now it is the gospel of God: God’s own announcement of what God is doing, not a proposal put forward for consideration. Proclaiming is a herald’s word: you either believe the report or you do not.

In everyday life. They silenced John, and God opened the mouth of his Son. If you are discouraged at how small your church or your witness looks, remember that the preaching tour that changed the world was conducted among farms and fishing boats.
verseByVerse.note: Galilee was the northern region of the land, around the lake. John was imprisoned by its ruler, Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time is fulfilled. The appointed time, the decisive moment, not the ticking of the clock. The long wait of the Old Testament is over. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4).

The kingdom of God. God’s reign: God acting as King to save his people and judge evil, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14). It is not a place, nor merely a future heaven. At hand means it has come near, within reach, arriving in Jesus himself. His healings and exorcisms show it (3:23–27).

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Both: where Jesus is, the kingdom has come near, yet it waits for its completion when he returns in glory (13:26). (See Luke 17:21 for the fuller answer.)

Repent. Turn around: a change of mind so thorough that it changes direction, away from sin and self-rule toward God. It is not an emotion or self-improvement. You can feel dreadful about your sin for years and never repent, because remorse looks at yourself while repentance turns to God. In practice it is concrete: naming the particular thing, agreeing with God about it, and turning, usually by a decision this week that costs something. Luther opened the Reformation by saying that the whole life of a believer is repentance.

Believe in the gospel. Rely on the good news, stake your life on it. What you rely on is a report: the news that the King has come and has done what was needed. Believing that a chair will hold you and sitting down in it are two different things, and only one of them is faith. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning, and they do not earn the kingdom; they receive it.

How do I know whether I have really repented and believed? Look at direction rather than intensity. Repentance is measured by which way you are facing, not by how much you felt on the day. Ask: is Christ my hope, and am I fighting my sin rather than making peace with it? And if you find you cannot turn, ask for it. Scripture speaks of repentance as something God grants (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25), which means the very thing commanded here can be requested from the one commanding it. That is why this is good news and not a hurdle. The King does not stand at a distance demanding that you climb; he has come near, and the command to turn is itself the outstretched hand.

Is it arrogant of Jesus to call everyone to repent? Only if he were saying that some people are better than others. He is saying the opposite. The call goes to everyone in exactly the same terms, to the religious leader and the tax collector, the respectable and the disgraced, because before a holy God the decent person and the notorious one need the same mercy (Romans 3:22–24). Arrogance looks down on others. Repentance is the one posture in which nobody can look down on anybody. And the command comes from a King who did not stay at a distance to issue it: he came near, and went to the cross to make the turning possible. A call to come home is not an insult. It is an invitation from the only one with the right to give it.

Is the kingdom of God the same as the church? Not quite. The kingdom is God’s reign; the church is the people gathered under that reign, the community where it is confessed, preached and lived. The kingdom is wider: Christ already reigns over all things for his church (Ephesians 1:22), and one day his rule will fill a new heaven and a new earth. But the church is where the kingdom shows its face now, in forgiven sinners worshipping their King, so belonging to a local church is not optional for a citizen of the kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: “The kingdom of God” means God’s reign, his rule as King. “At hand” means it has come near.

verseByVerse.quote: Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men." And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles long, ringed with fishing towns. Mark grounds the call in an ordinary working morning.

Casting a net. The circular casting net, weighted round the rim and thrown by hand, takes years to learn: a skill, an income and an identity. Mark’s Gospel probably comes from Peter’s preaching, so this is Peter telling the story of the morning his life changed.

Had they met Jesus before? Very probably. John’s Gospel records an earlier meeting: Andrew was a disciple of the Baptist, heard him point at Jesus and say, Behold, the Lamb of God, spent a day with him, and went to find his brother with the words, We have found the Messiah; and Jesus looked at Simon and renamed him (John 1:35–42). That happened at the Jordan, some time before. By the time Jesus comes up the shoreline, these are not strangers. This does not damage Mark’s point; it makes it firmer. Mark is shortening a history he assumes you know. What he records is not the moment they first believed but the moment they were called into his service: the men had believed already, and at the lake following came to mean leaving everything. That is the harder step, and the one Mark wants you to see.

Follow me. Literally come behind me. Students usually chose their rabbi, it seems; Jesus chooses his disciples, and calls them not to a set of teachings but to himself. The authority of the one calling is the point. He walked along a beach and spoke two words, and four working men walked out of their lives into his. That is the voice that called the worlds into being, and it has not weakened.

Fishers of men. Men means people. He does not tell them to abandon what they are; he tells them what they are for. Every instinct the lake taught them, patience, early starts, working all night for nothing, will be needed, aimed now at people. And I will make you become is a promise that takes time: he takes responsibility for forming them. The disciples in Mark are often confused, fearful and faithless, and yet they are the ones he is making. The calling comes before the competence.

Repent and believe, with a name attached. Verses 16–20 show what repenting and believing (v. 15) looked like for four particular men. Not every Christian must leave his job, but every disciple must put Jesus before everything.

I am not a preacher, so what does fishing for people look like for me? Mostly it looks like ordinary faithfulness where you already are. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ. Be the kind of neighbour and colleague whose life raises questions, and answer them gently when they come (1 Peter 3:15). Invite people to your home and to church. Tell your own story of what Christ has done, simply. Fishermen work in teams, and so do Christians: you may never be the one who draws the net in, but the one who cast it, mended it or rowed the boat is part of the catch.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about 13 miles long. A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mending the nets. The second pair are called off the unglamorous half of fishing, the half that never ends. James and John, with Peter, became Jesus’ inner circle (5:37; 9:2; 14:33). Jesus nicknamed them Sons of Thunder (3:17), and John became the disciple who wrote of love.

They left their father. Only Mark mentions the hired servants. Zebedee ran a business with employees, and the brothers left a prosperous family firm and their father in mid-work. But the detail also shows the business did not depend on the two sons alone: a real cost, and not a cruelty.

The Son who left his Father’s house. The one calling them knows that cost from the other side. The eternal Son came out from the Father into a world that did not receive him (John 1:11; 16:28), and before long his own family would come to take him home, convinced he was out of his mind (3:21). He never asks a disciple to leave anything he did not leave first, and more. And what he calls them into is a family of his own: whoever does the will of God, he says, is his brother and sister and mother (3:35). No one has ever left anything for him and found himself the poorer: he gives back a hundredfold, and in the age to come eternal life (10:29–30).

What if following Jesus divides me from my family? Jesus warned it would sometimes happen (10:29–30; Matthew 10:34–37), and promised that no one who leaves home or family for his sake will lose out, in this age or the next. Following him first does not mean despising your family. Keep honouring your parents, keep loving them, keep serving them in practical ways; the hired servants show that these sons did not leave their father helpless. But when their wishes and Christ’s commands collide, Christ comes first. Do it gently, without self-righteousness, and keep praying. Many families who were hurt by a believer’s choice have later been won by the same believer’s patient love.
verseByVerse.note: James and John left “hired servants” with their father, so Zebedee ran a working fishing business.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–45 — Authority in Capernaum and Beyond
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 21–45 show Jesus’ authority in one setting after another: in the synagogue, over teaching and a demon; in the house, over a fever; at the door after dark, over sickness and possession in great numbers; before dawn, the prayer behind it all; and on the road, the cleansing of a leper.
verseByVerse.theology: In the synagogue (vv. 21–28) the unclean spirit names Jesus accurately as the Holy One of God, and Jesus silences it. A demon is no fit witness to Jesus even when what it says is true; his identity has to be understood through the cross, not only through displays of power. Throughout Mark, Jesus will not let the wrong voices tell the right story.
verseByVerse.examples: The leper (vv. 40–45) prays the most honest prayer in the chapter. He does not doubt the power, only the willingness, and Jesus answers that question by touching him: I will; be clean. Then it was a man shut out of community, worship and human touch. Now it is anyone who comes to God unsure whether he really wants them. He does.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Capernaum. A fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, on the trade road, with a customs post and a Roman centurion stationed there (Luke 7:1–5), which became the base of the Galilean ministry (2:1). Archaeologists have found a later synagogue on what may be the foundations of the one Jesus knew, and a house venerated from early times as Peter’s.

The synagogue. The local meeting place for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture, the most public platform a town had. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:15).

As one who had authority. Astonished means struck, knocked out of their composure. The crowd’s point is not that Jesus was a better speaker; it is the basis on which he spoke. The scribes, as far as later Jewish writings show, taught by quoting earlier teachers, tracing a ruling back through a chain of rabbis; their authority was borrowed. Jesus quotes no rabbi. He teaches as a man reporting what is the case, and a room trained to expect footnotes is struck. They had come to hear the Scriptures explained. They got the one the Scriptures are about, in the room: the Author reading his own book aloud. Mark does not record what he taught here; the focus is on who he is.

One day in Capernaum. Verses 21–34 give one Sabbath from morning to night, a sample of the kingdom Jesus has just announced (1:15), and Mark puts the teaching first.

Should my pastor teach with authority like this? Only in a borrowed and lesser way, and that is right. Jesus’ authority was his own. A faithful preacher’s authority is exactly as great as his faithfulness to Scripture: when he says what the text says, he speaks with Christ’s authority, and you should receive it as God’s word (1 Thessalonians 2:13); when he goes beyond it, he speaks only as a man. So test what you hear by the Bible, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11), and when it is true, do not treat it as one opinion among many. The scribes’ failure was not that they quoted others but that they never brought people face to face with God’s own voice.

In everyday life. Pick one thing Jesus says plainly, about worry, money, forgiveness or anger, that you have been treating as advice, and treat it as a command from the one who has the right to give it, and who by his Spirit in you gives the strength to keep it.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee. Scribes were the trained teachers of the law of Moses.

parallels.desc: the same astonishment after the Sermon on the Mount

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, "What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An unclean spirit. A demon: a fallen angel, morally impure, which defiles and torments the person it controls. And look where it happens: not among the tombs, but in the synagogue, on the Sabbath, during the service. Whatever was in him may have sat quietly through the readings week after week, until Jesus walked in. The presence of Christ does not create the problem; it brings it to the surface. Things that have coexisted comfortably with religion for years become unbearable the moment he is actually in the room.

What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? A Hebrew idiom: what is there between us? Leave us alone. And us: the demon speaks for the whole kingdom of evil spirits. Knowing facts about Jesus is not enough; even demons know them, and know them accurately.

Have you come to destroy us? It is not defiance but panic. The demons know that Jesus has come to defeat them; the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). This spirit knows exactly who has walked in and exactly how the story ends.

The Holy One of God. The demon recognises what the people do not. Holy means utterly pure and set apart (Isaiah 6:3–5), and an unclean spirit cannot be at ease in his presence. Demons in Mark repeatedly recognise Jesus before the disciples do (3:11; 5:7), yet knowing who he is does not make them his followers; they believe and shudder (James 2:19). Some suggest that naming him was an attempt to gain power over him, as ancient magic believed that knowing a name gave control. If so, it failed in the next breath.

What is an unclean spirit, and does any of this happen now? This is the first exorcism in Mark and there will be many, so the question is best met here. Scripture treats demons as real personal beings, fallen and malevolent, not a first-century label for illness that we have since outgrown. And the Gospel writers themselves keep the categories apart. A few verses on, Mark says the people brought all who were sick or oppressed by demons, and that Jesus healed many who were sick and cast out many demons (vv. 32, 34): two groups, two verbs, listed side by side by a writer who plainly did not think they were the same thing. Luke, who was a doctor, keeps the same distinction. These men were not simply calling every illness a demon for want of a better word.
verseByVerse.note: An “unclean spirit” is a demon. “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him!" And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be silent. Literally be muzzled. Why, when it was telling the truth? Because Jesus would not accept testimony from demons, nor be proclaimed Messiah before the cross had shown what kind of Messiah he is (see below on v. 34).

Come out of him! Ancient exorcists named a superior spirit and used formulas, rings or roots; their power was borrowed, and it might not work (compare Acts 19:13–16). Jesus uses no name but his own, no formula and no delay. He tells it to be quiet and to get out, and it is quiet and it gets out. All the massed power of hell, in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, lasted one sentence against him.

Convulsing him. A final violent display, but it had to obey. Luke adds that it did the man no harm (Luke 4:35).

Two ditches. Does it still happen? Yes, and there are two ditches. One is to deny the whole category, a modern reflex rather than a biblical conclusion. The other, in our churches the more damaging, is to see a demon behind everything. Treating depression, epilepsy, trauma or a chemical illness as a spirit to be cast out has done real and lasting harm to people who needed a doctor and got an exorcism instead. When the apostles write about the Christian’s daily struggle, they speak overwhelmingly of sin, the flesh and the world, and the weapons they prescribe are ordinary: Scripture, prayer, truth, the armour of God, the company of the church (Ephesians 6:10–18). If you are unwell, see a doctor; that is not a failure of faith but an ordinary mercy God provides.

Could what happened to this man happen to a Christian? No. You cannot be owned by what has already been beaten. The man in the synagogue was held by an unclean spirit until Jesus spoke; a believer has already been spoken for. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4), and a person indwelt by the Spirit of God is not available for occupation: harassed sometimes, tempted certainly, but not possessed. You belong to Christ, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Some Christians believe a believer can be troubled by evil spirits more deeply than this; but the New Testament never describes a believer as possessed. So if you read a passage like this at night and feel afraid, resist the devil by the ordinary means and he will flee from you (James 4:7). And if you have dabbled in the occult in the past, renounce it plainly before God, get rid of anything connected with it (Acts 19:18–19), tell a pastor, and rest in Christ’s finished victory.

In everyday life. Whatever has a grip on you must obey his word. Bring it to him by name in prayer, and tell one trusted believer about it. Shame keeps things in the dark; Christ’s word brings them out.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus uses no ritual, no formula and no appeal to another power — a command alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him." And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is this? A new teaching with authority! They were all amazed, first at his teaching and now at his power. Read the crowd’s sentence carefully, because what they say is true but stops short. What is this? Not who is this. That question comes later in Mark, and it is the question the whole Gospel is driving at (4:41; 8:29). Here they ask what, as though it were a phenomenon rather than a person. New (kainē) means new in kind, fresh. And they connect the two things Mark has laid side by side, the astonishing teaching in verse 22 and the expulsion in verse 26. They are right to connect them. In this Gospel the word and the power are never separate. What he says happens, whether he is saying it to a room or to a spirit.

Even the unclean spirits. The evidence that the kingdom of God has arrived: Satan’s power is being broken; the strong man is being bound (3:27). But listen to what they call it. They have watched a man command a demonic power out of a neighbour with a sentence, and their category for it is a new teaching, a very good lesson. It is not wrong. It is nowhere near big enough. It was the voice of the Creator in a village synagogue, the word that said let there be light now saying come out, and being obeyed.

His fame spread. The news is out of the building before the Sabbath is over, and by the end of the verse it has the whole district. And that spreading fame is the thing Jesus will spend the rest of the chapter, and much of the Gospel, trying to manage: silencing demons, silencing the healed, withdrawing to desolate places. Not because the reports were false, but because a reputation built on power would fix in people’s minds a Messiah who was never going to be crucified. He is not building a following. He is going to a cross, and a crowd that wants a miracle worker will not follow him there.

Is it wrong to be amazed by Jesus without fully understanding him? No, it is often where faith begins. But amazement is a doorway, not a room to live in. These crowds were amazed and many of them later drifted away. The amazement that saves moves from what is this? to who is this? and then to you are the Christ, and finally to the trust that follows him even to the cross. If you are amazed by Jesus but not yet sure who he is, keep reading Mark. Its whole purpose is to take you from wonder to faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of Simon. From public ministry to a private home, from synagogue to kitchen. Jesus’ power is for ordinary households, not only for public spectacles.

Simon’s mother-in-law. Peter was married, and this domestic scene is very likely Peter describing his own front room. In the ancient world fevers killed.

Peter’s wife. The Roman Catholic Church names Peter the first pope and, in the Latin tradition, requires its priests to be unmarried, a discipline it acknowledges was not the apostles’ own rule. Years into the work Peter was still travelling with a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:5). This is no argument against celibacy freely chosen, which Paul commended and lived (1 Corinthians 7:7–8); but a rule that forbids marriage to those who hold Peter’s office cannot appeal to Peter. Scripture expects that a pastor may well be the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2).

Lifted her up. They brought her need to Jesus, which is the beginning of every answer to prayer. Lifted her up is the word used for resurrection (16:6): a small sign of the greater raising to come.

She began to serve. No time of recovery needed. The word is the one Mark used a few verses earlier of the angels ministering to Jesus in the wilderness (1:13), and the one Jesus will use of himself: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45).

Is it demeaning that the healed woman goes straight to the kitchen? Not in Mark’s eyes. He uses for her work the same word he uses for angels serving the Son of God and for the Son of God giving his life. Serving a meal to Jesus and his friends puts her in very high company. Hospitality is honoured throughout Scripture (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2), and many women served Jesus out of their means and were the faithful witnesses at the cross and the tomb (15:40–41). Every Christian, man or woman, is healed in order to serve, and no service done for Christ is small.

For worship. The kingdom’s first stop after the synagogue was a sickroom off somebody’s kitchen. That is the kind of King he is: Lord of angels, and not too great to take a feverish woman by the hand.

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening at sundown. The Sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules about carrying burdens.

At the door. The door was Peter’s, and the scene has the feel of a householder’s memory.

Healed many. Many here means a great number, and in Hebrew idiom it can mean all of a large company. Matthew writes that he healed all who were sick (Matthew 8:16), and the two fit: Mark stresses the scale of the night, Matthew that no one who came was turned away. Picture the door of that little house at dusk, the whole town pressing round it, and one man moving among them, touching, speaking, healing, until the last of them went home. He never turned anyone away for being too much trouble.

Why does Jesus keep telling people to be quiet about him? This silencing runs right through Mark, and scholars call it the messianic secret. It is not that Jesus is hiding; the crowds see everything he does. He refuses to let the word Messiah be shouted before it can be rightly understood. In first-century Galilee that word meant a conquering king who would drive out Rome; to be hailed as Messiah too early would light a political fire. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. So he controls the timing, moving deliberately toward Jerusalem, so that when the title is finally confessed it will be defined by his death and not by the crowd’s dreams. With demons there is a further reason: praise from liars to the core is no honour to the Holy One. The secret is not concealment but protection: the right truth, at the right time, on the right lips.

Does he heal everybody, and if not, why not me? Say the honest thing first. What happened in Capernaum that night was not normal and was never claimed to be. Such miracles clustered around Jesus and then his apostles to authenticate the message while it was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4); we are nowhere promised that abundance now, and anyone who guarantees it is promising what Scripture does not. At the same time God has not retired. He remains entirely free to heal, and still does, and the church is told plainly to pray for the sick and expect him to act (James 5:14–15). So we ask, honestly and often, and we leave the outcome where it belongs. Christians differ on how far gifts of healing continue: this commentary holds that the apostles’ sign-gifts ceased with them, because their purpose of confirming the apostolic message was fulfilled, while honouring brothers and sisters who expect them still; all agree that God hears prayer for the sick.

The signpost is not the country. Then say the deeper thing, where the comfort is. Every person healed in this chapter died later. Not one of these healings was the destination; every one was a signpost, a piece of the new creation pushed early into the old, so that we would know what the King is going to do with the whole of it. What is guaranteed to the believer is not healing now but resurrection then, and a body that will never need healing again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Revelation 21:4). If you are not healed, it is not that your faith was too small or that he was unwilling. It is that the signpost is not the country, and you are still on the road to it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick through the town without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, and they found him and said to him, "Everyone is looking for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Very early. After an exhausting evening, this verse shows what lay beneath it all. The authority was his own, as the eternal Son, yet he exercised it as a man living in unbroken dependence on his Father (John 5:19). The eternal Son, who shared the Father’s glory before the world was, slipped out of a sleeping house in the dark to be with him.

A desolate place. The word for wilderness. Mark shows Jesus praying at three key moments, each at night: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–39). The verse gives a time, a place and a priority: early, before anyone could reach him; alone, out of range; and first, before the day’s demands arrived rather than after they were met.

Do I have to pray at five in the morning? No. This passage often leaves readers feeling condemned, so it is worth working out properly. Many Christians have read this verse, set an alarm for five o’clock, managed it for nine days, and concluded they are second-rate. Mark is recording what Jesus did, not legislating an hour. Scripture nowhere commands a time of day, and the Lord himself kept no fixed slot: he prayed through an entire night before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12) and went up the mountain to pray in the evening after feeding the crowd (6:46). What is constant is not the clock but the withdrawal. The hour mattered only because of what it protected. He was not being austere; he was getting somewhere he could not be reached. In a life with no margin in it, prayer is never found. It has to be taken.

What should I actually do when I get alone with God? Keep it simple and scriptural. Open the Bible and read a passage slowly, perhaps a chapter of a Gospel or a psalm, and ask what it shows you of God and of yourself. Then pray from it: praise him for what you have seen, confess what it exposed, thank him for his mercies, and bring your requests and other people’s by name. The Lord’s Prayer is a pattern for exactly this (Matthew 6:9–13). Ten honest minutes most days is better than an hour you never reach. If your mind wanders, bring it back without fuss. You are not performing; you are a child talking to your Father.

Searched for him. The word means hunted him down, pursued him.

Everyone is looking. The disciples saw a great opportunity: popularity, crowds, success. In effect they tell him he is missing his moment.

In everyday life. Name the time and the place you will be alone with God, and guard them. If you have failed at this for years, do not start with guilt. He has prayed for you far more faithfully than you have ever prayed for yourself. Start tomorrow, small.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next towns. A whole town wants him, and it is a genuinely good thing being offered: more healing, more obvious fruit. And he says no. Prayer had clarified his purpose: the crowds wanted miracles; Jesus’ priority was preaching. The healings served the message, not the other way round.

For that is why I came out. Perhaps came out from Capernaum, or more deeply, came from the Father into the world (John 16:28). His mission was to proclaim the kingdom. He could say no to a good thing because he had already settled in the dark what the day was for. If you do not decide before the demands arrive, the demands will decide, and you will spend your life on whatever shouts loudest, which is usually good, and usually not what you were sent to do. And the voice hardest to refuse is not an enemy’s but a friend’s, telling you that everyone is looking for you. Being wanted is one of the strongest pulls on a human heart, and many people who would never chase money will bend their whole life to stay needed. Jesus loved those crowds, and still he would not let their approval choose his road. Everyone was looking for him, and he went looking for everyone else: the next village, the far country, the lost sheep.

Throughout all Galilee. Preaching and casting out demons go together. The word of the kingdom does not only inform; it changes the places it enters.

The order of the Gospel. Mark sums up weeks of work in a sentence, and sets the order for the whole Gospel: the healings follow the preaching and serve it. That is why chapter 2 opens with Jesus preaching the word to a packed house before anyone is healed (2:2).

How do I know what my main calling is? Start with what is plain in Scripture for every Christian: to love God, to love your neighbour, to belong to and serve a church, to make Christ known. Then add what your place in life gives you: a spouse to love, children to raise, a job to do faithfully, parents to honour. Your gifts, the church’s wise counsel and the needs in front of you help to fill in the rest. Most people do not need a new calling so much as the courage to say no to good things that crowd out the ones already given.

verseByVerse.quote: And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, "I will; be clean." And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A leper. Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases (Leviticus 13–14). A leper was ritually unclean, had to live outside the town, wear torn clothes, cover his lip and call out Unclean, unclean! (Leviticus 13:45–46). He was cut off from worship, from family and from all human touch, and curing leprosy was thought as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). This man breaks every expectation, comes close, and kneels.

If you will. His prayer is a small masterpiece of faith: he does not doubt the power; he leans his whole weight on it. He is uncertain only about the heart.

Moved with pity. Pity (splanchnistheis) is deep, gut-level compassion. But one ancient Greek manuscript and several early Latin translations read moved with anger (orgistheis). The two words look nothing alike in Greek, so a slip of the eye is unlikely; a scribe softening a startling anger to a gentle pity is the easier change to explain, which is why some scholars think the harder reading may be original. This commentary’s view: the evidence is divided; pity is better supported, though anger may be the harder and therefore original reading. Either way, Jesus is moved deeply. Most English Bibles read pity or compassion; the NIV follows the other reading and says Jesus was indignant.

If Mark wrote anger, at what? Not at the man; Jesus touches him in the same breath. At the thing that has him: at the disfiguring, isolating cruelty of the disease, at the whole ruin the enemy has worked in God’s good world. It is the same holy indignation with which he would groan in spirit at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:33, 38). Pity and anger are not rivals here. Love for the sufferer is fury at what is destroying him, and both bend the same hand toward the untouchable to make him clean.

He touched him. Jesus touched the untouchable. Perhaps no one had touched this man for years, and Jesus could have healed with a word, as he does elsewhere: the touch is deliberate. When Jesus touches a leper, the uncleanness does not pass to him; his cleanness passes to the leper. That is the direction grace always moves, and it is what he will do with the moral uncleanness of his people at the cross.

I will. The direct answer to the man’s question: not I might, or under the right circumstances. And he was not only healed but clean: restored to God’s people and to worship.

What it does not mean. Not that we should pray if you are willing about forgiveness. God has promised to forgive all who come to him (1 John 1:9). We may pray if you are willing about healing or circumstances, which he has not promised.

A guard on I will. What Jesus settles here for all time is his willingness to receive and cleanse the person who wonders whether he is wanted. It is not a promise that every disease will be removed on request: healing now remains his free gift, while resurrection is his promise. Whether he will heal your body today, you must ask him and leave with him. Whether he is willing to have you, unclean as you come, he has already stretched out his hand and answered.

What if what makes me feel unclean is something I did, not something that happened to me? Then this story is still for you, and even more so. The leper’s disease was a picture of sin: it spread, it defiled, it cut people off from God and from one another. The cleansing Jesus gives reaches the guilty conscience as well as the wounded body. The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), including the thing you are most ashamed of. Come as the leper came, kneeling and honest. You do not need to clean yourself up first. That is exactly what he came to do.

In everyday life. Ask who in your world is treated as untouchable: the lonely, the ill, the disgraced, the person everyone avoids. A hand on the shoulder, a meal, a visit may be the first human touch they have had in a long time.

For worship. The Holy One rested his hand on a ruined body and was not stained by it. Every outcast who has ever knelt and wondered whether he is wanted has the same answer, spoken once on a Galilean road and sealed at the cross, where the Clean One bore the uncleanness of his people: I will; be clean.
