verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart from others — so touching one was unheard of.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, and said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them." But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sternly charged. The word is a strong one, used of snorting with indignation, and it is the same verb John uses of Jesus at the grave of Lazarus. If Mark wrote anger in verse 41, verse 43 is of a piece with it: two fierce words in a scene otherwise pure tenderness.

Say nothing. The same command as at verse 34 (also 3:12; 5:43; 8:30), and here its practical reason shows: crowds that would make his preaching impossible, as happened (v. 45).

Show yourself to the priest. The law required a priest to examine and declare a leper clean, with offerings of birds, lambs, flour and oil (Leviticus 14:1–32). Jesus wants the man fully restored, not only in his skin but in his place among God’s people.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests that something extraordinary had happened, evidence they could not deny. The king of Israel had once cried that only God, who kills and makes alive, could cure a leper (2 Kings 5:7), and now a cleansed leper would be standing in front of them with his offering.

He began to talk freely. He disobeyed, out of joy. It is entirely understandable: he had been required to shout his own contamination at anyone who came near, and a man had put a hand on him. But disobedience, even happy disobedience, had consequences.

Out in desolate places. The man who had been shut out of the towns is now free to walk into any of them; and the one who freed him has taken his place outside. This exchange is a small picture of where the whole Gospel is heading: Jesus took the leper’s place, as he would take ours at the cross, when he suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). The clean man goes in. The one who made him clean goes out. And even there people kept coming to him from every quarter; he could not be hidden.

So should I keep quiet about what Jesus has done for me? No. This command was for a particular moment, before the cross, when talk of a miracle worker would hinder his mission. After the resurrection the command is the opposite: go and tell (16:7; Matthew 28:19–20). Even in Mark, the healed man of Gerasa, in Gentile territory, is told to go home and tell how much the Lord has done for him (5:19). The lesson for us is not silence but obedience: to tell what he has done in the way and at the time he commands, which now means gladly, plainly and often.
verseByVerse.note: The cleansing involved the priest’s inspection, two birds, and offerings on the eighth day.

1.theology:
Before his ministry begins, Jesus is identified from three directions: by the Father (my beloved Son), by Scripture (as it is written), and by his own announcement that the kingdom of God is at hand. So when the demons recognise him and the crowds are astonished, the reader already knows why.

Jesus silences the demons and tells the healed not to speak. This is not evasion but timing. Popular hope expected a military deliverer, and a following built on miracles would have pulled him away from the cross. Who the Messiah is had to be defined by the cross before it was proclaimed, and fittingly the great confession comes from a Roman soldier at the foot of it (15:39).
1.examples: The disciples here are responsive but unformed. They leave their nets and follow, and they come looking for him to report the crowds, but they do not yet understand whom they are following. Discipleship often begins like that: answering Jesus before you have the words to explain him. The understanding comes later, often painfully.

keyVerse.quote: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.

2.title: Who Has Authority to Forgive?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. <sup>2</sup>And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them. <sup>3</sup>And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. <sup>4</sup>And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. <sup>5</sup>And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” <sup>6</sup>Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, <sup>7</sup>“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>8</sup>And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you question these things in your hearts? <sup>9</sup>Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’? <sup>10</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— <sup>11</sup>“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.” <sup>12</sup>And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!” <sup>13</sup>He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. <sup>14</sup>And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>15</sup>And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. <sup>16</sup>And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>17</sup>And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>18</sup>Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <sup>20</sup>The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day. <sup>21</sup>No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. <sup>22</sup>And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins.” <sup>23</sup>One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. <sup>24</sup>And the Pharisees were saying to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” <sup>25</sup>And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>26</sup>how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?” <sup>27</sup>And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. <sup>28</sup>So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the first gathering of the storm. Four episodes, the paralysed man, the call of Levi and the dinner with sinners, the question about fasting, and the grain plucked on the Sabbath, each raise the same question more sharply: who does this man think he is, and by what right does he do what he does? Read on to 3:6, where the Pharisees plot to destroy him.

The key is the sentence spoken over the paralysed man: Son, your sins are forgiven. The scribes rightly see it as a claim to do what only God does. They are right that only God forgives; they are wrong about who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Paralytic and the Authority to Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and the house fills to the door while he preaches the word (vv. 1–2). Four men dig through the roof to lower their paralysed friend (vv. 3–4). Jesus forgives his sins, and the scribes silently charge him with blasphemy (vv. 5–7). He proves the claim no one can see by a healing everyone can see, and the man walks home carrying his bed (vv. 8–12).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first place in Mark where Jesus does what belongs to God alone. A priest could declare a man clean and a prophet could announce God’s pardon, but nobody in Israel forgave sins in his own name. Mark lets the scribes’ logic stand: if only God forgives, and Jesus is not blaspheming, then he is God. And the pardon is given on earth (v. 10), in a crowded house, to a man who had brought no sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: four men digging through a roof because the door was blocked, not by enemies, but by admirers who had arrived early and would not move. Now: the friend or parent who keeps carrying a name to God for years while the door seems shut; Jesus saw their faith. And a quiet warning: it is possible to be so pleased to be near Jesus that you become the reason someone else cannot reach him.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 2 sets the authority of Jesus against the religious leaders. He forgives a paralysed man’s sins and proves it by making him walk. He calls Levi and eats with sinners, as a doctor for the sick. He calls himself the bridegroom, a title that belongs to God, and claims to be lord of the Sabbath. In every scene the question is Mark’s first one, who is this, and the answer keeps coming back larger than anyone expected, and full of mercy.

The connection. Mark 2:1–3:6 is a series of five conflict stories: over forgiving sins (2:1–12), eating with sinners (2:13–17), fasting (2:18–22), and the Sabbath (2:23–28; 3:1–6). The opposition grows from silent questioning (2:6) to complaint to his disciples (2:16), to open challenge, to plotting, until the leaders agree to destroy him (3:6).

After some days. After his preaching tour of Galilee (1:39). At the end of chapter 1 the healed leper spread the news so widely that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (1:45). He had been driven into the countryside by his own success. Coming back to Capernaum was a deliberate return, and the town soon found out.

At home. Probably Peter’s house (1:29). Capernaum was a fishing village of perhaps fifteen hundred people, with single-storey houses of black basalt round a courtyard, roofed with beams, branches and packed mud; a family room might be eighteen feet square. The Son of God, in this Gospel, does not have a headquarters. He has a friend’s spare room.

No more room. The room, the doorway and the courtyard are packed, and people in the street crane at a window slot. Not the authorities, not enemies. People who had come to hear Jesus, had arrived first, and were not moving.

Preaching the word. The crowd has come because of a demon silenced, a fever broken, a leper touched, and what Jesus is doing is talking. The word is the message of the kingdom (1:15), and the miracles were never the main work; they were the proof that the message was true. The voice filling Peter’s front room is the voice that said let there be light, and within the hour it will forgive a man’s sins and stand him on his feet. When Jesus preaches, the word does what it says.

Is my faith fake if I first came to Jesus because I wanted help with a problem? No. Many came to him first for healing, and he received them. The four friends who brought a paralysed man to this very house came for legs, and he gave them more. What matters is where your coming leads. If you came for help and stayed for Christ himself, that is the ordinary story of countless believers. The danger is only in never moving past the problem: wanting Jesus as a means to something else rather than as the one worth having even if the problem stays.

In everyday life. If you are a regular in the crowded room, notice whether anyone is being kept outside because those already inside are comfortable where they are.
verseByVerse.note: “At home” probably means Peter’s house in Capernaum (1:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Carried by four men. Only Mark mentions that there were four, one at each corner of the mat. The man could not come on his own. His whole world was a piece of quilted matting and four friends. They are never named. Their whole recorded contribution to the kingdom of God is that they would not accept a blocked door.

They removed the roof. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase, because the roof was usable space: you dried figs on it and slept on it in summer. It was beams, branches and reed matting under a thick layer of mud and straw. Literally they unroofed the roof and dug it out: mud, straw and matting came down on a packed room, and then a man on ropes. Luke speaks of tiles (Luke 5:19), picturing it for Greek city readers; Mark gives you the dirt.

Whose roof? If this is Peter’s house, then a man who had just left his nets to follow Jesus watched his own ceiling come down into his own front room, and Peter, telling the story to Mark, would have remembered it. Mark records not one word of complaint from anybody. There was a man outside who needed to get in. The roof was only a roof.

The one beneath the hole. Nobody digs through a roof for a lecture. They were sure of two things: that Jesus could heal their friend, and that he would. There is one door in the world that is never finally blocked, because the one behind it has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Friends can carry a man to the edge. Only Christ can deal with what is lying on the mat.

What does carrying someone to Jesus look like today? Mostly ordinary things done stubbornly. Praying for someone by name, for years if necessary. Inviting them to church and offering to drive them there and sit with them. Reading a Gospel with them. Meeting a practical need so that a barrier comes down: the childcare, the lift, the meal. Bringing them into your home among other believers. Sometimes it means removing obstacles that Christians themselves have put up, like jargon, unfriendliness or a church that is hard for an outsider to enter. You cannot make anyone believe, but you can get them to the place where Jesus speaks.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. An opening could be dug through and repaired.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw their faith. Faith in Scripture is not a private feeling; it climbs stairs and digs through roofs. Their faith: the four friends, and perhaps the man himself, though Mark tells us nothing of what he believed. Jesus looked up through the dust and saw faith, and he loved it. He is the kind of Saviour who is glad to be interrupted by people desperate to bring him someone they love.

Can my faith do for someone else what these four did for their friend? Yes and no, and both halves matter. Yes: your faith can carry a person to the place where Jesus is, and that is precisely what intercession does. You can bring them, again and again, under the preached word, onto your prayer list, into the company of his people, and refuse to accept that the door is shut and the case is closed. And no: the man did not stay a spectator of his own healing. He heard your sins are forgiven, and he rose and walked. No one was forgiven in his place, and no one repented for him. Each must finally meet Christ himself. So your part is the roof and the ropes; the rising is God’s to give and theirs to receive. Many a believer walking with Christ today was once only a name on somebody’s stubborn, seemingly unanswered prayer list. Do not stop digging.

Son, your sins are forgiven. Son is literally child, a warm, domestic word, the word a father uses. The man has been lowered into a room full of strangers and religious professionals, filthy from the ceiling, at the centre of everyone’s attention, and the first word spoken to him is a family word. And are forgiven is present tense: it is happening now, on Jesus’ word. To be forgiven means that God cancels the debt and will not hold it against you again: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12).

Why this, and not the legs? The legs are what everyone in the room is looking at. Jesus saw the ruined man, not only the ruined body, and went first to his greatest need. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for ever. Hold the two outcomes side by side and the priority stops being abstract. A paralytic who walked home that afternoon and died unforgiven forty years later would still be lost. A paralytic forgiven and never healed, carried on that mat to the end of his life, would be eternally safe. Jesus will heal the legs to prove that he has dealt with the soul, but he leaves nobody in doubt about which was the emergency. He begins where you would not have begun, with the thing you were not asking about, because he is treating you as a whole person and not only as a problem to fix.

Sin and sickness. Was his paralysis caused by a particular sin? Not necessarily. Sometimes suffering is tied to a specific sin: Jesus tells another healed man to sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to him (John 5:14). Very often it is not at all: of the man born blind Jesus says it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:1–3). But all sickness belongs to a world broken by sin. Jesus deals with the root first.

How can I know that my sins are forgiven? In the same way this man did: by Jesus’ word. He did not feel forgiven first and then believe it; he was told, and the healing confirmed it. Your confirmation is greater than his legs, because you know the cross and the empty tomb. God promises that everyone who believes in Christ is forgiven and has peace with him (Acts 10:43; Romans 5:1), and that if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). Feelings come and go. Rest your assurance on what he has said and on what Christ has done, not on how you feel this morning.
verseByVerse.note: “Son” is a warm address, like “my child.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the scribes. Experts in the law, seated while others stood: men who had come to assess rather than to listen. And they question silently.

Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Blasphemy means speaking against God or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. It was punishable by death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Fix the word in your mind, because it is a death sentence, and it lands in chapter 2. When Mark reaches the night trial, the high priest tears his garments and says, You have heard his blasphemy, and they all condemn him as deserving death (14:63–64). The verdict that kills Jesus is reached, silently, in a crowded front room in Capernaum, twelve chapters before it is carried out. Everything in between is the trial.

Who can forgive sins but God alone? They were right: all sin is finally against God (Psalm 51:4), and only the one offended can wipe the account; no priest, prophet or rabbi ever forgave a man in his own name. (See Luke 5:21 for the fuller answer.)

No third option. Run the scribes’ logic honestly. Their first premise is true: only God forgives sins. Their second premise is true: this man has just forgiven sins. Either Jesus is blaspheming, or he is God. A sceptic may answer that the church invented the scene later; but the charge of blasphemy that finally condemned Jesus (14:63–64) is hard to explain unless he really made claims of this kind. What has never been available, whatever the century decides to say about him, is the comfortable middle position that he was a fine moral teacher who would be appalled at what his followers made of him. The scribes’ theology was correct; their conclusion about Jesus was wrong.

Did Jesus ever actually claim to be God? Yes, and here in exactly his usual way: by doing what only God does, forgiving sins, reading hearts (v. 8), and claiming lordship of the Sabbath (v. 28). His enemies understood the claim and called it blasphemy. (See John 10:33 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. The scribes’ teaching about God’s forgiveness was perfectly correct, and they used it to condemn the one who forgives. It is possible to hold every doctrine correctly and still reject the Person the doctrines are about. Before you enjoy their mistake, ask whether your settled convictions about how God works have room in them for God turning up and working.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: the same charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perceiving in his spirit. Jesus answers an objection that was never spoken. He reads the silence, and only God knows the heart: you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind (1 Kings 8:39; Jeremiah 17:10). So within moments he does two things that belong to God alone, forgiving sin and reading the heart, and the men best equipped to notice are the ones being read.

Why do you question these things in your hearts? He brings their hidden thoughts into the open, not to shame them but to answer them.

Which is easier. Easier to say: that is the exact wording, and it decides the argument. To say your sins are forgiven is the easy sentence, because nothing in the visible world changes when you say it. A charlatan could say it in every village in Galilee for a decade and never be caught. To say rise and walk is the hard sentence, because it is checkable in about four seconds in front of a packed room, and if the man does not move you are finished. But to actually do either requires the power of God.

The reverse of a fraud. So Jesus does the opposite of what a fraud does. He deliberately hangs the invisible claim on a visible, immediate, public test, and tells the room in advance that this is what he is doing. The apostles do the same with the resurrection. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to rest on an experience. He says that if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14, 17), and he lists the surviving eyewitnesses. Christianity has always staked itself on things that happened in public.

Can a modern person really believe a healing like this? The question is fair, and the honest answer turns on who Jesus is. If he is only a man, a paralysed man standing up at a word is impossible. If he is the God who made that man’s legs and holds every nerve in being (Colossians 1:16–17), it is no harder for him than speaking was at creation. Mark does not ask you to believe in miracles in general. He asks you to look at this person, his words, his claims, his death and his empty tomb, and decide who he is. Settle that, and the healing is no surprise; and, as Jesus warned, a heart set against him may not be persuaded even by a miracle (Luke 16:31).

Is my faith only a feeling, then? It should not be. A fair question to put to yourself is what your faith actually rests on. If what you find there is only a mood or an experience that no fact could ever confirm or disprove, it may be more fragile than you think. Christian faith rests on facts that are public and historical: a man who lived, died under Pontius Pilate, was buried and rose bodily on the third day, seen by many witnesses. Feelings are good gifts, but they are the weather; the facts are the ground. Read the Gospels as the testimony they claim to be, and let your trust stand on what God has done.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that you may know. The visible healing will prove the invisible forgiveness. Mid-sentence Mark notes that Jesus turns: he said to the paralytic. The argument is for the scribes; the command is for the man on the floor.

The Son of Man. This is the first time in Mark that Jesus names himself, and it is his favourite name for himself. In ordinary Aramaic the phrase could mean simply a human being, but Jesus is reaching for something enormous. It comes from Daniel 7, where the prophet sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before God, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom, so that all peoples and nations should serve him, an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). In the Old Testament the one who rides the clouds is God. Daniel sees a figure who is truly human and is given what belongs to God, and Jesus says that he is that figure. The Son of Man of Daniel’s vision, given an everlasting kingdom by the Ancient of Days, used his authority on a Galilean afternoon to forgive a paralysed man and send him home. Before Mark is finished, this name will carry both his throne and his cross: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

On earth. Two small words, and they move the place where forgiveness is found. Not in heaven, after you die. Not ninety miles south in Jerusalem, through a priest and a lamb and a curtain and a fee. Here, in a crowded front room, from the mouth of a man you could touch, to somebody who had brought no sacrifice and could not have carried one if he had.

Go home. Three commands, all impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own mat would show the healing was complete. And the third command is the tender one. He is not sent to the temple or to a rabbi. He is sent home, and whoever is waiting there, people who had learned to step around a mat on the floor, is about to look up and see him standing in the doorway on his own legs, carrying the thing that carried him. He does not merely repair you and leave you standing in the road. He sends you home.

Should I confess my sins to a pastor or priest to be forgiven? You do not need anyone but Christ to stand between you and God. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and you may go to him directly, any time, and be forgiven. Scripture does also tell believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), and there is great help in telling a trusted, mature Christian about a sin you are fighting. They cannot absolve you, but they can pray for you, hold you to account and remind you of the gospel. That is a mercy, not a requirement for forgiveness.

In everyday life. If there is something you keep confessing because you do not believe it has really been forgiven, take this verse as the receipt. Then go home today as someone forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before them all. Immediately: no convalescence. The command and the walking are the same instant, because the authority behind the command does not have to wait for nature to catch up. And before them all: Jesus staked a claim on a public test, and the test is settled publicly, in front of the very scribes who had silently convicted him. The crowd that had blocked the man’s way in now parted to let him walk out. The mat that had been the sign of his helplessness went home over his shoulder as evidence.

Never anything like this. Something new had come, and they glorified God. But weigh what they do not say. Mark records no one in that room saying: then the other thing he said must be true as well. No one asks aloud, if he can do that to a man’s legs with a word, what has he just done to a man’s guilt, and could he do it for me? They had been handed the proof, in the terms Jesus himself set, and their astonishment stopped at the miracle and never reached the thing the miracle was for.

Is it wrong to pray about my circumstances rather than my soul? No. The four friends asked about the legs, and Jesus did not scold them. God invites us to bring him everything, including health, money, work and family (Philippians 4:6). The danger is only when the whole list is legs: when we want him for what he might fix and never once come to him for what he came to forgive. A great deal of modern praying is exactly this. We ask him about the legs. He is waiting to talk about the sins. Ask for both, and put them in his order.

Pardoned and whole. God’s forgiveness and God’s power stood in one room in one man, and a paralysed sinner walked out pardoned and whole. Nobody had seen anything like it, because nothing like him had ever walked the earth. Glory to God, who in Jesus forgives all our iniquity and heals all our diseases, redeems our life from the pit and crowns us with steadfast love and mercy. The man had his legs for the rest of his earthly life. The pardon he walked out with, he has still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls Levi from his tax booth with two words (vv. 13–14). At Levi’s dinner for his disreputable friends the scribes complain, and Jesus answers with a sentence about a doctor (vv. 15–17). Asked why his disciples do not fast, he answers with a wedding and the first shadow of the cross (vv. 18–20), and two domestic pictures, cloth and wineskins, make one point: what he brings cannot be sewn onto what you already have (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The two small parables of vv. 21–22 are the hinge of the chapter. In both, the old thing is asked to hold what it was never made to hold. Jesus is not offering a reformed Judaism, or a reformed you. Adding a little religion to a self still in charge only makes a worse tear. But the last clause is the promise: new wine is for fresh wineskins. He supplies the skin as well as the wine: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26), a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks, and gets the only people he knows into a room with Jesus. Now: the newest Christian usually knows many people outside the church. Levi’s method needs no course: buy the food, make the call, be in the room, and go as a follower of Christ, not hiding whose you are.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside the sea. After the most spectacular thing yet seen in Capernaum, he goes outside and walks along the shore. As he walks he passes a customs post, and the whole chapter turns.

Levi the son of Alphaeus. Levi is called Matthew in the first Gospel (Matthew 9:9; 10:3), probably his birth name and his later one. The first Gospel, which the early church held to be Matthew’s own, adds the words the tax collector to his own name in the list of apostles, which nobody else does. A forgiven man is not embarrassed by his past. His booth was probably on the trade road near Capernaum, taking customs at the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip: a licence to print money. The man who once kept the accounts of Rome now keeps, in the first book of the New Testament, the record of the King.

Tax collectors. The collector bid for the contract, paid the authorities up front, and lived on whatever he could extract above that figure. Tax collectors were despised for serving the ruling powers, for cheating, and for contact with Gentiles that made them ritually unclean. They were classed with sinners and prostitutes (Matthew 21:31), and later rabbinic rules barred them as witnesses in court.

Beyond repair. And there was worse. The road back for a thief ran through restitution: you repaid what you took, and added a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). A tax collector could not do it. He had defrauded hundreds of people over years and could hardly trace them all. His repentance looked, to his own religion, impossible. That is the man Jesus stops for.

The debt he could not pay. Levi could not pay his own way. But the one who stopped at the booth had come to settle an account no tax collector could ever settle. The debt Levi owed to God, larger than everything he had taken from his neighbours, would be met by the man now calling him, who came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). God has cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Levi made out other men’s bills for a living. Christ came to pay his.

Follow me. The same call as to the fishermen (1:17), with no interview, no probation, and no requirement that he first put anything right. That is the grace of God in Christ: it does not wait for us to make ourselves acceptable; it calls us, and the call makes us new.

He rose and followed. Peter and Andrew left their nets, and the nets were still there (John 21:3). Levi stood up from a booth that somebody else would be sitting in by the afternoon. There was no going back to that job, ever, and everyone in Capernaum knew it. Money had been the centre of Levi’s life, the thing he had sold his good name for, and it was the one thing that could not come with him. When Christ becomes the treasure, the old treasure loses its grip, not because it is torn away but because something better has come in (Matthew 13:44).

Forgiveness, then a welcome. Mark puts this call straight after the healing of the paralysed man, and the order makes the point: Jesus has just shown his authority to forgive (2:10), and now he uses it on the most obviously sinful man in town. Forgiveness brings a welcome into his company.

If I become a Christian, must I leave a job that is morally compromised? It depends on what makes it compromised. Collecting taxes was not itself sinful; John the Baptist told tax collectors to collect no more than they were authorised to (Luke 3:12–13), and Paul tells Christians to pay taxes (Romans 13:6–7). What had to stop was the fraud. When Zacchaeus met Jesus he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). So if your work requires you to lie, cheat or sin, you must stop doing those things, even if it costs you the job. If the work is lawful but your practice in it has been crooked, change the practice, put right what you can, and serve Christ there. Ask a wise pastor to help you think it through.

In everyday life. Who have you written off: a relative, a colleague, yourself? Bring each of them to God this week. The man Jesus chose to be an apostle was the one man in town whose religion had already given up on him.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At table in his house. Levi’s first act as a disciple is to give a party: Luke tells us he made him a great feast in his house (Luke 5:29). Guests reclined on couches round a low table, the posture of a banquet.

Tax collectors and sinners. Levi invited the only people he knew. Sinners was almost a technical term for people known for immoral lives, or whose way of life put them outside the purity rules, everyone the religious establishment had written off. And they were already moving toward him, for there were many who followed him.

Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? The question comes from the scribes of the Pharisees, a name that probably means the separated ones, a movement devoted to strict keeping of the law and its traditions, including purity rules about food and who you ate with. A modern reader has to be told why this caused such offence, because we eat with anybody. In that world a shared table was not a neutral social event. It meant acceptance and friendship, peace between the people at it. You did not eat with a man you regarded as unclean, because you would be saying in the most public way available that there was no barrier between you. The Pharisees avoided eating with sinners to keep themselves pure. Jesus ate with them, and everybody in Capernaum could read what that said.

Said to his disciples. They take it to his new followers, who are easier to unsettle.

This man receives sinners. That is how Luke words the same complaint on another occasion (Luke 15:2). It is meant as an accusation, and it is the gospel. Isaiah had promised that on God’s mountain the LORD would make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). The peace Jesus offered over Levi’s food was real, because he would make it real: he came to reconcile enemies to God by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The Pharisees saw the company he kept. They did not see that the true host at this table was the LORD, beginning the feast Isaiah promised.

How do I keep real friendships with people far from God without condemning them or signing off on everything? Jesus gives the answer by being at the table rather than drawing a line around it. But look closely at how he is there. He is not blending in and hoping not to be noticed. He is not there as a fellow patient. Levi, the host, had given up his career to follow him, and Jesus ends the evening by calling the guests sick people who need a doctor (v. 17). So go, eat, listen, laugh and love; and go as yourself, a follower of Christ, unashamed of him. Most of us fail in one of two directions. The Pharisees would not go in at all and called it holiness. Others go in, sit down, say nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and call it grace. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

How far can I join in? Join in everything that is good: the food, the friendship, the conversation, the celebration. Do not join in what is sinful: drunkenness, crude talk, gossip, cruelty. Jesus was accused of being a drunkard (Matthew 11:19), but the accusation was false. If you find that time with certain friends regularly draws you into sin rather than giving you openings for Christ, you may need to change the setting: invite them to your home, meet over coffee, or take a Christian friend with you. Bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), but holy company can be the best thing that ever happened to a sinner.
verseByVerse.note: At a formal meal guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow — hence “reclined.” “Sinners” here means people known for ignoring the law.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No need of a physician. One sentence, and it is the whole gospel. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls, and his holiness is not contaminated by sinners; it heals them. He is not agreeing that the Pharisees are spiritually healthy. He is taking them at their own word: very well, if you are well, you will not want a doctor, and you will not get one. The man who will not admit he is ill does not take the treatment; he dies of something treatable, holding the position that there is nothing wrong with him.

I came. He states it of his whole mission. The words can mean simply that he came to do this work, as John the Baptist came (Matthew 11:18); but on the lips of the one who also says he came from the Father into the world (John 16:28), they carry more: he was somewhere before, and had business here.

Not to call the righteous, but sinners. The righteous are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, and so see no need of him. In truth no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sick. Luke adds: to repentance (Luke 5:32). And here is what makes it good news rather than merely fair-minded: the only thing that qualifies you for Christ is the very thing you thought ruled you out. Sickness is the entry requirement: what you bring is the sin you have been trying to hide.

It cuts two ways. If your fear is that you are too far gone, read the sentence again slowly. He did not come for the respectable and take the odd sinner as an exception. He came to call sinners. You are not the awkward case. You are the stated purpose of the visit. But if your quiet position is that you are basically all right, decent, churchgoing, never did anybody much harm, then this verse is not a comfort and is not meant to be. There are the sick who know it and the sick who do not, and only one of those groups ever sends for the doctor. The Pharisees went home from Levi’s house with their reputations intact and their sins intact.

If Jesus came for sinners, why should I try to be good? Because the doctor does not come to the sick to leave them sick. He calls sinners to repentance, and those he heals begin to get well. You do not try to be good in order to qualify for him; you could never manage that, and you do not need to. You try to be good because he has taken you on as his patient, and the medicine is working: his Spirit now lives in you (Romans 8:11). You will not be fully well this side of glory (1 John 1:8), and you need not be: the Physician was the one healthy man, his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and your halting obedience is accepted for his sake. Sin is the disease, not the freedom. Anyone who wants Christ’s forgiveness but not his healing has not understood what kind of doctor he is.

For worship. Consider what it cost the Physician. Doctors keep their distance; this one came into the ward, took the disease into his own body, and died of it, so that the patients would live. By his wounds we are healed. At Levi’s table he was beginning that work, and he has never lost a patient who came to him.

parallels.desc: “to seek and to save the lost”

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s disciples and the Pharisees. An odd alliance, united in bewilderment, because everybody serious fasts. The only fast required by the law was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29), but the Pharisees fasted twice a week; the man in Jesus’ parable says so with some pride (Luke 18:12).

Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Fasting was a sign of devotion and of mourning, and by any measure of the day a teacher whose followers did not fast was not a serious teacher. Jesus’ disciples seemed less devout. It was a fair question.

Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? Jesus does not defend his disciples. He changes the whole question, with a picture every person listening had stood inside. A Jewish wedding lasted up to a week, a time of feasting and joy. The phrase behind wedding guests is literally the sons of the bridechamber, the groom’s closest friends, who ran the celebration, and later rabbinic writings record that they were excused from certain religious duties for the week, because you cannot mourn and rejoice at once. Jesus is answering out of their own customs. Fasting at that moment would not be devotion. It would be a man sitting in the corner of a wedding feast refusing the food, with the bridegroom in the room.

Who is the bridegroom? Listen to what he has just said about himself while apparently talking about lunch. In the Old Testament that role belongs to one Person, and there is no second candidate. Your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name (Isaiah 54:5). As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isaiah 62:5). I will betroth you to me forever (Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes that title, God’s own, without a word of explanation, in the middle of an answer about diet. It is the second enormous claim of the chapter, and unlike the first, nobody in the room seems to have noticed. And it tells you what he thinks his own presence is: not an examination, not an inspection, but a wedding, the happiest week in a village’s life, food and wine and noise and a groom who cannot stop smiling. His presence is a time of joy, not mourning. If your religion feels nothing like that, it is worth asking whether you have understood who is in the room.

When the bridegroom is taken away. Then the light goes out of the sentence. Bridegrooms are not removed from their own weddings. Taken away may suggest violent removal: this is Jesus’ first hint in Mark of his death, dropped into a cheerful answer about fasting in chapter 2, before any opponent has laid a finger on him.

Then they will fast. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). So are Christians meant to fast now? Jesus plainly assumed so. He did not say fasting was abolished; he said its time was coming. And when he taught about it he did not say if you fast but when you fast (Matthew 6:16–17), which is not the language of an optional extra for specialists.

What fasting is for. It is not a way of getting God’s attention or paying something off. It is a way of making the body say what the heart means: deliberately going hungry for a few hours so that a real, insistent ache reminds you, every twenty minutes, that there is a deeper hunger you have been feeding with everything except God. And remember the reason Jesus gives: we fast because the Bridegroom has been taken away and we want him back. It is not gloom. It is longing for someone who has promised to return.

How do I start fasting, and who should not? Start absurdly small. Miss one meal this week, tell nobody (Matthew 6:17–18), and spend the time you would have spent eating with the Bible open, praying about one specific thing. Drink water. Expect to feel hungry and irritable; that is part of the lesson. If you are pregnant or nursing, diabetic, on medication that must be taken with food, elderly and frail, or have ever struggled with an eating disorder, do not fast from food without medical advice. You can fast instead from something else, a screen, a habit, a pleasure, for the same purpose. Fasting is never a measure of your standing with God, and no one should be pressured into it.
verseByVerse.note: A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

parallels.desc: the one yearly fast the law commanded
a Pharisee who fasted twice a week

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unshrunk cloth. Two domestic pictures, one mistake. New cloth off the loom is unshrunk. Sew a piece of it onto a garment that has been washed a hundred times, and it looks like a decent repair until it gets wet; then the patch pulls tight, and it rips away and takes the old fabric with it. Mark’s summary is bleak and exact: a worse tear is made, and the repair did it.

New wine. Wine in that world was carried in whole goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; it gives off gas and swells hard against the container, which is why it went into a new skin with stretch left in it. An old skin has done its stretching and become stiff and brittle. Pour fermenting wine into it and it bursts: the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins.

Different in kind. Neither picture attacks the old thing; it is asked to hold what it was never built to hold. The new life Jesus brings cannot simply be patched onto the old system of Pharisaic religion, with its traditions, fasts and purity rules. It is different in kind, and the joy and freedom of the kingdom need new forms.

Patchwork religion. Most of us instinctively approach religion as patchwork. We take the life we have, with the self firmly in charge of it, and sew something on: church on Sunday, a habit of prayer, a tidied-up vocabulary, a few things given up. This is why a certain kind of half-Christianity makes people more miserable than before. Something in them keeps tearing every time life puts strain on them, and they conclude that faith does not work, when what has failed is the repair job.

Fresh wineskins. The gospel is in the last clause: he gives the skin. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). Paul says that whoever is joined to Christ is a new creation, the old gone and the new come (2 Corinthians 5:17): the fresh wineskin, made by God. This does not mean that your personality is erased; it means that God gives you new desires at the root: you begin to want him, to hate the sin you once enjoyed and to love his people, and a heart like that can hold the life Christ pours in without tearing (Philippians 2:13). The making of a vessel that can hold what he pours is his work and not yours, which is exactly why you can ask him for it.

The wine he would pour. The new wine is the life of the kingdom, and Mark will show what it cost. At the last supper Jesus took the cup, called it his blood of the covenant, poured out for many, and said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God (14:24–25). The wine that bursts old skins was pressed out of him. That is why it can never be stitched onto anyone’s religion as an improvement: it is a covenant made in his blood, and it makes a people new.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless. Jesus fulfils it (Matthew 5:17). The old garments and old wineskins are the human traditions of the religious system, not God’s word itself.

Does this mean new church styles are always better than old ones? No. Jesus is not contrasting old-fashioned with modern, or hymns with new songs, or liturgy with informality. He is contrasting the gospel of his kingdom with a religion of human effort and tradition. A brand-new church can be as much a patch on the old self as an ancient one, and many old forms, rooted in Scripture, are excellent wineskins for the new wine. The question to ask of any practice is not whether it is old or new but whether it serves the free grace of Christ or competes with it.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disciples pluck grain on a Sabbath, which the law allowed; the Pharisees count it as reaping, threshing and winnowing (vv. 23–24). Jesus answers with the story of David, the rejected king, eating the holy bread with his men (vv. 25–26). Then two sentences reset everything: the Sabbath was made for man, and the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: To be lord of the Sabbath is a very large claim. The day goes back to creation, when God rested and made the seventh day holy (Genesis 2:2–3), and it was written into the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 20:8–11). It pointed past itself to a rest Israel never fully entered (Hebrews 4:9), and now the Giver is standing in the field, being scolded. The rest the day pointed to is found in a Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: hungry men eating grain on a walk, and experts who had gone out into a field on a Sabbath to watch for an infringement. Now: the same instinct wherever keeping a form matters more than the person it was meant to serve: the church that notices a visitor’s clothes before his face, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the grainfields. The Sabbath was the seventh day, Saturday, when God commanded rest from work, remembering creation and the exodus (Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It was the sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:13). This is not a story about stealing. The disciples are walking a path through standing grain; field boundaries were unfenced and paths ran between them.

Pluck heads of grain. Luke adds that they rubbed them in their hands (Luke 6:1), loosening the husk so that the chaff could be blown away and the grain eaten. It is what a hungry man does on a walk, and the law of Moses expressly allowed it: travellers could pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field, though not put a sickle to it (Deuteronomy 23:25). The Pharisees do not accuse anyone of theft. The issue was the day. And the Lord of the harvest walked through his own fields with his hungry friends, and let them eat.

Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? The Pharisees’ traditions listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, and the disciples had touched three of them in a single mouthful. Pulling the head off was reaping. Rubbing it in the hands was threshing. Blowing away the husk was winnowing. By their count a man did a whole harvest’s work in the time it takes to eat a handful of wheat. The list was written down later, in the Mishnah (about AD 200), but it gathers rulings already taught in Jesus’ day.

The charge is brought to the Master. The Pharisees accuse the disciples, but they bring the accusation to Jesus, and he takes it up as his own. A teacher answered for his disciples, and this one never leaves his people to face their accusers alone. He stands between them and the charge, a small scene of something far larger: Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God interceding for us, and no charge against God’s elect can stand (Romans 8:33–34).

The climax of the conflicts. The earlier disputes ended in an answer; the two Sabbath scenes end in a plot (3:6), because the Sabbath was the most visible mark of Israel’s faithfulness, and a teacher who claimed to be its Lord was touching the centre.

How did the Pharisees see it? They were there. On a Sabbath, out along a path through the fields, close enough to watch a group of working men to see whether any of them would put a hand out. And their first word, look, is almost a shout. They had been waiting for this. The scene deserves a second look, because the same energy is alive in every generation and it always dresses as faithfulness. It is possible to be scrupulously careful about a rule and hard as flint about a person; to notice at a glance everything that is out of place in somebody’s life, and never once notice that he is hungry. Their own Scriptures had told them what to look for: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

Is it wrong to have rules in a church or a family? No. Rules can be wise and loving: a family that eats together on Sundays, a church that asks its children’s workers to be checked, a habit of daily prayer. The trouble comes when human rules are treated as if they were God’s law, used to judge other believers, or kept in a way that crushes the people they were meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we decide it? If we decided it, hold it humbly and do not bind other consciences with it (Colossians 2:20–23). That includes the Lord’s Day itself: because the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest as a gift, out of joy and wisdom, not as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). And never let a rule stop you from seeing the person in front of you.

In everyday life. The next time you are sharply critical of another Christian, how he brings up his children, what he does with his Sundays, ask whether you are standing at the edge of the field with a clear view of the rule and none at all of the man.
verseByVerse.note: The objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work.

parallels.desc: picking grain by hand was allowed

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What David did. Jesus answers with a story: 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David is already anointed king and not yet on the throne. He is running from Saul with a few men, in need and hungry, and he comes to the tabernacle at Nob and is given the holy bread by the priest. Human need is the point.

In the time of Abiathar the high priest. An honest reader with a reference Bible will notice something, and it is better dealt with plainly than hurried past. 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar was there (he escaped the massacre that followed, 1 Samuel 22:20) and later became the more famous high priest under David. There are good answers. In the time of Abiathar may mean in the days of Abiathar, who was a priest then and became the better-known high priest, as we might say in the days of King David about events before he was king. Or the phrase may mean at the passage about Abiathar: with no chapter numbers, a teacher located a text by its best-known figure, as Jesus does with the passage about the bush (12:26). On that reading Jesus is giving a reference, not a date. Or the names were sometimes interchanged (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 have Ahimelech son of Abiathar). None of these answers is certain, and careful believers weigh them differently; each is reasonable. This commentary’s view: no error; the phrase identifies the period or passage by its most famous priest. And nothing in the argument depends on it. Jesus is not resting his case on which priest was on duty, and the Pharisees, who knew that chapter far better than we do, are not recorded raising the objection.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves placed fresh before the LORD each Sabbath, and the old ones afterwards eaten by priests only, as a most holy portion (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The argument. David ate the holy bread and gave it to those who were with him, breaking a ceremonial law, and Scripture does not condemn him; neither God nor the narrator rebukes him. Human need takes priority over ceremonial rules. But there is a second point in the choice of this story, and it is sharper. Jesus picks the anointed king, rejected, unrecognised, on the road with his men, being fed from the holy table. David was God’s anointed; Jesus is the greater Son of David. If David’s men could eat the holy bread because of who was with them, how much more the disciples of David’s greater Son. He is the true bread of the Presence, the bread of God come down from heaven, and he does not keep the holy things from his hungry people.

Does this mean I may break any rule when I am in need? No. Jesus is speaking about ceremonial rules, like the bread of the Presence, and about the Pharisees’ additions to the Sabbath law. He never suggests that need excuses breaking God’s moral law. Hunger does not justify stealing, and loneliness does not justify adultery. God’s moral commands, to love him and our neighbour, are themselves the shape of mercy. The point is that God’s laws were given for our good, and a reading of them that leaves a hungry man unfed has misunderstood the God who gave them.
verseByVerse.note: On the name Abiathar (1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech), see the commentary.

parallels.desc: the bread of the Presence, eaten by priests

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Made for man. Only Mark records this saying. Its roots go back before there was a Jew in the world. God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy at the end of the creation account (Genesis 2:2–3), centuries before Sinai, though the command to keep it was first given to Israel (Exodus 16:23–30; Nehemiah 9:14). It was a kindness: rest for weary people, a day to delight in God (Isaiah 58:13–14; Exodus 23:12). The Egyptians had given Israel no such day, and in Deuteronomy the command is set out with the memory of slavery attached (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Pharisees had taken a day designed to lift a burden off a man’s back and turned it into a burden to carry, as if people existed to serve the rules. The gift had become an examination.

Lord even of the Sabbath. The Sabbath was the LORD’s day (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it: the right to say what it means and how it should be kept. Only God could make this claim. If the day was made for man, then the Son of Man, the one Daniel saw given dominion over all peoples, is its lord. He is telling a group of experts, in a cornfield, that the day belongs to him.

The Sabbath and Christ. The Sabbath always pointed past itself, to the rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Every seventh evening for more than a thousand years, a nation rehearsed something it did not yet have. Then the rest itself walked through the standing grain with a handful of hungry men, and was told off for it by the people guarding the rehearsal. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). This is what is meant by saying the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ: not that rest no longer matters, but that what the day pictured has arrived in a person. Whoever trusts him stops working to earn God’s favour and rests in a finished work, as God rested from his (Hebrews 4:10).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Christians who love the Bible have not landed in the same place on this, and it is only fair to say so. Some keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, holding that the fourth commandment, rooted in creation and written into the Ten, still binds one day in seven, now observed on the day of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8); it is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as a Sabbath, pointing to Paul: one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike (Romans 14:5–6), and let no one pass judgment on you with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17); Sunday is then the Lord’s Day for gathering. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest. The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Believers who keep a stricter Sabbath should be honoured, not judged.

What neither side disputes. The day is a gift and not a scoring system. Do you stop? Not slow down; stop. Most of us now miss the gift of rest not by putting a hand to grain, but by never taking a hand off anything. And be honest about why stopping is frightening. If you stop, things carry on without you. You find out you were not holding the world up. That is the humiliation in it, and it is also precisely the rest in it. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2). A day of rest is a weekly, physical confession that you are not God.

What if my job requires me to work on Sundays? Then you are in good company: doctors, nurses, carers, police, firefighters and many others do necessary and merciful work that cannot stop, and Jesus himself defended doing good on the Sabbath (3:4). Because the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and the Lord’s Day is a gift, not a law with rules about work, you are not sinning by doing it; and even those who hold the stricter Westminster and 1689 view count works of necessity and mercy as right on the Lord’s Day (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Do your work as service to Christ. Then guard what you can: gather with God’s people whenever possible, perhaps at another service or a midweek meeting, and take a real day of rest at another point in your week. If you have a choice and Sunday work keeps you from the church week after week, take that seriously, and ask whether you could rearrange things. The aim is not a rule kept but a heart that gathers with God’s people, worships and rests.

For worship. He is still the one who says, Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). He is Lord of the Sabbath because he made it, and he gave its rest at the cost of a Friday on which he had no rest at all, and lay in the tomb through the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of a new week. Because he finished his work, we may cease from ours, and the rest he won is the one Sabbath that will never end.

2.theology:
The scribes and Pharisees are not cardboard villains. They are serious people defending serious convictions, and on forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to, and they try to fit him into their old forms, like new wine into old skins.

So the chapter shows four reasons Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religion of his day: he forgives sins directly, not through the temple; he welcomes the excluded to his table; he calls his presence a wedding, not a fast; and he claims lordship over the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law’s Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees’ unease at Jesus eating with sinners deserves a fair hearing: their concern for purity was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God commanded, under pagan occupation. But they assumed that eating with a sinner meant approving of his sin. Jesus was among sinners as a physician among the sick, and a cure requires nearness.

Then: Pharisees keeping their distance to stay clean, while the one truly clean man in Capernaum reclined at a tax collector’s table. Now: any Christianity that has confused holiness with keeping away, and, on the other side, any that sits at every table and never says whose it is.

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
In chapter 3 the opposition to Jesus hardens into a decision, and a new community forms around him. The Pharisees and Herodians, parties who agreed on nothing, walk out of a Sabbath service together to plan his death (v. 6). His own family thinks he is out of his mind (v. 21). Scribes from Jerusalem say he is possessed (v. 22).

Against that, Jesus appoints twelve men to be with him and to be sent out (vv. 13–15), and explains his work: a stronger man has entered the strong man's house, tied him up, and is carrying off his goods (v. 27). The chapter ends by naming who belongs to him: not those related by blood, but those who do the will of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus enters a synagogue where a man with a withered hand is waiting, and so are men watching to see whether he will heal him.

The question (vv. 3–4). He sets the man in the middle and asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm. They say nothing.

The anger (v. 5). Jesus looks on them with anger and grief. Then a command the man cannot obey, and a hand made new.

The plot (v. 6). Two parties who despised each other walk out together to plan his death.

The crowds (vv. 7–12). Crowds from every region follow him to the lake. He silences the demons who know exactly who he is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does Jesus silence the demons when what they say about him is true (vv. 11–12)?

First, timing. In Galilee, to be proclaimed Son of God before a crowd would have been heard as the call of a king come to drive out the Romans. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. The title is spoken openly only at the cross, by the Roman officer (15:39), where his death shows what kind of Son of God he is.

Second, what the spirits say is correct, and it saves them from nothing. James says it plainly: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him, and this chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a withered hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed.

Now: obedience that makes a person visible before the outcome is known: the first time you say at work that you are a Christian; an apology with no guarantee it will be received. He was exposed first and healed second.

And the watchers saw a crippled man made whole and were not moved at all. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be occupied only with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 3 draws the lines around Jesus. A Sabbath healing ends in a plot to kill him; crowds pour in from every region; he chooses twelve, the beginning of a renewed Israel. His family says he is out of his mind; the scribes say he is in league with Satan. He answers that he is the stronger one who has bound the strong man, warns of the one sin never forgiven, and calls those at his feet his mother and his brothers. Every reader must ask: outside, or inside with him?

Again he entered the synagogue. The fifth of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6), and the second about the Sabbath. A Galilean synagogue was small: stone benches round the walls, the congregation facing inward, everybody able to see everybody.

A withered hand. The hand was dried up, the muscle wasted. Luke, the doctor, notices it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), which in a world of manual labour is the difference between a tradesman and a beggar. An early Jewish-Christian gospel, quoted by Jerome in the fourth century, has him say: I was a mason, earning my living with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, give me back my health, that I need not beg my bread in shame. His condition was not life-threatening. The scribal rule, later written down in the Mishnah (Yoma 8:6), allowed healing on the Sabbath only when life was in danger. This could wait a day, which is precisely why the case suited the Pharisees.

They watched Jesus. Watched means kept under observation, the way you watch a man you have already decided about. They had no doubt he could heal; their question was whether he would break their rules, so that they could bring a charge. They were using a disabled man as bait.

Religion detached from love. The most religious men present have looked at a man with a wrecked livelihood and seen a test case. That is what happens to religion when it comes away from love. It does not usually collapse into open wickedness; these men would have been horrified to be called wicked. It happens by degrees, until a suffering man in your own congregation is to you mainly an issue to be handled. A man with a withered hand, and men with withered hearts. Only one of them knew he needed healing.

Why did Jesus heal on the Sabbath when he could have waited a day? Because waiting would have conceded that their rules were God’s, and that doing good to a suffering man was work God forbade. Jesus was not being provocative for its own sake. He was showing what the Sabbath was for. Every day the man waited was another day of shame and begging, and the Lord of the Sabbath saw no reason to make him wait. Mercy delayed for the sake of a human tradition is not holiness. He chose the day deliberately, so that everyone would learn what kind of rest God gives.

The rest the day was waiting for. The Sabbath was a weekly picture of God’s rest: burdens lifted, the creation enjoyed with its Maker. Here is a man who cannot work at all, and on the day of rest the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28) gives him back the use of his hand. The rest the Sabbath pictured is found in Christ’s finished work (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17).
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. Healing a condition that was not life-threatening could wait a day — which is why they watched.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
