“Come here”. Literally rise into the middle. He does not heal secretly to avoid trouble. If the healing is to be treated as a crime, he will commit it where everyone can see. He set the man in the middle and put his own life at risk for him. That is how he has always loved: openly, at cost, in the full view of his enemies. And spare a thought for the man, who has not asked for any of this. He has probably kept the hand out of sight for years, and now he is exposed first and healed second.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? Jesus changes the question. They were braced for an argument about what counts as work: whether healing counts, whether the case is urgent, which earlier rulings apply. Jesus will not argue on those terms. He asks not what work is permitted, but what the Sabbath is for. And he leaves no third option. On any given Sabbath you are either doing good or doing harm, saving life or destroying it. To have the power to do good and to withhold it is itself a choice, and it does harm. James says it plainly: whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (James 4:17).

To save life or to kill. The second half of the question cuts close. By the end of verse 6 the men in that room will have spent the Sabbath planning a death. The Sabbath on which he restores a hand is the Sabbath on which they begin to plot a murder, and of the two it is the plot that breaks the Sabbath.

Was healing on the Sabbath forbidden in the law? No. Moses forbade work on the Sabbath but nowhere forbade healing. The ban came from the scribal rules built around the law, which allowed treatment only when life was in danger. Jesus was not breaking Moses; he was breaking the fence the teachers had built around Moses. As for Christians today, the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28). The Lord’s Day is a gift that believers gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly brothers, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold it as the Christian Sabbath, and they are to be honoured. And the question Jesus asks still stands over every day of the week.

But they were silent. They could not answer without condemning themselves: the question has only one honest answer, and it costs them the case. Most of us have used that silence: you do not deny what has been said, and you do not act on it either. A man who says nothing has not stayed neutral; he has decided, and avoided the cost of saying so. Two verses later the same silent men walk out of the building and start planning his death.

In everyday life. Think of the last time a clear word from Scripture met you and you answered it with silence. Silence before God is not a hiding place, and you need none: the voice that searches you is the voice that heals. Answer him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With anger. He looked round the room, face by face. This is the only place in the Gospels where the word anger is used of Jesus; Matthew and Luke leave it out, and Mark keeps it. This was righteous anger: anger at cruelty, at religion that used people instead of loving them, at hearts that cared more about rules than a suffering man. God is angry at such things (Psalm 7:11).

The picture that cannot fit. A picture of Jesus as endlessly mild and never provoked is not from the Bible. The Jesus of the Gospels was angry here, made a whip and cleared the temple courts (John 2:15), and called men whitewashed tombs to their faces (Matthew 23:27). And he never sinned once. So it is possible to be angry and holy at the same time. Be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26) is not a contradiction: anger is allowed, but it must stay clear of sin.

Grieved at their hardness of heart. His anger and his grief came together, in the same look. Hardness comes from a word for a callus, skin thickened until it can no longer feel. They were not merely mistaken; their hearts were closed. Righteous anger is never without sorrow for the sinner.

How can I tell righteous anger from sinful anger? Mark answers in the same sentence, and the answer is the word grieved. Sinful anger enjoys itself. It wants the other person diminished; it rehearses the argument in the shower; it would be quietly disappointed if they repented, because then there would be nothing to be right about. Righteous anger grieves. It hurts to feel it. It wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and it would be delighted to be made unnecessary. Try that test on the last thing you were angry about. Did you want the person changed, or did you want them beaten? You will know the answer in about four seconds.

“Stretch out your hand”. A command he could not obey in his own strength; if he could stretch out that hand, he would have done it long ago. Jesus’ word gave the power to obey.

His hand was restored. Healed by a word, with no interval and no gradual return of movement. He obeyed, and in the obeying the power was there. Jesus did not touch the man or lift a finger: there was nothing to accuse him of except the healing itself.

The order of obedience. The order here is the order of the Christian life. The stretching is where the healing happens. Faith is not a feeling of confidence you wait to receive before you move; faith is moving on his word while you still feel exactly as incapable as you did a minute ago. That answers a thought many believers are quietly stuck on: I would obey if I had more faith. No. You will find you had the faith in the doing of it. Make the phone call; open the Bible when nothing in you wants to. The strength arrives in the stretching, never before it, and it is the strength of the Spirit Christ has put in you (Philippians 2:13).

For worship. One hand withered and useless, held out at his command and made new. And his own hands, sound and strong, a workman’s hands, stretched out one Friday on a piece of wood and ruined, so that the ruined might be restored. His anger at sin and his grief over sinners met at the cross, and there he made us whole.
verseByVerse.note: Mark alone records Jesus’ anger and grief here; Matthew and Luke do not mention them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees went out. After an undeniable miracle, done to a man they have probably seen in that synagogue for years, they walk out. Nobody congratulates the man.

Counsel with the Herodians. Immediately: no interval of reflection. And the alliance would have seemed almost unbelievable. The Herodians supported Herod Antipas’ rule and cooperated with Rome: worldly, political, comfortable. The Pharisees were strict separatists who regarded collaboration with Rome as filthy compromise. On religion, politics, money and nationhood they agreed on nothing. Now they unite against Jesus within minutes, as they will again (12:13). Nothing on earth makes allies like a shared hatred of the light.

Against the LORD and against his Anointed. Psalm 2 had foreseen this alliance: the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed. The church in Acts named its fulfilment: Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against your holy servant Jesus, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:25–28). This meeting in Galilee is the first small beginning of that alliance, and Psalm 2 already says how it ends. He who sits in the heavens laughs, and the Son they plot against is the King set on Zion.

How to destroy him. Not discredit him: destroy. This is the first plot to kill Jesus in Mark, as early as chapter 3 of sixteen, and it is made on the Sabbath. From here on Jesus walks, with his eyes open, toward a verdict that has already been reached, and he heals somebody in nearly every chapter on the way.

Correct theology is not a preservative. This is what a hardened heart looks like from the inside: entirely convinced it is defending God, while it plans a murder. And here is the sober word for anyone who takes doctrine seriously, as we should. These were the orthodox party. They believed in the resurrection, the authority of Scripture, the coming Messiah and the moral law, and they left a service in which God had visibly acted and went straight into a meeting about how to kill him. The safeguard was never the doctrine on its own. It was whether the doctrine was still attached to love for God and pity for people, and in these men it had come away.

How do I guard my heart against this kind of hardness? Hardness grows by small refusals: hearing God’s word and not doing it, seeing a need and looking away, being corrected and defending yourself. So the remedy is small obediences, made promptly. When Scripture convicts you, act on it the same day. When you are shown to be wrong, say so. Keep company with believers who will tell you the truth, and exhort one another every day, so that none of you is hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Pray that God would keep your heart soft. And pray over what you believe: truth that is not prayed and loved soon becomes a weapon. If you are afraid your heart has already hardened, take comfort from this: the men in this verse felt no such fear. A heart that grieves over its own coldness is a heart God is already softening (Ezekiel 36:26).

For worship. They planned his death on a Sabbath, and he did not stop healing. Months later, on another Sabbath, he lay in a borrowed tomb, resting from a finished work, while his enemies posted a guard. Then came the first day of the week, and the stone was rolled back. The one they met to destroy has destroyed death itself, and every counsel taken against him has ended at an empty grave and a throne.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family’s rule — unlikely allies for the Pharisees.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea. Away from the synagogue and the plot. He does not escalate. He goes down to the lake, and the ministry gets bigger: what was meant to shut him down pushed him onto a shoreline that could hold thousands.

A great crowd followed. Mark rarely stops to name places, and here he lists six. Galilee is home. Judea and Jerusalem are the religious heartland several days’ walk to the south. Idumea is ancient Edom, forcibly converted and thought barely Jewish; Herod’s own people. Beyond the Jordan is the east bank, Gentile-mixed. Tyre and Sidon are not in Israel at all: Phoenician port cities to the north-west. Almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, and beyond: Jews and Gentiles.

The shape of the list. The list runs outward from the centre in every direction and takes in Jew, half-Jew and Gentile. It is a small picture of the church that is coming, and the first sign of an older promise being kept. To Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3). To the Servant: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6). By Acts the list will have kept going until it reaches Rome. The crowd on that shore was only the first trickle of a river that has not stopped flowing, and will not stop until a multitude no one can number stands before his throne.

In the flow. Verses 7–12 are a turning point: the leaders walk out, and the whole land walks in. Rejected by the old leadership, Jesus begins to form a new people around himself (vv. 13–19).

All that he was doing. Many came for healing, not for the teaching. This is a crowd assembled by reports of power, and much of it will not last. The day comes when he says something hard, and many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66).

Is a large crowd a sign of God’s blessing? Not by itself. Crowds gathered around Jesus, and crowds also shouted for his crucifixion. Some of the people on that shoreline came because of what they had heard he could give; some because of who he was. The beach looked identical either way, and only those who came for Jesus himself keep following when it becomes costly. A large church may be blessed, or merely popular; a small one may be faithful, or merely stuck. The measure Jesus uses is not attendance but whether people hear his word and do it (v. 35). Pray for crowds, but pray more for disciples.
verseByVerse.note: Idumea (old Edom) lay south of Judea; Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the coast to the north. The crowd came from every direction.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A boat ready. A small fishing boat kept just offshore: a platform to teach from (4:1) and a way out.

Lest they crush him. The verb is the one you would use of a mob pressing a man against a wall. This is a crowd of desperate, sick people, every one of them trying to get a hand on him. And Jesus, who could have stilled them with a sentence, quietly asks his friends to get a boat.

He did not despise the means. The Son of God, in a real human body with real exhaustion, took an ordinary practical precaution. He did not let himself be trampled to prove something about faith, and he did not stay available every hour that people wanted him. He withdrew (v. 7). He slept in boats (4:38). He got up before dawn and went where they could not find him (1:35).

Isn’t it selfish to set limits when people need me? No. It is part of being a creature. Having limits is not a character flaw; it is how you were made, and the Lord himself lived within them. The needs around you are truly endless and your strength is not, and pretending otherwise is not devotion; it is a slow way of becoming useless to everybody. If you are the person everyone comes to, in a family, a church or a job, take the boat. Rest, sleep, say no to some things, let others help. The aim is not to protect your comfort but to stay able to serve for the long haul. And remember that you are not the Saviour. He is, and his strength has no limit.

All who had diseases. The word translated diseases is the ordinary word for whips: illnesses that had flogged people for years. They believed that touching him would heal them (5:27–29; 6:56). And he heals them. This is a crowd with no theology and no understanding of who he is. He does not lecture them about their motives first.

In everyday life. Remember the mercy here when you come to him yourself with mixed motives and a bad attitude, wanting relief far more than you want him. He has never yet turned away a person for coming to him badly. Come as the crowd came, and let him sort out your motives once you are near enough for him to reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They fell down before him. Not in worship but in terror. In that whole crowd, the only voices that say exactly who he is belong to the demons, and they bow because in his presence they cannot do anything else. It is a small, unwilling foretaste of a day that is coming, when at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Philippians 2:10). Every knee, including these. The only question any creature gets to decide is whether it bows now in love or later in ruin. And the same Lord before whom demons cower calls sinners to come near and bow in love, and lifts them up as brothers and sisters.

“You are the Son of God”. The demons know who he is (1:24, 34): the truth the Father spoke at the Jordan (1:11), more than the disciples have yet said. And it does the demons no good at all.

A creed can be word-perfect and worthless. James puts it bluntly: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). These spirits fall down and confess his identity aloud, and they remain exactly what they are. The difference between the demons’ confession and a Christian’s is not accuracy. One says you are the Son of God and means keep away from me; the other says the same words and means have me. Mark will end this very chapter by showing you which you are: not by what you can recite, but by whether you do the will of God (v. 35).

Not to make him known. Jesus would not accept testimony from demons. The truth about the Son of God is not going to be carried on the tongue of the father of lies; that commission belongs to a fisherman, a tax collector, a Zealot, and to you. And he would not have his identity broadcast before people understood that the Son of God must suffer (8:29–31). Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. His full identity will be revealed at the cross, where a Roman officer says the words (15:39), and nobody can mistake what kind of King he is.

If every knee will bow, will everyone be saved in the end? No. Every knee will bow, but not every knee will bow in love. The demons here bow and remain his enemies. Paul’s words in Philippians 2 describe the universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship on the last day, willing or unwilling. Scripture is clear that those who reject Christ will go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). That is why the invitation is so urgent now. Today you may bow willingly and be received as a child. One day you will bow regardless. Bow now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Twelve (vv. 13–19). Jesus goes up the mountain, calls those he wants, and appoints twelve, first to be with him and then to be sent out. The list ends with Judas.

Two accusations (vv. 20–22). His family says he is out of his mind; scribes from Jerusalem say he is possessed.

The answer (vv. 23–27). Satan is not fighting himself: a stronger man has bound him and is carrying off his goods.

The warning and the family (vv. 28–35). The widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, with one solemn exception, and then his mother and brothers arrive outside, and he calls those sitting around him his family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The picture of the strong man in verse 27 is the key to the chapter. Jesus grants that there is a real kingdom of darkness; he denies that he serves it. He has come to rob it: first he ties up the strong man, Satan, and then he carries off the people Satan held. So the New Testament says God delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13).

And he bound the strong man by being bound himself. At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15), so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed to be with him, and only then sent out. They spent a long season watching him before they were sent to preach (6:7–13).

Now: it is possible to be very busy for God and seldom with him: to run a rota, lead a group and defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. Work that does not flow from being with Jesus becomes performance, and performance ends in exhaustion or pride.

And there is comfort in the same verse for the person who can no longer do much: the first calling of every disciple is one that illness, age and obscurity cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up on the mountain. Mountains are places of revelation and covenant in Scripture. At Sinai Moses went up and came down with a nation ordered around twelve tribes. Luke adds that Jesus spent the whole night there in prayer before he chose (Luke 6:12).

Those whom he desired. Jesus’ choice, by his will. Not those who volunteered or qualified: those whom he wanted. You did not choose me, but I chose you (John 15:16). If you belong to Christ today, that is the reason: he wanted you. There is no reason behind that except his own free love, and since it never rested on anything in you, nothing in you can undo it.

And they came to him. He calls, and they come: his wanting produces their coming. The call is not an offer left on the table but a summons that creates the answer, the way the same voice once said let there be light, and there was light.

Does those whom he desired mean that God chooses who will be saved? Yes, and that is a comfort, not a threat. This verse is about the choice of the Twelve for their office, but it shows the pattern of all God’s saving work. Scripture teaches that God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything foreseen in them but in love, according to the purpose of his will (Ephesians 1:4–5), and that those he calls he effectually draws (John 6:44). Effectually means that the call actually does what it intends: it does not merely invite, it brings. This never makes anyone’s coming unreal: they truly came. And it never closes the door on anyone who wants to come, for whoever comes to Christ will never be cast out (John 6:37). If you have come, it is because he wanted you first, and he will not let you go. And if it sounds unfair that he chooses, remember what is being chosen out of: rebels who deserve nothing. Grace is by definition not owed to anyone, and the wonder is not that God passes some by but that he sets his love on any of us at all (Romans 9:15–16). Many faithful Christians understand election differently, as God choosing those he foresaw would believe; the Reformed reading rests on texts like these, which ground the choice in his will and love alone.

And he appointed twelve. Literally he made twelve. Nobody in Israel could miss what that number meant: twelve sons of Jacob, twelve tribes. Ten of those tribes had been scattered for seven hundred years, and the prophets had promised they would be gathered again. Jesus does not preach a sermon about restoring Israel. He appoints twelve men, and the claim is made without a word of argument. This is Israel, beginning again, around him: the restored people of God. The Lord of the new Israel chose his people before they could choose him, and called them first of all to himself.

Whom he also named apostles. Apostle means one who is sent, an envoy carrying the sender’s authority. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, lack this phrase here, though several early ones have it; it is certainly in Luke 6:13.

So that they might be with him. The first purpose of the Twelve is not to be useful. Their first task is simply to be in his company: some three years mostly watching him pray, handle a hostile room, touch a leper. Almost none of it will feel like ministry. All of it is the training.

Sent out to preach. The second purpose: mission, proclaiming the kingdom. And the two are in an order that never reverses. Those he sends must first be with him. When a church or a Christian swaps those round, the work hollows out from the inside. That is the diagnosis for a common kind of Christian tiredness: not too much work, but too much work done on too little time with Christ. The cure is simple: go back and be with him. And they go with authority to cast out demons, sharing his own power over evil (6:7, 13).

Do Christians have this authority today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do, and practise deliverance ministry, and they are often sincere brothers and sisters. But this authority was given to the Twelve when Jesus sent them out, as part of the signs that marked the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12). The New Testament letters never tell believers to cast out demons. They tell them to resist the devil (James 4:7), to put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18), and to pray. The devil is real and still works, but Christ has bound the strong man (3:27), and the believer facing evil fights with the word, prayer and the fellowship of the church. This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such sign-gifts belonged to the apostles’ founding work (Ephesians 2:20); continuationist brothers read the evidence differently, and both agree that God still delivers the oppressed in answer to prayer, and that the victory is Christ’s alone.

In everyday life. There is a mercy here for anyone who can no longer do much of anything: the elderly, the ill, the housebound, the one whose usefulness has been taken away. The first calling on every disciple is one no illness can revoke. You are called to be with him, and you can do that from a bed.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent.

parallels.desc: the Twelve and the twelve tribes

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter). Peter means rock. When the name was given, Simon was anything but a rock: impulsive, loud and only a few years from swearing in a courtyard that he had never met the man. Jesus named him for what grace would make him, not for what he was.

He gave the name. In the Old Testament the great covenant renamings are God’s own work. He made Abram into Abraham and Jacob into Israel, and each new name was a promise that God himself would keep (Genesis 17:5; 32:28). Now Jesus does on a Galilean hillside what the God of Abraham did, as his own right, because the one speaking is the one who calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17). Peter would become a rock only by being joined to the true foundation, the stone the builders rejected (1 Peter 2:4–8). What these men became was Christ’s gift before it was their achievement.

Sons of Thunder. Only Mark records this nickname. It is affectionate, and it is also honest about them. These are the brothers who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that would not receive him (Luke 9:54), and who came privately to ask for the two best seats in the kingdom (10:35–40). Jesus knew their temperament on the day he chose them, gave it a name, and appointed them anyway. And John, the son of thunder, became the apostle of love (1 John 4:7–21).

Andrew. Peter’s brother, who spends his New Testament career bringing people to Jesus and then disappearing: his brother, a boy with some bread and fish, some Greeks (John 1:40–42; 6:8–9; 12:22). If your service is small and nobody attaches your name to it, Andrew is your man.

The middle of the list. Bartholomew is probably Nathanael (John 1:45). Matthew is Levi, the tax collector of chapter 2 (2:14), the collaborator his own people would have written off. Thaddaeus is probably the Judas son of James of Luke 6:16. We have not one line from James the son of Alphaeus. They are known to history as names in a list, and their names are written on the foundations of the city of God (Revelation 21:14). If it troubles you that your life will leave no trace anyone can point to, look hard at the middle of this list.

Simon the Zealot. Literally the Cananaean, from the Aramaic for zealous. He may have belonged to the Zealots, who wanted to overthrow Rome by force. To them a Jew who collected taxes for the occupiers deserved a knife. Jesus placed a former tax collector and a man whose very name spoke of zeal against Rome in the same group. They shared the same meals for three years. Nothing in the politics of the day could have reconciled them; nothing did, except the man in the middle.

Can my temperament really change? Yes, though usually slowly and never by willpower alone. The Spirit does not turn you into someone else; he makes you more truly yourself, with the sin burned out of your strengths. Peter stayed bold, but his boldness became courage for Christ. John stayed intense, but his intensity became love. Bring your temperament honestly to Christ: the temper, the anxiety, the coldness, the need to control. Name it, confess its sinful expressions, ask for the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), and stay close to him and to his people. Look back in ten years, not ten days.
verseByVerse.note: Peter means “rock.” Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas Iscariot. Judas is always last in the lists, and every list attaches a clause about the betrayal. Iscariot may mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee; but that is uncertain.

Who betrayed him. Mark tells the reader from the start how the story will go. Judas was appointed with the rest, there with him at every private explanation of every parable. He was sent out with the others to preach and given authority to cast out demons (6:7, 13), and there is no hint that his mission failed or that the others suspected him. When Jesus said at the last supper that one of them would betray him, they did not single out Judas; they each asked whether it was themselves (14:19). Being close to Jesus, and even serving in his name, is not the same as belonging to him.

Did Jesus know? Yes. Jesus chose Judas knowingly (John 6:70). John says it without qualification: Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him (John 6:64). The appointment of Judas was not an error later regretted. And there is a strange comfort in it for anyone who has been betrayed by someone close. Your Lord chose his betrayer with his eyes open, kept him at his own table, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden. He was not caught out. Nothing that has been done to you has caught him out either.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced to betray Jesus. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), and Judas acted freely and was responsible (14:21). The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed. Both are true: God planned it, and Judas chose it.

Can I fall away like Judas? This is the question that keeps sensitive people awake, so let it be answered plainly. Judas was never a believer who lost his salvation; he was a man who was near Christ without ever being in Christ, and John tells us how it went wrong: he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). The rot was private, ordinary and financial, and it ran for years under a spotless public record. He did not fall in one night; years of small thefts brought him to that night. So no, a true believer cannot be snatched out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). But do not use that as a reason to skip the examination; use it as the reason you can bear to make it. The honest test is not whether you have ever sinned badly. Peter denied him with oaths that same week and was restored on a beach. The test is what you do afterwards. Judas felt remorse, threw the money into the temple and went out to a rope. Peter wept, and came back. Remorse looks at itself and despairs; repentance turns to Christ and lives. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is not the mark of a Judas. Go to Christ with the thing you are afraid of. That is the one move Judas never made, and it was always open to him.

For worship. Behind Judas stood the Father, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and the Son himself, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Judas handed him over for money, the Father for love, the Son out of love for his Father and for us. The darkest deed of the night served the brightest purpose of eternity: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25).
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They could not even eat. Home is probably Peter’s house in Capernaum (2:1). The Son of God missed meals because of the volume of human need at the door.

To seize him. Word travels some twenty-five miles to Nazareth. His family (literally those beside him) includes his mother and brothers (v. 31). The verb is strong and physical, to take hold of, to arrest, the same word used later of the mob that comes for him in the garden (14:46). They intend to take him home before he embarrasses the family any further or gets himself killed.

“He is out of his mind”. They mean that he has lost his senses: he is neglecting food, provoking the authorities and claiming divine authority. They probably meant well, trying to protect him and the family’s reputation. That is a pressure every family knows: what will people say? Reputation is a quiet idol, and Jesus would not bow to it, even for his mother. But they did not understand him. His brothers did not believe in him until after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14). They called him mad, the people who had watched him grow up, and he went on loving them. He is patient beyond all our patience, and his love outlasts our blindness.

A stranger to his mother’s sons. Psalm 69 is the psalm the New Testament keeps quoting about Christ, at the temple and at the cross (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3), and it describes this afternoon: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s sons. For zeal for your house has consumed me (Psalm 69:8–9). What his family called madness was zeal: a love for his Father’s will so complete that meals and reputation counted for nothing beside it. Measured by the world, a man who will go to a cross for his enemies is out of his mind. Measured by heaven, it is the sanest love there has ever been.

The structure. Mark sandwiches the scribes’ accusation (vv. 22–30) inside the family story, and the sandwich invites comparison: the family’s misunderstanding, though less hostile, is uncomfortably close to the scribes’ rejection.

Mary among them. The first name in verse 31 is his mother: Mary, who had heard the angel and treasured the shepherds’ words (Luke 1:26–38; 2:19), on the road to Capernaum to take him home before it gets worse. Mary was not a woman of finished faith standing serenely above ordinary disciples. She had to grow, sometimes painfully. The Mary who stands outside here is the Mary who stands at the foot of the cross when nearly all the Twelve have run (John 19:25), and who is found praying with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). She moved from outside to inside, from misunderstanding to worship. So if your own coming to Christ has been uneven, with long stretches where you did not understand him at all, you are in the company of his mother.

Should I neglect food and rest for ministry, as Jesus did here? Not as a rule. This was a season of extraordinary demand, and the same Gospel shows Jesus withdrawing, sleeping, and later telling his disciples to come away by themselves and rest a while, because they had no leisure even to eat (6:31). There are times when love means missing a meal or a night’s sleep for someone in crisis, and that is right. But a life that never eats, never rests and never stops is not more spiritual; it is usually less wise. Jesus’ family were wrong about his sanity, but your family may be right about your exhaustion. Listen to them.
verseByVerse.note: “His family” means his relatives.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes from Jerusalem. The second verdict comes with authority: an official delegation from the religious capital, some ninety miles away.

What they cannot do. They cannot deny the exorcisms. The people best placed to expose a fraud admit that the demons were driven out and dispute only the power behind it. That is strong evidence that these things happened: no church would invent such a charge against its own Lord, and centuries later the Talmud still remembers Jesus as a sorcerer (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a).

He is possessed by Beelzebul. Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23). Behind it stands Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), lord of the flies, or Baal-zebul, lord of the dwelling. By Jesus’ day it had settled as a title for the prince of demons. They accuse Jesus of being in league with the devil, and more: they say that Satan lives in him.

The Anointed called unclean. At the Jordan the Spirit came down on Jesus (1:10–11), and every demon driven out in this Gospel has been driven out by that Spirit. Isaiah had promised a Servant on whom God would put his Spirit (Isaiah 42:1), and in Matthew Jesus draws the conclusion the scribes will not: if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Matthew 12:28). The men who came to judge him called the Spirit-filled Messiah the devil’s house.

Three verdicts. Mark has set two accusations side by side. His family says he is mad; the theologians say he is evil. Between them they cover the ground people have covered ever since: he is deluded, or he is dangerous, or he is what he says he is, and the third verdict is costly, because if it is true he must be obeyed. Some today suggest a fourth, that his followers later inflated a simple teacher; but even the earliest accounts, like this one, show a man claiming an authority no mere teacher claims. What is not on offer is the comfortable modern option of a wise and gentle teacher whom everyone can admire. Even the crowds who called him a prophet (6:15; 8:28) were not admiring a gentle moralist: a prophet speaks with God’s authority and demands an answer. People loved him or they wanted him dead.

Why didn’t the miracles convince them, and would miracles convince people today? These scribes had the best religious education in the world. They had the Scriptures largely by memory. They had walked ninety miles and watched the power of God set human beings free before their eyes, and they went home and wrote it up as demonic. The problem was never the evidence. When a heart has decided, it will build a theology to house the decision, and the better educated it is, the better the theology it can build. Abraham said the same in Jesus’ parable: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). Evidence matters, and Christianity rests on it, but only the Spirit opens closed hearts. So when you share the faith, give reasons, and pray.

For worship. They have called the master of the house Beelzebul, Jesus said (Matthew 10:25). He is indeed master of a house, but it is God’s: Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:6). The one they named Beelzebul is building a temple for the Holy Spirit out of sinners, living stones taken from the very house he was accused of serving.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called them to him. They have accused him of being possessed by the devil, and he invites them closer. The Lord of glory did not crush them with a word, though he could have. Parables here means picture-sayings, comparisons.

How can Satan cast out Satan? Then he takes the charge apart, with cold logic rather than outrage. The accusation is absurd. Why would Satan destroy his own work, freeing the people he has enslaved? When the most serious accusation in the Gospel is laid against him, Jesus reasons. There is a place for argument in the defence of the faith, and the Lord uses it.

A kingdom divided. Civil war destroys nations. Israel had split in two after Solomon, and the northern kingdom had ended in exile.

A house divided. Division destroys families, as anyone who has watched one tear itself apart knows.

Coming to an end. The scribes’ theory requires that the devil is expelling his own troops. If that were true, his kingdom would be destroying itself, and they would be announcing the end of the kingdom of darkness, which is exactly what they came to deny. Either the exorcisms are not from Satan, or Satan is finished. In fact Satan is coming to an end, not because he is divided, but because someone stronger has come (v. 27).

How Jesus argues. First, he grants them what is true: he does not deny the devil, but shows that their theory will not carry the weight they have put on it. That is how a Christian should handle an argument: take seriously what is right in it, and press the part that fails. Second, the argument changed nobody we hear of. Argument can clear away an obstacle, but it has never on its own changed a heart. That work belongs to the Spirit, the very Person these men are about to be warned against resisting.

Does a house divided mean churches must never divide? Unity is precious, and most church splits come from pride, not principle; Paul begs believers to be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit (Ephesians 4:3). So work hard for peace, forgive quickly, and do not leave over preferences. But Jesus’ point here is about Satan’s kingdom, not a rule that Christians must stay together whatever is taught. Where the gospel itself is denied, faithfulness may require separation (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10–11). Even then, go with grief and humility, and never with contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong man’s house. Now Jesus goes on the attack, with one picture that turns the accusation inside out. The strong man is Satan, and the goods are people: every possessed man in Galilee, every reader of this page before Christ came for them.

First binds the strong man. To rob a strong man you must first overpower him and tie him up. Jesus is the one stronger than Satan. John the Baptist had called him the mightier one (1:7). Isaiah asks whether the prey can be taken from the mighty, and God answers that the captives of the mighty shall be taken and he himself will contend with the contender (Isaiah 49:24–25). The scribes have said he works for the owner. But a servant does not tie up his master and carry off his goods. Jesus is in the house as the raider, and the owner is on the floor with his hands tied. And the order is exact: binding first, plundering afterwards.

Then he may plunder. Every exorcism, every healing, every sinner forgiven is Jesus plundering Satan’s house, freeing his captives. The New Testament keeps the picture when it describes what happened to you: God delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13), and transferred is a word used of moving whole populations from one land to another.

When was the strong man bound? The binding began in the wilderness (1:12–13) and was completed at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). And here is the strangest and best turn in the faith. He was bound by a stronger man who let himself be bound first. In a garden, soldiers put their hands on Jesus and tied him, and he did not resist. They led him away bound to a high priest, bound to a governor, and fastened him to a cross with his arms open and immovable, the posture of a man who can plunder nothing. And that was the binding of Satan. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15); through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). The strongest man who ever lived walked into the house, and instead of overpowering the owner he let the owner tie him up, and died, and that is how Satan came to be the one tied up.

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is now inactive. He still prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). But he cannot stop the gospel or hold those whom Christ frees. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he cannot deceive the nations. This commentary reads that thousand years as the present gospel age, between Christ’s two comings, partly because Jesus speaks of Satan as bound already; brothers who expect a future thousand-year reign on earth read Revelation 20 differently, and both rejoice that the decisive victory is already won.

If Satan is bound, why is there still so much evil? Because a bound enemy can still do damage within the length of his chain. Satan is defeated but not yet destroyed; that final destruction comes at Christ’s return (Revelation 20:10). For now he cannot stop the spread of the gospel among the nations, or keep a single one of God’s elect in his house, or separate a believer from Christ. But he still tempts, accuses and deceives, and the world still groans under sin. Christians live between the binding and the end: the decisive battle won, the war not yet over. So we resist him firmly in the faith, knowing that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under our feet (Romans 16:20).

In everyday life. If you are in Christ, you are not a volunteer who signed up. You are rescued property. Somebody broke in and carried you out over his shoulder, and the price of the raid was his life. Live today like someone who has been carried out.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you. The word behind truly is amen, the formula Jesus uses to put his own authority behind a statement.

All sins will be forgiven. He begins with the widest promise in the Gospel. All sins, and every blasphemy men speak: the things said in rage, the years spent mocking him, the words you would not repeat to another human being. Blasphemy means speech that insults or slanders God, and even that can be forgiven: no sin is too great to be forgiven if it is repented of. Paul was a blasphemer and was forgiven (1 Timothy 1:13). Do not hurry past this on the way to the exception: it is one of the most sweeping sentences about mercy Jesus ever spoke, and he spoke it to men who had just called the Holy Spirit a devil.

Whatever blasphemies they utter. How can a holy God promise this? Because the man speaking was on his way to bear those sins himself. Mark uses the same word at the cross: those who passed by derided him, literally blasphemed him, wagging their heads (15:29). From the middle of the blasphemy he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34; the prayer is missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, though many scholars judge it authentic). He came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and that ransom is big enough to cover every word ever flung at him. The promise of all sins rests on the blood of the one who was sinned against most.

An eternal sin. Then the one exception. An eternal sin is one whose guilt is never lifted, because it is never forgiven, in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). What is it? Mark tells us in the next sentence.

“He has an unclean spirit”. Mark ties it to what was said in that room. The scribes saw the Holy Spirit’s work in Jesus clearly, and deliberately called it the work of Satan. This is blasphemy against the Spirit: not a careless word, doubt or confusion, but a settled, wilful rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, looking straight at the light and naming it darkness. It is unforgivable not because God’s grace is too small, but because it refuses the only way to be forgiven. The Spirit convicts of sin and leads to Christ (John 16:8–11); a person who calls his work satanic has shut the door on the only way back. He is never forgiven because he never repents, and he has no wish to be forgiven.

Have I committed it? Let the answer be given straight, because you may be living inside this question and you do not need a survey of opinions. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, you have not committed it. That is not a comforting fiction. The sin is the final hardening of a heart against the Holy Spirit, a heart grown so hard that it can see God at work and call it the devil without a tremor. Fear of this sin requires that you want to be forgiven, that you care what God thinks of you, that being cut off from him horrifies you. That does not come from a hardened heart. Hardened hearts do not lie awake worrying about their standing with God; they sleep very well. The scribes went home untroubled. Your distress is itself the evidence of a conscience still alive under the Spirit’s hand, and the Spirit does not trouble a man he has abandoned. The hardness that commits this sin does not tremble. It calculates.

Then come. Can you say honestly that if he would have you, you would come? Then come. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and there is no clause in that sentence excepting people afraid they have gone too far. A person who wants pardon is not in the position of the scribes. Your fear is not your danger.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers. The family who set out to seize him (v. 21) arrive, and a message comes from the door.

Standing outside. Outside: Mark says it twice (vv. 31, 32), and the word carries the scene. They do not come in. They send for him, which is what you do when you expect to be obeyed: family authority, requiring the eldest to come out so that they can take him home.

A crowd was sitting around him. Inside, they sit listening, the posture of disciples (Luke 10:39). Where people stand shows the lesson of the whole chapter: being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. You can be his mother and be outside, while a crowd of strangers sits at his feet.

Who were his brothers? Jesus’ brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (6:3), most naturally Mary’s later children. Matthew names them and adds sisters (Matthew 13:55–56); John says that not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5); and Acts sets them beside Mary but apart from the apostles (Acts 1:14). Two other views arose in the early church, both to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin all her life, a belief many Christians through history, some Reformers among them, have sincerely held: that they were Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, or that they were cousins. But Scripture never says either, and Matthew says that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), which most naturally implies that afterwards they lived as husband and wife. The more likely reading is that these were Jesus’ younger brothers. It does not lessen Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord.

In the room, or at the door? This is the most searching thing in the passage for religious people, and it is not really about Mary. It is about anyone whose connection to Christ is a matter of nearness rather than surrender. Raised in it, related to it, married into it, employed by it, on the rota, in the building, known by name to everyone in the congregation, and still, in practice, outside, sending messages in, wanting Christ to come out and fit into a life that has been organised without him. So ask, without panic but without dodging it: am I in the room, or at the door? Not, have I been around this a long time; the family had been around him for thirty years. The question is whether you have sat down in front of him as someone who wants what he says more than you want a Christ you can manage.

He went outside for those outside. At the end of the Gospel the places are reversed. He is led out of the city, as the sin offering was carried outside the camp, and Hebrews makes the connection: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). He went out into the place of rejection so that people standing outside, strangers to God and to his covenants, could be brought in. You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13). That is how his own mother and brothers came in, and it is the only way anyone does. If someone you love is still outside, take heart from this family: nobody in that street was beyond the reach of the man in that house.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are my mother and my brothers? A startling question in a culture where family was everything. It is asked in order to be answered, and the answer is astonishing news for ordinary people.

Looking about. Only Mark mentions the look. Earlier he looked around at hard men with anger (v. 5). Here he looks around at a floor full of nobodies, face by face.

Here are my mother and my brothers! Those who sit at his feet and listen are his true family. He said it while his mother was standing in the street, but not at her expense. This is not the demotion of the natural family. It is the announcement of a second one.

Whoever does the will of God. Whoever: no pedigree or record required. Does the will of God: membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth but by doing God’s will, hearing his word, repenting, believing and obeying (1:15). Not whoever admires it, or believes the correct things about it; the demons on the beach had the doctrine right and were no relation of his. And in case anyone turns that into a place to be earned by performance, John records the Lord’s own definition of the work God requires: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29). And none of us does God’s will perfectly (James 3:2); the one Son who did it without fault did it in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), which is why our faltering obedience is welcome in the family. My brother and sister and mother: he reaches for the closest words the language has, and he says sister, at a time when a rabbi’s disciples were all men. The church is a family.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus rejected his mother or family. He provided for his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27), and he is the one who said that setting aside duty to parents for a religious excuse makes void the word of God (7:11–13). His brothers later came to faith. But blood ties are not the deepest ties. And this passage gives no support to praying to Mary as one who pleads for us with her Son. Jesus pointed away from family to faith.

Does this mean I should put church above my family? Not in the sense of neglecting them. Scripture is fierce that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8), and your husband or wife, children and parents are people God has given you to love first and most practically. What this passage does is set the order of loyalties: Christ above all, and his family as a real family, not a club. Where your natural family and your church family both need you, you will usually serve them in different ways at once. Where your natural family opposes Christ, you follow him while still loving them. And where you have no natural family, or have lost them, the church is meant to be home.

In everyday life. Who in your church family sits alone this week: the widow, the student far from home, the believer whose relatives have cut them off? Invite one of them to a meal. The awkward, mismatched congregation you sit among on a Sunday is not a social arrangement you could improve on by finding people more like yourself. It is your family, given to you by Christ, and he named them before you did.

For worship. To the believer with a family gone quiet, the empty chair at Christmas, the brother who does not call, and to the one with no family left at all, the Lord Jesus Christ looks round a room and says: here. These are mine. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He said it on the afternoon he was called mad by his family and demonic by the theologians, on his way to a cross where he would make a family out of people who had none.

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark come in this chapter.

Was Jesus's anger sinful? No, and verse 5 shows how to tell, because it puts the anger and the grief in one breath: he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Sinful anger wants the other person diminished; righteous anger grieves, and wants the wrongdoer restored.

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in verse 30: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. It is the settled, deliberate calling of the Holy Spirit's plain work the work of Satan, by men who have seen it with their own eyes. It is not a slip or a doubt. And the person terrified of having committed it has not, because that fear needs a conscience still alive to the Spirit, which is exactly what this sin destroys.
3.examples:
The chapter sets two alliances side by side.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians, strict separatists and worldly courtiers who despised each other, agreeing within minutes on one thing: how to destroy him. So Pilate and Herod became friends over him (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve, reconciled by nothing except the man in the middle.

Now: a congregation can be held together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity without being unity. Or it can be people with little in common except Christ. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is the evidence of his work.

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is Mark's great block of teaching, and it answers the question chapter 3 raised: if Jesus is the King, why does his kingdom look so small? The kingdom seems to be a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve ordinary men.

The answer comes in seed. A sower scatters over ground he cannot see into, much of the seed is lost, and still the harvest is thirty, sixty and a hundredfold (vv. 3–20). Seed grows while the farmer sleeps (vv. 26–29). The smallest seed becomes the largest garden plant, with birds nesting in its branches (vv. 30–32).

Then Jesus says let us go across, and the crossing nearly kills them. The chapter about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a storm, and with a question: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The boat (vv. 1–2). The crowd is so large that Jesus teaches from a boat a few yards offshore.

The parable (vv. 3–9). Seed falls on a path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil. Three losses, and one harvest far beyond what a farmer could hope for.

Why parables (vv. 10–12). Jesus quotes Isaiah: the stories give understanding to those who come and ask, and confirm the refusal of those who will not.

The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25). What is hidden now is hidden so that it may be revealed, and what we do with what we hear decides what we receive next.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matthew 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven.

First, the words quote Isaiah 6:9–10: this is judgment on hardened refusal. Second, so that speaks of fulfilment: the parables confirm a choice already made, as God gives people over to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24). Third, the door is never bolted. The disciples understood nothing either; the difference was that they asked.

So the same parable is judgment and mercy at once: it hardens the scornful and keeps the truth within reach of anyone who will come and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer scattering seed by hand over ground he has not sorted, some of it landing where it has no chance.

Now: every preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. If you have taught a class for years or raised children in the faith and cannot see a harvest, your task was the sowing.

And the harvest is not in doubt. Jesus names thirty, a bumper crop, as the lowest of the good outcomes.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 4 is Jesus’ chapter of parables, ending in a storm. Why do some receive him and others not? The word of the kingdom falls on four kinds of ground, and only one bears fruit, but that fruit is an astonishing harvest. Then a lamp, a measure, seed growing while the farmer sleeps, and a mustard seed: the kingdom is small and hidden now, and certain of harvest. On the lake at night Jesus silences the storm, and his disciples ask the question of the whole Gospel: who then is this?

He got into a boat. The boat prepared in 3:9. Jesus has it pushed out a few yards and sits down in it, the posture of a teacher. Near Capernaum there are coves where the ground rises from the water in a natural curve, and a man in a boat could be heard by thousands without shouting.

I will open my mouth in a parable. One voice goes out over farmers and fishermen and Pharisees listening for errors: one seed, many kinds of ground. Matthew saw a psalm fulfilled in this teaching: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world (Matthew 13:35, from Psalm 78:2). Asaph, who wrote Psalm 78, told Israel’s history in riddles; the Son of David tells the secrets of God’s kingdom, and he can utter what was hidden since the foundation of the world because he was there when it was laid (John 1:1–3).

Many things in parables. We remember the miracles; Mark records that the bulk of the Lord’s time went on teaching. A parable is a story or picture from ordinary life placed beside a spiritual truth to illuminate it: farming, lamps, measures, seeds. The Creator used his own creation as his pulpit and his illustrations, and he spoke so that farmers and fishermen could understand. A parable is not a children’s illustration or a code. Parables usually make one main point, and they make you work.

Why stories? A straight statement, such as people respond differently to the word of God, is easy to agree with and easier to forget; you can nod at it without a flicker of self-suspicion. But hand a man a picture of a field with four kinds of ground in it, and he will find himself walking round the edge of it wondering which patch he is standing on. He has to enter the story to understand it, and once he is inside it, it has him. A story slips past the defences that an argument runs straight into. Nathan did not open by telling David that he was the man. He told him about a poor man and one little ewe lamb, and let David pass sentence on himself first (2 Samuel 12:1–7). So read this chapter expecting to be handled the same way. Jesus is not about to give you information about four types of hearer. He is about to walk you out into a field and ask you where you are standing.

How should I read a parable? Start with the setting: who Jesus is speaking to and what question is in the air. Look for the main point, often found in the surprise or the ending, such as the enormous harvest or the mustard plant that shelters birds. Where Jesus explains a parable, as he does with the sower, let his explanation govern yours. Do not press every small detail for a hidden meaning; a story needs scenery. And always ask the question a parable is designed to make you ask: where am I in this? Then come to Jesus with what you do not understand, as the disciples did (v. 10).
verseByVerse.note: Teaching from a boat let the whole crowd on the shore see and hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen! He opens with a command, and will end with he who has ears to hear, let him hear (v. 9). The great issue of the chapter is how we listen.

The sowing. A Galilean farmer carried the seed in a fold of his cloak or a bag at his hip and threw it in a wide arc as he walked, often before the ground was ploughed, so it fell everywhere: on paths, on limestone a few inches down, on last year’s thorn roots. The sower is not careless. He cannot see what is six inches under the surface.

The first comfort. Hold on to that, because it is the first comfort in the chapter, and it is for anyone who has ever taught, preached, raised children in the faith, or talked about Christ to a friend and watched nothing happen. You are not asked to survey the soil first. You could not do it if you tried; you cannot see into another human being. Sow. The results were never the part assigned to you.

A sower went out. The first sower in this parable is the man telling it: the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man (Matthew 13:37). That is why I came out, he said (1:38). He came out from the Father to sow the word in a world of paths, rocks and thorns, and he flung it wide: to Pharisees and fishermen, to Judas and to Peter. He does not ration his mercy to the promising. Every faithful preacher since is only scattering from his bag.

Along the path. The path is not bad soil by nature. It has been walked on so often that it has set like a floor. Nobody decided to make it hard; the same feet went over it, day after day, until nothing could get in.

The birds devoured it. At once. Jesus will tell us in verse 15 who the birds are: Satan comes at once and takes the word away. So the most ordinary religious experience in the world, sitting through a sermon and remembering none of it by lunchtime, is not always a neutral failure of concentration. Something can be at work in it. And the path is the soil nobody worries about being, which is its danger. It feels nothing at all. The word arrives, lies there and is carried off, and the man goes home to his lunch undisturbed and slightly bored.

I forget sermons by lunchtime. What can I do? Several simple things help the seed go in before the birds arrive. Pray before the service that God would open your heart to his word. Read the passage beforehand if you know it. Listen with a pen: write down one sentence you want to remember. Talk about the sermon over lunch with your family or friends, and ask each other what struck you. Come back to it during the week, perhaps reading the passage again on Monday. And above all, act on one thing it said. Truth that is obeyed is not easily stolen.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rocky ground. Not soil full of stones but a thin skin of earth over limestone bedrock, common in Galilee. From above it looks exactly like the rest. And here is the cruelty of it: this is the ground that performs best at first.

It sprang up. The logic is the opposite of what you would expect. It came up fast because the soil was shallow. The shallow soil warmed quickly; the seed could not go down, so everything it had went up. It looked promising. The fastest, greenest, most impressive growth in the whole field is the growth that is going to die. Anyone who has been in church life for twenty years has watched this: the new convert whose enthusiasm makes everyone else feel lukewarm, who is at everything, telling everyone, radiant, and who is not there in three years, and nobody can quite say when they stopped coming. The rate of early growth told you nothing.

It withered away. The same sun that made it sprout killed it. Yet the sun also ripens the harvest in the good soil; the difference is underground, where nobody can see. Trouble is the weather in which real growth ripens and shallow growth is exposed. The same bereavement or diagnosis will strengthen one believer and break another, and the difference was decided long before the heat arrived. But if a loss has shaken you badly, that is not the same as withering: a believer can be struck down without being destroyed (2 Corinthians 4:8–9), and the very fact that you still reach for him in the dark is a root holding.

A root out of dry ground. The deepest roots in Scripture belong to Christ. Isaiah says the Servant grew up before the LORD like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2), with nothing around him to explain his life. He never withered, because his life was drawn from his Father. Faith that lasts is not rooted in our own depth of character but in him. Paul prays that believers be rooted and grounded in love, and tells them to walk in Christ, rooted and built up in him (Ephesians 3:17; Colossians 2:6–7). Shallow faith rests on an experience of Jesus; rooted faith rests on Jesus.

Roots are grown in private. So the practical question is not how green you look this month but what is happening in the dark. Roots go down in the unglamorous stretches: the half-hour with a Bible on a wet Tuesday when nothing in you wants it; the prayers that feel like talking to the ceiling; the Sundays you attend when you would rather not; the doctrine you take the trouble to understand before you need it. None of that shows. That is precisely the point of it.

How can I tell whether my faith has roots, or whether I am rocky ground? Look below the feelings. Rooted faith keeps going when the feelings go: you still pray when prayer is dry, still trust when God seems silent, still belong to his people when church is disappointing. It rests on Christ and his word, not on an atmosphere. It has survived some heat already, a loss, a temptation resisted, a cost paid for being a Christian, and come out clinging to Christ rather than resenting him. If you are unsure, do not torment yourself with introspection. Go to Christ, ask him to root you, and start digging: Scripture, prayer, church, obedience, day after ordinary day.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among thorns. The thorns are not visible at the sowing: last season’s roots, burned off at the surface, the earth above them looking as good as any other.

Choked. Then the rains come, and wheat and thorns come up together, drawing on the same water and light. The thorns grow faster. Choking is silent, but it is total. Nobody digs up the wheat. It is simply crowded, shaded and starved by things that are also alive, also growing, also using the ground.

It yielded no grain. Only Mark adds this. The plant is still there, green and standing. It simply never produces anything.

Thorns and the crown. Thorns entered the Bible with the curse: cursed is the ground because of you; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Genesis 3:17–18). Every heart crowded by care is the same curse at work inside. Then, on the morning of his death, soldiers twisted a crown of thorns and pressed it on Jesus’ head (15:17). The King wore the curse of the ground as his crown. He took our thorns on himself so that ground choked by the fall could be made good. So the cure for a choked life is not first a better schedule. It is a Saviour who has already borne the curse that makes the thorns grow.

The thorns are not scandalous sins. Jesus explains them later in the chapter (v. 19): the thorns are the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things. Not adultery, theft or blasphemy, but worry, money and the wanting of ordinary things. So this soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct. A man in this field is worrying about the mortgage, working for a promotion he does not need, keeping up with the news. None of it is wicked. All of it is alive, and all of it uses up the room and strength the word needs.
