And the sign is not a sin you have committed but a fruit you cannot find: the prayer that has quietly stopped happening, the Bible opened on Sunday because someone else opens it, the conversation about Christ you have not had with anyone in a year, not because you decided against it, but because there has been no room.

Is it wrong to plan, work hard and provide for my family? No. Scripture commands it: work with your hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11), provide for your household (1 Timothy 5:8), learn from the ant (Proverbs 6:6–8). The problem is not that these things exist but that they take first place and leave no room. A good test is not whether you work hard but whether your work and plans are done before God, with prayer, and whether they leave room for him: for worship, for his word, for his people, for generosity. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33). Thorns grow where good things are allowed to grow unweeded.

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good soil. Three failures, and now the harvest. The good soil does nothing to become good. It simply receives what falls on it and lets it go down. Whatever this parable asks of you, it is not asking you to manufacture your own fertility; a field is worked on by its farmer; it does not improve itself. Mark alone says the grain was growing up and increasing: this growth takes its time. Fast is not the same as fruitful, and slow is not the same as dead.

A hundredfold. A normal harvest was perhaps seven to tenfold, out of which next year’s seed had to come. Thirty was excellent; a hundred was astonishing, the kind of blessing Isaac received in the year God prospered him (Genesis 26:12). Jesus names thirty as the lowest of his three good outcomes. Three of the four kinds of ground are a loss, and the harvest is still extravagant. Despite all the losses, God’s word will not fail.

The grain that dies. Where does a harvest like this come from? From the Sower’s own death: in the week he died, Jesus said of himself, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). The hundredfold of the gospel age, the church gathered from every nation, is the fruit of one grain buried in a garden tomb and raised on the third day, the firstfruits of all who will rise (1 Corinthians 15:20).

The accounts at the end. It looked, in Galilee that year, as though this was going badly. The professionals had declared him demonic, his family thought he was mad, the crowds wanted healings and not much else, and the kingdom of God consisted of a preacher in a borrowed boat and a dozen unimpressive men. Jesus tells them what the accounts will say at the end, and the harvest far outweighs the losses. Hold that when you look at your own field and see mostly loss: the children who are not walking with God, the years of teaching that seemed to change nobody, the church that is smaller than it was. The losses in this parable are real and named honestly. But they are not the end of the story. He who supplies seed to the sower will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness (2 Corinthians 9:10).

Ears to hear. A call to hear with understanding and respond; the refrain will sound again over the seven churches (Revelation 2–3). Everyone on that beach had ears, so the sentence is a warning: a person can hear the sound and miss the meaning. Spiritual hearing is a gift, and the man who wants it has only to ask the one in the boat for it.

What is the fruit, exactly? Not only converts, though bringing others to Christ is part of it. The fruit is a life changed by the word: the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23); good works done for God’s glory (Colossians 1:10); repentance that shows in what you do (Matthew 3:8); praise to God (Hebrews 13:15); and generosity (Philippians 4:17). Fruit grows slowly and is often seen more clearly by others than by yourself. Ask someone who knows you well whether they see Christ in you more than they did five years ago.

In everyday life. Bring to mind one person you have been sowing into for a long time with little to show for it, and pray for them, trusting the harvest to the one who promised it.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him. The crowd goes home, and a smaller group stays behind and asks. The insiders are not insiders because they understood; verse 13 shows they did not. They stayed and asked.

The secret of the kingdom. Secret in the New Testament does not mean a puzzle for clever people. It means a truth once hidden, now revealed by God. The secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but in a hidden, unexpected way: like seed, not like a conquering army; in a carpenter from Nazareth who is going to a cross. Has been given: understanding is God’s gift (Matthew 16:17). The kingdom is a gift, and so is the understanding of it, and so is the faith that receives it.

Those outside. Those outside are those who have rejected Jesus. Mark used the same word of his family, standing outside the house (3:31–32).

See but not perceive. The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must not be smoothed over. It sounds as though Jesus speaks in stories so that people will not repent. Three things open it up. First, these words quote Isaiah 6:9–10. God sent Isaiah to a people who had refused the truth for generations. Jesus’ parables have the same effect on those who have already rejected him: the truth is there, but they do not grasp it. It is a judgment on hearts already closed, and it is the passage the New Testament reaches for again and again to explain unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27). Second, so that here means that Scripture is being fulfilled: when they hear and do not understand, Isaiah’s word comes true. It is the pattern Paul describes when God gives people over to what they have already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28), the darkness they preferred, finally granted.

Lest they should turn. Turn is repentance: not just feeling sorry, but a change of mind that turns the whole person round, away from sin and toward God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). And third, decisively, the door is never bolted against anyone who knocks. The proof is sitting in the room: the only thing separating the Twelve from the crowd walking home is that they asked. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matthew 7:7).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus wanted to prevent willing people from being saved. Those who wanted to understand came and asked, and he explained (v. 34). The hardening falls on those who refuse. And Jesus’ purpose in parables is also to reveal: a lamp is meant to be seen (v. 21). God is sovereign in revealing and hiding (Matthew 11:25–26), and people are responsible for refusing.

Am I one of those outside if I do not understand much of the Bible? No. The disciples did not understand either; Jesus had to explain everything to them, and they were still slow years later. Being inside is not about how much you understand but about whether you have come to Jesus and keep coming. If you love him, want to know him better, and bring him your questions, you are among those to whom the secret has been given. Understanding grows over a lifetime. Keep reading, keep asking, keep listening to faithful preaching, and be patient with yourself.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? There is a sigh in that, and Mark is not embarrassed to record it. But it is not a refusal to explain; it is a remark made in the middle of explaining. He says, do you not understand? and then tells them. That is a mercy for slow disciples, which is all of us. The men who were with him some three years were, by any honest reading of this Gospel, consistently baffled, and the Lord kept teaching them. This parable is the key to the rest. If you understand how the word is received, you can understand everything else.

The sower sows the word. The seed is the word: not a mood, but sentences that can be spoken and heard. The sower is Jesus, and all who preach his word after him. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17); we are born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). So an unremarkable sermon in a half-empty building on a wet Sunday is not a low-grade activity. It is the sowing.

Satan immediately comes. Jesus names the birds. Satan is a personal being, not a figure of speech, and he takes the word, by distraction, mockery, doubt or forgetfulness. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4). Immediately: in the car park, on the walk home. The word did not fail to be good; it was removed before it could get in.

If Satan takes the word away, are people who reject the gospel still responsible? Yes. Satan blinds, but he blinds people who prefer the dark (John 3:19). The path was hardened by traffic it allowed, and the hearer is not a passive victim but a willing participant in his own forgetting. Scripture never lets us blame the devil for our unbelief, any more than Eve could (Genesis 3:13). And the remedy is offered to every hearer: God is able to break up hard ground and to open blind eyes, and he invites everyone to ask. Responsibility and the need for grace stand together.

In everyday life. If you have started to find God’s word dull, take that seriously and take it to God tonight, in exactly those words. He has never once refused a man who asked him to break up his own hard ground: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). The path cannot plough itself. It does not have to.

parallels.desc: the god of this world has blinded the minds

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Received with joy. It looks like conversion. And there is nothing wrong with the joy, which needs saying, because this soil frightens sensitive people. Real conversion is glad: the man who found treasure in a field sold everything in his joy (Matthew 13:44). The problem is not that they were happy. It is that happiness was all there was.

No root in themselves. The diagnosis is in the words in themselves: not no root in the church, but no root in themselves. Something was never made their own. Their faith lived on its surroundings: the music, the friendships, the feeling in the room, a preacher they admired. It never went down into the private ground where nobody could see it. And they endure for a while: that is why it takes time to tell. For a season this soil looks the same as good soil, and at first even better. Mark gives no timescale. It might be two years.

On account of the word. The heat is specific: trouble that arrives on account of the word, the cost of the faith itself: the friendships that cool once you are known as a Christian, the promotion that goes elsewhere, and in much of the world today far worse. Mark’s first readers, probably in Rome, knew exactly this. This is the soil that discovers Christianity is expensive, and had assumed it was free.

They fall away. Fall away means stumble, be tripped up; from the same root comes the word Paul uses when he calls the cross a stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23). Mark uses immediately at every stage of this soil: it springs up, receives and falls away immediately (vv. 5, 16–17).

You will all fall away. Jesus uses the same verb on the night he is arrested: you will all fall away (14:27). And they did. Every one of them fled (14:50). So what separates the Twelve from the rocky ground? Not the strength of their roots that night, but the grip of their Shepherd. In the same breath he promised, after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:28), and to Peter he said, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:32). The disciples stumbled and were brought back, because the root of their faith was in a Saviour who intercedes. Rocky ground has no such root. Every true believer does.

Were these true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians (who hold that God’s grace can be resisted and true faith finally lost), brothers who take the Bible’s warnings seriously, read the parable that way: the rocky soil received the word with joy, so it must have been real faith, which was then lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6). But Jesus says they have no root in themselves; something was missing from the start. The joy was real, but it was not the life of a new heart. John says of such people that they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The more likely reading is that the fruitless soils describe profession without possession: people who claim the faith without having its life. A true believer may stumble and struggle, but the word that has truly taken root goes on to bear fruit, because God who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

How do I help a new believer put down roots? Do not dampen their joy; build under it. Read the Bible with them regularly, perhaps a Gospel, a chapter at a time, and show them how to pray from it. Bring them into the life of a church where people will know them, not just greet them. Teach them the basics of the faith, so they know why they believe. Warn them honestly that following Christ will cost something, so the heat does not take them by surprise. And keep in touch when they go quiet. Roots grow best in company.

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third soil. The word takes root and grows. This is the particular danger of churchgoers in a comfortable country, and Jesus names its three weeds.

The cares of the world. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd God out. The Greek word for cares is the ordinary one for anxiety, the same one Peter uses when he says to cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Peter 5:7). The mortgage, the scan result, the parents growing frail: most of these cares come with real duties. And they strangle the word, because worry takes the time and mental room that hearing God requires.

The deceitfulness of riches. Not riches, but the deceitfulness of them: the lie that a little more will make you safe. It makes people feel they do not need God (10:23–25; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). That lie is told to the man with very little as loudly as to the man with a great deal, which is why this weed grows in every income bracket.

Desires for other things. Only Mark adds this: the extension, the holiday, the hobby that has quietly become the thing you think about while other people are talking. None of it is wrong, which is why it is so hard to see from inside. Good things can become thorns when they take first place.

The surpassing worth. Thorns are not cut out by willpower alone; they are crowded out by a greater love, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). Paul counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8). That is the remedy this soil needs. Not a life emptied of ordinary goods, but a heart in which Christ has become the treasure for which a man sells all that he has (Matthew 13:44), so that money, plans and worries are put back in their place beneath him. A choked heart does not need less to love. It needs to see how much more there is to love in him.

It proves unfruitful. Enter in: these things were let in, one reasonable thing at a time, until the word was crowded to the edge. And it proves unfruitful. The faith is never renounced; the plant survives, but bears nothing. A person may stay in church for years with no real fruit.

Is this hearer a Christian at all? Some teach that he is a carnal Christian, saved but fruitless and unrewarded (compare 1 Corinthians 3:15). But in the parable only the good soil yields a harvest, and Jesus says elsewhere that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down (Matthew 7:19). The more likely reading is that a life that bears nothing at the harvest shows a faith that never truly lived. A believer may go through seasons of little fruit and be pruned (John 15:2); but the word that is truly received does not stay barren for good.

Is it wrong to be wealthy? Not in itself. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. But Jesus warns that wealth is unusually dangerous, because it deceives (10:23–25). Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). So if God has given you money, hold it with an open hand: give regularly and generously, live below your means, and ask honestly whether your security is in your savings or in your Saviour. The test is not how much you have but how easily you could give it away.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear and accept. Three verbs, in an order that cannot be rearranged: hear, accept, bear fruit. Hear: the path heard it too; hearing is where everyone starts and where three of the four stop. Accept (paradechontai) means welcome, receive it fully, take it in as your own, the way you receive a guest rather than a leaflet. The good soil hears, welcomes the word into the heart, and holds it fast (Luke 8:15). It is the difference between a man who takes a letter at the door and a man who opens it, reads it and does what it says. And accepting is not merely agreeing that the sermon was true. It means letting the word in with authority: allowing it to contradict you and change what you do on Monday.

And bear fruit. And the order matters, though we keep turning it round. Fruit is not the price of acceptance but its result. No plant produces grain by straining; it receives light and water, and the fruit comes out of that. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4). That answers a way of living that exhausts many sincere Christians: trying to squeeze fruit out of themselves by effort. You are not asked to manufacture fruit. You are asked to receive, and keep receiving, and let it go down.

All three are good soil. Here is the kindness in the last clause: the yields are different, and all three are good soil. The thirtyfold Christian is not second-class. The Lord of the harvest makes his fields good and then rejoices over what they bear, thirty or sixty or a hundred, and calls it all his.

Where does good soil come from? Every heart is hard by nature. God makes the soil good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), he opens hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14), and he gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Our part is to receive the word humbly (James 1:21). The Sower who scattered his seed across your life knew exactly what was under the surface when he threw it, and threw it anyway, and he is the one who breaks up the ground.

What if I see very little fruit in my life? First, be careful of measuring yourself by others. Some believers are given health, gifts, years and opportunity, and their lives are visibly fruitful. Some are ill, or poor, or obscure, or worn down by circumstances they did not choose, and what they produce is thirty: a marriage held together, a few people prayed for by name for decades, a faith kept in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in this verse, and both are gathered into the same barn. Second, fruit is often invisible to the tree. Ask a mature friend what they see. Third, if there really is nothing, go back to the root: are you abiding in Christ, in his word, in prayer, among his people? Fruit comes from there, not from trying harder.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? After hard words about seeing and not perceiving (vv. 11–12), Jesus picks up a household object and asks a question a child could answer. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick, giving about as much light as a candle. The basket (modios) was a grain measure, a bushel bowl. The bed was a low couch. And the question is faintly comic on purpose: no one lights a lamp to hide it. You would put it out and save the oil. Literally the Greek says, does the lamp come? and some see Jesus himself as the lamp who has come into the world.

Hidden to be made manifest. If the parables conceal, has God gone into the business of hiding things? No. The kingdom is now hidden (vv. 10–12), but the whole purpose of the hiding is the eventual showing. One day every hidden thing will be revealed, and the brightest thing revealed will be the glory of the Lamb.

Nothing secret. The secret will be proclaimed after the resurrection (9:9). Jesus silences demons, hushes the healed, tells the disciples to say nothing, and then dies in public in the busiest week of the year, and a Roman officer says aloud what nobody was allowed to say (15:39). The secret was being protected until it could be understood, the way you shield a flame with your hand while carrying it. He was shielded for a while, his glory veiled in flesh and his name hushed, and then he was lifted up in the sight of all, and the light broke out over the nations.

The dark parts of your own story. This is a comfort for the parts of your life that make no sense yet, and for situations you have prayed about for years. The verse does not promise an explanation next Tuesday. It promises that nothing in the hands of God is hidden for the sake of being hidden. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Will my secret sins be exposed on the day of judgment if I am a Christian? The New Testament does say that nothing is covered up that will not be revealed (Luke 12:2), and that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But for those in Christ, the judgment is not condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your sins were brought into the light at the cross, judged there, and removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). Whatever is shown on that day will be shown as forgiven, and will magnify his grace. So you do not need to live in dread of exposure. You can bring your secrets into the light now, to God and, where wise, to a trusted friend, and walk in the light (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to what you hear. Literally see what you hear (Luke 8:18: take care then how you hear). Listening is something you do, well or badly.

Listen to him. Whose voice? On the mountain the Father answered: this is my beloved Son; listen to him (9:7). Long ago God spoke by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and therefore, says Hebrews, we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it (Hebrews 2:1). The attention we bring should match the worth of the one speaking. To give the eternal Son only a little of it is not caution. It is a small view of a great Saviour.

The measure you use. A merchant’s picture: bring a thimble and you carry home a thimbleful, however generous he is. So with listening: the attention and response you give to God’s word determines how much understanding you receive.

Still more will be added. Then Jesus goes beyond the picture. A shopkeeper gives exactly what your measure holds; God gives more than you brought room for.

To the one who has. It sounds like the rich getting richer, but Jesus is speaking of understanding God’s word, and that is simply how understanding works. Everything you take in and act on enlarges the vessel you bring back next time, as a man who learns a little of a language starts hearing words where he used to hear only noise.

Even what he has. Spiritual understanding not used is lost. A truth heard and never obeyed hardens, and next time it will be easier to ignore. That is how the hard path of the parable is made.

Does this mean God gives more to clever people? No. The measure is not intelligence but obedience. A child who believes and obeys a simple truth receives more from God than a scholar who studies Scripture and does nothing with it. Some of the most spiritually wise people in any church have little formal education; they have simply spent decades doing what God says. The container that grows is a heart that hears and obeys, and anyone can bring that.

In everyday life. Recall the last thing God said to you that you knew you were meant to do: the conversation, the person to forgive, the money to give. Did you do it? If yes, expect more. If no, he has not stopped speaking to you; but the next thing he says will be fainter. He is asking for obedience, because obedience is the only container that ever gets bigger. None of us brings a full measure (James 3:2); Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and so your small, real obedience, worked in you by his Spirit (Philippians 2:13), is accepted for his sake. And if your feelings have gone flat through grief, illness or depression, do not read this as your case: numbness is not disobedience, and he does not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Seed growing secretly (vv. 26–29). A parable only Mark records: a man sows, sleeps and rises, and the seed grows, he knows not how.

The mustard seed (vv. 30–32). The smallest seed becomes the largest garden plant, with room for birds to nest.

As they were able to hear it (vv. 33–34). Parables for the crowd; everything explained to the disciples in private.

The storm (vv. 35–41). Crossing the lake was Jesus' own idea, and the storm meets them while they obey. He sleeps; they bail; and they end by asking, who then is this?
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm shows who is in the boat. In the Old Testament it is God who rules the sea: you rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Psalm 89:9); thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:11).

Jesus was asleep because he was exhausted, and he silenced the sea with a word. Fully man in his tiredness, fully God in his voice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen bailing with their hands, sure they were about to die, while their Lord slept beside them.

Now: believers in a storm still ask do you not care? The Psalms are full of such prayers: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Psalm 44:23).

He stilled the storm first and asked about their faith afterwards: he does not wait for us to pray well before he acts. And after the calm they were filled with great fear, more afraid of the man in the boat than of the wind. That is the beginning of knowing who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seed on the ground. Only Mark records this parable, and it is the most restful thing in the chapter. The farmer does his part: he sows. And then Jesus tells us what he does next, and it is the surprise of the story: nothing.

In the flow. Three seed parables, three worries. The sower answers why so few bear fruit; this one answers the worry that nothing is happening; the mustard seed (vv. 30–32) answers the worry that it is all too small to matter. The kingdom is not failing. It is growing in the ground.

He sleeps and rises night and day. He goes to bed; he gets up. There is no anxious digging up of seed to see how it is doing. Underneath much of our anxiety about other people’s growth is a wish to be in control, and the parable gently takes it out of our hands: the growth belongs to God, and so does the timing. He gives to his beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2), because the growth was always his.

He knows not how. His ignorance does not slow the crop by a single day. This was spoken to twelve men just appointed to a mission and unqualified for it: you scatter, and then you sleep. The power was never in the sower.

The earth produces by itself. By itself (automatē, from which we get automatic) means without visible cause: not without God, but without the farmer. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

First the blade. The tenderest line for anyone worried about slowness. A blade is not a failed ear; it is a blade, which is exactly what a healthy plant looks like in April. God is not disappointed with a young Christian for not being an old one, and he is not finished with an old one either.

The harvest has come. The words are lifted from Joel: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13), a text about the final judgment of the nations. The harvest pictures the end of the age (Matthew 13:39), and it comes when the grain is ripe. The long, quiet middle of history, where the kingdom looks small and slow, is not drift. It is growing season. The life of the kingdom is his life, hidden in the soil of the world, rising in its seasons, unstoppable.

One like a son of man, with a sickle. Who puts in the sickle? John saw one like a son of man, with a sharp sickle in his hand (Revelation 14:14–15). Jesus says the same in Mark: the Son of Man will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds (13:26–27). The sower who sleeps in this parable cannot make the seed grow, but the reaper at the end is the Lord himself. The one who sowed the word in Galilee is the one who will gather the grain, and he knows the day.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be passive. The farmer sows and reaps. But we cannot force growth, in our children, our church or ourselves.

How should I pray for a child or friend who shows no sign of growth? Keep sowing and keep praying, and then actually go to bed. Pray specifically that God would open their heart, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14), and give them a new heart. Keep living out the faith in front of them with warmth rather than pressure, and keep the door open. Do not dig up the seed every week to see whether it has sprouted; nagging rarely helps. Many a believer looks back on years when parents or friends saw nothing, while the seed was quietly at work underground. And leave the timing to God. The harvest comes when the grain is ripe, not when we are ready.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this parable of the seed growing by itself.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe
the farmer waits for the precious fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? Jesus invites his hearers to think with him, asking aloud, as a teacher does when he wants the class leaning in. And the answer he reaches for is deliberately, almost comically, small.

A grain of mustard seed. The black mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the rabbis’ standard picture of tininess. You could lose it in the creases of your palm.

Was Jesus wrong that mustard is the smallest of all seeds? No. He was not giving a lecture in botany or making a claim about the seed catalogue of the world. He was using the everyday proverb of the people in front of him, about the seeds a Galilean farmer actually handled, exactly as we say the sun rises without being wrong about astronomy. Of all the seeds his hearers sowed in their fields and gardens, the mustard seed was the smallest, and everyone knew it. Speaking in the ordinary language of his hearers is not error; it is how all clear speech works.

Larger than all the garden plants. The plant could grow three metres high in one season. Nothing in the seed announces it.

Nests in its shade. In the Old Testament a great tree with birds in its branches pictures a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 31:6; Daniel 4:12). In Ezekiel 17:22–23 God takes a tender sprig from the top of the cedar, the royal line of David, and plants it on the mountain height of Israel, and under it every kind of bird will nest. The birds are the nations.

A shoot from the stump of Jesse. That sprig is the King. The prophets call the Messiah the Branch, a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and Isaiah adds that the nations shall inquire of him, and his resting place shall be glorious (Isaiah 11:10). So the kingdom is small at first because the King came small: a tender shoot from a felled royal house, laid in a manger. The tree that shelters the nations grows from him, and to rest in its shade is to rest in Christ. And the King who was planted in the ground like a seed on a Friday rose on the Sunday as the firstfruits of a harvest without end.

The meaning. Hear who is listening: a dozen men on a beach in a provincial district of an occupied country, following a village carpenter whose family thinks he is unwell and whose national leaders have ruled him demonic. Rome has legions and roads and an emperor. This kingdom has a boat. And Jesus says: the kingdom of God is that speck in your hand. Yet it would grow into a worldwide kingdom, as it has. What turns the speck into the sheltering tree is not strategy or numbers. It is the life God has put in the seed. Small is not the same as weak, and slow is not the same as failing, and it is only ever in the hand that a mustard seed looks like nothing.

What it does not mean. Not that the world will become Christian before Christ returns, as postmillennialists (who expect the gospel to bring a long golden age before his coming) teach, a hope many godly Reformed believers have held. The parables of growth stand alongside the parables of mixed fields and continuing evil (Matthew 13:24–30). This commentary’s view: amillennial (Christ reigns now, through the whole age between his two comings, with no separate earthly millennium still to come): the kingdom grows powerfully through the whole gospel age, and comes to its fullness when Christ returns.

In everyday life. If the part of the kingdom you can see is discouragingly small, the ageing congregation, the one believing member of a family, remember that you are not looking at the tree. You are looking at the seed, and you were never given the ability to tell the difference by looking.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many such parables. Mark steps back for two verses to tell us how the Lord taught.

As they were able to hear it. One of the kindest clauses in the Gospel: he measured what he said to what they could bear: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (John 16:12). The Son of God, with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him, stooped to the measure of fishermen. Parables were both a mercy, making truth memorable and accessible, and a test, concealing it from the unwilling.

He explained everything. The difference between the two audiences is not intelligence but willingness to come to Jesus: the crowd got the story, the ones who stayed got the meaning (v. 10). The door into the private room was never locked.

Two lessons. To yourself, if you are impatient with your own understanding: he is not withholding out of displeasure. He gives at the rate a person can receive. And to how you handle other people: if the Lord matched what he said to his hearers, so should we. Some zealous Christians unload every hard truth at once onto a new believer or a person just bereaved, and call it faithfulness. Say what they can take in now. There will be other days for the rest.

How do I ask Jesus to explain Scripture today? He explains his word by his Spirit through his word, so the ordinary means are the way. Pray before you read, asking him to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Read slowly, and read the surrounding chapters, since Scripture interprets Scripture. Bring your questions to faithful preaching and to mature Christians, and use a good study Bible or commentary. Discuss passages in a small group. And obey what you do understand, because understanding grows through obedience (John 7:17). He does not give new revelation, but he does give light on what he has already said.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening had come. After a long day of teaching, and it is getting dark.

To the other side. To the eastern shore, largely Gentile territory (5:1). And here is the detail that changes how the storm is read: going out onto that lake was his idea. The storm that nearly killed them was met in the middle of doing exactly what he told them. And Jesus said they would go to the other side. His word was a promise that they would arrive.

Does a storm in my life mean I have disobeyed God? Not necessarily. A great deal of Christian thinking assumes it: when trouble comes we search backwards for the wrong turn, what did I miss, where did I disobey, is this because I stopped praying. Sometimes there is a wrong turn, and it should be found and repented of. But this boat is in this storm because Jesus put it there, and they sailed into it by obeying him. Job did not suffer because he had drifted; the book opens by insisting he was blameless. Paul was in the will of God on the ship that broke up under him (Acts 27). The storm you are in may not be evidence of anything having gone wrong at all. It may simply be part of the cost of going where he sends you.

In the flow. The teaching ends and the deeds begin: four mighty works, over the sea, a legion of demons, a long illness and death itself (4:35–5:43), each answering who then is this? a little more fully.

Just as he was. He was already in the boat (v. 1): no going ashore, no meal. They pushed off with him exhausted where he sat, which explains verse 38.

Other boats. Only Mark mentions this, and it is easy to skip. It means the storm did not fall on one boat. There were other people out on that water in the dark, in other boats, with no one aboard who could still a wave. Mark says nothing about what happened to them, and the silence is its own comfort: when the calm came, it came over the whole lake. Some who benefited from the miracle may never have known who had done it. Some of what God does in answer to the church’s terrified praying spills a long way past the church, and is never traced back.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great windstorm. A furious squall that hits without warning. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air rushing down onto the warm lake can take it from glass to breaking waves in minutes.

The boat was already filling. Not spray, but waves coming in over the side. At least four of these men are professional fishermen who have worked this lake since boyhood. When men like that conclude they are about to drown, they are almost certainly right.

Asleep on the cushion. Only Mark mentions the cushion, the kind of detail an eyewitness remembers. And the sleep is a window onto who Jesus is. He is worn out. The Son of God got properly tired. He was hungry (11:12), he was thirsty (John 19:28), he wept at a graveside (John 11:35). And his sleep showed complete trust in his Father: in peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). He can sleep in a storm on a lake he made.

And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing”? Only Mark records this question, and he did not tidy it up. It is not a request; it is an accusation. They do not ask him to do anything. They do not say save us; they say, do you not care? That is what fear does to us. It goes past the danger and attacks the character of God. The real terror in that boat was not only the water but the sudden conviction that the one in charge had gone quiet and might not be bothered. The disciples thought he did not care. In storms we often feel the same: God, do you not care? But he did care. He was with them in the boat.

Is it wrong to complain to God like that? Scripture is full of honest complaint, and it preserves this sentence rather than hiding it. Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Psalm 44:23). How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Psalm 13:1). God would rather have that cried out to him from four feet away than have you drown politely at the other end of the boat. What is wrong is not bringing your fear to him but accusing him and walking away. These men got one thing right in the middle of getting everything else wrong: when they were sure they were dying, they went to him. So pour out your heart, and then, as the psalmists did, remind yourself of his steadfast love.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common. The cushion was probably the helmsman’s seat or a sandbag in the stern.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm
awake! why are you sleeping, O Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rebuked the wind. He does not take the helm or pray for deliverance. He wakes and speaks to the weather. Rebuked is the word used for silencing demons (1:25), as for a hostile thing that has no business being there.

Be muzzled. The second word literally means be muzzled, the word used to the demon in 1:25. To Israel the sea was chaos, the old enemy, and only God can rule it. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Psalm 89:9; 65:7). Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). And this is a carpenter, standing in a fishing boat, wet through, speaking to a storm in the dark.

A great calm. Normally the swell outlives the storm. Here, instant calm. A great storm (v. 37), a great calm, and one sentence between them. And there is the difference between him and every other help you have ever had. Everything else that assists you works with the situation, manages it, gets you through it. He speaks to it.

If Jesus rules the wind and the sea, why does he allow storms and disasters? Scripture does not give us a full explanation, but it gives us enough to trust him. Natural disasters belong to a creation subjected to futility because of human sin, groaning as it waits to be set free (Romans 8:20–22). God rules them still: not one storm escapes his hand, and he works through all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). Sometimes disasters are warnings to a careless world to repent (Luke 13:4–5). And this story shows us his heart and his future: the one who stilled one storm on one lake will one day remove every storm from a renewed creation, where there is no more sea of chaos (Revelation 21:1). Until then, we bring our fears to the one who rules the waves.

For worship. The wind and the sea obeyed him in the dark. There is one other moment in Mark when the world goes dark and then quiet. On a hill outside Jerusalem the sky turns black at noon for three hours, and a man cries out that God has forsaken him, and then he dies (15:33–37), and it goes quiet. That day nobody rebuked the storm. He went into it and let it break over him with nothing held back, and it was not muzzled, and it did not stop until it had finished with him. The voice that could have silenced anything said nothing at all, so that when the storms come for us they come as hard weather and never as God’s wrath against us.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? It sounds hard. Two things take the sting out of it without taking away the point. First, the order of events. He stilled the storm and then asked the question. He did not require a better standard of praying before he would act. He dealt with the water first, because they needed it dealt with, and only afterwards turned to what was wrong inside the boat. Remember that the next time you are ashamed of how badly you prayed in a crisis. He is not waiting for you to pray well. Second, hear what the question asks. The word (deiloi) means timid, cowardly, and the point is not that they felt fear but that they feared as if he were not there. They had every reason to be afraid of the lake and no reason at all to be afraid with him in the boat. The rebuke is not, you felt something. It is, you forgot who was aboard.

Still no faith. Still is the sad word: after a leper made clean, a paralytic walking, demons obeying him. Faith here means trusting Jesus to keep his word (they would go to the other side, v. 35). We know that gap ourselves: the distance between what you believe on a Sunday and what you can hold on to at three in the morning. Faith is tested by whether what you believe bears weight when the water comes over the side.

Is fear always a lack of faith? No. Fear is a natural response to real danger, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). Scripture does not command us never to feel fear; it tells us what to do with it: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). The disciples’ problem was not that they felt afraid in a sinking boat, but that their fear made them doubt his care and forget his power. So when fear comes, do not add guilt to it. Take it to Christ, tell him plainly, and remind yourself who is in the boat.

A great fear. Literally they feared a great fear. The danger is over, the lake is like glass, and the disciples are more frightened than during the storm. They had been afraid of drowning. Now they are afraid of the man standing in the boat with them, dripping wet, an arm’s length away. This is not a failure of faith; it is the beginning of understanding. This is the fear of God, as the sailors in Jonah’s storm feared the LORD exceedingly when the sea grew calm (Jonah 1:16). When Isaiah saw the Lord he said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, and it has to begin somewhere. It is not the cringing dread of a slave before a cruel master. It is the awe of a creature who has seen how great and holy God is, and it draws him near in worship rather than driving him away: with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4).

And said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him”? The question of the whole Gospel. They ask it of each other, in the dark, on flat water, and they do not answer it. Mark leaves it hanging at the end of the chapter, because the whole Gospel is the answer, and it will not be complete until the cross and the empty tomb. But their own Scriptures had already answered it, and they knew those Scriptures by heart. Psalm 107:29 says of the LORD that he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Jesus has done what only God does. There is one name in the whole Old Testament that fits, and no second candidate. The answer to their question is in Mark’s first verse: the Son of God.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always removes the storms of life when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms us in it. The story is first about who he is.

For worship. The man asleep on the cushion is the one who said to the ocean, thus far shall you come, and no farther, before there was a man alive to see it. That is who was in the boat. The Lord of the wind and the sea, tired out in the stern, in a body he took so that he could sleep, and thirst, and bleed, and die, for the men bailing water round his feet. Who then is this? He is the Son of God, and he is ours.

parallels.desc: who stills the roaring of the seas

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 quote Isaiah 6:9–10: the parables confirm the refusal of those who will not hear, while the disciples, who understood no more than the crowd, were given the meaning because they stayed and asked.

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament only God rules the sea: he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Psalm 107:29). So the disciples' closing question has one answer. And Mark shows that he is both man and God within a few feet: a man asleep from exhaustion on the cushion, and a voice that silences the storm.
4.examples:
The four soils are four possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday.

The path was made hard by traffic, not by a decision: hearing about God so often that the sound becomes familiar.

The rocky ground grows fastest because the soil is shallow, and the same sun that ripens the good grain withers it. Roots are grown in private, long before the heat comes.

The thorns are not scandalous sins but cares, riches and the desires for other things. This soil is diagnosed less by what you have done than by what has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the conversation about Christ.

The good soil yields thirty, sixty or a hundred, and all three are good soil. A few names prayed for over decades belong in the same barn as the most visible ministry.

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is three impossible cases in a row: a man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, and a child who has already died.

It is also a chapter about uncleanness. Under the law a grave, a discharge of blood and a pig all made a person unclean, and all three are here. Jesus lands among tombs and pigs to free a man who lives in a graveyard; an untouchable woman takes hold of his clothes; and he takes a dead girl by the hand. Each contact should have made him unclean. Instead his cleanness and life pass to them.

The two halves are tied together by twelve years, the length of the woman's suffering and the whole life of Jairus's daughter, and by one word: Jesus calls the woman Daughter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The landing (vv. 1–5). The man who meets Jesus lives among the tombs, breaks every chain and cuts himself with stones: beyond human help.

The encounter (vv. 6–10). He falls before Jesus, and the spirit in him tries to put Jesus under oath. Asked its name, it answers: Legion.

The pigs (vv. 11–13). The demons are permitted to enter a herd, and the herd rushes into the sea.

The town (vv. 14–17). The people find the man clothed and in his right mind, are afraid, and ask Jesus to leave.

The commission (vv. 18–20). The freed man asks to go with Jesus and is sent home to tell what the Lord has done for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Under the law, contact with a grave (Numbers 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Leviticus 15:25–27) or a pig (Leviticus 11:7) made a person unclean, and uncleanness spread while holiness did not. This man lives among tombs, near pigs, in Gentile country, and Jesus walks straight in.

Jesus is not setting the law aside here. He is fulfilling its purpose. The law taught Israel that sin and death spread, so that they would recognise the one whose holiness spreads instead.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a town given back a neighbour, clothed and in his right mind, alongside a hillside of lost livestock, and it asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same choice is made by ordinary people who have counted what Christ might disturb (a business practice, a relationship, a habit, a plan) and would rather keep things as they are. Nobody denied the miracle; they decided it cost too much.

Jesus did not argue; he got into the boat. But he left a witness behind, and when he returned to that side of the lake, the crowds came to him (7:31–37).

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 5 is a chapter of three rescues, each harder than the last: a legion of demons sent out of a man among the tombs, a woman healed of twelve years’ bleeding, and Jairus’ dead daughter taken by the hand. In every scene the same thing happens: what is unclean and dead does not defile him. His holiness and his life flow out to it.

The connection. Mark 4:35–5:43 shows Jesus’ authority over four enemies: the storm (nature), a legion of demons (the spiritual powers), chronic disease, and death itself. Each is a power no human can defeat, and each is made to obey him.

The other side. They land where Jesus said they would (4:35). The whole stormy night on the lake was the journey to this one man. Jesus made the crossing, at the cost of a night that nearly drowned a boatload of men, for a man whose own town had given up on him.

To the country of the Gerasenes. Gentile territory on the eastern shore of the lake: the region of the Decapolis, ten Greek cities, pagan country with pig farms on the hillsides. It is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus sets foot outside Jewish land, and he goes there to fight.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? A reader with a map will notice a real puzzle, and it is better dealt with than hurried past. Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes (Matthew 8:28; the KJV reads Gadarenes here too) and Gergesenes. Gerasa was a large city about thirty miles southeast, far too far for a herd to run down a steep bank into the sea; Gadara was closer, about six miles off, but still not on the shore; Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi) was on the shore itself, where steep slopes come down to the water. The likeliest answer is that the names refer to regions. Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that shore, and each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might say a village lies in greater London. The place was probably near Kursi, where a steep bank still comes down to the water. This is a likely explanation rather than a certain one, but it needs nothing more than the ordinary looseness of naming a place by a well-known city, and the shoreline fits the story.

One man or two? Matthew says two (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke and was sent home to tell his story, and neither says there was only one. (See Luke 8:27 for the fuller answer.)

Out of the tombs. The boat grounds and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks. Tombs were often caves cut in the hillside. A man is living in a graveyard, and the town knows it, and nobody has come to bring him home.

Unclean three times over. Under the law a grave defiled anyone who touched it for seven days (Numbers 19:16). This man is unclean three times over: demon-possessed, living among the dead, in a Gentile land near pigs. He is shut out of the town, shut out of worship, and counted with the dead rather than the living.

The Holy One walks into the graveyard. Under the law uncleanness was catching: touch the dead and you became unclean. With Jesus it works the other way round: his cleanness spreads to the unclean. The Holy One of God (1:24) walks into a cemetery and the cemetery is cleansed. Holy means set apart for God and utterly pure, a purity so bright that in Israel a man who handled the ark carelessly died on the spot (2 Samuel 6:6–7). Holiness like that ought to consume the unclean. In Jesus it comes to them to make them clean. And this beach is a preview of everything he came to do. He would be counted among the transgressors, led out of the city to die where the unclean were sent (Hebrews 13:12), and laid in a tomb cut in the rock like the caves on this hillside. He went into our graveyard, not to be held by it, but to empty it from the inside. The man coming down out of the tombs is running towards the one who will walk out of a tomb himself.

Does demon possession happen today? The New Testament treats it as real, and nothing in it says the devil’s work ended with the apostles. Missionaries in places of open idolatry have often met things they could only describe this way. But Scripture also distinguishes the possessed from the sick (1:32–34), and most suffering of mind and body has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Two errors are to be avoided: seeing demons behind every illness, and denying that the devil works at all. And what drives out evil is not a technique, a ritual or a gifted specialist, but Christ himself, sought in prayer and trusted through his word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7).

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer is indwelt and sealed by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19; Ephesians 1:13); he can be tempted and attacked, but the one in him is greater than the one in the world (1 John 4:4). (See Acts 5:16 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. Think of the person you know who is furthest from God. Pray for him by name this week, and be ready to cross some small storm of your own (an awkward conversation, an inconvenient visit) on his account.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gergesenes, some Gadarenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived among the tombs. Three verses of description come before a word is spoken, and every clause establishes that this man was past help.

No one could bind him anymore. Anymore tells the history: the town had tried force, repeatedly, and had stopped.

Chains wrenched apart. Superhuman strength (compare Acts 19:16): this was no ordinary illness.

No one had the strength to subdue him. The word means to tame, as of an animal. They had failed at that too, and written him off.

The stronger man has come. Jesus has already said that no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (3:27). The strong man is Satan. Here is his house, a graveyard, and here are his goods, a human being. The town tried to bind the man and could not. Jesus binds the power that owns him, and he does it with a word. And this is a foretaste of the greater binding: at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), so that the devil’s captives, chained far more deeply than this man, could walk free.

Always crying out. The screaming never stopped; the town may well have gone to sleep hearing him.

Cutting himself with stones. This should be handled gently, because a great many people know exactly what this verse is describing. First, it tells us about the power in him. The demons have taken him out of his home, his town, his clothing and his mind, and now they are using his own hands against his own body. That is the settled programme of the enemy wherever he is given room: not pleasure, not power, but ruin, and ruin worked where possible through the victim’s own hands. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy (John 10:10).

What it does not mean. Not that people who harm themselves or suffer mental illness are possessed. The Gospels distinguish illness from possession (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness are enough to explain most of what human beings do to themselves. Those who self-harm need compassion, safety and care, medical and spiritual. Going to a doctor is an ordinary mercy from God and not a failure of faith. But this man’s torment was demonic, and only Jesus could free him.

How can I tell whether a struggle is spiritual or medical? Usually you do not need to choose, because every human trouble is both: we are bodies and souls together, living in a fallen world with a real enemy. So do both things. See a doctor, and if a counsellor or medication is advised, accept it with thanks, as you would for a broken leg. And bring the whole thing to Christ in prayer, Scripture and the fellowship of his people, asking your pastor and elders to pray with you (James 5:14). Be wary of anyone who offers a quick spiritual diagnosis without knowing you well, and of anyone who tells you that faith means refusing treatment. The man in the tombs was beyond every remedy; most of us are not, and God normally heals through means.

The direction the story runs. If you are a person who hurts yourself, or you love one, take from this passage the direction the story runs. The man in the tombs, whom nobody could hold and nobody could help, is soon sitting quietly, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the one who put him back together did not flinch at meeting him at his worst, in a graveyard, screaming, bleeding and out of control. He came to that beach on purpose.

In everyday life. If you or someone you love is self-harming, please tell someone and seek help today: a doctor, a trusted friend, your pastor, or an emergency line if you are in danger. That is not weakness; it is taking hold of the help God has put within reach.

parallels.desc: who sit in tombs, who eat pig’s flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He ran and fell down. He ran from a distance and went down on his face. Who did the running? A man who has wanted help for years, and a power that cannot do anything else in the presence of the Son of God but bow. Both arrive at the same feet. The powers that hold men in chains cannot hold their ground before Jesus; they fall on their faces, and they know his name better than his friends do.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? The question means, leave me alone; what is there between us (1:24)? And what the demon says about Jesus is exactly true: not for the first time in Mark, the clearest statement of who he is comes from a demon (1:24; 3:11). “Most High God” was a title often used by or to Gentiles for the supreme God: it is Melchizedek’s name for him (Genesis 14:18–22), and Nebuchadnezzar’s (Daniel 3:26), and the slave girl’s spirit uses it in Philippi (Acts 16:17). On the pagan side of the lake even the demons use the local title for God, and this one knows exactly who Jesus is.

I adjure you by God. To adjure is to put under oath. It was the standard technique of an exorcist, a person who drove out spirits: he named a higher power and bound the spirit by it. So the demon is trying to drive away the one who has come to drive it out, calling on God to bind the Son of God. It does not work for even a moment.

Before the time. Matthew records the fear underneath: Have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29). Demons know judgment awaits them, and all they can argue about is when. The kingdom of darkness in this Gospel is not confidently opposing Christ. It is already defeated, and is pleading for a delay.

If demons believe the truth about Jesus, what makes my faith different? Saving faith is not only knowing who Jesus is; it is trusting him and coming to him to be saved. James says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). They know he is the Son of God and they hate it; they want him to go away. A Christian knows the same truth and wants him to come nearer. So the test is not whether you can say the right words about Christ, but whether you rest on him, love him, and want to be with him. If you find in yourself even a weak longing for him, and grief that it is not stronger, that is not the faith of demons. It is the work of his Spirit.

In everyday life. If the powers of evil frighten you, look at who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark shout, beg, bargain and go; he never has to raise his voice. So when fear comes at night, or temptation presses, do not argue with it on its own terms. Go straight to Christ, speak his name in prayer, and stand on what he has already done.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come out of the man. Jesus had already commanded it; the screaming and bargaining of verse 7 are what a thing does on its way out. The command has no ritual, no formula, no invoking of a higher name. Jesus does not appeal to any authority above himself. The authority is his own.

And Jesus asked him, What is your name? This is the only occasion in the Gospels when Jesus asks a demon its name, and it is worth asking why, because he plainly does not need the information. He is not gaining power over it by learning its name, as the magicians of the day believed. Two things are being done. The first is for the man. Everything that has happened to him has happened in the dark, unnamed and unexplained, for years. The thing that owned him is about to be forced to identify itself out loud, in front of witnesses, before it is thrown out. What has been destroying you is made to say what it is. The second is for the record. Mark wants his readers to grasp the extent of the possession, the scale of what they are watching, and only the enemy can supply that figure.

Legion. The word would have chilled anyone in that district. A Roman legion had up to about six thousand soldiers, no figure of speech there: legions had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies and stays. It cannot be resisted, cannot be negotiated with, and does not leave. The name suggests a vast number of demons, organised like an army, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also tells you why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain one man, when an army was holding him.

Two occupations. The man was occupied, as the land was occupied by Roman legions (the tenth legion later carried a boar among its emblems, which gives the pigs a sharp edge). One occupation everybody could see; the other nobody could do anything about. Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence. He will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a cross outside Jerusalem and finds that it cannot hold him either.

Not out of the country. Mark’s word is begged: the strongest power in the district has been reduced to asking. Luke tells us what they were most afraid of: they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the prison of evil spirits.

Should Christians name demons, or bind spirits over places? No. This scene is not a method to copy. Jesus asked the name for the man’s sake and for ours, not because naming gives power; the demon’s own attempt to use a formula failed. Nowhere does the New Testament tell believers to interrogate spirits, map territorial demons, or command the devil by special words. The apostles, with their unique authority, cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Acts 16:18), but the instructions given to every Christian are plainer: be sober and watchful, resist the devil, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), take up the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). Our weapon is not a technique but the Lord himself.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great herd of pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and no Jewish district would have two thousand of them on a hillside. A herd that size shows this was Gentile country, and a valuable business: the pigs are somebody’s livelihood.

Send us to the pigs. The demons can only plead. The Legion cannot go anywhere without Jesus’ permission. Nothing in this world lies outside his control.

Down the steep bank. Two thousand animals over a cliff. A reader who cares about somebody’s ruined business is entitled to ask what this was for. Three things answer it.

The demons did this. First, the demons drove the herd, not Jesus. He permitted their request, and let their intention show in the open: everything they enter goes straight over the edge. The pigs are the man’s story acted out in a few seconds on a hillside. And it shows that the man was truly freed: everyone could see that the demons had gone.

The arithmetic of heaven. Second, one human being matters more to Jesus than two thousand pigs. Jesus had already said it in a synagogue argument: Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matthew 12:12). And a man than a pig. God’s care for animals is real: he feeds the ravens, he counts the sparrows, and Proverbs says the righteous man has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). But when the two are set against each other, there is no contest, and there never was. This Lord counts one person worth more than any property.

The real price of his freedom. Yet the pigs were not what this man’s freedom cost. The true price was paid on another hill. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). You were ransomed, says Peter, not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). The town counted the cost at two thousand pigs. Heaven counts it as the life of the Son of God.

Why would Jesus grant a request from demons at all? Because their going into the pigs served his purposes, not theirs. It gave visible proof that the man was free, it exposed what the demons are, and it put the town’s heart to the test. Throughout Scripture God permits evil powers to act only within limits he sets, and he turns what they intend for harm into good (Job 1:12; 2:6; Genesis 50:20). The demons got what they asked for and lost everything: they wanted a home and ended in the sea. That is the pattern of every concession evil wins from God. It is never a defeat for him.
