It is always a rope by which it hangs itself.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a herd of two thousand shows this was Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The herdsmen fled. Soon the whole district knows.

The one who had had the legion. Even now that is his name in this town. Then Mark gives three small details.

Sitting there. This man has probably not sat still in years. Luke adds where: sitting at the feet of Jesus (Luke 8:35), which is the posture of a disciple at his teacher’s feet.

Clothed. He had been naked (Luke 8:27); now his dignity is restored along with his mind.

The one who would be stripped. Mark’s readers knew how this Gospel ends. The man who gave this naked man back his dignity would himself be stripped, and soldiers would divide his garments among them, casting lots (15:24). He would hang uncovered under the shame that the tombs had put on this man and that our sin has put on us all. That is how clothing is given in the kingdom of God. The Lord God covered Adam and Eve with skins after the fall (Genesis 3:21), and Christ gives his people the robe of his own righteousness (Isaiah 61:10) because he went out naked to Golgotha in their place. So when God looks at a believer, he does not see the stained record of what we have done but the perfect obedience of Christ, counted as ours (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). We are accepted not because we have cleaned ourselves up but because we are dressed in him.

And in his right mind. A single word: sound-minded. He can hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

A case everybody else had closed. No process, no gradual rehabilitation. He came down out of the rocks screaming and he is sitting on the ground with a borrowed coat on, listening. The town could only chain him. Christ loved him, and his love was stronger than all their iron. That is what Christ does with a case that everybody else has closed, and it is a picture of what he does for everyone he saves: peace, dignity and a renewed mind. And it is worth saying to anyone praying for a person who has been beyond reach for a long time, the addict, the one who is not in his right mind, the family member nobody knows how to help, that this town had reached the settled conclusion that nothing could be done. They were right that they could do nothing, and wrong that nothing could be done. The one who could do it arrived by boat.

And they were afraid. They were not glad for him. They were afraid of the power that had done it, as the disciples were in the boat after the storm (4:41): the fear of a power you can neither explain nor control. In itself it is not a wicked reaction; awe in the presence of God is right. But what this town does with it in the next two verses is another matter entirely.

Is the change always this sudden? The freeing was instant, and so is the new birth: God gives a new heart, and a person passes from death to life (John 5:24; Ephesians 2:4–5). But what follows is usually slow. This man had to learn to live in a town, rebuild trust, and face people who remembered him; the sitting, the clothing and the right mind were the beginning of a life, not the end of it. So when you pray for someone, ask boldly for the decisive work only Christ can do, and then be patient with the long recovery afterwards, in them and in yourself. Christians are being transformed by the renewal of the mind (Romans 12:2), and that is a lifetime’s work.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man and the pigs. The witnesses report two things, what happened to the man and what happened to the pigs, and the town has to weigh one against the other.

They began to beg Jesus to depart. The demons begged not to be sent away; the townspeople beg Jesus to go away. Nobody disputes what has happened. They have their neighbour sitting in front of them in his right mind, and their unanimous request is that the man who did it should get back in his boat.

Why did they want him gone? Mark does not explain, and he does not need to. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the one who sets people free. His power threatened their way of life. They had just watched a hillside of assets go into the water, and they had understood something about Jesus that many people who admire him never grasp: he is not safe, and no one can set a limit on what he may cost. A man who can do that to a herd of pigs might do it to anything. They preferred a misery whose cost they knew to a mercy whose cost they could not control. So they chose the graveyard they knew, and the terrible thing is how ordinary that choice is.

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him. He makes no argument and no second attempt. Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone (Hosea 4:17) is a real sentence in the Bible. The most frightening answer God can give is to leave people alone, as they asked.

The first of many who sent him away. What happens on this shore will happen again in Jerusalem. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11): Nazareth next (6:1–6), and at the last Jerusalem, which will lead him out of the gate to be crucified. Yet that rejection is the very road of salvation. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (12:10). He let himself be sent away so that those who sent him away could be brought near.

Not the end of the account. He leaves the district the one thing it cannot chain, cut or drive away: a man with a story. And when Jesus returns to that side of the lake, the crowds come out to meet him (7:31–37; 8:1–10). He is the God who is rejected and still sends messengers, who is shut out and still knocks (Revelation 3:20), and whose mercy outlasts the refusals of whole towns.

If I have pushed Jesus away before, has he left me for good? Not if you want him now. The danger in this passage is a settled preference for life without him, not a single moment of fear or refusal. The Gerasenes sent him away, and by chapter 7 that same region is bringing him their sick. Peter denied him three times and was restored on a beach (John 21:15–19). The very fact that you are troubled by having pushed him away is a sign that he has not left you to yourself. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). So do not wait to feel worthy: ask him back today, and he will come.

In everyday life. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus stayed away, because his presence might cost you something: the relationship, the way you make your money, the evening habit? Name it to him today, and ask him to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. And he did not permit him but said to him, "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That he might be with him. The last begging in this scene, and the best. That he might be with him is the phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve: so that they might be with him (3:14). The man is asking to be a disciple in the strictest sense.

And he did not permit him. He permitted the demons. He did not permit the man. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus refuses a request to follow him, and not because he did not want him, but because he had a different calling for him.

When the best prayer is refused. If you have prayed the best prayer you know and been refused, you are in good company. Paul asked three times to have the thorn removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked in a garden that the cup might pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ is not a sign that you asked badly or that he has stopped caring. Sometimes he is sending you to serve somewhere else.

Go home to your friends. Look what he is given instead: not a place in the boat but a whole district to reach, not nearness to Jesus but a task from him. And see where he is sent. Home: to his friends, to the town that chained him, to the neighbours who had heard him screaming on the hills for years, to the family that gave up. That is often the hardest mission field on earth. These are people who knew him before and will remember what he was. But that is exactly why they cannot argue with his story: they saw for themselves what he had been.

Why is this man told to tell, when others are told to be silent? Elsewhere Jesus tells people to keep silent (1:44; 5:43). Here, in Gentile territory, where there was no crowd waiting for a Jewish Messiah to lead a revolt against Rome, and where Jesus would not be staying, he sends the man to tell. The danger that made silence wise in Galilee did not apply here. And the man is to tell what the Lord has done for him, not to proclaim a title. “The Lord” means God.

How he has had mercy on you. His testimony was simple: what God had done, and God’s mercy. He had no training, no years with Jesus. He had one thing: what happened to him. If you have ever thought you were not equipped to say anything about Christ to anybody, this man is the answer, and he had been out of his mind that morning.

In the Decapolis. The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan. Jesus told him to tell what “the Lord” had done; he told what “Jesus” had done. He had been a believer for a matter of hours, and he had already worked out that the man who had spoken to him on the beach and the Lord God of Israel were one and the same. Mark’s point: what Jesus did, God did, and the mercy of God has a human face. On his first day he understood who Jesus is better than the disciples did, and they had been with him for months.

And everyone marveled. Ten cities, and one man telling the only story he had. The town that begged Jesus to leave got him back, because the man they could not chain would not stop talking.

What if my story is not dramatic? Then tell it anyway, because the heart of this man’s message was not the drama but the mercy. Every Christian has the same two things to say: what the Lord has done for me, and how he has had mercy on me. Perhaps you grew up in a Christian home and cannot remember not believing; that is a story of mercy too, of God keeping you from what this man went through. Speak simply about what Christ means to you, what he has forgiven, how he has held you. Point to Jesus rather than to yourself, as this man did. You are not asked to impress anyone, only to be honest about the Lord.

In the flow. The first person in Mark to preach Jesus to Gentiles is a man who that morning was naked among the tombs. It is a foretaste of what Jesus will say later, that the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (13:10), and a sign that the mercy shown on this beach was never meant to stay on the Jewish side of the lake.
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

parallels.desc: Jesus later returns to the Decapolis

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The father (vv. 21–24). Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus' feet because his daughter is dying, and Jesus goes with him.

The interruption (vv. 25–34). A woman who has bled for twelve years touches his garment from behind and is healed, and Jesus stops to find her and call her daughter.

The news (vv. 35–36). Messengers say the girl is dead; Jesus answers, Do not fear, only believe.

The house (vv. 37–43). Mourners laugh when he says she is sleeping. He puts them out, takes her by the hand and tells her to get up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark sets one story inside the other, and they explain each other. Both involve twelve years. Both women are called daughter. Both are healed by touch: she takes hold of his garment, he takes hold of her hand. And the same verb runs through both: made well is the word for saved.

And the delay matters. To Jairus it looks fatal: while Jesus speaks to a woman already healed, his child dies. But in that delay he hears your faith has made you well before he hears your daughter is dead.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman who had tried everything, coming from behind in a crowd, hoping to be healed without being seen.

Now: everyone who comes to Christ after the money, the specialists and the years have run out, and finds that he should have been the first resort.

Jesus drew her out, not to shame her, but because he wanted more for her than a cure: a word about her faith, peace, and a name, Daughter. She came for healing and went home welcomed.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live." And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back across. Back to the Jewish western shore, and the crowd is waiting on the beach. Then a man comes through it who should not be there.

Jairus by name. Mark names him, which he rarely does, perhaps because Jairus was known in the church afterwards. A ruler of the synagogue was the senior layman who appointed the readers and kept the building. He belongs to the religious leadership, and leaders of that kind have already plotted to destroy Jesus (3:6). Every professional instinct and every social pressure in this man’s life points away from the beach he is walking down.

He fell at his feet. In front of everyone: a dignitary on his face in the sand before a preacher his colleagues have written off. A dying child burns away everything a man was worried about the week before. And there is a mercy hidden in it. The very grief that is destroying him has got him to the only place where help was.

My little daughter. The Greek is a diminutive. She is twelve (v. 42): old enough in that world to be nearly a woman, and still his little girl.

Lay your hands on her. He has a method in mind: Jesus must be present and must touch her. Most of us pray the same way, telling God how he should do it. God is not offended by that; he did not correct Jairus. He simply intends to do more than Jairus asked (Ephesians 3:20).

That she may be saved and live. “Made well” is the verb usually translated saved. Without knowing it, Jairus has named the two gifts Jesus came to give: salvation and life. And Jesus can give both because of what he is. In him was life (John 1:4); he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), and death has no claim on him. But he would give that life to others only by going down into death himself. The man walking with Jairus towards a house where a child is dying is walking, in the end, towards a cross, where he will die so that daughters and sons beyond counting may be saved and live.

He went with him. Jesus goes at once. The Lord of glory can be stopped in the street by a frightened father and turned towards a sickroom. He sets no conditions, and does not ask whether this synagogue ruler had sided with those who plotted against him (3:6).

A great crowd. The crowd is an obstacle: a man with a dying child is moving at the pace of a mob, and it is about to stop altogether.

The structure. Mark again sandwiches one story inside another: Jairus’s daughter (vv. 21–24, 35–43) frames the woman with bleeding (vv. 25–34). The two stories interpret each other: two daughters (v. 34), twelve years, uncleanness, faith, and the power of Jesus over disease and death.

Does “saved” here mean healed or saved from sin? Both, in the way Mark tells it. The same Greek word covers rescue from illness, from danger, and from sin and judgment, and Mark uses it on purpose. Jairus means: heal her. But in this Gospel every healing is a sign of the larger salvation Jesus brings. The body made well points to the whole person made right with God, and one day to the body raised. So when we pray for healing we are asking for a small piece of what Christ will finally give in full. He may give it now; he will certainly give it at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

In everyday life. Bring your children to Jesus by name, whatever their age and state. And ask whether pride or reputation is keeping you from going to Christ, or from asking his people to pray with you, over something you cannot fix. Jairus lost his dignity on that beach and found the Lord of life.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve years. Mark breaks off the journey to tell her story. Her condition was probably bleeding from the womb that never stopped. And the twelve years match the girl’s age (v. 42): about the time Jairus’ family received a child, this woman’s life began to fall apart.

Her situation. Under the law, a woman with a discharge of blood was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted, and anyone or anything she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been excluded from the temple courts and from normal social contact, probably unable to marry or to stay married. No embrace, no worship, no place at anyone’s table. Whatever the bleeding was doing to her body, the loneliness had been doing something worse.

Under many physicians. Only Mark adds this frank detail, and his word is strong: she suffered under them. Ancient remedies for such conditions included unpleasant and useless treatments; the Talmud preserves a list of them, including carrying the ash of an ostrich egg in a linen rag. Twelve years of that, each course of treatment a fresh humiliation. Luke, a doctor, softens it: no one could heal her (Luke 8:43). And she had spent everything. Whatever her family had, it is gone. She is not merely ill; she is penniless, and penniless in the way that leaves a person feeling foolish: she paid for all of it herself, one hopeful appointment at a time.

Rather grew worse. This sentence will find some readers exactly where they live. If you have a chronic illness, or a chronic anything, a marriage that every attempt has made colder, a child who has moved further away with each intervention, a sin you have fought with every weapon you own and are visibly losing to, this verse is in your Bible on purpose. Mark does not hurry past it to the good part.

A flow of blood that cleanses. Her own flow of blood had made her unclean for twelve years. What would make her clean, and keep her clean before God for ever, was another flow of blood: the blood of the man whose cloak she was about to touch. The law could only declare her unclean; it could not cure her. But the prophet had promised that on that day a fountain would be opened for the house of David to cleanse from sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1), and at Calvary it was opened. The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). In Scripture blood stands for a life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11). When Christ died he bore the guilt of his people’s sin in their place, so that God no longer holds it against those who trust him (1 Peter 2:24).

Was God saying her body was sinful? No. Ritual uncleanness in the law was not the same as sin. Childbirth, a skin disease, touching a dead relative while burying him: all made a person unclean, and none was wrong. The laws of cleanness were a living lesson for Israel that life and holiness belong together, and that death and everything that leaks life away are out of place in God’s presence. They pointed forward to the one who would make the unclean clean. Those ceremonial laws were fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind Christians (Hebrews 9:9–14; Westminster Confession 19.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3). No woman today is less welcome before God because of her body.

Is it wrong to keep seeking medical help? No. Mark is not mocking doctors, and Luke, who was one, tells the same story. Medicine is a good gift of God, and Paul himself travelled with the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14). The lesson is not that doctors are useless, but that they are limited, and that the last word on any case belongs to Christ, not to them. So keep the appointments, take the treatment, and bring the whole thing to him, the remedies that work and the ones that do not. Trust him above the means, and do not despise the means.

In everyday life. Look around your church for the person whose trouble has made them lonely. A hand on the shoulder or a meal at your table may be the first in years.
verseByVerse.note: A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch; twelve years meant twelve years of exclusion.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She had heard the reports about Jesus. That is all she has. Faith, at its beginning, is very often no more than this: something you have heard about Christ, taken seriously enough to move on. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17).

From behind. She came from behind, probably ashamed: to approach openly would mean explaining what was wrong with her, and admitting that she had no business being in that crowd at all.

The risk she ran. The real risk was not embarrassment. Every person she pushed past was defiled by her under Leviticus 15. If she were recognised, there would be an uproar. Think what it took for an untouchable woman to walk into a crowd.

The fringe of his cloak. Matthew and Luke say she touched the fringe, the tassel at the corner of the outer cloak that every Jewish man wore under the command of Numbers 15:38–39, to remind him of the commandments of the LORD. It was the furthest, lowest edge of him. And yet the tassel that reminded Israel of the law was worn by the one man who had kept every commandment it stood for, and even its edge was enough.

If I touch even his garments. “Made well” is again saved. Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition, as though the power were in the cloth. But it was directed towards Jesus, and Jesus does not correct the theology. He never refuses somebody for coming to him with a poor grasp of how it works. What saved this woman was not the accuracy of her understanding. It was that she put out her hand.

The flow of blood dried up. Instantly, after twelve years.

The contagion went backwards. Every law of uncleanness in Israel ran one direction: what is unclean contaminates what is clean, and never the reverse. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse is not raised (Haggai 2:11–13). This woman put her hand on a clean man and, by every rule she had been taught, she should have made him unclean. Instead she was made clean. Jesus is not breaking the law here. He is what the law was preparing for: Israel had been taught that sin spreads and holiness does not, so that when a man came whose holiness was catching, they would know what they were looking at.

She felt in her body. “Disease” is the word for a whip (as in 3:10). She had been flogged by her own body for twelve years, and she felt it stop.

Should Christians use prayer cloths, relics or holy objects? No. The power was not in the cloak, and Jesus says so in a moment: her faith, resting on him, made her well. God did once do unusual miracles through cloths taken from Paul (Acts 19:11–12), but those were signs confirming the apostles’ message in a unique moment, not a pattern for us. Scripture never tells us to seek healing through objects, and the medieval trade in relics shows where that road leads. We have something better than his cloak: direct access to Christ himself, at the Father’s right hand, through prayer in his name (Hebrews 4:16).

parallels.desc: touching the fringe of his garment

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, "Who touched my garments?" And his disciples said to him, "You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, 'Who touched me?'" And he looked around to see who had done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Power had gone out from him. This is not an electrical charge that leaked out of him. A power that simply drained away would not go looking for anybody. He stops and looks for the person, and he will say your faith has made you well, not my cloak has. It was personal from both ends.

The cost of giving. Something went out of him. Healing costs him something, and at the end of this Gospel saving his people will cost him his life.

Immediately turned about in the crowd and said, Who touched my garments? Jesus stopped, though a dying girl was waiting. He would not let the woman slip away unseen. And now the scene stops dead: a crowd in a village street, a man with a dying child beside him, and Jesus turning round to ask an apparently unanswerable question.

Did Jesus not know who had touched him? His question was not for his own information but to draw her out, as God asked Adam, Where are you? (Genesis 3:9). God knew where Adam was; he wanted Adam to come out. Even so, Mark does not hide that in his earthly life the Son accepted real human limits; Jesus says of himself that the day of his return is known only to the Father (13:32). He is fully God and truly man, and he wanted her face to face.

You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, Who touched me? You can hear the exasperation, and Mark has never minded making the Twelve look foolish. Peter thinks the question is absurd (Luke 8:45): everyone was touching him. It is a fair objection. But they have missed the distinction the whole Gospel turns on. The crowd was pressing against him; one woman took hold of him. Many touched him by accident; one touched him in faith. Jesus knows the difference. Contact is not faith. There were hundreds of hands on Jesus that afternoon and exactly one of them got anything.

He looked around. Jesus will not let her stay hidden. It is a kindness, though it will not have felt like one to her. She could have gone home cured, and nobody would have known. He is willing to keep a dying child waiting rather than let that happen. He has something for this woman that she did not think to ask for, and it is worth the delay.

How do I reach out to him, rather than just being in the crowd? By coming to Christ yourself, personally, with your own need. Stop thinking of faith as something your family or church has and you share by being near it. Speak to him directly: tell him you are a sinner, that you have nothing to bring, that you trust him alone to forgive and make you clean, and ask him to receive you. Then keep reaching: in his word, read as his voice to you; in prayer, as to a person who is listening; at the Lord’s Table, receiving him by faith. The crowd brushes against Jesus. Faith takes hold of him and will not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. And he said to her, "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In fear and trembling. She comes forward in fear and trembling, afraid she will be condemned in front of everybody for touching him in her uncleanness.

The whole truth. Twelve years of shame told in front of the crowd, and not a summary. That is what confession is, and it is why we avoid it. Not the general admission that we are sinners, but the whole truth, in particular words, to the one person entitled to hear it. She was already healed. He draws her out because he wants more for her than a cure taken from behind and carried off in secret.

Daughter. That one word is the reason he stopped the procession. She is the only woman in the Gospels whom Jesus addresses as daughter. She has been nobody’s anything for twelve years: untouchable, unwelcome in worship, a name people lowered their voices about. And the first word out of his mouth gives her a place in a family. Remember what Mark is doing with this chapter. Jairus is standing a few feet away with his own daughter dying at home. Jairus has a daughter dying; Jesus has a daughter healed. And Jesus turns to a destitute, unclean woman nobody in that street would have looked at twice, and calls her the same thing. The most respected man in the town and the least respected have come to the same feet with the same empty hands. His standing will not buy his daughter’s life, and her shame will not keep her from his welcome. Both depend entirely on his grace.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” is saved you (sesōken): both healed and saved. He says where the power lay: not in her touch or his cloak, but in her faith in him. And her faith was small, frightened, muddled in its understanding, and reaching from behind. That is all it has ever taken. Faith saves not because it is impressive but because of who it takes hold of. The public declaration also restored her socially: everyone heard that she was healed and clean.

Go in peace. Behind the words stands the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, peace with God, the whole person put right. She came for a healed body and is sent away with a whole new life. Peace with God means the war is over: God is for her and not against her. Paul calls the root of it being justified, God declaring a sinner right in his sight, not because of anything in her but because of Christ, received by faith (Romans 5:1).

Be healed of your disease. A word of permanence: after twelve years she might have spent her life waiting for it to start again. He tells her it is over. And then, into the silence at the end of that sentence, the messengers arrive from Jairus’s house.

Does this mean that enough faith guarantees healing? No. Faith is the hand that reaches; Christ is the one who heals, and he heals as he wills. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be taken away and was told, My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Timothy had frequent ailments and was told to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23), not to believe harder. A believer who is not healed has not necessarily failed to believe. Faith trusts Christ whether he heals now or raises us whole at the last.

Do I need to confess my sins publicly like this? Not usually. Confession is first to God, who already knows and wants to hear it from us (1 John 1:9). Confess to the person you have wronged, and seek their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). James tells us to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), which normally means a trusted brother or sister, a pastor or an elder, especially with a sin you cannot break alone. Public confession before the church is for public sins that have harmed the church. The point of this scene is not the size of the audience but the honesty: the whole truth told to Christ, who receives it with the word daughter.

In the flow. A few hours earlier Jesus had asked his disciples, Have you still no faith? (4:40). Now the faith he commends belongs to an unclean woman reaching from behind. Her story prepares the next scene, where Jairus, who has just heard the word faith praised, will be told to keep on believing when there is no human hope left at all.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, "Do not fear, only believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking. Mark’s timing is exact and merciless. The word about the woman’s peace is barely out of his mouth when the men from the house arrive: while Jesus stopped for her, Jairus’s daughter died.

Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? In two kindly meant sentences they say all that the world believes about death: once it comes, nothing more can be done. The fact is true. But the conclusion rests on what they think Jesus is: a teacher. A teacher is a fine thing to bring to a sickbed and no use at all at a graveside. They are not hostile. Their view of him is simply too small, and it leads to advice that sounds entirely reasonable: stop praying about this one. It is finished. Do not bother him.

The kindly advice of unbelief. That advice still gets given, kindly: the marriage is over; he is seventy-eight and hardened; stop praying. It is always said gently, and it is always based on a true fact and too small a view of Christ.

Matthew says the girl had already died. Matthew has Jairus say at the start that his daughter has just died (Matthew 9:18). Matthew tells the story briefly and gives its outcome from the beginning; Mark and Luke tell it in sequence. Both are true accounts of the same event, told at different lengths.

The cost of the delay. From where Jairus is standing, the interruption killed his daughter: a stranger’s twelve-year complaint, which could have waited an hour. It is one of the hardest things about the way God works. His delays are real, they cost real people real things, and they are not accidents.

Overhearing. The word can mean overhearing or ignoring, and here it seems to mean both: he heard it and refused to let it stand.

More than a Teacher. The messengers had the right fact and the wrong Christ. The one they called Teacher is the one the prophet saw coming to swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:8). And this is how he will do it. He shared our flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:14–15). That is why his first word to Jairus is do not fear. The man telling Jairus not to be afraid is the only man who has ever had the right to say it at a deathbed.

Do not fear, only believe. Both are commands, and in the Greek both speak of something ongoing: stop being afraid, keep on believing. He means: nothing has changed about who I am. Jairus had believed Jesus could heal; now he must believe Jesus can raise the dead. And only is the tender word. He is not asking Jairus to feel confident or to understand why the woman came first. Just this one thing.

What the delay was for. And see what the delay was for. Jairus has just watched a hopeless twelve-year case healed and heard her called daughter: the last lesson he would need, ten minutes before he needed it. God’s delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are how he teaches us what we will need next.

What does only believe mean when Jesus did not raise the one I lost? It means trusting him with what he has not yet done. Jesus raised only a handful of people in his earthly ministry, and each of them died again. Those signs were not a promise that every Christian’s child will be restored this side of the grave, but a pledge of what he will do for all his people at the last day (John 11:25–26). If you have buried someone who trusted Christ, only believe means: he is not dead to Jesus, and Jesus will wake him. If you are unsure of the person’s faith, it means trusting the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25), and resting on his character. Fear says it is over. Faith says he has the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and James and John. The first time in Mark that these three are taken aside from the others, as they will be to see his glory (9:2) and his agony (14:33). They are first taken to watch him in a dead child’s bedroom, and if the early tradition is right, one of them told the story to Mark years later.

Weeping and wailing. Mourning was loud, immediate and public. A later Jewish rule says that even the poorest husband must provide two flute players and one wailing woman when his wife dies; a man of Jairus’s standing would probably have had a houseful. Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). Burial was usually the same day.

Nobody sends for the mourners while there is a pulse. Nothing was false about the sorrow, and nothing contemptible about the mourners. But their presence settles what Jesus means by sleep. She was dead.

Jesus saw the commotion. He did not push through it or shout over it. He stood in the doorway and looked at it. The Lord of life does not stand far off from death. He will stand at another graveside later and weep (John 11:35), knowing perfectly well that he is about to empty the tomb. The knowledge that he can undo it has never once made him indifferent to it. He is not embarrassed by grief and he does not hurry anyone through it, which is worth knowing if you are in a house like this one, or have been.

Is loud grief a lack of faith? No. Jesus wept, and so did Paul’s friends at Ephesus (Acts 20:37–38); devout men made great lamentation over Stephen (Acts 8:2). Paul tells believers not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), which is not a command to stop grieving but to grieve with hope. Tears at a graveside are not unbelief; they are love, and death is an enemy worth weeping over (1 Corinthians 15:26). What Jesus rebukes in that house is not the tears but the certainty that death has the final word.

In everyday life. Jesus does not avoid places of grief, and so his people walk into them. If someone you know is newly bereaved, do not wait until you know the right thing to say; go, sit, bring food, and let your presence say that they are not alone. And if you are the one grieving, do not hide your tears from him. He stands in the doorway and sees.
verseByVerse.note: Peter, James and John were the inner three, with Jesus again at the transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Hired mourners were customary at a death.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered, he said to them, "Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping. This sentence has been seized on for two hundred years. The claim is that she was never really dead, a coma, a faint, a lucky misdiagnosis, so this is no resurrection at all. The reading does not survive a careful look. She was truly dead, and everyone present was certain of it: the messengers reported it as fact, and the house was already full of professional mourners in full cry. They laughed at Jesus precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one, and they had seen this one. Luke, who was a physician, states plainly what happened when Jesus spoke: her spirit returned (Luke 8:55).

So what does sleeping mean? It is not a second opinion on her pulse. It is his settled way of speaking about the death of people he intends to raise. For Jesus, death is like sleep, because he is about to wake her. Of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said, Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and when the disciples took it literally he told them plainly, Lazarus has died (John 11:11–14). The New Testament uses sleep for the death of believers because they will be raised: those who have fallen asleep, and Christ the firstfruits of them (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:20). So by calling it sleep Jesus is not claiming less than a raising from the dead. He is claiming far more. To the mourners in that house, death was the end of the sentence. To the one standing in the doorway, it was as temporary as a night’s sleep, and waking this child would cost him no more effort than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning. He does not deny that she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has just become something you get up from.

Does sleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. The word describes how death looks from this side and how temporary it is, not what the soul experiences. It is the body that lies down and will be raised. Scripture is clear that believers who die go at once to be with Christ, conscious and blessed. Jesus told the dying thief, Today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The Westminster Confession puts it simply: the souls of the righteous, made perfect in holiness, are received at once into heaven (Westminster 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory. The Christian dead are awake in the presence of Christ, waiting for the morning of their bodies.

They laughed at him. Their grief turned to mockery, and the swing is worth noticing: these people were wailing a moment ago and they are jeering now. Their laughter also shows what the world does with the resurrection. It does not usually argue against it. It laughs, and feels clever for laughing (Acts 17:32). That room contained the only person present who knew what he was talking about, and he was the one being mocked. The laughter of unbelief has been echoing for two thousand years, and it has never once kept him from walking into the room.

He put them all outside. Firmly, all of them. “Put outside” is the word Mark uses for casting out demons. Jesus removes unbelief from the room.

The father and mother. Five people go in with him: Peter, James, John, and a father and a mother. The parents are not left in the corridor. The mother appears here for the only time in the story, unnamed, having probably been in that house all afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: Taking her by the hand he said to her, "Talitha cumi," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise." And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand. Before a word is spoken, he takes hold of a dead child. Under the law, touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days and required a specific rite of purification (Numbers 19:11–13).

The third touch. The third time in this chapter that Jesus goes straight to where uncleanness lives: the tombs, an untouchable woman, a corpse. Each contact should have made him unclean, and each time the opposite happened. The tombs did not defile him; the man came out of them. The bleeding did not contaminate him; it dried up. And death does not make him unclean for seven days. He takes hold of it, and it lets go. There is also, quite simply, the tenderness of it. He could have spoken from the doorway. He takes her hand, because that is what you do for a twelve-year-old, and because her mother and father are watching.

He said to her, Talitha cumi. Mark, writing in Greek, keeps the actual Aramaic Jesus spoke, perhaps because Peter never forgot it. It is not a magic formula, but the words a parent might use to wake a child in the morning. Talitha means little girl; it may come from a root used of a young lamb, though in use it simply meant a young girl: little one, get up.

I say to you, arise. No prayer, no invocation. He tells her to get up, and the authority in I say to you is the same authority that told a hurricane to be quiet. “Arise” (egeire) is the word used for resurrection (16:6), the word the angel will use of Jesus himself: he has risen.

She got up. Not weak and slowly recovering: she got up and started walking about the room, in front of her mother.

Twelve years old. An incidental detail that ties the chapter together: twelve years of a girl’s life, twelve years of a woman’s suffering, both touched on the same afternoon by the same hands. And they were immediately overcome with amazement, literally amazed with a great amazement. There is no adequate reaction to this and they did not manage one.

Can a thinking person really believe a dead girl got up? Everyone in that room already knew that dead girls do not get up; that is why they laughed. What matters is not whether this normally happens, but whether Jesus is who he says he is. If God gave life in the first place, giving it back is no strain for him. And notice the marks of an eyewitness rather than a legend: a named synagogue ruler people could ask about, the Aramaic words kept in a Greek book, the embarrassing laughter, the order a moment later to give her something to eat. None of these details proves the event on its own; they show that Mark tells it as a report, not a fable. In the end it all hangs on Jesus’ own resurrection, which Paul says was seen by more than five hundred people, most of them still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).

Was this the same as the resurrection Jesus will give us? Not quite. The girl was brought back to ordinary mortal life, and years later she died again. Jesus’ own resurrection was different: he was raised never to die again, in a body glorified and immortal (Romans 6:9), and he is the firstfruits of that harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). What happened in this room was a sign and a promise. The same voice, with the same authority, will one day speak to all who sleep in him, and they will rise not to die again but to live for ever, with bodies like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

The cost of the word. Here raising the dead cost him two words in a child’s ear. But raising all his people will cost far more: the hand that took this girl’s hand will be pierced by a nail, so that everyone who sleeps in him can be told, one morning, to get up.

In everyday life. Read 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as the long answer to this short scene. And if you are afraid of dying, or of the death of someone you love, picture this room: the hand that takes hold, the gentle word, the girl walking. That is what death is for those who belong to Christ. And if you have buried a child of your own, this room is not set before you as a reproach that yours was not raised now. It is a glimpse of the Lord into whose hands you may commit your child, the Judge of all the earth who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and who took this girl so tenderly by the hand.
verseByVerse.note: “Talitha cumi” is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke; Mark keeps his very words.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That no one should know. The command is emphatic, and impossible for long: the girl will be seen in the village tomorrow.

Why the secret? This is what is often called the messianic secret, Jesus’ habit of hushing the news of who he is (1:44). Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder-worker, or to stir up political hopes, before his identity could be understood through the cross. In Galilee at that moment, a man who raises the dead becomes a national event within a week, and the word Messiah in that year meant, for many, a king who would drive out Rome. He will not be hailed as King until he has been lifted up on a cross. He keeps the news quiet as long as he can, because people will only understand what kind of King he is once they have seen the cross.

Not a performance. He does not do this for show. A father and a mother get their daughter back in a quiet room with four other people in it. He is not using this family. He is helping them.

Something to eat. It is proof that she was truly alive, not a ghost (compare Luke 24:41–43). And it is Jesus’ practical care: the girl needed food. Her parents are past speech, and the Lord of life says, in effect: she will be hungry. The one who raises the dead also thinks about lunch.

The enormous and the domestic. In him the greatest power and the smallest household kindness belong together. He did it again after his own resurrection: the risen Christ, having conquered death, lit a charcoal fire on a beach and cooked breakfast for seven tired disciples (John 21:9).

Why was this kept quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because the time was different. Before the cross, the news of a wonder-worker would have been misunderstood as a political Messiah, and the crowds would have tried to make him king by force (John 6:15). After his death and resurrection, the full truth could be told: who he is and why he came. So the commission changes. Jesus himself sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). We are not under the secret; we are under the command to tell, and to tell it as Mark does, with the cross at the centre.

In the flow. The storm ended with the disciples asking, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (4:41). Chapter 5 is Mark’s answer: demons, disease and death obey him too. Yet the next scene is his home town of Nazareth, where people who know his family take offence at him and he marvels at their unbelief (6:1–6). Power alone does not create faith. And the command to silence holds back the full answer to who he is until it can be seen at the cross.

For worship. The chapter began with a man nobody could chain and ends with a girl being handed a plate. This is our Lord: mighty enough to command the abyss, humble enough to send for bread. There is nothing too great for his power and nothing too small for his love, and the one who conquered death for one little girl has conquered it for ever, for all who are his.

5.theology:
Legion. A Roman legion had up to about six thousand soldiers, the empire's means of occupation. The town had tried to chain one man, when an army was holding him. Jesus evicts that occupation with a word.

Why the pigs? The demons drove the herd, not Jesus. In permitting their request he let their purpose be seen: whatever they enter goes over the edge. And one man restored is worth more than the herd: Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matthew 12:12).

Not dead but sleeping. The girl had not fainted. The mourners laughed because they knew she was dead, and Luke records that her spirit returned (Luke 8:55). Sleep is Jesus' way of speaking about the death of those he will raise (John 11:11–14). He is claiming more than a single raising, not less: for his people death is no more final than sleep.
5.examples:
Then: the freed man begs that he might be with him, the phrase used of the Twelve (3:14), and Jesus says no.

Now: anyone whose best prayer has been refused. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). A no from Christ is not proof that you asked badly; sometimes it is a new assignment. This man was sent home with one commission: tell them how much the Lord has done for you.

He had no training and no Scriptures, only what had happened to him. And he told what Jesus had done, where Jesus had said the Lord. Within hours of being freed he had grasped that the two were one.

6.title: Refused at Home, Broken Bread, and a Prophet’s Head
6.text: <sup>1</sup>He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. <sup>2</sup>And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands? <sup>3</sup>Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household.” <sup>5</sup>And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. <sup>6</sup>And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 swings widely: a village that will not have him, a mission that works, a prophet murdered at a birthday party, a hillside fed until it could eat no more, and a man walking on water in the last watch of the night.

At Nazareth the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones, where did this man get these things?, and the conclusion drawn is the worst in the book.

Mark sends the Twelve out (vv. 7–13), then tells how John the Baptist died before he lets them come back (v. 30). Anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told.

The second half answers the first. The crowd that ruins the disciples' day off is met with compassion, because he sees sheep without a shepherd; five loaves in his hands feed a district with twelve baskets over; and he comes to his struggling disciples across the sea, saying, it is I.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Home (vv. 1–6). He preaches in the synagogue he grew up in, and the village is offended. They know his trade and his family, and he could do no mighty work there, and he marvelled at their unbelief.

The sending (vv. 7–13). Twelve men are sent out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits, carrying almost nothing, before they understand very much at all.

The dungeon (vv. 14–29). Mark then tells, out of sequence, how John the Baptist died: a birthday party, a dance, a rash oath and a head on a serving dish. Herod is not a monster but a weak man who liked listening to a preacher and would not be changed by him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened: Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the words that follow settle the sense: he healed a few sick people that afternoon, so his power had not failed. He could not because it would not have been right. In a village that had decided in advance what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle, and he refused exactly that to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and to Herod (Luke 23:8–9).

Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

And he marvelled. Only two things in the Gospels are said to have astonished Jesus: the faith of a Roman officer with no Bible (Luke 7:9), and the unbelief of the village that had raised him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod feared John, knew he was a righteous man, and heard him gladly.

Now: Herod is the thorny ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: the word received with real pleasure, and choked. A man who will not repent will eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to. So the honest question is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether it is changing anything. And if you hate the sin you still fight and keep bringing it to Christ, you are not Herod: he never tried.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 6 sets side by side two ways of meeting Jesus. The people who know him best are offended by him; Herod, the false shepherd-king, feeds the powerful and kills the prophet; and against that dark feast Jesus, the true Shepherd, feeds five thousand in the wilderness. The town that thought it knew him stayed as it was; those who knew they needed him were made well.

His hometown. Nazareth, the small village in the Galilean hills where he grew up (1:9), a place of a few hundred people where he had lived for something like thirty years. Joseph has vanished from the record by now; Mark names only Mary. Jesus knew the very seats they were sitting in.

And his disciples followed him. This is not a private visit. He has come home as a rabbi with a following, which is exactly what a village finds hardest to swallow, and the disciples see how his own town receives him before he sends them out.

He began to teach in the synagogue. As a visiting teacher, invited to read and explain Scripture. Luke records a visit, probably an earlier one, when he read from Isaiah 61 and said, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16–30). Mark gives only the reaction.

Astonished. The same verb was used of the crowd in Capernaum (1:22), where it led people towards faith. Here it turns into offence. Astonishment is not faith.

Where did this man get these things? Listen to their questions, because every one of them is the right question to ask. This first one has an answer they would not accept: from God. As far as they knew he had had no rabbinic training (compare John 7:15), and nobody in Nazareth had taught him this.

What is the wisdom given to him? They can hear that it is wisdom. They are not pretending it was a poor sermon. And note the word given: they recognised that his wisdom came from somewhere beyond himself. They have half the answer in their own question and do not follow it.

The Branch from Nazareth. The answer to their question had been written centuries before. Isaiah saw a shoot coming up from the stump of Jesse, and on him the Spirit of the LORD would rest, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might (Isaiah 11:1–2). He does not merely have wisdom; he is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Nazareth was asking where the wisdom came from while the Wisdom of God was standing in front of them. That is the humility of our God: he comes near enough to be overlooked.

How are such mighty works done by his hands? They had heard of his miracles, and they do not dispute them. News from Capernaum has reached them, and their objection is not that the reports are false.

Near is not the same as in. Here is a village asking precisely the right questions about Jesus and arriving at one of the saddest answers in this Gospel. A person can grant that the teaching of Jesus is extraordinary and his influence hard to explain, and still stop there, permanently, because the next step would rearrange his life. They were near the kingdom, and near is not the same as in.

Is it enough to admire Jesus as a great teacher? No, and in the end it is not even possible. A man who claimed to forgive sins (2:5–10), to be Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), and to be the one whom the prophets foretold, was either telling the truth or was not good at all. Admiration that stops short of worship is not a compliment to him; it is a refusal to answer his question. The Nazareth question, where did he get these things, has only one honest answer: from the Father, because he is the Son. To admire him without bowing to him is to stand in the doorway of the synagogue and never go in.
verseByVerse.note: His hometown is Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not this the carpenter? Here is where the astonishment curdles, and it turns on one word. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus himself is called a carpenter; Matthew’s version has the carpenter’s son (Matthew 13:55), and a few manuscripts of Mark read that way too, though most Bibles follow the better-supported reading, the carpenter. The Greek tektōn means a builder or craftsman in hard materials: wood, and in that stony country very often stone as well. He made ploughs, yokes, doors, roof beams, furniture and houses.

They had his furniture. For perhaps eighteen years the eternal Son of God did a trade in a village workshop, and the people in front of him very likely had his work in their houses. The Word through whom all things were made took up a carpenter’s tools and made doors for Nazareth. To the townspeople this settled it: you cannot easily worship a man who fixed your door.

The son of Mary. A small phrase with a barb in it. Normally a man was called son of his father, even if the father was dead. To call a grown man his mother’s son in his own village was a slight, and there may be a whisper behind it. A village can count the months between a wedding and a birth, and rumours about Jesus’ origins seem to surface elsewhere too (compare John 8:41).

And brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? They name the brothers and gesture at the sisters, who are apparently sitting in the room. Jesus had four brothers and at least two sisters. James later led the church in Jerusalem and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude. The most natural reading is that they were Mary and Joseph’s children born after Jesus. Matthew says Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7), a word that suggests other children followed.

Where Christians differ: Jesus’ brothers. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, and takes the brothers to be cousins (so Jerome). Orthodox tradition takes them to be Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Some of the Reformers, Luther among them, also kept the older belief, so this is not a line between the godly and the ungodly. This commentary’s view: the natural reading of the Gospels is that they were Mary’s younger children, Jesus’ half-brothers and half-sisters, born in the ordinary way. Nothing in Scripture requires otherwise. Mary’s honour is not a lifelong virginity. It is that she bore and raised the Son of God, believed God’s word (Luke 1:38, 45), and then mothered his brothers.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? It matters a little, and in a particular direction. Nothing in the gospel hangs on it: Christ was born of a virgin, and that is the article of faith. But the idea of Mary’s perpetual virginity grew alongside the view that married love is somehow less holy, and that Mary should be honoured as more than a believing servant of God. Scripture gives her great honour as the mother of our Lord, and calls her blessed (Luke 1:48), but it never makes her an object of prayer or a mediator. The honour of standing between God and sinners belongs to one person only, the son she bore, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Reading the brothers plainly keeps Mary where she placed herself: among those who need a Saviour (Luke 1:47).

The brothers who came to believe. During his ministry these brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). Here in Nazareth they are among the offended, and three chapters back they came to take him home as a madman (3:21, 31). Afterwards they are in the upper room, praying with the believers (Acts 1:14). James becomes a pillar of the Jerusalem church and writes the letter that opens, James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ; Judas writes Jude. Brothers are the hardest people to impress. Something happened between Nazareth and Acts 1, and Paul names it in a single line about the risen Jesus: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7).

They took offense at him. “Took offence” (eskandalizonto) is the root of our word scandal: they stumbled over him, and the thing they tripped over was that they knew him. They could not imagine the incarnation, God the Son becoming man: without ceasing to be God, he was truly man, with a real body, a real trade and a real family (John 1:14). And here is a warning for anyone raised in a Christian home: familiarity does not produce faith. It can leave you so used to the most extraordinary Person who ever lived that he no longer astonishes you: just one of the things you have always known.

Were those years in the workshop wasted? No. For most of his life on earth the Son of God did ordinary work for ordinary customers, and that was not a delay before his real work but part of his obedience. He was keeping the law perfectly in a carpenter’s shop, honouring his parents, giving fair measure, doing good work for people who would later despise him, and all of that is part of the righteousness credited to those who trust him. It also means your ordinary work matters to God. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23). A plumber, a nurse, a mother at home, a clerk at a desk, can serve Christ in the work itself, because Christ himself did.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet is not without honor. Probably a proverb already. Only Mark adds among his relatives, and the sentence narrows, getting more painful as it goes: the town, then the extended family, then the house he grew up in. And he is speaking of himself; his own brothers are in the room (3:21; John 7:5).

When your own family does not understand. If your family think your faith is a phase or a mild derangement, he was not spared this either, and he had to rise from the dead to convince his own brothers.

He could do no mighty work there. One of the most startling sentences in Mark, and it should not be smoothed away. Matthew says he did not do many mighty works there (Matthew 13:58); Mark says could not. The words that follow settle what it means.

Except that he laid his hands on a few. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power: sick men and women in that village got up well. He could not because it would not have been right. Miracles were signs meant to lead to faith; in a place that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle, and Jesus does not perform (8:11–12; Luke 23:8–9). And people did not bring their sick to someone they despised.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that controls whether God can act, as though God were a machine and belief the coin you put in. Faith receives what God gives; unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it on a town that has made up its mind.

He marveled. Only twice in the Gospels are we told that Jesus marvelled: at a Roman officer with no Bible and no synagogue behind him, who asked him only to say the word (Luke 7:9), and here, at the village that had raised him and taught him the Scriptures. The people with none of the advantages astonished him by their faith. The people with all of them astonished him by their unbelief.

He went about among the villages. Rejection at home did not stop him for a single day: he moved on to the next place and kept preaching.

Can my unbelief stop God from working in my life? Your unbelief cannot defeat God’s purposes, but it can keep you from receiving what he is offering. God is not limited by our weakness of faith; he heals the father who says, I believe; help my unbelief (9:24). What closes the door is not weak faith but settled refusal, the kind that has decided in advance what Jesus can and cannot be. So if your faith is small, bring it to him as it is, and ask him to increase it. If you notice that you have stopped expecting anything of him in some area of your life, confess that to him, and begin to pray about it again.

How do I love a family that rejects my faith? Patiently, warmly and without either preaching at every meal or hiding what you believe. Honour your parents (Ephesians 6:2), keep showing up, serve them in practical ways, and let your life speak before your words do (1 Peter 3:1–2). When they ask, answer gently and honestly. Do not take their scorn as a judgment on Christ or on you; he met it first. And pray for each of them, steadily, because their coming to faith will not depend on your arguments but on the risen Lord showing himself to them, as he did to James.

For worship. He carried the dishonour of Nazareth all the way to Golgotha, where the sign over his head named him Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (John 19:19). The town that would not honour him gave him the title he wears for ever, and he wears it as a crown.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to send them out. The word is apostellō, from which comes apostle, a sent one. These men have not yet grasped who he is (4:41), and they will fail to understand the loaves before this chapter is out. He sends them anyway, with real authority. If you have been waiting to feel qualified before you say anything about Christ to anyone, remember that nobody in this group was.

The Sent One sends. Behind the sending of the Twelve stands a greater sending. Jesus is himself the apostle of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), and everything the Twelve carry is his: As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). Their authority over unclean spirits is his own victory over Satan, the strong man of 3:27, lent to them. And the mission does not finally depend on how well they understand him. It depends on his hold on them.

In the flow. The town that knew him best has shut its door, and his answer is to multiply his voice: twelve men in six pairs. Between their going out and their return (6:30), Mark tells how Herod killed John, so that the mission and its cost stand side by side.

Two by two. Never alone: for support, safety and credible witness, since a charge stood on the evidence of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and these men are bearing testimony. The early church followed the pattern: Paul and Barnabas, Peter and John. Each of the Twelve probably went with a colleague he had not chosen, and someone had to walk the roads with Simon the Zealot, someone with Matthew the tax collector.

Authority over the unclean spirits. It is his own authority, lent to them, not a skill built up or a technique learned by watching. That is exactly why they will fail in chapter 9, when they try without depending on God in prayer (9:28–29).

Nothing for their journey except a staff. Matthew and Luke say not even a staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3). With Matthew the difficulty eases when the verbs are compared: his word is acquire, Mark’s is take along, so Mark may mean take the staff you have, while Matthew means do not get another. Luke uses Mark’s verb, so there the answer must lie elsewhere, perhaps a walking staff in one and a club for defence in the other. No suggestion settles it beyond doubt, and believers can hold the Gospels true while admitting this small question is not fully resolved. One plain instruction stands behind all three: do not equip yourselves for this journey; travel light.

No bread, no bag, no money in their belts. Coins were carried in folds of the belt. The bag was a traveller’s pack, or quite possibly a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts, which would have made them look like the wandering religious tricksters of the day. They must depend entirely on God’s provision through those who welcomed them.

Not two tunics. A second tunic was the ordinary traveller’s blanket. This is not hardship for its own sake. Jesus is making them dependent on purpose: they will eat only if somebody feeds them, so they cannot keep their distance from the people they are sent to.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. This was the instruction for one short mission in Galilee. Later Jesus reminded them of it, When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?, and then told them that things were now different: let the one who has a moneybag take it (Luke 22:35–36). The principles remain: urgency, simplicity and dependence on God.

Does this mean Christian workers should not be paid?
