No. The point of the instruction is that those who preach should live from those who receive the message, and that is exactly what Jesus says next: the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7). Paul argues the same: the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). So it is right for churches to support their pastors and missionaries generously. And it is right for those workers to live simply, avoid the appearance of greed, and trust God rather than their reserves.
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt; the “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay there. A visiting teacher with a following would attract offers, and the temptation was to move up from the first house that took you in to a wealthier host. Take the first door that opens and stay behind it.

What it protects. Two things. The poor family that risked something to receive them is not to be used as a stepping stone and then quietly left. And the message: a preacher visibly working his way towards the best address in town has already said something about himself that will drown out what he says about Christ. Every church has its own version of this: being warmer to people the more influential they are.

If any place will not receive you. Rejection was expected, as at Nazareth. He assumes refusal, names it, and gives them a way to leave that is neither bitter nor guilty.

Shake off the dust. Jewish teachers regarded the soil of Gentile lands as unclean, and strict Jews coming home from abroad are said to have shaken its dust off their feet rather than carry it into the holy land. For the apostles to do this to a Jewish town was startling: by rejecting God’s message, the town had made itself like pagan territory. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A solemn warning, leaving them to God’s judgment, done in sorrow, not anger: you have put yourselves outside, and the responsibility now rests with you. To refuse the King’s messengers is to refuse the God who sent them, and Scripture asks how we shall escape if we neglect such a great salvation (Hebrews 2:3).

Whoever receives you receives me. The dust carries such weight because of who sent them: whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me (Matthew 10:40). A door opened to two tired fishermen was a door opened to the Son of God. That is still what happens when the gospel is told at a kitchen table: the King himself is asking to come in.

The mercy in the instruction. They are told in advance what to do when it does not work: say your piece, and if they will not have it, go, and do not carry the weight of that town away with you. If you have talked to somebody about Christ for years and got nowhere, his unbelief is not necessarily a verdict on your competence; where the message was brought faithfully and refused, the refusal belonged to the hearer.

When should I stop talking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never stop praying for him. The dust-shaking was a solemn act given to the apostles on a particular mission, marking towns that had heard and rejected the message; it is not a licence to write off a friend. But there is a lesson in it for us. When someone has clearly heard the gospel and has asked you to stop, respect that. Do not nag, argue at every meeting, or turn every conversation into a sermon. Keep the friendship, keep loving, answer if asked (1 Peter 3:15), and keep praying, because God can open a heart long after you have run out of words (Acts 16:14).
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That people should repent. The same message as John and Jesus (1:4, 15). Repentance is not the same as being sorry: remorse looks at yourself and feels bad; repentance turns round and goes the other way. It is a direction, not a mood.

They cast out many demons. The authority he had given them turned out to be real in their hands, and when the seventy-two were sent out later they came back astonished at the same thing (Luke 10:17).

Anointed with oil. Olive oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6), and as a sign of God’s blessing and presence. This is the only place in the Gospels where anointing with oil accompanies healing, and James tells the church to do the same: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15).

So what is the oil for? It is not working as medicine here: these are miracles, not cures by ointment. And it is not magic: nothing in the New Testament suggests the oil has power in it. It is a sign: something visible and physical, laid on the body of a sick person, saying that God is being asked to act here, on this man, now. In the Old Testament oil marked out a person or thing as belonging to God and set apart for his purposes: kings, priests, the tabernacle furniture. And before anyone builds too much on the oil, see where James puts the power: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. The Lord will. Not the oil, and not the elders.

The oil and the Anointed One. Messiah and Christ both mean the Anointed One, and Jesus had read it of himself: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me (Luke 4:18). Peter later summed up the whole ministry: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38). The apostles anointed the sick because they had been sent by the Anointed, and the oil on a fevered forehead was a small sign of the Christ.

What it does not mean. Not the sacrament of extreme unction or last rites, as the medieval church developed it, for preparing the dying for death. The anointing here was for healing. Reformed churches do not treat anointing as a sacrament, though some practise it in prayer for the sick, following James 5.

Should we expect healings like these today? These were signs given through the Twelve as they were sent out, part of the apostolic witness that confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, expect gifts of healing to continue today; this commentary holds that such sign-gifts belonged to the apostles’ founding work (the view called cessationism), while gladly agreeing that God still heals in answer to prayer. What continues is what James describes: the elders praying over the sick, with oil as a sign of setting them before the Lord. God hears such prayers and sometimes heals, often through ordinary means and sometimes beyond them. But no one is promised that every prayer for healing will be answered with recovery, and when healing does not come, the prayer has not failed. The final healing waits for the resurrection.

Should I ask my elders to pray over me when I am ill? Yes, if you are seriously ill. The instruction in the New Testament is not to suffer privately and hope somebody remembers you in a service. It is to send for the elders of your church and ask them to come and pray over you. That is a specific, concrete thing you are entitled to ask for, and it is in your Bible. Many churches have quietly let it drop, which is a pity. James joins it to confession and forgiveness (James 5:15–16), so it is also a time to make sure all is well between you and the Lord, and then to rest in his will.
verseByVerse.note: Olive oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing.

parallels.desc: anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Herod heard of it. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. His official title was tetrarch, a minor ruler (Matthew 14:1), but people called him king, and Mark uses the title the locals used. He later asked Rome for the title of king, and was exiled instead.

For Jesus’ name had become known. Twelve men in six pairs have covered the district, and the noise has reached the palace.

Like one of the prophets of old. Some said John the Baptist raised from the dead; others said Elijah, the prophet expected before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). All honourable opinions, all inadequate. The crowd reaches for the greatest kind of person it already knows. Ask people today and you will hear the same kind of answer: a great teacher, a moral genius, a revolutionary. All respectful, all far too small, and often for the same reason: none of those answers asks anything of us. He is not one of the prophets come back; he is the one all the prophets were pointing to.

In the flow. Herod’s verdict is one more answer to Mark’s driving question: who is this? The demons know (1:24), the disciples ask it (4:41), Nazareth thinks it knows (6:3), and here the crowds and the king guess wrong, until Peter answers it with this same list in front of him (8:27–29).

John, whom I beheaded. A chilling sentence, because of one word in it: I. He could have said, John, who was beheaded, and blamed his wife, the oath or the guests. When the news of Jesus reaches him, the sentence comes out in the first person.

What guilt does. A guilty conscience keeps an accurate record. Guilt does not fade because it is ignored; it goes underground and comes out in other ways: in dreams, in irrational fears, in the inability to enjoy anything. Herod had a prophet in his cellar who pointed to the Lamb of God, and he preferred to keep listening rather than obey. Now he has a ghost.

The resurrection Herod did not expect. Herod’s guilty guess named the wrong man, but something like it was going to happen. A prophet was going to be put to death by a ruler who knew he was innocent, and he was going to be raised: not John, but the one John had pointed to, rising not as a ghost to haunt his killers but as the Lord who forgives them. Herod would meet him face to face in Jerusalem, and ask him for a trick (Luke 23:8–11).

What do I do with a guilty conscience? Bring it to Christ, specifically and honestly, and do not try to manage it by yourself. Name the sin to God without excuses: not it happened, but I did it. Believe that the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works (Hebrews 9:14), and that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). If your sin has injured another person, go to them and repair what can be repaired, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8). And if the guilt keeps returning after you have confessed and been forgiven, that is no longer conscience but accusation: answer it with the cross, where the debt was fully paid (Romans 8:1, 33–34).
verseByVerse.note: “King” Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea; his official title was tetrarch.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound him in prison. According to the historian Josephus, John was held at Machaerus, a grim hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea: the man who had baptised thousands in the open air of the Jordan valley, shut in a cell in a desert castle.

His brother Philip’s wife. The mess of the family arrangement is the point. Herodias, granddaughter of Herod the Great, was the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’ half-brother (called Philip in the Gospels); Antipas fell in love with her, and both divorced their spouses to marry each other. Antipas put away his first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, which would eventually cost him a war.

It is not lawful. “Had been saying”: repeatedly, to the ruler’s face. The law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John confronted the ruler with God’s law, like Elijah before Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21).

How John spoke. That sentence is a model of something the church constantly gets wrong. It is short: no treatise on marriage. It is specific: not a general denunciation of immorality in high places, which costs nothing and changes nobody, but this man and this marriage. It is said to Herod, not about him to a crowd who already agreed. And it is about Herod’s sin, not his politics: he confronted him on the thing he was answerable to God for.

The friend of the Bridegroom. It is fitting that John, who came to prepare the way for Jesus, should die defending a marriage. John called himself the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29), and the Bridegroom was Jesus. From the beginning marriage was a picture of the covenant love of God for his people, and in the end of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Herod’s marriage was a lie about that love; John’s rebuke guarded the picture. And the Bridegroom himself would keep his covenant by laying down his life for a bride who had been unfaithful, to make her clean (Ephesians 5:25–27).

The cost. It cost him his freedom and then his head. It is safe to denounce sins in general; the moment a name is attached, it becomes expensive. Yet this is no licence for the sharp tongue. John was not rude, and he was not indiscriminate: he had a word for the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers too (Luke 3:10–14), tailored to each.

Was Herod’s marriage wrong only because of the law about a brother’s wife? No; it was wrong twice over. Each of them abandoned a living spouse without any ground God allows, and then they married within a forbidden degree of kinship. Scripture permits divorce only for adultery or for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15; Westminster Confession 24.5–6), and Jesus calls remarriage after any other divorce adultery (10:11–12). Persistent, serious abuse can itself amount to desertion, as the elders judge each case, and anyone abused should seek safety at once. John’s sentence named the most public offence, but the whole arrangement was built on two broken covenants. The point is not that the powerful are worse sinners than others, but that their rank does not exempt them from God’s law about marriage.

Should Christians speak out against the sins of leaders today? Yes, with John’s wisdom. Pray for rulers first (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honour them (1 Peter 2:17). When you speak, speak about what God’s word plainly says, not your political preferences dressed up as prophecy. Speak to the person where you can, not merely about him. Speak with grace, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6), and be ready to pay for it. And remember that the first sins to deal with are your own: John’s courage before Herod grew out of a life that had already bowed to God.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herodias had a grudge. Literally held it in: a nursed, settled hatred, not a flash of temper but a campaign, waiting for its chance. Bitterness kept and fed becomes murderous (Ephesians 4:31).

What the truth does to some people. John’s sentence was aimed at Herod, but it was Herodias who could not live with it, because it named her position exactly: she was not his lawful wife. Some people, when a sin is named, repent. Some argue. And some set out to destroy the person who said it, as if the sin would disappear with the person who named it. It never does.

Herod feared John. Only Mark tells us about Herod’s inner conflict, and it is searching, because Herod is not a monster. He feared John with awe, the respect a morally careless man cannot help feeling in the presence of a serious one. He is not deceived about John’s character for a moment, and against his own wife he used his authority to keep John alive.

The Holy and Righteous One. Herod had a righteous and holy man in his cellar, and could not bear either to obey him or to lose him. John was only a lamp (John 5:35). The truly Holy and Righteous One was walking the roads of Galilee, and Herod would one day dress him in splendid clothing to mock him (Luke 23:11). What Herod needed was not a better preacher in the dungeon but a new heart, and by his Spirit Christ gives one that actually wants what God wants (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that his word is no longer a voice you visit in the cellar and leave there, but the voice you live by.

Matthew says Herod wanted to kill John. Matthew says that Herod wanted to put him to death but feared the people (Matthew 14:5). Both are true: a man can want a voice silenced and still be drawn to it.

He heard him gladly. Picture the ruler of Galilee going down into his own prison to listen to the man he has chained there, being upset by what he hears, and returning to be upset again. He enjoyed hearing John, but would not give up Herodias.

A divided heart. One of the most dangerous spiritual conditions in this Gospel, because it looks so much like the real thing: interest, respect, emotion, protection of the preacher, genuine disturbance of conscience, and no repentance. Herodias stayed. He is the thorny ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace (4:18–19). And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to. Herod did not want John dead, but a sin that is not repented of leads only one way, and it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before. If you fear you are Herod because you still fight a sin you hate, see the difference: Herod did not want to give up Herodias and never tried. A believer who hates the sin he still falls into, and keeps bringing it to Christ, is not divided like that; the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in him (Galatians 5:17).

Is it wrong to enjoy sermons? Not at all. Delight in God’s word is a mark of grace (Psalm 119:103), and it is right to be moved by faithful preaching. The danger is not enjoying it but stopping there. Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves (James 1:22). A simple test: after a sermon that moves you, ask what one thing it calls you to do, believe or stop, and tell someone. Enjoyment that leads to obedience is the Spirit at work. Enjoyment that replaces obedience is Herod in the dungeon, nodding.

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An opportunity came. Literally a good day, a well-timed day. Herodias has been waiting for one.

On his birthday. Everything turns on the guest list: every man in the region whose opinion Herod cares about is in one hall, on the most public night of his year.

Two kings, two feasts. Mark has set this banquet deliberately beside the meal that follows it. In the palace, a king gives a feast for the powerful, and the last course is a prophet’s head on a platter. In the wilderness, the true King spreads a meal for the shepherdless poor, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. At Christ’s table the King himself is the one who dies, and his people feed on his life. Take, this is my body (14:22). Every Lord’s Supper is the answer to Herod’s birthday.

Herodias’s daughter. Josephus tells us she was called Salome; Mark calls her the girl, probably a teenager. The reality is squalid. For a princess to dance before drunken men at a banquet was shameful, and suggests a performance very possibly arranged by her mother. If Herodias did send her own daughter in, she was willing to use her child that way to get what she wanted. That is the measure of the grudge.

Up to half of my kingdom. A drunken, extravagant promise. It is for show: Herod is performing for the room (oaths, plural, v. 26). It is empty: he ruled at Rome’s pleasure and had no kingdom to give. And it is borrowed: it echoes the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2), where the offer is used by a brave woman to save a nation from slaughter. Here the same words fetch a prophet’s head on a plate.

A man who cannot say a small true sentence. Herod could never say a small true thing, such as I was wrong, yet he cannot stop himself making a large empty promise. A man who inflates his words to impress a room will one day find himself standing behind a promise he never meant, in front of people he cannot bear to disappoint.

Should Christians take oaths at all? Yes, when it is solemn and lawful, but never casually. Jesus forbade the everyday swearing that props up our words because we are not otherwise trusted (Matthew 5:33–37). Yet God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as his witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and Reformed and Baptist confessions alike teach that a lawful oath in a court or on a solemn occasion is a proper act of worship (Westminster Confession 22.1–3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 23.1–3). What is forbidden is the rash oath, the oath to do evil, and the oath as performance. Let your ordinary word be so reliable that you rarely need more.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And she went out and said to her mother, For what should I ask? She goes out: the girl does not know what she wants. She has been given, in front of the whole court, an open cheque from a ruler, and she has to leave the room and go and ask her mother. That shows whose will is driving this story. The girl was the instrument of her mother’s hatred.

The head of John the Baptist. No hesitation: Herodias seems to have had the answer ready for months. Offered half a kingdom, she asks for nothing for herself or the girl. That is what a nursed grudge does to a person’s appetites: it eats everything else.

Immediately with haste. Before Herod could sober up and change his mind.

At once, on a platter. She has improved on her mother’s answer: at once, and on a platter, a serving dish, as if it were another course at the feast. Mark does not comment. This is what happens to a child raised in that house.

Exceedingly sorry. The word is strong, deeply grieved, and Herod’s distress is entirely real.

Two men exceedingly sorrowful. Mark uses this word only once more, of Jesus in Gethsemane: My soul is very sorrowful, even to death (14:34). Herod, sorrowful, does evil to keep his word to a girl and his face before his guests, and another man dies. Jesus, sorrowful to death, does the Father’s will and keeps his word to his people, and he is the one who dies. Herod would not lose face to save a righteous man; the Righteous One lost everything to save the unrighteous. The sorrow is the same word; the love beneath it is the whole difference between this world and the gospel.

Because of his oaths and his guests. There is the whole reason a man is beheaded tonight. And there is a terrible show of religion in it. Herod keeps his word. He is careful to keep an oath and ready to murder a prophet, and he would have told you, quite sincerely, that a man must stand behind what he has sworn.

Was Herod bound to keep his oath? No. An oath to do evil binds no one; it should be repented of, not carried out (Westminster Confession 22.4, 22.7). The law made provision for someone who had sworn rashly (Leviticus 5:4–6), and Jephthah’s vow stands in Scripture as a warning, not an example. Herod’s real bond was not to God but to the faces around his table. What he could not face was being the man who backed down in front of that room. Not conscience: he had already lost that argument, and he knew John was righteous and holy. Not law: no law said a prisoner should be executed to settle a dinner-party promise. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

The fear of man. One of the most ordinary motives for the worst things people do: backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable. The snare Proverbs describes was laid for Herod by a room full of faces, and only trust in the LORD could have kept him out of it (Proverbs 29:25). Christ is the King who was never once trapped by the opinion of a room, and he frees his people from the snare of the fear of man by giving them a better fear, the fear of the Lord.

What if I have already made a promise I should not have? If keeping it would mean sinning, do not keep it; confess the rash promise to God and to the person, apologise, and bear the embarrassment. If it is merely costly or inconvenient, a godly person keeps his word even when it hurts (Psalm 15:4), unless the other person releases him. Either way, go humbly to the one you promised, explain honestly, and seek a way to make it right. The cross covers rash words too, and it is far better to look foolish before people than to do wrong before God.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An executioner. Immediately: as long as it takes a soldier to walk down to the cells and back. Mark uses a Latin word (spekoulatōr) for a soldier of the guard, perhaps because he was writing in Rome.

Beheaded him in the prison. Mark will not embellish it: a door opening in the dark and a soldier with an order, and that is all we are told. This is the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11), the man who baptised the Son of God, saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit descend, and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29). And he died alone in a dungeon, killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride, with no last word recorded.

There is no rescue. The Gospel does not soften it. Jesus was alive and a few days’ walk away, healing strangers, and John, who had been shut in that fortress long enough to send messengers asking, Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? (Matthew 11:3), was not delivered. The answer he got back was not, I am coming to get you, but a message about the blind seeing, and a blessing on whoever did not lose faith in him (Matthew 11:6). So John died with the question answered and the door still locked.

Faithfulness is not a contract with providence. If you are serving God faithfully and your circumstances are getting worse rather than better, that is in your Bible on purpose, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Hebrews knows this: some by faith stopped the mouths of lions and escaped the edge of the sword, and others, by exactly the same faith, were sawn in two and killed with the sword (Hebrews 11:33–37). The chapter puts them in the same list and calls it all faith.

The girl gave it to her mother. Told plainly, without comment. Herodias has what she wanted.

Took his body. The one clean act in the whole squalid story, by men with no power and everything to lose. They could not save him. They could not avenge him. They could carry him, and they did.

Why Mark tells this story. It is almost the only story in Mark not directly about Jesus, and every detail foreshadows his death: Pilate will know Jesus is innocent, yield to pressure, and Jesus will be laid in a tomb by friends who came and took the body (15:15, 45–46). The difference is what happened next. Herod’s dungeon kept John. The tomb outside Jerusalem could not keep the one John had pointed to, and because it could not, John’s story does not end in that cell: he too will rise.

Why did God let John die like that? God was not absent, John’s work was complete, and death was not the end: nothing, not even the sword, can separate his servants from his love (Romans 8:35–39). (See Matthew 14:5 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. Herod silenced the voice, and could not touch the Word. The voice crying in the wilderness fell quiet in a cellar, but the one it announced was already speaking in every village of Galilee. The head on Herod’s platter was a trophy of a night; the Lamb John named reigns for ever, and John lives before his throne with every martyr since (Revelation 6:9–11). The world has the last word only until the morning, and the morning belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rest that never happened (vv. 30–34). The apostles come back, and Jesus's first word is not a debrief but a retreat. The crowd is waiting when they land, and he meets a wrecked day off with compassion.

The feeding (vv. 35–44). The disciples do the sums and propose sending the crowd away; Jesus hands the problem back, and five loaves and two fish leave more at the end than at the start.

The lake in the fourth watch (vv. 45–52). From the mountain where he prays, he sees them straining at the oars, and comes to them on the water.

Gennesaret (vv. 53–56). Whole villages carry the sick into the marketplaces, and everyone who touched even the edge of his clothing is made well.
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not what it sounds like. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible: to Moses, while my glory passes by (Ex. 33:22); to Elijah, behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). And Job joins the God who trampled the waves of the sea with the God who passes by me (Job 9:8, 11).

Then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi, I am: an ordinary way to say it is me, and, spoken on that water, also God’s own name from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd, and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: the parent who has run out of wisdom, the pastor of a small church looking at a large town. Jesus asks the practical question: How many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many you need, but how many you have, because the multiplication happens in his hands and not in theirs. And the men who had nothing to give carried back the surplus, one basket each.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles returned. Almost the only time Mark calls them apostles, those sent, as they return from being sent (compare 3:14). They are full of what has happened: demons had come out, sick people had got up. It had worked.

In the flow. The apostles come back straight after John’s death, and its shadow falls across this scene: the world kills God’s messengers, and the Lord gathers his own to himself. The quiet place they sail to will become the wilderness where he feeds five thousand.

Rest a while. Only Mark records this tender invitation. No strategy session about building on the momentum: rest. He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). He notices when we have not eaten, and he calls us away to himself before we break.

Come away with me. The rest is by yourselves, with him. The one inviting them is the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28): Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The deepest weariness of these men is not their feet but their souls, and he is the only rest for that: rest from earning, rest from proving, the rest of those whose work is finished because his is (Hebrews 4:9–10). You now serve because God has accepted you, not in order to be accepted. The one who sends them out is also the one who holds them up.

Christians are peculiarly bad at this. There is a way of serving God that treats tiredness as a badge and rest as a shameful concession, and it is not in this Gospel. With a district newly stirred up, the Lord of the harvest took twelve effective men away from the work for a rest. Often what drives our overwork is not love for people but a quiet idol: the need to be needed, or the hope of proving by exhaustion that we are worth something. If the Lord can do without you for a day, you were never the one holding things up.

No leisure even to eat. Not a hard week, but a pattern (3:20). When the ordinary human things go, meals eaten standing up, sleep treated as the thing that can always be cut, days off that quietly became nothing, something has gone wrong that no fruitfulness justifies, and Jesus treated it as a reason to stop.

They went away in the boat. The desolate place (erēmos) is the wilderness, where God fed Israel (Exodus 16), and what follows will recall that. The rest he arranged will in a moment be ruined by the crowds; planning rest is right, and it will still sometimes be taken from you.

Is it selfish to rest when there is so much need? No. Jesus himself sent his apostles to rest while crowds were still coming. God built rest into creation and into his law (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11). The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed brothers keep it as the Christian Sabbath, and they are to be honoured. All agree that a weekly rhythm of worship and rest is God’s gift, and that you are not the Saviour of the world. The need will always be greater than your strength. Rest is an act of trust that God keeps the world running while you sleep (Psalm 127:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Got there ahead of them. The plan fails immediately: twelve exhausted men, promised a quiet day, see the empty shore covered with people. Anyone who has needed a day off knows what would rise in the chest. Jesus too is tired.

He had compassion. Not irritation, but deep, gut-level compassion (splanchnizomai), built on the word for the inward organs.

Like sheep without a shepherd. The phrase is from the Old Testament, and it carries a great deal. Moses prayed that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd (Numbers 27:17). Behind it stands Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises that he himself will shepherd his people through a new David: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep (Ezekiel 34:15).

The false shepherd and the true. Mark has just shown what kind of shepherd Galilee had: Herod fed his nobles and devoured the prophet. Jesus is the true Shepherd those promises were waiting for, and he will now feed his flock in the wilderness.

He began to teach them. See what the compassion produces first: not the loaves, but teaching (2:2), because the deepest thing wrong with sheep that have no shepherd is that nobody has been feeding them (Deuteronomy 8:3). He will get to their stomachs before the day is out.

How do I find compassion when I am exhausted? Not by trying to feel it, but by looking at people the way Jesus did, and by drawing on his compassion rather than your own reserves. Ask him to show you what he sees: not interruptions, but sheep without a shepherd. Remember how he has had compassion on you when you came to him at inconvenient times. And be honest about your limits; Jesus’ compassion did not stop him from sending the crowds away that evening and going to pray. Compassion is not saying yes to every demand. It is meeting people with his heart, and then trusting him with what you cannot do.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is a desolate place. The disciples are being sensible, and they are right about the facts.

Send them away. A reasonable suggestion, and the standard shape of religious problem-solving: the need is real, the resources are insufficient, therefore reduce the need. It simply never occurs to them that the man standing next to them might be a factor in the calculation.

You give them something to eat. The pronoun is emphatic: you. He hands twelve tired men a responsibility plainly, mathematically beyond them, to show them their inadequacy and his sufficiency. It is one of his settled habits: the command that cannot be obeyed out of your own resources (3:5; Matthew 28:19), which is always an invitation to depend on him. Our Lord gives commands bigger than our resources because his resources are bigger than his commands. He is never caught by surprise at nightfall in a desolate place; he knew all along what he was going to do (John 6:6).

Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat? And out comes the arithmetic. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. Two hundred denarii was some seven or eight months’ wages: far more than they had, and they could not have spent it in a village at dusk anyway. They have evidently done the sum on the spot. Their answer is probably half sarcastic, and you can almost hear the tone: it is not quite rude and it is not quite faith. It is a man showing his working to prove the thing cannot be done.

Can God spread a table in the wilderness? Israel once asked that very question in unbelief, in the desert, though God had just split the rock and given them water (Psalm 78:15–16): Can God spread a table in the wilderness? (Psalm 78:19). The disciples are asking it again with a calculation. And the answer is standing beside them. This is not a prophet who will ask God for bread; it is the God who fed Israel for forty years, come in the flesh to a desolate place to do it again. Every human sum about the wilderness leaves him out, and every time he is the whole of the answer. He would one day give a bread no money could buy, his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51).

A spreadsheet beside the Son of God. These men have seen a paralytic walk, a girl raised from the dead and a storm muzzled, and their considered response to a catering problem is a spreadsheet. Before we use that to beat them with, be honest: we pray about the things we already half expect to manage and quietly do arithmetic about the rest. The disciples’ sum was correct, and completely beside the point, because they had left Jesus out of it.

Is it wrong to plan and count costs? No. Jesus himself told his hearers to count the cost (Luke 14:28), and careful planning is part of good stewardship. The disciples’ fault was not that they counted but that they counted without him, as if the Lord of heaven and earth were not standing beside them. Plan, budget and prepare, and then bring the plan and the shortfall to him in prayer, expecting him to act according to his will. The question is not whether you do arithmetic, but whether Christ is in the sum.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How many loaves do you have? Go and see. He does not answer the objection; he asks a different, practical question. Not how much do you need: they have already worked that out and it paralysed them. How many have you got? And then, gently: go and count it. That is exactly what to do when a need is obviously beyond you. Stop calculating the gap. Go and find out precisely what is in your hands, however little that is, and bring it to him. The gap is his business; counting what you have is yours.

Five, and two fish. John says they came from a boy in the crowd, and that they were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish would have been small and salted, the relish you ate with bread rather than a meal. Little as it was, it was right to bring it. Christ has never once been hindered by the smallness of what was brought to him; he has often been hindered by its being kept back.

On the green grass. Only Mark mentions that the grass was green, a detail that fits the early church’s report that Peter’s memories stand behind this Gospel; the hills are green for a few weeks in spring, near Passover (John 6:4). And it puts a psalm into the scene: He makes me lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:2). The Shepherd is making his shepherdless sheep lie down in green pasture, and will feed them.

By hundreds and by fifties. Literally, in garden beds: from the hillside the crowd would have looked like a garden laid out in plots. Hundreds and fifties recalls how Moses organised Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 18:21, 25). Jesus is forming a new Israel in the wilderness and feeding it like a new Moses, and he is greater than Moses, who never made a loaf in his life.

What if what I have really is too little? Then bring it anyway, because the miracle did not begin with a large gift. A boy’s lunch was all it took for Jesus to feed thousands, and he chose to work through that lunch rather than without it. Your time, your small gift of money, your stumbling words to a friend, your weak prayers: none of them is impressive, and none of them is the point. He is the point. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27). The only gift he cannot use is the one we keep.
verseByVerse.note: The groups of hundreds and fifties recall the way Moses organised Israel in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He looked up to heaven. Like the head of a Jewish household at a meal. The blessing was not said over the food but to God for it, probably in words like the familiar Jewish grace: blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. He is thanking his Father over food that is obviously not enough, before a single extra crumb exists. Gratitude offered before the provision arrives is one of the plainest marks of faith there is.

Broke the loaves and gave them. He took, he blessed, he broke, he gave: the same four verbs as the Last Supper (14:22), and the sequence by which the Emmaus disciples will recognise him (Luke 24:30–31). This is not the Lord’s Supper, but Mark has laid the two scenes on top of each other on purpose. The man who feeds a hillside with broken bread is going to be broken himself, and the church has been fed from that ever since.

The bread went out through their hands. He hands it to the Twelve. Somewhere between the Lord’s hands and the hundredth row, there kept on being more, and the carriers were the men who had proved by arithmetic that it could not be done. That is how he still works: he gives his provision to his church to carry, and the carriers discover that there is enough only as they hand it out.

They all ate and were satisfied. A full meal, not a taste: a plain, earthy word for being fed until you want no more, and each had fish as well as bread. In the wilderness God gave Israel manna, and they were satisfied (Exodus 16:12; Psalm 78:24–29). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. He is greater than Moses and Elisha. John records his explanation: I am the bread of life (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that people simply shared hidden lunches, as some have suggested. The Gospels describe a miracle of creation. If it were a lesson in sharing, nobody would have tried to make him king that night (John 6:14–15), and nobody would have needed twelve baskets for the leftovers.

Should we give thanks before every meal? It is a good and biblical habit, though no rule requires a set form. Jesus gave thanks before eating here, at the Last Supper, and at Emmaus; Paul gave thanks for bread in front of a shipload of pagans in a storm (Acts 27:35), and says that everything created by God is good and is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A few honest words before a meal remind us that our food comes from our Father’s hand, keep gratitude from going stale, and teach children where their daily bread comes from. Say it, and mean it.

Can a thoughtful person today believe this really happened? Yes, and the question is really about Jesus, not about bread. If God made the world out of nothing, making bread from five loaves is no strain on him; the miracle is impossible only if there is no God, and that is the very thing in question. So the real issue is whether Jesus is who he claimed to be, and the strongest evidence for that is his resurrection, reported by people who had seen him alive and would die rather than deny it (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The feeding is told in all four Gospels, with details that fit the memory of people who were there: the green grass, the barley loaves, the count of baskets. Details alone cannot prove a miracle, and some reply that the church made such stories up later; but the Gospels were written while many who had been on that hillside were still alive, and the weight finally rests on the witnesses to the risen Christ. Faith here is not believing against the evidence. It is trusting the one the evidence points to.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Broken pieces. John tells us the gathering up was commanded: Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost (John 6:12). The one who has just created bread out of five loaves will not have scraps trodden into the grass. Abundance in the kingdom of God never licenses waste.

Twelve baskets. One for each disciple, or a sign for the twelve tribes, and perhaps both. Each man who went out among the rows with an impossible task comes back carrying a full wicker basket (kophinos).

The arithmetic comes out backwards. More food at the end than at the start: that is how things add up in God’s kingdom, and it is why asking about two hundred denarii was the wrong question. God is able to make all grace abound to you (2 Corinthians 9:8).

Five thousand men. Almost a footnote. The word means adult males; Matthew adds, besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). Perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand people altogether, probably more than any town in Galilee except Tiberias and Sepphoris.

What the crowd did not understand. John records that they tried to make him king by force that night and had to be dispersed (John 6:15). They had eaten from his hands and concluded that a man who can do that should be running the country. They were nearly right, and entirely wrong. He had not come to be the kind of king who keeps a nation fed. He had come to be the bread, and when he said so the next day, many of them left (John 6:66).

Does this mean God will always give me plenty? No. God promises to supply every need of his people according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19), but he does not promise wealth or comfort, and Paul learned to be content in hunger as well as plenty (Philippians 4:11–13). Many faithful Christians are poor, and some go hungry for Christ’s sake. What this miracle promises is that the Lord knows our needs, cares about our bodies, is never short of resources, and will give us everything we need to do his will and reach his kingdom. And it points beyond bread to himself: the abundance he guarantees without limit is grace.

For worship. With Christ there are always more fragments than there were loaves, and not a crumb of what he gives is lost. He is the King who would not be crowned by a full crowd because he had come to be broken for an empty world. As he gathered the fragments from the grass, so he will lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He made his disciples get into the boat. The word (ēnankasen) means compelled; the disciples plainly did not want to go. Why the urgency? John tells us: the crowd wanted to take Jesus by force to make him king (John 6:14–15). Five thousand fed men in an occupied country is a rebellion looking for a leader, and one of the Twelve was a Zealot, from a movement that fought Rome. So he sent the disciples ahead to Bethsaida (John 1:44) before they were swept up in it.

While he dismissed the crowd. He refused the crown they offered: a crown offered freely, by the shout of a crowd, without a cross. The shortest road to glory has been laid in front of him before, by the devil in the wilderness (1:13; Matthew 4:8–9). He will not take a kingdom on those terms, because a king who feeds you is not the same as a king who saves you. He walked away from a crown that would have cost him nothing, because he had come to wear one that would cost him everything.

On the mountain to pray. Here is the pattern of his life. He has had no rest; he has taught for hours, fed thousands and defused a political crisis. What he does with the first free hour is climb a hill in the dark to pray.

Three nights of prayer. This is the second of three times Mark shows Jesus praying alone at night (1:35; 14:32–39), each at a moment of temptation or decision. The three moments are success, the offer of glory and the approach of death, and he meets all three the same way. We tend to pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at all at the first two. We treat prosperity as a season that needs no prayer, yet it is the season in which many are most easily lost (Deuteronomy 8:10–14).

Alone on the land. They cannot see him, and night has come down between them. That is what a hard stretch feels like from inside the boat. But a man alone on a mountain at night, praying, is not absent from the boat. He is keeping watch over it.

Why did Jesus refuse to be made king? Because he was already King, and because the crown they offered was the wrong one. They wanted a ruler who would drive out Rome and keep the bread coming. He had come to deal with a deeper enemy, sin and death, and that could only be done by the cross. To accept their crown would have been to bypass the cross, which is exactly what Satan had offered in the wilderness. He would be crowned, but with thorns first, and then at the Father’s right hand (Philippians 2:8–11). His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36); it comes by word and Spirit, not by force.

Should Christians then avoid politics? Not necessarily. Christians may serve as rulers, judges and officials, as Joseph and Daniel did, and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7). What this passage warns against is confusing Christ’s kingdom with any political cause, or trying to bring in his rule by force, popularity or votes. No party is the kingdom of God. Serve faithfully wherever you are placed, pray for those in authority, and keep your deepest hope fixed on the King who refused a crowd’s crown and will return in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He saw. This may be the most comforting sentence in the chapter. He is up a mountain in the middle of the night, and they are three or four miles out on the lake (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing this was, he was watching them the whole time. Every fact available to them said they were alone. He sees every boat in the dark, and none of his people rows unwatched.

Making headway painfully. The word (basanizomenous) means tormented, tortured. This is not a storm that threatens to sink them, as in chapter 4. It is worse in a particular way: hours of grinding, exhausting, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore does not get closer.

For the wind was against them. They are out there because he sent them: obedience put them in the wind. Here is the shape of a great deal of Christian experience: you are where he put you, pulling as hard as you can, nothing is moving, and he appears to be somewhere else. And the verse tells you what you cannot know from inside the boat: he went up the mountain to pray, and from that mountain he saw them. Those two facts are still true together: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25), and the Father always hears the Son (John 11:42).

The fourth watch. Between about 3 and 6 a.m., after perhaps nine hours of rowing. He came in the last watch, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling. He is never early, as we would arrange it, and he has never yet been late.

Walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. Job says that God alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); the psalmist says, Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19). Mark’s readers knew those books.

He meant to pass by them. A puzzling phrase, found only in Mark. In the Old Testament, God passing by is how he reveals his glory: he passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock and proclaimed his name (Exodus 33:19–22; 34:6), and passed by Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11). And Job, describing the God who trampled the waves, says three verses later, Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:11). So he is showing them who he is. He was not passing them by. He was passing before them, so that they could see who had been watching from the mountain.

If Jesus sees me struggling, why does he wait so long? Because his timing serves purposes we cannot see from the boat. The disciples learned that night what they could not have learned at the first hour: that he watches, that he comes, and that he is the Lord of the sea. Delay is not neglect. The Lord is not slow as some count slowness (2 Peter 3:9), and his help comes at the hour he has fixed. Meanwhile he is not idle; he is interceding. Keep rowing where he has put you, keep praying, and expect him, not on your schedule, but certainly on his.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They thought it was a ghost. Of course they did. Mark’s word is phantasma: an apparition, perhaps an evil sea spirit, in the dark before dawn.

The Lord in the shape of their worst fear. Their instinct was not stupid; it was human. The one thing that could actually save them looked, in the dark, like the thing most likely to kill them. God has a way of coming to his people wearing the shape of what they most dread. Joseph’s brothers did not recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. The thing bearing down on you out of the dark this year may be the Lord at work, and you will not necessarily know it at the time.

They all saw him. This was not one man’s imagination: four of them were professional fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night. Their terror is more fitting than they know. When the holy God draws near, sinful people tremble, as Isaiah did in the temple and Peter did in another boat (Isaiah 6:5; Luke 5:8). What they took for a ghost was the Holy One himself, and that is why his first word to them is mercy.

Immediately he spoke. His voice comes first. Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is the order in which he deals with frightened people.

It is I. In Greek egō eimi, literally I am. It can simply mean it is me; in everyday speech it is how you identify yourself in the dark. But it is also God’s name revealed to Moses at the burning bush, when Moses asked for his name (Exodus 3:14), and God’s words in Isaiah: I am he; before me no god was formed (Isaiah 43:10), and I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 51:12). And they are spoken here by a man standing on a sea that the Scriptures say God alone tramples.

Do not be afraid. God’s words when he reveals himself (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10). The command rests entirely on the middle phrase, it is I: the reason not to fear is not the weather but a Person, and the name he uses is the name from the bush. He does not tell them the wind will drop; he tells them who is with them, and treats that as sufficient. It is. That is the whole of Christian comfort in three phrases, and every one of them was spoken from the middle of the water they were afraid of.

Is Jesus really claiming to be God here? Yes, though he does it in the way Mark loves: by deeds and echoes rather than a lecture. Walking on the sea is what Scripture says God alone does; passing by is how God shows his glory; I am is God’s name. Any one of those might be a coincidence; all three together, in one scene, are a revelation. The same Jesus will say I am before the high priest and be condemned for blasphemy (14:62–64). The disciples would not grasp it fully until after the resurrection, but Mark wants his readers to grasp it now: the man in the boat is the LORD.

What do I do with fear that will not go away? Listen to the order of Jesus’ words. He does not first remove the storm; he first tells you who he is. So when fear grips you, do not only ask him to change your circumstances. Remind yourself who is with you: the Lord who made the sea, who walked on it, who died and rose and holds your life. Speak his promises aloud (Isaiah 41:10; Hebrews 13:5–6). Bring the fear to him in prayer as it is (Philippians 4:6–7). If anxiety is constant and crippling, seek help from a pastor or a doctor as well; that is not unbelief. And expect that faith may coexist with trembling for a while. Courage is not the absence of fear but trust in the One who is greater.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wind ceased. After a night of terror, the ending is almost domestic: a man climbs over the side and sits down with them. Mark does not even say he rebuked the wind this time. It simply stops, because he is aboard. (Mark does not record Peter walking on the water; Matthew does, Matthew 14:28–31.)

Utterly astounded. Beyond measure astonished, as when the little girl got up (5:42). And then Mark says something about his own leaders that a church inventing flattering stories would hardly have written.

They did not understand about the loaves. Only Mark adds this, and the connection is not the one we would expect: the walking on water astonished them because they had not understood the loaves. That afternoon they had carried food out of his hands to thousands and drawn no conclusion from it about who he was. The reason a new trouble knocks us flat is very often the same: we drew nothing from the last deliverance.

Their hearts were hardened. The same root word was used of the Pharisees who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to plan a murder (3:5). These are the apostles, and their hearts are described in the words Mark used for his opponents; disciples suffer from it too (8:17), and it does not announce itself. It is not disbelief; the Twelve believed a great deal. It is slowly becoming unable to be moved: the same truths arrive and produce nothing, and a man can carry the bread and never taste it. If Peter is Mark’s source, Peter told this story against himself.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were unbelievers like the Pharisees. But it shows that even true followers need God to open their eyes again and again (8:22–26). The hardening was real and it was not final. He kept them, was denied by them, and after the resurrection fed them breakfast on a beach. He does not give up on hard-hearted disciples. He gets into the boat with them. He does not wait for us to understand before he comes aboard. And if you fear this describes you because your feelings have gone flat, remember that grief, exhaustion and depression can numb a believer whose heart is still turned towards Christ; that is weakness to be carried, not hardness to be feared.

In the flow. Mark will press the point again in another boat (8:17–21), and then Peter at last confesses, You are the Christ (8:29). The slow eyes of the Twelve, and the patience of the One who opens them, run through the whole Gospel.

How can I stop forgetting what God has done? By deliberately remembering, which is what Scripture keeps telling God’s people to do. Israel was told to set up stones, keep feasts and tell their children (Joshua 4:6–7; Deuteronomy 6:12). So keep a record of answered prayers and deliverances, and read it back when trouble comes. Speak of God’s past mercies to others, at home and in church. Come to the Lord’s Supper as a feast of remembrance (1 Corinthians 11:24–25). And ask the Spirit to soften your heart, because remembering is not merely a technique; it is grace. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Psalm 103:2).

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gennesaret. A fertile plain on the northwest shore, between Capernaum and Magdala. He had sent them towards Bethsaida; the headwind of the night is the likeliest reason they land somewhere else. The boat touches the shore, and the people immediately recognise him.

On their beds. Carried on mats, as the paralysed man had been (2:3). They are chasing a moving target: he is walking, so the beds are being carried from place to place after him, all day, by relays of neighbours and relatives.

In the marketplaces. The square where everything happened, and the sick laid out in rows in the way of everybody. These people have stopped caring how it looks. There is a certain kind of desperation that has burned through embarrassment entirely, and Christ has never once despised it.

Even the fringe of his garment. The fringe was the tassel on the corner of a Jewish man’s garment, commanded as a reminder of the commandments of the LORD (Numbers 15:38–40). A woman with twelve years of bleeding had reached from behind to touch his garments (5:27–34), and now a whole region is doing what she did: somebody tells what happened to them, and a district comes.

As many as touched it. The word for made well can also mean saved. Not one was turned away, and Mark does not tell us that anyone’s theology was corrected first. Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious, as hers had been. He does not lecture them about the tassel. He heals them. His power is undiminished by our ignorance, his mercy undeterred by our superstitions, and his welcome as wide as the marketplaces of Galilee.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power. The power was his own, received by faith.

The contrast. The chapter began in Jesus’ hometown, which rejected him and saw few miracles. It ends with crowds who sought him eagerly and were healed. The difference is faith. Nazareth had every advantage and would not stretch out a hand. Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat. What separated them was never how much they knew. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him. That is good news for the irreligious, who fear they know too little to come to him, and a warning to the religious, who are sure they know enough not to need to.

In the flow. In the very next scene Pharisees from Jerusalem complain that his disciples eat with unwashed hands (7:1–5). Here the sick touch him and are made whole; there religious men worry about the dirt on other people’s hands. What matters is not how clean you are when you come, but whom you touch.

Why does Jesus not heal everyone like this today? Because these mass healings were signs of who he is and of what his kingdom will finally bring, given in a unique moment as the King arrived. They were not a promise that every illness will be removed in this life. Christ still heals, in answer to prayer and through medicine, as he wills. But the full fulfilment of this scene is still ahead: on the last day, every one of his people will be raised with a body that no disease can touch, and there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain (Revelation 21:4). Gennesaret was a preview. The resurrection is the whole picture.

In everyday life. Who is the sick or burdened person you could carry to him this week, in prayer, by a visit, by bringing them to church? Be one of the neighbours who carry the beds; no one who comes to him is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
The loaves and the sea are one lesson. The feeding shows the Shepherd of Psalm 23 and a greater Moses; the walking on the sea shows the God who alone tramples the waves (Job 9:8) and speaks his own name in the dark. The disciples were astonished at the sea because they did not understand about the loaves (v. 52).

And their hearts were hardened is said of the apostles, in the word used of the men who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). It is not disbelief. It is slowly becoming unable to be moved by what you see and hear, so that a man can carry the bread and never taste it. It was real and it was not final: he got into the boat with them.
6.examples:
Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests. It was not conscience: his conscience told him John was righteous. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Now: people often do the worst thing they ever do because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable. Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25). The way out is to fear God more than people: someone who already has God’s approval in Christ can afford to lose face rather than do wrong.

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes down a wall, and then walks through the gap.

A delegation from Jerusalem has travelled ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands. Jesus quotes Isaiah at them, and proves the charge with one example: Corban, a vow that could put a man's money beyond his parents' reach by declaring it dedicated to God.

Then he tells the crowd that there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, and Mark adds, thus he declared all foods clean. The food laws had kept Jew and Gentile apart, so that boundary goes too.

Having removed it, he crosses it: a Phoenician mother takes his own hard saying and finds hope in it, and a deaf man in the Decapolis, brought by friends, is given his hearing with one Aramaic word. The crowd's verdict is bigger than they know: he has done all things well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The complaint (vv. 1–5). A second delegation arrives from Jerusalem, and what they have come to raise is that the disciples do not wash their hands before eating.

The answer (vv. 6–13). Jesus quotes Isaiah: their lips are near, their hearts far, and they teach human rules as though God had given them. Then he gives one example, the Corban vow.

The principle (vv. 14–23). Nothing that goes into a person can defile him. Mark adds thus he declared all foods clean, and Jesus tells the disciples in private where defilement actually comes from.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost or hidden. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16. Later copies add if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear, a sentence Jesus certainly said and Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23), probably first written in a margin and later taken for part of the text.

The verse numbers were added only in the sixteenth century, so translators left the number empty and put the words in a footnote, telling you so rather than quietly leaving them in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban, a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God's name.

Now: the same thing still happens, and almost never with conscious dishonesty: the man so committed at church that his mother has not had a visit in four months. So the passage supplies its own question: is keeping any tradition of mine currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them? Jesus attacks not tradition as such but tradition set level with Scripture and then used against it. And the test case he chooses is one anyone can measure: not prayer or fasting, but whether the old people in your family are being looked after (Jas. 1:27; 1 Tim. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 7 asks where uncleanness really lives. Inspectors from Jerusalem complain that Jesus’ disciples skip the elders’ ritual hand-washing; Jesus answers with Isaiah and with the Corban rule, and tells the crowd that defilement comes out of the heart, not into the stomach. Then he walks into Gentile country, where a mother receives the crumbs and a deaf man is opened. The experts go home unmoved; the outsiders receive the bread.

Setting. This is the second delegation from Jerusalem in this Gospel; the first decided that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (3:22). These men have come some ninety miles as inspectors, and they do not seem to be here to learn. The crowds are being fed, healed and taught (6:30–56), and the experts’ concern is how the disciples hold their bread.

The Pharisees gathered to him. They collect around him, the way a committee collects. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law, including the purity rules that the Old Testament gave to priests, which they applied to ordinary daily life. The scribes were the professional experts in the law, many of them Pharisees.

Hands that were defiled. This is what they came for. They are standing in front of a man who has raised a dead girl and fed a district on five loaves, and they have taken notes on his catering. The word (koinais) literally means common: not set apart as holy, and therefore ritually unclean. Mark explains it, that is, unwashed, for Gentile readers.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about hygiene. The washing in question had nothing to do with germs; it was a religious rite that the law of Moses did not command for ordinary people.

The hands that make clean. Jesus touched a leper, and instead of the leper’s uncleanness passing to him, his cleanness passed to the leper (1:41–42); a bleeding woman touched his garment and was healed (5:27–29). With Jesus the contagion is reversed, and holiness is what spreads. The inspectors are checking the disciples’ hands while standing beside the only man in Israel of whom Psalm 24:4 is wholly true, clean hands and a pure heart.
