The two men in all Scripture who had asked to see the glory of God and been given a glimpse of it are standing on another mountain, looking straight at it. They asked to see. Now they see, and it has a face and a name and is going to Jerusalem to die.

And they were talking with Jesus. Luke tells us they spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and the word is exodos. Moses led the first exodus, out of slavery in Egypt, and here he is discussing the greater one, out of slavery to sin and death, with the man who will lead it. This time the way out is opened not through a sea but by a cross, and the blood that shields the people is not a lamb’s but his own. Six days ago Peter tried to talk Jesus out of the cross. Now the Law and the Prophets appear in glory and talk about nothing else. Heaven’s greatest saints are not interested in themselves. They are absorbed in what he is about to do at Jerusalem.

Will I know my loved ones in heaven? This scene gives real grounds for hope that you will. Moses and Elijah were themselves, recognisable, and the disciples knew who they were without being introduced. Death does not dissolve the person God made. The believer who dies is with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), awaiting the resurrection of the body. Scripture does not answer every question about what that life is like, but it never suggests that we become strangers to one another. What it promises above all is that we will know him, and in knowing him we will not lose those who are his.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to Jesus, "Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah." For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Peter is not wrong about that, and there is nothing to criticise in the gladness. But “Rabbi”, teacher, falls far short of what he has just seen.

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters of branches; the word also means tabernacles, like the tabernacle in the wilderness where God’s glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34). Peter very likely had the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which the prophets had made a picture of the age to come, when God would dwell with his people at last (Zechariah 14:16–19). So Peter is thinking: this is it, the age of God dwelling with men is beginning. Let us set up and stay. But Peter wanted to build the Lord a shelter, and the Lord was about to build Peter one: not of branches but of his own body, broken and raised, the true tabernacle in which God dwells with men for ever.

One for Moses and one for Elijah. Three things are wrong with it. He wants to stay: six days ago he heard that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed, and he objected; now, on a mountain full of light, his instinct is to make the moment permanent. It is the same instinct in a nicer form: anything but the road down to the cross. He wants to build something: faced with the unveiled glory of God, his impulse is to get busy, to organise, to be useful, when the moment called him simply to stand still and behold. And he makes it three: equal accommodation, equal honour. It is the kindest possible mistake and it is still a mistake, and the voice from the cloud is about to correct precisely that.

Jesus in a row of great men. Peter’s error is not disbelief. He is being warm, reverent, hospitable and enthusiastic. He is also arranging the Son of God as one of three, and that is a thing people still do: Jesus placed respectfully in a line of great teachers, given his own shelter, honoured among the founders of the world’s religions. He fits nowhere in such a row. He is not the best of the prophets. He is the one the prophets came to see.

They were terrified. Early tradition says that Mark wrote down what Peter preached. If so, this is Peter, years later, telling the church: I had no idea what to say, so I said something. When Isaiah saw the Lord he cried, Woe is me (Isaiah 6:5), because a sinful man before perfect holiness sees at once what he is. The fear on the mountain was not foolishness. It was the right reaction to the holy God, and only the Son’s presence made it survivable.

Filling the silence. In the presence of something too large, real glory, real grief, the impulse is to fill the space. Job’s friends were faultless for seven days while they said nothing, and ruined it the moment they opened their mouths. At a graveside or a hospital bed the pressure to produce a sentence is enormous and almost always better resisted. Be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10). Peter could not be still, and Mark did not hide it. And the Son of God bore with a frightened fisherman’s nonsense in the very hour of his glory, and did not withdraw.

Is it wrong to want to stay on the mountain? Not to love it. The longing to remain in God’s presence is holy, and it will be fully satisfied in the age to come, when God will dwell with his people and the tabernacle will be permanent (Revelation 21:3). Peter’s mistake was timing. He wanted the glory without the cross, and the end before the road. So treasure the moments of nearness God gives you, in worship, in Scripture, at the Lord’s Table, and do not despise them. But do not try to live in them. They are given to strengthen you for the valley, not to excuse you from it.
verseByVerse.note: The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a cloud overshadowed them. The cloud is not weather. It went before Israel out of Egypt, settled on Sinai and filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 13:21; 24:15–18; 40:34–35): the visible sign that God himself has come down. “Overshadowed” is the word used of the cloud settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), and the word the angel used to Mary (Luke 1:35). So Peter, who wanted to build three shelters, is enveloped in the real one. God does not need his branches. He has brought his own dwelling, and it has covered them.

And a voice came out of the cloud. The Father speaks, as at the baptism (1:11), the only other time in Mark that God speaks from heaven. At the Jordan the voice spoke to Jesus: You are my beloved Son. Here it says, This is my beloved Son: the same testimony, turned outward, addressed to three men standing there. God is telling somebody else who this is.

This is my beloved Son. This answers Peter’s mistake. Jesus is not one of three equals; he is the Son. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). “Beloved” may also carry the sense of only, as with Abraham’s only son Isaac, whom he loved and was told to offer on a mountain (Genesis 22:2). The Father loves the Son, and on that mountain he could not keep it to himself. The eternal delight of God in his beloved broke through the cloud in words, and the words were for us. And consider the timing. The Father’s public endorsement comes six days after the Son announced that he was going to be rejected and killed, precisely at the point where the plan looks like failure, as if to say: this is the one I love, and the road he has just described is the road I sent him down.

Listen to him. The only command the Father speaks from heaven in the whole Gospel of Mark. Not build for him, which is what Peter proposed. Not feel something, which is what the moment was producing. Listen. There is an echo underneath it that Moses would have recognised, since he is standing there: God would raise up a prophet like him, and to him you shall listen (Deuteronomy 18:15). The voice from the cloud is telling three Jewish fishermen that the promise has arrived.

Listen to him about what? About the last thing he said, which they had refused to accept. The command is aimed straight at the argument at Caesarea Philippi. Jesus had said he must suffer and die (8:31), and that they must take up their cross (8:34), and Peter had rebuked him for it. The Father says: do not correct him; hear him. Which is the plainest practical word in the chapter. Whatever else God wants from you, this is what he has said out loud: listen to his Son. Not to your instincts about what the Christian life ought to look like. Not to the version of Jesus you find manageable. To him, including the parts you would rather he had not said.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Through his word: he speaks now by the Spirit through the Scriptures, and listening means reading and hearing them with the intention of obeying, especially where it costs. (See Acts 3:22 for the fuller answer.)

Jesus only. This is the phrase the whole scene exists for. The Law has done its work and stepped back. The Prophets have done theirs and stepped back. Everything Israel had been given over more than a thousand years was pointing at this man, and when he is fully in view the pointers are not needed. What is left standing is what was there before the vision began and will be there after every vision any Christian ever has: an ordinary-looking man from Nazareth, who is the Son of God, and no one else. And he is enough.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence at Sinai and over the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were coming down the mountain. The shelters were never built, and within a paragraph the three are back in a shouting crowd. Nobody lives on the mountain.

Tell no one. Not even the other nine. But for the first time in Mark the ban has an expiry date: not tell no one, full stop, but tell no one until.

Until the Son of Man had risen. The limit is the resurrection, which tells you what the secret was always for. It was never permanent concealment. It was timing. The truth about him was kept back until the cross and the empty tomb could show what kind of Messiah he is. Tell people of his glory without his cross, and they will expect exactly the conquering Messiah Peter had in mind six days ago. After the resurrection the glory can be told, because then it will be understood.

So they kept the matter to themselves. They obeyed, and for once in this Gospel people told to keep quiet about him actually do: the healed leper and the crowds in the Decapolis had spread the news at once (1:45; 7:36). But they were puzzled.

What this rising might mean. These three have just seen the Son of God shining, and they walk down the hill arguing about what he could mean by rising from the dead. It is not that they disbelieved in resurrection as such. Jews who believed in it, as the Pharisees did, expected it at the end of the age, for all the righteous together (Daniel 12:2; John 11:24). What they could not fit together was a Messiah who dies and then, alone, in the middle of history, gets up. They had no place in their thinking for that, nor for a Messiah who must die at all.

A story nobody expected. This counts against the idea that the disciples simply made the resurrection up. People do not easily invent a story they were plainly not expecting, had no framework for, and did not understand when it was explained to them in advance. Someone may reply that the church wrote the confusion in later; but a church inventing stories would hardly make its own leaders look so slow. Mark records their bafflement without embarrassment, most naturally because it is what happened.

What if I have read something many times and still do not understand it? Then you are in good company, and it is not necessarily unbelief. These three heard the words plainly and could not take them in. Sometimes a truth is bigger than the categories you have, and it will not fit until something makes room for it. For them it was an empty tomb; for you it may be years of reading, a trial, or a sermon that suddenly joins two passages. Keep reading, keep asking, and read with the cross and resurrection in view, because they are the key that opens the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?" And he said to them, "Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come? The question follows naturally: they have just seen Elijah. The scribes taught it from the closing words of the prophets: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (Malachi 4:5). Elijah comes first, to turn hearts and prepare the people; then the Day. So if Elijah has only now appeared, to three men in private, where does that leave the order of events? If Jesus is the Messiah, where was the forerunner who should have come first? The scribes were very likely making exactly that objection: he cannot be the Christ, because Elijah has not come.

To restore all things. Jesus agrees with the teaching: the scribes are right about the order, and Elijah’s work is restoration, turning the hearts of fathers to their children and of children to their fathers (Malachi 4:6).

And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? Then, in the middle of answering, he turns a question back on them, and it is the more important one. Since you are so attentive to what is written about Elijah, what have you done with what is written about the Son of Man? “Treated with contempt” (exoudenēthē) means regarded as nothing. And he assumes they know where it is written. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows (Isaiah 53:3); all who see me mock me (Psalm 22:7); the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22); they will look on him whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10). It had been read and sung in Israel for centuries, and a nation had built a Messiah out of the conquering passages and quietly stepped over the suffering ones. Both sets of passages are true. Elijah would come and restore, and the Messiah would still be rejected.

The verses we skip. That temptation is not only an ancient one; it is ours too. We assemble a picture of God from the verses we like and treat the rest as background noise: the promises without the warnings, the comfort without the cost, the Jesus who accepts without the Jesus who commands.

Elijah has come. The forerunner has already been and gone, and they missed him, because he did not look like Elijah returned in fire. He looked like a man in camel’s hair by a river, dressed like Elijah himself (1:6; 2 Kings 1:8). Matthew says the disciples understood that he was speaking of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:13), and the angel had said it before John was born: he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

Was John the Baptist Elijah come back? Not in person. When asked directly, John said he was not Elijah (John 1:21), and he was right: he was not the Tishbite returned from heaven, and Scripture gives no support to the idea of souls returning in new bodies. But he came in Elijah’s spirit and power and did Elijah’s work. Malachi’s promise was fulfilled not by reappearance but by a new prophet in the old mould. So both statements are true: John was not Elijah, and Elijah has come.

Whatever they pleased. Herod arrested and beheaded him, and his head was carried into a banquet on a dish because a girl danced well (6:17–29). As Jezebel had sought to kill the first Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), so Herodias destroyed the second. As it is written of him points not to a single prophecy of John’s death but to the pattern of Elijah’s life in Scripture: a prophet persecuted by a wicked king and queen.

The herald and the King. The point of this exchange is not the order of end-time events. God’s plan often looks like failure, and what happened to the herald will happen to the King: they did to John whatever they pleased, and they will do the same to the Son of Man. He is walking down that mountain with the glory barely faded off him, telling three men that the road runs the same way it ran for John.

For worship. He did not walk into his death by accident. He read it in his own Scriptures and walked toward it with open eyes, because those same Scriptures said it would bring many sons to glory. The Christ the scribes could not imagine, crowned with thorns, is the only Christ who could save us.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah, in Jesus’ words, is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. And he asked them, "What are you arguing about with them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the mountain to the valley. Mark’s cut is deliberate: from the light on the mountainside straight into noise at the bottom. Raphael’s last painting puts the transfigured Christ in the upper half of the canvas and this scene in the lower, the convulsing boy and the pointing hands, because the two belong in one frame. The glory of the mountain does not take Jesus away from the misery of the world; it sends him into it.

Scribes arguing with them. A great crowd: this is public. Scribes, the professional opponents, who have found the disciples in a failure and are pressing it in front of everybody, probably to discredit their master. Nine men had promised something and not delivered it, with a sick child on the ground and their critics in full voice.

The come-down. The come-down is not a sign that the mountain was false. The three had genuinely seen the glory of God, and it did not exempt them from walking into a shouting match. The retreat ends and Monday arrives with nothing changed: that is the shape of the Christian life, and Mark has arranged his Gospel to prepare you for it.

Greatly amazed. The whole crowd turns. Mark’s word is strong, the one he uses for the women’s alarm at the empty tomb (16:5–6). Mark does not say why. Some think something of the glory still lingered on him, as Moses’ face shone when he came down (Exodus 34:29–30), though here people ran toward him rather than away. It may simply be the shock of his arrival at the exact moment of a public humiliation. Either way, the argument stops and everybody runs.

What are you arguing about with them? With one question he takes possession of the scene. He does not upbraid the nine in front of the crowd. He asks what the argument is about, and by asking he moves himself into the middle of it, and the scribes are now arguing with him. He steps between his failed disciples and the men attacking them, and that is the first act of the rescue. Whatever he has to say to the nine he will say inside a house, privately, at the end (v. 28).

In everyday life. If you lead or correct others, treat them as he treated the nine: defended in public, dealt with in private.

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, I brought my son to you. Teacher: the smallest title in the chapter. I brought my son: he has done the one thing available to him. Luke adds that he was his only child (Luke 9:38). And to you: he came looking for Jesus, and Jesus was up a mountain, and he got the disciples instead.

A spirit that makes him mute. The boy cannot speak, and verse 25 adds that he cannot hear either. He has never told his father what it is like.

It throws him down. It is a father’s detail; he has watched this many times. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses the ordinary word for a person with seizures (Matthew 17:15). But Mark is clear that the cause here was a demon, which Jesus casts out (v. 25); a demon could cause physical symptoms. Not all illness is demonic, and the Gospels list the sick and the demonised separately (1:32–34). But this case was.

Should seizures or mental illness be treated as possession? No, and it must not be made to follow from this passage. That inference has done immense harm to suffering people, and the Bible does not license it. Scripture routinely distinguishes ordinary illness from demonic affliction; this is a specific case in which the two were bound together, and Jesus knew it because he knows all things. We do not. If your child has epilepsy, this passage is not a diagnosis. Take them to a doctor, which is an ordinary mercy of God, and pray for them, which is another. Medicine and prayer are not rivals.

Is belief in demons just ancient superstition? It is a fair question, and the Gospels do not answer it by blaming everything on demons; as we have seen, they keep illness and possession apart. Jesus spoke of Satan and evil spirits as real persons, and he spoke of them calmly, as a master speaks of servants who must obey. If he is who the voice from the cloud said he is, his view of the unseen world is better informed than ours. And the modern world has not made evil smaller. It has only made it harder to name.

They were not able. Said quietly, without accusation, and everything that follows turns on it. It was a painful failure: Jesus had given them authority over unclean spirits (6:7), and they had cast out many demons (6:13). Now they could not. Jesus will give the reason in verses 19 and 29: unbelief, and prayerlessness.

To you, and not to them. The father came for Jesus and found only his followers. Their authority had always been his, lent and never owned, and what the servants could not do, the Master will do with one sentence. The church can fail a sufferer; Christ never has, and the father’s to you was aimed at the right person all along.

What if I am caring for someone who cannot be fixed? Then this man is in your Bible on purpose. He has spent years watching his child thrown to the ground. He has never had a conversation with him. He has lifted him off floors, cleaned him up and lived with the sound of it, and Jesus is about to give him a great deal of time. Your long, unseen labour is known to the Lord, and he is not impatient with your weariness or your questions. Bring the one you care for to him, as this father did, again and again. And if the church has let you down, do not let that become your final word about Christ.

In everyday life. Find someone carrying a long burden, a sick child, a disabled spouse, an ageing parent, and do one concrete thing for them this week: a meal, an hour so they can sleep, a message that says you are praying.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O faithless generation. One of the sharpest things Jesus says in the Gospel, and a hasty reading turns it into impatience with a suffering father, which it is not. Mark says he answered them, plural: a generation, not a man. It takes in the nine who failed, the scribes who were arguing, and the crowd who came to watch. It is not aimed at the father, who is the one person there doing the right thing. The words echo God’s own complaint against Israel in the wilderness: a crooked generation, children in whom is no faithfulness (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20).

How long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? And the tone is not irritation at inconvenience. It is God’s language. The LORD in the wilderness said: How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs? (Numbers 14:11). It is the grief of a God who has done everything and been believed by almost nobody. These are the words of one who does not belong to this world, who has come from the Father and is going back, a visitor among unbelievers. “Bear with” (anexomai) means put up with, endure. It shows the real cost to Jesus of living among sinners, even his own disciples. And there is a shadow of the cross in it: he is not going to be with them much longer, and he knows it. He is a man measuring the little time he has left against how slowly his people are learning. He bore with them in Galilee, and at the cross he bore far more than their slowness: he bore their sin.

A second Sinai. Moses came down from the mountain of glory to find Israel worshipping a calf (Exodus 32); Jesus comes down to find a faithless generation. But where Moses broke the tablets, Jesus calls for the boy.

Bring him to me. The rebuke ends and the rescue begins in the same breath. He does not say: come back when you have more faith. Whatever his grief, he does not turn the child away.

Does Jesus get tired of me? He feels the weight of unbelief; this verse proves it, and you should not make his patience cheap. But look at what his weariness does. It does not withdraw; it calls the boy over. His patience is not a fuse that will one day run out on a believer who keeps coming. It is the patience of the God who passed before Moses as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). If you have hesitated to bring something to him because you were ashamed of the state of your faith, this chapter holds a hard word about unbelief and an immediate invitation, spoken by the same voice. The rebuke is real. It is not a refusal.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the spirit saw him. The demon recognises Jesus and rages, as demons have since chapter 1 (1:24; 3:11). And there is a hard mercy in the timing, though it will not have felt like it to the father. The worst seizure the boy has, he has in front of Jesus. What had been happening in fields and houses where nobody could help is now happening in the one place where something can be done about it.

And Jesus asked his father, How long has this been happening to him? This question is one of the most surprising things in the passage. There is a boy convulsing at his feet. Jesus has driven out a legion of demons and silenced a storm with a word. And he turns to the father and asks about the case history. Whatever he already knew, the question is not mainly for information. It is for the father. Nobody has asked this man anything. He has carried this alone for years; he has just been let down in front of a crowd; and the Son of God stops the scene and asks him how long it has been going on. That is pastoral care of a kind most of us never manage. Faced with a crisis, we go straight to the problem. He goes to the person, and lets him talk. The father needs as much attention as the son.

From childhood. Not a recent illness: a hard case, long established. The father may never have heard his son’s voice; the boy has hardly known a normal day.

Into fire and into water. Every hearth and every well in that man’s life has been a threat for years, and he has pulled his son out of them often. And he understands what he is dealing with: to destroy him. He is not describing bad luck. There is an intention behind it. That is Satan’s purpose for every human being: the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy (John 10:10).

But if you can do anything. He did not arrive with that clause. The doubt has got in through the crack the nine’s failure made, and it still works that way. People’s confidence in the Lord is regularly damaged by his people: the church that let them down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell. They come to Christ afterwards with an if you can that was not there before.

Have compassion on us. Not on him; on us. It is the whole family’s affliction, and he asks for the one thing he knows to ask for: compassion, the word used of Jesus’ own heart for the crowds (6:34).

Why does God allow a child to suffer for years? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, and we should not pretend it does. But this passage gives us what we most need. It names the evil for what it is: not God’s delight but an enemy’s work, aiming at destruction. It shows that the suffering is seen, in detail, by Jesus, who asks about it. And it shows him overthrowing it. God permits evil for a time for purposes he has not fully explained, but he is not its author in the way the destroyer is, and he has not left it unanswered. The final answer is a cross where he took the worst of it upon himself, and a resurrection that promises an end of it.

In everyday life. When you are with someone in trouble, copy the Lord’s question: ask how long it has been, and listen to the answer before you offer anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If you can”! Jesus hands the man’s own words back, abruptly. It is not mockery. The if is in the wrong place: the father has attached it to Jesus’ ability, and the question is not whether Jesus can but whether the father will trust him. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read If thou canst believe, which puts the if on the father’s faith; the earliest have Jesus simply handing the father’s words back to him, as most modern Bibles do. Either way the point stands: Jesus’ power was never in question.

All things are possible for one who believes. This sentence has been made to say something cruel that it does not say. It is not a formula: believe hard enough and you will get what you want. That doctrine has crushed a great many suffering people, who have been told that a diagnosis stands because their faith was insufficient. Faith is not a force that makes things happen. It is trust in God, for whom all things are possible (10:27; 14:36): empty hands held out to someone who has everything.

Cried out. From the depths. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add with tears; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles leave it out. It is a shout, not a carefully worded statement.

I believe; help my unbelief! One of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and only Mark records it. I believe: he will not deny the faith that brought him here. Help my unbelief: he will not pretend it is more than it is. He does not ask for stronger faith so that he can then qualify. He asks Christ to help the very thing that disqualifies him. And Jesus accepts it. He meets trembling faith, shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the doubt said he could not do. Our salvation never rested on the strength of our grip, but on the strength of the hands that hold us.

Believing and doubting in the same hour. That is why this verse has been the lifeline of honest Christians for two thousand years. We can affirm every article of the creed and lie awake unable to feel a word of it. And the great temptation is to sort yourself out before you come, to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man did the opposite. He brought both halves and laid them at Christ’s feet. And the boy was healed.

All things are possible for you. In Gethsemane Jesus himself will pray, Abba, Father, all things are possible for you (14:36). There is the one man whose faith had no unbelief in it at all, and the cup of suffering was not taken from him. He trusted the Father perfectly and was handed over, so that people whose faith is half doubt might be heard for his sake. The father in the valley could bring his ragged prayer because the Son would bring a perfect one, and drink the cup anyway, in the father’s place.

If my prayer is not answered, was my faith too weak? Not necessarily, and usually not. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and was told no, because God’s grace was sufficient and his power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith does not dictate outcomes to God; it trusts him with them. Sometimes he heals; sometimes he gives grace to bear what he does not remove; always he hears. Never let anyone tell you that a sickness persists because you did not believe hard enough. The father in this passage confessed that his faith was mixed with unbelief, and he was not turned away.

Is doubt a sin? Unbelief that refuses God’s word is sin, and Jesus has just grieved over it (v. 19). But the struggling faith of a believer who wants to trust and finds it hard is not the same thing. It is weakness, and the remedy for weakness is to bring it to Christ, exactly as this man did. Doubts are best fought not by staring at your faith but by looking at the one you trust: his word, his promises, his cross and empty tomb. Feed faith with Scripture, pray this prayer, stay among God’s people, and do not make major decisions to walk away in a dark hour.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You mute and deaf spirit. He names it precisely: the thing has shut the child in, both ways. And the “I” in I command you is emphatic. He calls on no one, uses no set form of words and appeals to no higher name. The master commands in his own authority.

Never enter him again. Nowhere else in the Gospels does Jesus add this clause. Why here? Because the father has just told him it has been happening from childhood, and the fear in that household is not only that it might happen but that it will keep happening. Jesus is not simply ending an episode. He is closing the door and telling the father it is closed, as he told the woman with the bleeding, be healed of your disease (5:34): a word of permanence for someone who would otherwise wake every morning waiting for it to come back.

It came out. The last thing it does on the way out is hurt him as much as it can. The powers of darkness in this Gospel are malicious to the final second, and they always obey.

Like a corpse. The crowd concludes that the healer has killed him. The father has just prayed the truest prayer of his life, and his son is lying on the ground looking dead. The moment before deliverance can look exactly like the disaster you feared. Israel was never more trapped than with the sea in front and the chariots behind.

Lifted him up, and he arose. Took him by the hand, as with the dead girl in Jairus’ house (5:41–42). Lifted him up and arose are the two words used for Jesus’ own resurrection (16:6; 8:31), in the chapter where he spoke of rising and nobody understood (vv. 9–10). Here, in front of a crowd that has pronounced the boy dead, the Son of Man takes a child’s hand and raises him: a small, dusty rehearsal of what he is walking to Jerusalem to do for the world. Our Lord does not merely drive out the enemy; he lifts us up, and one day he will take every sleeping believer by the hand and say, arise.

Can Christians be possessed, and should we be casting out demons today? Christ’s victory here is the reason for confidence, not fear. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ; Scripture never describes a Christian as possessed, and greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Believers are tempted and attacked, and we resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). The extraordinary sign gifts that marked the apostles’ ministry served to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and this commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that once that message was complete in Scripture those gifts ceased. Many faithful believers, Pentecostal and charismatic brothers among them, hold that they continue, and we hold our view without doubting their love for Christ; but God still hears prayer for the afflicted, and Satan still flees from Christ. Where real spiritual oppression is suspected, the remedy is the ordinary means: the gospel, repentance, prayer by the elders, and patient care, without theatre and without neglecting medical help.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why could we not cast it out? Notice first where the conversation happens: indoors, afterwards, in private. He never humiliated them in the valley. The correction is real and it is coming, but it is not delivered in front of an audience. And their question is a fair one. They are not making excuses. They had done this before, on the mission he sent them on. They are not amateurs, and they know something has gone wrong that they cannot account for.

Anything but prayer. “This kind” suggests that some demons were stronger than others. But the answer is not a technique, a better formula or more authority; they had all the authority they needed. It is prayer, and he is not prescribing a step they omitted on the day. He is diagnosing a life.

Prayer as the posture of a life. Jesus himself does not pray in this passage: he speaks a sentence, and it is done. His praying was done very early in the morning in a desolate place (1:35), and he has just come down from a mountain of communion with the Father, while the disciples had been arguing with scribes. So prayer here means settled, daily, unspectacular dependence on God, the only way such authority ever works.

The drift from dependence. These men had come back from their mission delighted. Somewhere between that success and this valley, the authority had quietly become a possession: something they had, something that worked, a capacity they carried about rather than a gift held moment by moment from the hand of the one who gave it. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending. And the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside, until a day comes when the thing does not work. Every generation of the church faces the same drift: serving on skill and experience, without the closeness to God that gives the work any power.

The Son who never drifted. Set beside the nine the one man who never treated his power as a possession. The eternal Son chose to live as a man in moment-by-moment dependence: the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19). And his praying did not end with his earthly life. He lives now at the Father’s right hand to intercede for his people, so that what the disciples lacked in the valley, their Lord supplies from the throne.

Faith and prayer. Faithlessness (v. 19) and prayerlessness are the same thing from different sides: prayer is faith expressing its dependence on God. A prayerless believer is a person who has quietly concluded that he can manage.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “and fasting”. The words are missing from the two earliest and most reliable manuscripts, and were probably added later as the church came to practise fasting more. The ESV puts them in a footnote. Fasting is good, and Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), but it is not the secret here. Jesus’ point is dependence on God in prayer.

How do I build a life of dependent prayer? Start small and real rather than large and short-lived. Set a fixed time each day, even ten minutes, with your Bible open, and pray back what you read. Pray before the things you think you can do, not only the things you know you cannot: before the meeting, the lesson, the hard conversation. Keep a short list of people and situations, and pray through it. Pray with others, in your church’s prayer meeting and with your household. And when you find you have gone days without real prayer, do not wait to feel spiritual again. Confess it and begin again today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second telling (vv. 30–32). Passing quietly through Galilee, Jesus tells them again that he will be delivered up, killed and raised. They do not understand, and are afraid to ask.

The argument (vv. 33–37). At Capernaum it comes out that they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. He sets a child among them and redefines greatness.

The outsider (vv. 38–41). John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus' name because he was not one of them. Jesus tells them to leave him alone, and promises that even a cup of water given to a disciple will be rewarded.

The warnings (vv. 42–50). A millstone for anyone who trips up a little one; a hand, a foot or an eye better lost than kept; and at the end, peace with one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two sayings that seem to collide. The one who is not against us is for us (v. 40) sits beside whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23). They answer different questions. Toward a fellow worker plainly on Christ's side, do not treat an ally as an enemy; toward Jesus himself there is no neutral ground. Be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

The verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48 three times, at verses 44, 46 and 48. The two extra lines are absent from the earliest manuscripts, so modern Bibles footnote them; nothing is lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men argued about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument runs with better manners: who was consulted, who was thanked from the front, who was asked to do the thing you were not asked to do. Jesus does not abolish the wish to be first; he turns it round: last of all and servant of all. And the test is the child in his arms: how you treat the people who cannot do a thing for you, when nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Galilee. Quietly and unrecognised, through his own home region. The public Galilean ministry is over; from here the Gospel narrows to fewer crowds, more instruction, and the road to Jerusalem.

For he was teaching his disciples. His priority now is to prepare the Twelve, and there is not much time.

Delivered into the hands of men. This second foretelling of his suffering and death (the first was 8:31) has a new word in it, the darkest in the sentence. “Delivered” means handed over, betrayed: the word is used of Judas (14:10), of the priests handing Jesus to Pilate (15:1), of Pilate handing him to be crucified (15:15), and of God giving up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32). Here it does not say who is doing it, and behind all of them stands the Father’s purpose. There is a play on words too: the Son of Man is handed over to men. That means humanity in general, and so it includes the reader.

If God handed him over, are the betrayers less guilty? No. Scripture holds both truths together without embarrassment. Peter preached that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same sentence that his hearers crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordains what happens without being the author of the sin, and human beings act freely and are fully responsible for their wickedness (so the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession: Westminster 3.1; 1689 3.1). Said simply: God planned the cross and steered every event toward it, yet the greed in Judas’ heart was Judas’ own, and God did not put it there (James 1:13). Judas was not a puppet; he chose for silver. And God, in his wisdom, used the worst thing ever done to accomplish the best. That is why the cross is both the guilt of the world and the gift of God.

After three days he will rise. Flat, unadorned, and with the resurrection attached again, as it was the first time. In none of his plain predictions of his death does he leave out the rising.

Afraid to ask him. Two failures. They did not understand: forgivable, and by now familiar. And they were afraid to ask him: that is not ignorance but a choice. Perhaps because last time Peter raised it he was called Satan (8:33); perhaps they suspected they would not like the answer.

The questions we do not ask. There are questions Christians decline to ask God because we half-know the answer and the answer would require something: the passage you skip, the area of your life you have agreed with yourself not to discuss with him. It is not doubt; doubt at least engages. It is avoidance. And the disciples do not ask him about the cross, and then they fill the rest of the walk with an argument about which of them is the most important. The unasked question leaves a space, and something always moves into it.

For worship. He knew every hand that would pass him along: the friend’s, the priest’s, the governor’s, the soldier’s. And he walked toward them, because behind every one of those hands stood the Father who did not spare his own Son. Every handing over was love going all the way down.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Capernaum. Probably Peter’s house (1:29). Whatever Jesus heard on the road, he says nothing until the door is shut, the same restraint he showed with the nine.

What were you discussing on the way? Jesus very likely knew already; Luke says he perceived the reasoning of their hearts (Luke 9:47). The question is gentle; he does not accuse, he asks. And “on the way” is loaded in Mark: it is the way to the cross, where Jesus was going to give his life. That was the road on which they had been arguing about greatness.

But they kept silent. The silence is a confession: you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with. Some talk cannot be repeated in front of him, and that it cannot is itself the verdict on it; yet he asks gently, as one who has come to serve them.

Who was the greatest. Jesus had just told them, for the second time, that he would be killed, and the men walking behind him were arguing about rank. Perhaps the choosing of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy. It kept coming back (10:35–45; Luke 22:24). Pride is among the most persistent of sins, even in disciples.

The silent argument in church. Nobody in a church says I am the greatest. But the argument runs anyway, silently and constantly: who was consulted and who was not, who got thanked from the front, whose name is on it, who was asked to do the thing you were not asked to do, who is regarded as sound. It can be conducted entirely without words, and everybody in the room knows the standings.

He sat down. The posture of a teacher giving formal instruction: what follows is a lesson for the men who will lead his church.

Last of all and servant of all. If anyone would be first: the wanting is allowed to stand. He tells them where the front of the queue actually is, and the word all, used twice, makes it impossible to soften. Last of all: bottom. Servant of all: diakonos, the table-waiter, from which comes our word deacon. Not servant of the deserving or the useful. Of all.

The first who made himself last. The man saying this had the right to the first place in every room he entered. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to hold on to, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He asks the Twelve to go nowhere he has not gone first. The quarrel about rank was conducted behind the back of the only one who truly outranked them all, while he went down to serve them.

Is it wrong to want to do great things for God? No. Jesus does not rebuke the desire to be first; he redirects it. It is right to long that your life should count, that God should be honoured greatly through you, that you would hear well done at the end. What is wrong is wanting greatness measured by the world’s scale: being seen, consulted, thanked, above others. So ask what your ambition is for. If it is for his glory and others’ good, pursue it by serving. If it is for your name, it will show itself in resentment when someone else is chosen.

What does servant of all look like on an ordinary week? It is measurable, which is what makes it hard. It is easy to feel humble; it is not possible to be a servant in the abstract. It looks like doing the job nobody notices: stacking chairs, washing up, visiting the person who is hard work. It looks like letting someone else have the credit, and being glad. It looks like putting your spouse’s and children’s needs before your evening, and your colleagues’ success before your own advancement. And it looks like serving people who cannot repay you. Service of that kind can be looked up in a diary.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the table-waiter’s word for himself. And he has promised that when he returns he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The first of all will wait at his own feast, and there is no greatness in heaven or on earth like the greatness of that servant.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A child in the midst. An acted parable: the argument was about the highest place, and he puts a child in the centre of it. We have sentimentalised this scene. Children were loved, but they were not counted important; they had no legal standing and no voice, and in the wider Roman world unwanted babies were often exposed at birth. A child could not advance you or repay you. So the lesson is not be innocent like this; children are sinners too (Psalm 51:5). It is: here is a person who can do absolutely nothing for you.

And taking him in his arms. Mark alone records this, here and again at 10:16. Someone in that room never forgot it: while he was explaining greatness to us, he was holding a child.

Whoever receives one such child. To receive is to welcome a guest. “In my name”: for my sake. Not whoever loves children, but whoever makes room for one who has nothing to give in return. Jesus identifies himself with the least important people. The way you treat the least is the way you treat Christ (Matthew 25:40).

Him who sent me. The chain goes all the way up: welcome a nobody in Jesus’ name, and you welcome God himself. The greatness of an act is measured not by the person you did it for but by who is standing behind them. It is also a claim: Jesus is the sent one, who represents the Father fully. And the Son of God, whom the Father sent, put his arms around a child no one counted. That is the God we worship: the high and lofty One who dwells with the lowly, who stoops to take up the small, and who reckons a welcome given to a nobody as given to himself.

Does this mean every child belongs to Christ? Not in that sense. In my name means receiving the child for Jesus’ sake, because he cares for such little ones and commands us to. It does not teach that children are born saved or that they enter the covenant by birth or baptism; each child needs to be born again and to come to Christ by faith, which is why we pray for our children and teach them the gospel. Our paedobaptist brothers (who baptise the infants of believers) hold that such children belong to the covenant community and should receive its sign; they too insist that each child must come to personal faith, and we differ from them in love. But Jesus’ arms around this child show how warmly he welcomes the little ones brought to him, and we believe that those who die in infancy are safe in the hands of a merciful God who saves his elect, that is, those he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). If you have laid a little one in the grave, you may picture that child in these same arms. Every child is to be welcomed, protected and taught, because the Lord who made them takes them up in his arms.

In everyday life. Welcome the people who can do nothing for you: the lonely, the elderly relative whose conversation goes in circles, the child in your own house at the end of a day when you have nothing left. You came to him with nothing to give and he took you in; in them you welcome him.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John said to him. The only time in Mark that John speaks alone, and the timing is superb. Jesus has just said that receiving a nobody in his name is receiving him, and John’s contribution is to report an occasion when they stopped somebody acting in that name. Perhaps he expected approval: he is a Son of Thunder (3:17).

Someone casting out demons. Someone outside the Twelve, using Jesus’ name, and succeeding, when the disciples had just failed (v. 18). There may be a little jealousy here.

He was not following us. Not following you, but us. The man plainly was following Jesus; the objection is to his membership, not his master. Joshua made the same mistake about Eldad and Medad prophesying outside the camp, and Moses answered: Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29).

Party spirit in one clause. There is a way of caring about the kingdom that has quietly become caring about our part of it, where the first question asked about a man’s ministry is not whether Christ is being preached but which group he belongs to. It flourishes among people who are entirely orthodox and entirely sincere, and it produces the strange spectacle of Christians uneasy rather than glad when good work is done by somebody outside their circle.

Soon afterward to speak evil of me. The reasoning is practical: having just seen that name work, he is not about to start slandering it. Whatever is lacking in his understanding, he is not on the other side.

Not against us is for us. In the war between the kingdom of God and Satan (3:23–27), anyone casting out demons in Jesus’ name is fighting on the right side. Elsewhere Jesus says the reverse: Whoever is not with me is against me (Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23). The two sayings do not contradict; they answer different questions. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil’s: toward Jesus there is no neutral ground. Here the subject is a fellow worker plainly on Christ’s side who does not belong to the disciples’ circle: do not treat an ally as an enemy. Read together they are a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

The power in the name. The man had no commission among the Twelve, and the demons went anyway, because the authority was never in the group. His name did what the nine had just failed to do, which is the plainest proof of who he is: the name at which demons flee is the name God has exalted above every name, at which every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–10). John wanted to guard the name. Jesus shows that the name guards itself, and belongs to him, not to any group.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer (Matthew 7:22–23). Nor that doctrine does not matter: the issue here is group loyalty, not truth. Paul could rejoice that Christ was preached even by rivals with bad motives (Philippians 1:15–18), and in the same years curse anyone who preached a different gospel (Galatians 1:8–9). The line is the gospel itself, not our party.

How can I tell whether someone outside my circle is truly on Christ’s side? Look at what he does with Christ and the gospel. Does he confess Jesus as the eternal Son of God come in the flesh, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith in him, not by works? Does he submit to Scripture as God’s final word? If so, he is a brother even if he differs from you on baptism, church order or the end times, and you should be glad when God uses him. If he denies the heart of the gospel, he is not doing a work in Christ’s name, whatever words he uses, and love for the sheep means warning against him.

In everyday life. Pray by name for another gospel church in your town, and thank God for something good he is doing through it.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cup of water. Jesus puts his solemn Truly, I say to you in front of a cup of water. He could have said whoever preaches, whoever heals. He says a drink of water, the smallest kindness in a dry land, costing almost nothing and heard of by no one. And it will not be forgotten.

Because you belong to Christ. Literally in the name that you are Christ’s. Not because the giver was impressive or the act large, but because of whom the receiver belonged to, exactly as he said about the child. Kindness shown to a disciple because he belongs to Christ is kindness to Christ.

Will by no means lose his reward. “By no means” is the strongest negative in Greek: not overlooked, not too small to register. Nothing done for Christ is lost; God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of what flows from love for Christ, not wages that put God in our debt (Luke 17:10). It is grace upon grace: he gives the faith, works the love, and then crowns his own gifts as if they were ours.

What is the reward? Scripture does not give us a price list, and it is better not to imagine one. The heart of it is the Lord himself: his well done, his joy shared, a deeper capacity to know and enjoy him in the age to come (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:14). Rewards in the New Testament are never a ladder of merit within salvation that makes some saints proud, but the Father’s delight in his children’s love. Every believer’s cup will be full, and every one will cast his crown before the throne.

The list nobody sees. Most Christian work is small and unnoticed: meals cooked, lifts given, a message sent to somebody having a bad week, prayer for people who never learn they were prayed for. None of it will be described from a platform. All of it is on a list. And he will read the list out one day, and the people named will not recognise their own lives in it: Lord, when did we see you thirsty and give you drink? And he will answer that as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:37–40).

The cup he was given. The Lord who promised a reward for a cup of water knew what it was to be thirsty. On the cross he would say, I thirst, and be handed sour wine on a sponge (John 19:28–29; Mark 15:36). And he knew of another cup, the one he would ask the Father to remove: the cup of God’s judgment, which no kindness could ease. He drank that one to the dregs, so that every cup handed to one of his people might be gathered up and honoured. The one who notices the water is the one who drank the wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of these little ones who believe in me. The child is still in the room, so children are not excluded. But who believe in me points wider: any humble believer whose faith is genuine and not yet strong, the recent convert, the person hanging on by their fingernails, anyone whose grip on Christ could be loosened by what you do.

To sin. The verb is skandalizō, to trip up: to lead a believer into sin or away from faith, by false teaching, bad example, abuse, pride or contempt. It is anything you do that makes it harder for a weak believer to keep walking.

Who believe in me. Jesus speaks of faith in himself as the prophets spoke of trust in the LORD, and he binds the little ones to himself so closely that to wound their faith is to strike at him. He is the Servant of whom Isaiah wrote, a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3). He handles weak faith with infinite care, and the severity that follows is the measure of it. The millstone is what his tenderness sounds like when it turns to face those who would crush what he is guarding.

A great millstone. Literally a donkey’s millstone: not the hand-mill of a kitchen but the huge upper stone an animal walked in circles to turn, weighing hundreds of pounds.

Thrown into the sea. Drowning with a weight was a Roman form of execution, especially horrifying to Jews because the body would not be buried. Then hear the comparison: it would be better for him. Not that he should be drowned, but that judgment for such a sin will be worse than the worst death imaginable. He does not speak like this about doubters or the confused. He keeps words like these for the gravest sins, such as the betrayal of the Son of Man (14:21), and here for damaging the faith of the small.

Who is this word for? For anybody with influence over somebody weaker, and that is a great many of us. It is a word for parents, whose children’s picture of God is being assembled largely out of what they see at home, and whose faith can be quietly ruined by a father who is one man on Sunday and another on Tuesday. It is a word for anyone who teaches or leads in a church, and for anyone whose conduct is watched by a younger Christian who thinks well of them. And it is a word about ordinary talk. You do not need to preach heresy to trip somebody up. It is done with a cynical remark about a fellow believer in front of a new convert, with running commentary on the church’s failings that a fragile person overhears, with the joke that makes something holy look small. The father in the valley had his faith damaged by disciples who let him down. Somebody put that if you can in his mouth.

What about abuse in the church? This verse is among the most severe Jesus ever spoke, and it bears with full weight on anyone who abuses a child or a vulnerable believer, especially under cover of Christ’s name. Abuse is never to be tolerated, hushed up or managed quietly to protect a reputation, a ministry or a family. Jesus’ concern is for the little one, not for the institution. A church that loves Christ will report abuse to the civil authorities, who are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), will protect and believe and care for victims, and will remove offenders from any position of trust. Forgiveness for a repentant abuser is real, but it never means restoring access or silencing the harmed. If this has happened to you, it was not your fault, and Christ is on your side.

In everyday life. Ask who is watching you who is weaker than you are, and whether anything you do makes it harder for them. In the strength of his Spirit, change the thing; where you have already tripped someone, confess it to the one who forgives, and go and help them up.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From others to yourself. Having warned them about tripping up others, he turns to the more likely danger, yourself; the same verb, to trip up, runs through. Deal with sin in your own life as ruthlessly as God will deal with those who harm his little ones.

Cut it off … tear it out. Not literal self-mutilation, which would not work: the trouble comes out of the heart (7:21), and a blind man can still lust. But do not let that soften it into nothing. This is deliberate overstatement, and he is in deadly earnest: whatever leads you into sin, however precious, get rid of it. He deliberately chose things you cannot spare.

Making it concrete. Keeping it vague is how we take the edge off this passage. The hand is what you do. The foot is where you go. The eye is what you look at, and in our generation that is very often one object, in your pocket and lit up at midnight. And the surgery is not moderation; it is removal. In practice that means the concrete, slightly embarrassing measure: the app deleted rather than managed, the phone that does not come upstairs, the account closed, the friendship stepped back from, the route changed, the arrangement told to another Christian so that it can be asked about. Every one of those feels disproportionate. That is the feeling of amputation, and it is exactly the feeling he is describing.

It is better for you to enter life crippled. “Life” means eternal life, the kingdom of God of verse 47; the alternative, three times over, is hell. Better to lose something precious now and enter life, than keep everything and lose your soul (8:36).

To go to hell. The word translated “hell” (geenna, Gehenna) was the name of a real place: the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where apostate Israel burned its own children to Molech (2 Chronicles 28:3; 2 Kings 23:10), and which Jeremiah called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:31–32). Jesus takes a valley every pilgrim knew, with a history of fire and death, and makes it his picture of final judgment.

To the unquenchable fire. Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. The closing line is a quotation of the last verse of Isaiah (66:24), which pictures the corpses of those who rebelled against God. The worm devours and the fire burns, and neither ends. These are pictures, but the reality they point to is more terrible than the pictures, not less.

The tenderest voice speaks of hell. Nobody in the Bible speaks about hell as often as Jesus does. The man who held a child while he taught is the one who will not let this subject alone. It runs too deeply through all four Gospels to be peeled off as a later addition. It is on the lips of the Saviour, and he says it three times in six verses because he means his people not to go there. The Judge who warns of the unquenchable fire is the Saviour who went into the fire for us. He was cut off from the land of the living, forsaken, so that every one who flees to him might enter life whole.

Where Christians differ: the nature of hell. Some (conditionalists or annihilationists) hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, taking unquenchable fire to mean a fire that does its work completely, and noting that in Isaiah 66:24 the worm and fire consume dead bodies. Others (universalists) hope that all will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: the historic Christian view is that hell is conscious, eternal punishment. The undying worm and unquenched fire speak of punishment that does not end: in Isaiah the picture is of corpses, but Jesus applies it to people thrown into hell, and for them the punishment never finishes. Jesus elsewhere sets eternal punishment alongside eternal life as equally lasting (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night (Revelation 14:11). Jesus’ warnings are given in love, so that none would go there. It is meant to drive us to the one who bore judgment for all who come to him.

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy as well as loving, and a God who shrugged at evil would not be good. The marvel is not that God judges but that he came himself, in his Son, to bear that judgment for all who come to him. (See Luke 3:17 for the fuller answer.)

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, both repeating verse 48. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain three times; here the numbers run 43, 45, 47, 48. The two repetitions are missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and were probably added to make the three warnings match. The ESV puts them in footnotes. Nothing has been lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah.

If I keep failing at the same sin, am I going to hell? Not if you belong to Christ. These verses are not a threat hung over the believer who fights and falls; they are a warning to the person who will not fight at all, who keeps the hand because he loves it more than he fears the fire. A Christian still sins, and grieves, and confesses, and gets up (1 John 1:8–9). You may find that part of you still loves the sin while the rest of you hates it. That divided heart is what Paul describes in Romans 7:15–25, and the hating and the fighting are the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17), not proof that he is absent. What marks a true believer is not that the battle is won but that he is in it, on God’s side, using the means God gives. Your hope is not the strength of your surgery but the Saviour who was cut off for you. Cut off what feeds the sin precisely because he has already saved you, and keep running to him.

In everyday life. Name the hand, foot or eye in your life, cut it off today in a concrete way you could explain to a friend, and ask one trusted Christian to check on you next week. Your surgery will never be clean or complete; Christ’s obedience was, kept whole in your place, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19). So you cut as one already accepted, not to become so.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone will be salted with fire. One of the strangest sentences in Mark. Fire is the last word of the previous paragraph, where it meant judgment, unquenchable, in Gehenna. Salt comes from somewhere else entirely: you shall season all your grain offerings with salt; you shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing (Leviticus 2:13). Salt was rubbed into every sacrifice laid on the altar, and many were burned with fire. So the saying covers two groups of people at once, and fire does opposite things to them. The unrepentant meet the fire that consumes. The disciple, who has just been told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish, meets the fire that purifies: the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

Which fire? Everyone will meet fire. The only question is which kind. Peter says the same thing to Christians under persecution: do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you (1 Peter 4:12), for tested faith is more precious than gold that is refined by fire (1 Peter 1:7). Other readings have been offered: that every believer’s work will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13), or that the wicked will be preserved, as salt preserves, in the fire of judgment. The reading given here keeps the link with the fire of verse 48 and the salt of the sacrifices, and is the more likely: everyone meets God’s fire, either as judgment or as the refining of a life given to him. Since Jesus is speaking to the Twelve, his main point is for the disciple: the fire he must meet is the refining one. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and every sacrifice will be salted with salt, probably added from Leviticus 2:13 to explain the saying.

Salt is good. Salt preserved and seasoned, and in the Old Testament it sealed a covenant of salt, lasting and unbreakable (Numbers 18:19). So a disciple is meant to stop the rot, give savour, and be bound to God for good.

The sacrifice salted and burned. Every salted offering pointed to one. Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2), and he went wholly into the fire of judgment, the same fire the unrepentant will meet. Because he was consumed in the place of his people, the fire that reaches them now is never the fire of Gehenna. It is a Father’s refining fire, burning off the dross and leaving gold. The disciple is salted with fire as one who stands inside a covenant of salt that Christ’s blood has made unbreakable.

But if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But much of the salt of Palestine probably came from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals, and damp could leach out the actual salt, leaving a white powder that looked identical and did nothing. You could not restore it. You threw it out (Matthew 5:13). That is the sober question under the sentence. A disciple who has quietly lost the thing that made him different is not obviously distinguishable from one who has not. He looks the same. He is in the same place on Sunday. He simply no longer preserves anything or gives savour to anything.

Can a true Christian lose his salt and be lost? A true believer cannot finally fall away, because the God who began the work will complete it (Philippians 1:6) and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28–29). But Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps us. Christians can grow cold, compromised and useless for a season, and the warning is meant to wake them. And someone who looked like salt for years may prove never to have been the real thing at all (1 John 2:19). So do not use this verse to torment yourself, and do not use the doctrine of perseverance to ignore it. Go back to Christ, the source of the salt.

Have salt in yourselves. The salt is the self-denial Jesus has been describing since 8:34: taking up the cross, being servant of all, cutting off whatever leads you into sin.

And be at peace with one another. The chapter comes full circle: men who had failed in a valley, argued about greatness (v. 34) and stopped a man who was not of their party are told to be at peace. Have salt in yourselves comes first; peace follows from it. Peace in a church is not produced by managing personalities. It is what happens when a group of people have each dealt honestly with themselves. People who have been salted with the fire of the cross have nothing left to fight over.

What if peace with someone seems impossible? Do what lies with you (Romans 12:18). Examine yourself first and own your part without excuses. Go to the person privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15). Forgive as you have been forgiven, which does not mean pretending wrong was not done, but releasing your claim to pay it back. If they will not be reconciled, keep your heart free of bitterness and keep praying for them. Peace does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring serious sin; sometimes the church’s elders must be involved. But it does mean you will not be the one keeping the quarrel alive.

For worship. He was going to Jerusalem to make that peace at his own expense, by the blood of his cross. And on the night he was handed over, John tells us, he got up from the table, took a towel, and washed the feet of every one of them. He is our peace.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark's own arrangement answers it: the next words are and after six days, and Mark almost never gives intervals. Some standing there would see the kingdom come with power, and six days later three of them did. The kingdom came in power again at the resurrection, at Pentecost and in AD 70, but the mountain was the first sight of it.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not for lack of a technique or of authority. Prayer here is the posture of a whole life. Somewhere between their earlier success and this valley the authority had become a possession rather than a gift held moment by moment. They did not stop believing; they stopped depending, and from the inside the two are hard to tell apart.
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out. The disciples' failure put it there, and the same thing still happens when a church lets someone down or a leader falls.
