Then watch what the man does with the little faith he has: I believe; help my unbelief! Jesus does not tell him to come back when he is sure. He meets the faith that is there and heals the boy. So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve before you pray.

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 takes the three things people build their lives out of, marriage, children and money, and puts each of them in the hands of a man walking to Jerusalem to die.

The Pharisees ask about divorce, the question that cost John the Baptist his head, and Jesus goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. The disciples turn children away, and Jesus is indignant with them. A rich man runs, kneels, asks how to inherit eternal life, is looked at and loved by Jesus, and goes home, because there was one thing he would not give.

The second half is a road. Jesus walks ahead and tells the Twelve for the third time what is waiting in Jerusalem. James and John ask for the two best seats, and out of that squabble comes the centre of the Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. At Jericho a blind beggar calls him Son of David, throws away his cloak and follows him. The chapter opens with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–12). In Herod's territory the Pharisees ask him about divorce. Jesus goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, joined by God.

The children (vv. 13–16). The disciples turn children away, Jesus is indignant, and he takes the children in his arms and blesses them.

The rich man (vv. 17–22). A man asks the best question in the Gospel, is loved, is asked for the one thing he will not give, and goes away sorrowful.

The impossibility (vv. 23–31). A camel through a needle's eye, disciples asking then who can be saved?, and the answer: with man it is impossible, but not with God.
verseByVerse.theology:
"Why do you call me good?" (v. 18) Jesus is not denying that he is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word. He holds it up to the light. Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone: it is a door held open to his deity, not a denial of it.

Why point him to the commandments? Not because keeping them saves, but because the law is a mirror. With one demand Jesus exposes the rival god the man had kept on the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by Jesus, and went home.

Now: he is alarming precisely because there is nothing obviously wrong with him. So the question the passage asks is not whether you are a good person, but what your one thing is: what you would be unable to say yes to if Christ named it tonight. He asks for it because he loves you and is better than it, and the Spirit he gives is stronger than its grip.

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 10 is the road to Jerusalem. Jesus teaches what life in his kingdom looks like in marriage, with children and with money; foretells his death a third time; and explains his whole life: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The rich man had everything and went away; the blind beggar had nothing and followed.

The setting. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32), and this chapter gathers what he taught along the road, ending with the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life (v. 45).

Beyond the Jordan. Perea, east of the river, ruled like Galilee by Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias and beheaded John the Baptist for saying it was unlawful (6:17–18); Josephus says John died in Herod’s fortress of Machaerus, in this very region. Jesus has walked into the jurisdiction of the man who killed John, and the very next thing he is asked about is divorce. He would not be trapped, flattered or frightened: our Saviour is the defender of the defenceless, and he is never afraid of kings.

As was his custom. The pattern of the whole ministry: they came, and he taught (1:38).

In order to test him. Mark tells us the motive first. The Pharisees did not want instruction. They wanted a trap. If he took a strict line, he might offend the crowds, and also Herod, and so risk the same end as John. If he took a loose line, he could be accused of undermining Moses.

Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? All Jews agreed that divorce was permitted. The debate was over the grounds. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found some indecency in her, and the whole argument turned on that phrase. The school of Rabbi Shammai said it meant sexual immorality only. The school of Rabbi Hillel said it meant anything that displeased him, even spoiling a dish; a later rabbi, Akiba, said finding a prettier woman was enough. Matthew records the question in this form: for any cause? (Matthew 19:3). Mark gives the bare question, the more radical one: is divorce lawful at all?

Nobody has mentioned the wife. The question is asked entirely from the man’s side, and a woman put away had no property, no standing and very little future. The Pharisees are debating the limits of a man’s freedom to dispose of a person. Jesus is about to mention her.

Testing the Bridegroom. The irony runs deep. The prophets had called the LORD Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:16), the faithful partner of an unfaithful bride, who in Hosea goes after his wife and buys her back (Hosea 3:1–2). Jesus had already called himself the bridegroom (2:19). So the men asking how easily a husband may put away his wife are putting the question to the one Husband whose love has outlasted all his people’s unfaithfulness, and whose errand on this road is to win a bride at the cost of his life.

In everyday life. When you find yourself asking whether something is allowed, stop and ask why you want to know. The question of the outer boundary is usually asked by someone who has already decided what he wants.
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas, who had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What did Moses command you? Jesus goes to Scripture, as always. And he answers a question with a question, and his question is a trap of its own, because the verb is precise. He asks what Moses commanded.

Moses allowed. They correct him: allowed, not commanded. They are right, and they have just made his point for him. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 does not command divorce or even approve it. It regulates something already happening. Its only command is that if a man has divorced his wife and she has married another, he may not take her back. The certificate of divorce protected the woman. It proved she had been released and was free to remarry; without it she could live under suspicion, and in poverty, for the rest of her life. Even in his concessions God was kind: in a hard-hearted world he put a paper into the hand of the discarded woman so that she would not be left with nothing. Moses was not opening the door to divorce. It was already open, and he was limiting the damage.

Your hardness of heart. A heart that has thickened until it cannot feel (compare 3:5; 8:17). The law of divorce was a concession: because men would divorce their wives anyway, God set limits to protect the vulnerable. A law can regulate sin without approving it. And notice the pronoun: he wrote you this commandment. The concession was granted to people like you, for hardness like yours, and you have turned it into an entitlement and come here asking how far it extends.

What God permits and what God intends. A distinction we constantly lose. The Bible regulates polygamy, slavery, warfare and divorce in a fallen world; it does not commend them, and the regulation is a restraint on a fallen practice, not a blueprint. With slavery, the law made kidnapping a man to sell him a crime punished by death (Exodus 21:16), and Paul calls a slave his master’s brother in Christ (Philemon 16); Christians have at times twisted these texts to their shame, but Scripture’s direction runs toward freedom. To read a concession as an endorsement is exactly the mistake being made in this conversation.

Greater than Moses. Jesus explains why Moses wrote what he wrote, and then goes behind him to the beginning, as one who knows the Lawgiver’s mind from the inside: Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Moses could only limit the damage hard hearts do. The Son came to do something about the hearts.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from the beginning of creation. The most important move in the passage. Asked about the rules for ending a marriage, he goes to what a marriage is. Before sin and before Sinai, God established marriage, and that design is the standard. Deuteronomy 24 was a concession; Genesis 1 and 2 are the pattern.

God made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. Marriage is not a human invention that societies may adapt. It is built into the way people were made, before any culture and before the fall: the foundation of the Christian understanding of marriage as between one man and one woman.

Leave and hold fast. Genesis 2:24, the words of the writer of Genesis, which Jesus treats as God’s own. Leave: a new primary loyalty replaces the old one, and a marriage in which one party has never actually left home, emotionally or practically, will feel the fault line for decades. Hold fast: be glued, cleave, the word used of clinging to God himself (Deuteronomy 10:20). It is not a mood. It is a decision that is renewed, and does not depend on how the week has gone.

The Maker in the conversation. The Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) is standing in Perea explaining his own design. He knows what a marriage is because he made the first one. No one has ever had a better right to say what God has joined, and no one has ever honoured a bride as he will honour his.

One flesh. A union of the whole person, of which sexual union is both the expression and the seal. The two now share one life, one home, one purse, one future, so that what wounds or gladdens one belongs to the other as well. Paul draws the conclusion that a husband who loves his wife loves himself, because no one ever hates his own flesh (Ephesians 5:28–29).

No longer two. Jesus’ own comment on the text, and a statement of fact rather than an ideal: the union is real whatever either of them feels about it on a given morning. Which is why the ending of a marriage is never just paperwork. You cannot separate one flesh without tearing something, and everyone who has been through it knows this in their body long before they can say it.

Let not man separate. The weight falls on who does what. God has joined: not the couple or the registrar but God creates the bond, in every genuine marriage, including those of people who have never given him a thought. Let not man separate: no husband, wife or court has the right to tear apart what God did.

What this means on the bad days. This verse is chiefly about how you regard the marriage you are in. You are not in an arrangement that continues as long as it works; you are in something God did. That changes what to do in the year that is going wrong. The question in that hour is not, is this still working? It is: what did God join, and what am I doing to keep it? Marriages are rarely separated by one decision. They are separated by a thousand small permissions: the conversation not had, the resentment kept, the friendship at work that becomes the place you are understood. Let not man separate is addressed to the man in the mirror, and the Bridegroom who has held fast to you through all your unfaithfulness gives grace to hold fast too.

What if my marriage is very unhappy? Unhappiness is not a ground for divorce, but it is a reason to act, not to drift. Pray honestly about it together and alone. Ask for help early: a wise pastor or older couple, and good Christian counselling. Look first at your own part, and confess it. Keep doing the ordinary acts of love when the feeling is absent, because feelings often follow faithfulness. Many couples who came close to the end have found, years later, a deeper marriage than they had at the start. And if the unhappiness is fear because you are being harmed, that is a different matter: you do not have to stay in danger, separation for protection is not sin, and the church must believe and protect you.

What about people who never marry, or who experience same-sex attraction? Jesus’ words define marriage; they do not say that everyone must marry. Jesus himself was single, and Paul calls singleness a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7). A single life given to Christ is full and honourable, not second-class. Those who experience same-sex attraction are not beyond the love or the family of God; the call to them is the same as to every believer, to deny themselves and follow Christ, and the church must be a real family to them (v. 30). But Jesus’ grounding of marriage in God making them male and female means the church cannot bless any other union as marriage. The reason is not dislike of anyone. Jesus defines marriage by creation, the man and the woman made for each other and joined as one flesh, and Paul sees in that union of two different partners a picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The church has no authority to redraw what God made; what it can and must give is friendship, belonging and patient love.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house. A public statement, then a private question. They were startled; Matthew records what they said in the house: If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry (Matthew 19:10). Jesus’ teaching was stricter than either rabbinic school.

Adultery against her. Since God’s bond still holds, remarriage after a divorce God does not recognise is adultery: the certificate does not touch what God joined. And “against her” was revolutionary. In Jewish law a man could only commit adultery against another man, by taking his wife. Jesus says a husband can commit adultery against his own wife. She has rights.

The wife at the centre. In a conversation that began with men debating how freely a man may dispose of a wife, Jesus names her as the one who has been wronged. The raising of the dignity of women in the societies Christianity touched is not a modern correction applied to an embarrassing text; it starts here, in a house in Perea, with a rabbi telling twelve men that a discarded wife has been sinned against.

If she divorces her husband. Jewish law did not normally allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did, and Mark, writing probably for Roman readers, records that the teaching applies to both; Herodias had divorced her husband. There is no double standard here.

The exceptions. Mark gives the principle without exception. Matthew records an exception: except for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9; 5:32). Paul adds another: if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). These exceptions do not contradict Mark. They show that some sins so break the marriage covenant that the innocent party may lawfully end it.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; remarriage while the spouse lives is never permitted, though an annulment may declare that no true marriage existed. Some Protestants hold that remarriage is never right while a spouse lives, even after divorce for adultery. Others allow divorce for many reasons, such as abuse, or simply breakdown. This commentary’s view: the Westminster Confession states the position best grounded in Scripture (Westminster 24.5–6): God’s design is lifelong marriage, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and be free to remarry. Whether persistent, serious abuse amounts to such desertion is for the elders to weigh in each case; but no one is ever required to stay where they or their children are in danger, the abused should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered. Those who have divorced and remarried wrongly may repent and find full forgiveness in Christ, as with any sin.

Not a list of loopholes. Even where Scripture allows divorce, it never requires it. Adultery and desertion give the innocent party freedom, not an obligation, and where there is genuine repentance, reconciliation is better where it is possible. Some marriages wounded by adultery have been rebuilt, slowly and at great cost, into something stronger. But that is the wronged spouse’s free choice before God, and no one may shame them for using the freedom Christ gives.

What if I am being abused? Abuse is never to be tolerated, excused or covered up, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires you to remain in danger. If you or your children are being hurt, threatened or controlled, your first duty is safety: get to a safe place, call the police where there is violence or threat, and tell someone you trust. Separation for protection is not sin. A husband who abuses his wife is himself breaking the covenant he vowed; headship in Scripture means self-giving love, never domination (Ephesians 5:25). Elders and churches must believe, protect and support victims, involve the civil authorities, and call the abuser to account. Whether divorce is then lawful is a further question, and persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, which the elders help judge in each case, but you do not need to settle that question before you get safe.

What if I divorced and remarried before I became a Christian, or on wrong grounds? The sin is real and should be confessed. But a second marriage, once made, is a marriage, and the answer is not to break it, which would add another sin; Moses’ law itself forbade going back to the first spouse after remarriage (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). Christ forgives the repentant fully, and you are to live faithfully where you now are, honouring the vows you made. Paul tells believers to remain in the condition in which they were called (1 Corinthians 7:17–20), and that includes your present marriage. Your past does not disqualify you from grace or from serving God.

A word to the divorced. To the reader who is divorced, perhaps remarried, and reading these hard sentences with a sinking heart: the standard has not moved, and a church that lowers it to seem gentle has only made grace unnecessary. But hear this clearly. There is no sin named here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no marriage so broken, by your fault, another’s, or the tangle of both, that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel does not meet you in the marriage you should have had. It meets you in the life you actually have, with a Saviour who came to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45), the divorced among them.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That he might touch them. After marriage, children: Mark is showing what a household looks like under Jesus’ rule. Luke says some were babies (Luke 18:15). It was ordinary to bring a child to a respected rabbi for a blessing, and that is all these parents ask.

And the disciples rebuked them. The verb is the one used of rebuking demons: they told them off. By any ordinary measure their reasoning was sound: the Master is on the road to Jerusalem and somebody has to manage the diary. It is the second time in two chapters they have tried to control access to Jesus (9:38). There is something in religious people that likes to stand at the door and decide who gets in.

He was indignant. A strong word, used of Jesus only here. The Son of God, days from the cross, became visibly angry because somebody turned away a queue of toddlers. What made him angry was not the interruption but the gatekeeping. That is the heart of God laid open: not a busy king who tolerates the small, but a Saviour who wants them near.

Do not hinder them. Nothing must stand between children and Jesus.

Who hinders children now? It is rarely done deliberately. It is done by treating them as a distraction to be managed until they are old enough to matter: the church that has no room for them, the family in which faith is discussed but never with them, the parent who is too tired at bedtime and always will be. And it is done by the hypocrisy children see at home. Nobody rebukes anybody. The children simply do not get brought.

To such belongs the kingdom. Note the wording: to such, not only to these. He is not saying that children are automatically in and adults are not. The kingdom belongs to people of this kind: those who, like children, have nothing to offer and simply receive. Not because children are innocent, but because they are dependent.

Where Christians differ: children and baptism. Paedobaptists (Presbyterians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Catholics) often appeal to this passage for infant baptism: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. Credobaptists (Baptists) answer that Jesus did not baptise these children; he blessed them, and the passage is about how all must receive the kingdom, not about a sacrament. This commentary’s view: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, which both sides agree on. It does not mention baptism, and it cannot settle the question. The New Testament pattern links baptism to repentance and faith, so the credobaptist position is best. This is a disagreement among brothers, held charitably.

So how do Baptist parents bring their children to Christ? In every way except the sign that belongs to those who profess faith. Pray for each child and with them, from the cradle. Teach them the Scriptures and the gospel at home (Deuteronomy 6:6–7; 2 Timothy 3:15). Bring them to worship, where they hear the word and see the people of God. Many churches hold a service of thanksgiving and dedication, in which parents give thanks and promise to raise the child in the Lord. Speak to them of Christ as one who welcomes children, and call them to trust him themselves. Then, when they profess faith and show its fruit, they are baptised. Our brothers who baptise their infants share every one of those aims.

What of children who die young? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no formula, and we should say no more than it says. But it gives firm ground for hope. Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). David expected to go to the son who died in infancy (2 Samuel 12:23). And the one who took children in his arms and was indignant when they were kept from him is the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). Grieving parents may entrust their little ones to that mercy with confidence. If you are one of them, the Lord who was indignant when children were kept from him is not indifferent to your empty arms; he knows the child you lost, and has not forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you. Jesus puts it negatively, shall not enter it, which makes it a condition for everyone rather than a compliment to children: no one enters any other way, and adults cannot come in as adults, with their merits.

Like a child. What is it about a child? Not innocence: children are not morally blank, and David says he was brought forth in iniquity (Psalm 51:5). Not simplicity of mind either, as though faith required us to stop thinking; this is the same Lord who tells us to love God with all our mind (12:30). It is dependence. A small child in that world owned nothing, earned nothing, and could contribute nothing. He did not negotiate for his dinner; he was fed. He did not qualify for his place in the family; he was born into it. Everything he had came to him as a gift from someone bigger, and he took it without embarrassment. The kingdom must be received in exactly that way, as grace, not achievement.

Why this is so hard for competent adults. Every other sphere of life rewards the self-sufficient. Here, the qualities that recommend you everywhere else are the disqualifying ones. The only thing anyone can do with the kingdom is receive it. The rich man who comes running next is the opposite of the child: he asks, what must I do? (v. 17). A child comes with empty hands and is welcomed. A rich man comes with full ones and cannot get in.

What does receiving like a child look like for me? It means coming to God with no bargaining position. You stop presenting your record, your church attendance, your efforts, as reasons God should accept you, and you simply trust what he has promised in Christ. It means believing that he loves you because he is your Father, not because you have performed well this week. And it continues all through the Christian life: you keep receiving forgiveness, strength and guidance as gifts, rather than turning the Christian life into a new way of earning. It does not mean being naive or passive; children who trust their father also obey him. But the obedience grows from being loved, not the other way round.

And he took them in his arms. Only Mark records it, as in 9:36; the verb, to fold in the arms, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. When the Lord of glory dealt with children he did not pat them on the head. He gathered them up. The people brought the children for a touch; he gave them an embrace.

And blessed them. The verb is a strengthened form: he blessed them fervently, one child at a time, while grown men stood by wishing he would get on. They were the same hands that had taken a dead girl by the hand (5:41) and lifted a convulsing boy from the ground (9:27), and which within weeks would be nailed down and unable to hold anybody at all.

For worship. The hands he laid on those children, soon to be nailed down, he lifted over his disciples as he was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51), and from there he has never withheld his blessing from anyone brought to him with empty hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ran up and knelt. Everything about the approach is right. He ran, when men of position did not run; he knelt, in the dirt, in public. Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), Luke that he was a ruler (Luke 18:18). He had everything, and still lacked something.

Good Teacher. Jewish teachers were not normally called good, a word reserved for God. It is warm and sincere, and also the kind of compliment a man pays to a respected figure on his way to asking a favour.

What must I do to inherit eternal life? The best question anybody asks in this Gospel, and nobody else asks it. The Pharisees ask about divorce law and signs from heaven; the disciples ask about seats and greatness; this man asks how to be saved. So hold the whole picture before the passage turns hard, because the point is nearly always missed by making him a villain. He is not one. He is eager, humble, urgent, morally serious, and asking the right thing. If he walked into your church you would thank God for him. But note the word do. He thinks eternal life is something to be achieved. And inherit is a strange word to pair with doing: an inheritance is precisely the thing nobody does anything for. You receive it because of who you are in the family. He has used the language of gift and attached it to the language of achievement, and he does not notice. The child two verses ago received. This man wants to know the price.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. This has been seized on for centuries as though Jesus were denying that he is good, or denying that he is God. He is doing neither, and notice that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Do you know what you have just said? Goodness in the full and final sense belongs to God and to nobody else. Which leaves two possibilities, and the man never works out which one he is in. Either you should not have called me good, in which case you have come running and kneeling to the wrong person; or the word is right, and you must reckon with who is standing in front of you. It is not a denial of his deity. It is a door held open to it. He came asking what he must do, and the deeper question, the one he never reaches, is who is this?

What it does not mean. Not a confession by Jesus that he is a sinner: the New Testament is clear that Jesus was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). If only God is good, it is the rich man who is not good, whatever he thinks of his record.

Compliment or confession? There is a hard little test here for the way we talk about Jesus. It is possible to say very warm things about him and mean very little: to call him wonderful, loving, good, the greatest teacher who ever lived, and to be paying a compliment rather than making a confession. Many people today will happily call Jesus good who will not call him Lord. He is quite capable of stopping a man mid-sentence and asking whether he knows what he is saying. If he is good as only God is good, then he must be worshipped and obeyed, not merely admired.

For worship. Every perfection of God was there in a human face in that road: holiness without hardness, truth without coldness, goodness that could not be flattered. He is not merely a good teacher. He is the Good, come down to seek those who are not.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments. The question was what must I do, so Jesus goes to God’s law: not because keeping it is how anyone is saved, but because it is the mirror the man needs.

The list. Jesus lists the commandments about our neighbour. Not one of the first four, about God, is mentioned. That is deliberate, and very gentle: the man’s problem is going to be a rival god, so Jesus recites only the commandments the man believes he has kept, and waits.

Do not defraud. Not one of the ten, but in the law elsewhere (Leviticus 19:13), and perhaps standing for the tenth, since defrauding is covetousness in action. It is the one commandment on the list that a wealthy landowner in first-century Palestine would have been most likely to break, and least likely to notice himself breaking: withholding what is owed, especially to a labourer. He is being probed, kindly, at the exact point of his danger, and he does not feel a thing.

All these I have kept. This time he drops the word good. His claim is sincere, and by outward standards perhaps true; Jesus does not contest it. Paul could say the same of his life before Christ: as to righteousness under the law, blameless (Philippians 3:6). But it is the most self-condemning sentence in the chapter. He has not understood how deep God’s law goes, reaching the anger and lust of the heart (Matthew 5:21–28). He has treated it as a checklist and is waiting to be told the remaining item. Yet the law that condemns us is in Christ’s hands a tool of mercy, and its whole demand was met by him, who alone could say with truth, all these I have kept, and kept them in our place.

What he still assumes. He thinks one more good deed will complete his record. What he is about to be shown is not one more item to add. It is that his heart belongs to something other than God.

Why does Jesus point him to the law if we are not saved by keeping it? Because the law shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he has kept it needs to see that he has not, and Jesus is leading him there with great care. The law is also good as a guide for those already saved, showing how to love God and neighbour. What it can never do is make us right with God, because no one keeps it from the heart. Christ kept it perfectly for us, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him. Scripture’s word for this is justification: God pronounces a guilty person right with him, not because that person has become perfect, but because Christ’s perfect record is credited to him and his sins were paid for at the cross (Romans 4:5; 5:19).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking at him, loved him. Only Mark records this, and it is one of the tenderest half-sentences in the Bible, and the key to the passage. The verb for looking means to fix the eyes on somebody: a deliberate, held gaze, not a glance. And then: he loved him. It is the only place in this Gospel where we are told that Jesus loved a particular individual. Everything hard that follows must be read inside that. What follows is not harsh. It is love. Jesus saw his sincerity and his need, and the demand he makes is the loving cure for what was killing him.

You lack one thing. For about two seconds that sounds like a relief: only one thing. But the one thing is the centre of his life. His wealth had his heart. It was his god. He had broken the first commandment, you shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3), and the tenth.

Sell all that you have. The surgery: cut out the idol. The man had passed the whole list about neighbours; one sentence finds out whether he has any other gods, and the answer comes back at once.

Is this required of every Christian? No, and the Gospels themselves settle it. Jesus does not ask everyone to sell everything. Peter kept his house in Capernaum (1:29). Zacchaeus gave away half, and was told that salvation had come to his house (Luke 19:8–9). Joseph of Arimathea, Matthew tells us, was rich (Matthew 27:57), and his money bought the tomb. Jesus does not issue this command to anyone else in the New Testament. It is not a universal rule. It is a scalpel, and it goes to one man’s one thing. He asks this man to give up the thing that stood between him and God. For him, it was money. But the principle is universal: Christ has the right to ask for anything you love more than him.

Treasure in heaven. Not a payment for salvation, and not a rule that poverty is holier. Jesus tells him to trade: give away treasure on earth and receive treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21), which is the better end of any bargain ever offered to a human being.

Follow me. Selling everything was the means; following Jesus was the end. Eternal life is not earned by giving away money but found in following Christ. He is being invited into the company that walks behind Jesus on the road, and Jesus himself is the real prize, not the treasure.

He went away sorrowful. The only person in Mark whom Jesus personally calls who refuses. He wanted eternal life, but not more than he wanted his money. He is not angry or scoffing; he knows exactly what he is refusing and refuses it anyway, and he is miserable about it. There is such a thing as sorrow that is not repentance, grief over the cost of obedience that never actually obeys, and this man is its portrait. Mark gives the reason last, flat, without comment: he had great possessions. In truth it was the other way round. They had him.

Jesus let him go. He does not call after him or offer a smaller figure. The Son of God, who loved this man, let him go. That is what love looks like when it will not lie to you. A love that lowered the price would have been the crueller thing: it would have sent him home comfortable, with his idol intact, thinking himself safe. Few sights in the Gospel are sadder than a man walking down a road with everything he came with still in his hands, and without the one thing he came for.

How do I know what my one thing is? Ask what you could not bear to lose, what you turn to for security when you are afraid, what you think about when your mind is free, and what you would be most angry to have taken away. Ask what you are most reluctant to bring under Christ’s word: your money, a relationship, your reputation, your comfort, your career, your plans for your children. The one thing is usually not a wicked thing but a good thing loved too much. And the test is often money, because money is the most portable god there is. Look at your bank statement and your diary; they tell the truth about the heart.

In everyday life. He looks at you with the same love, and asks for your one thing only because he is better than it; the Spirit he has put in you is stronger than its grip. Loosen it this week with something concrete: a generous gift that costs you, an hour given that you wanted for yourself, a plan surrendered in prayer.

For worship. Where this man would not let go of his riches to follow Christ, Christ let go of all his riches to come after us: though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How difficult it will be! Riches give a sense of not needing God (Deuteronomy 8:11–14), and make it hard to receive the kingdom like a child, with empty hands, because full hands cannot receive.

Amazed at his words. In the Old Testament prosperity is often a sign of God’s favour (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and people commonly concluded that a rich man is a blessed man. And the rich could afford to give alms, offer sacrifices, keep the law scrupulously and study it at leisure. If anyone was going to make it, surely he was. If the rich can hardly enter, what hope for anyone?

Children, how difficult it is! The second time he leaves out the rich: verse 24 says how hard it is for anybody. The rich man only makes visible a difficulty everyone has. And he begins, Children, the only time he addresses the disciples this way in Mark. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, and he opens it the way a father does.

The man who refused the kingdoms of the world. Only one man has faced the pull of wealth at its largest and not given an inch. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and offered him the lot for one act of worship, and he answered that God alone is to be worshipped and served (Matthew 4:8–10). The rich man could not let go of his estates. The Son turned down the world, and chose instead the road to a cross, so that people whose hands are full of lesser things could be given the kingdom.

A camel through the eye of a needle. The largest animal anyone in Palestine handled, the smallest opening anyone used: deliberate, comic exaggeration, meaning impossible.

Two ways of softening it. The idea of a small gate in Jerusalem called the needle’s eye has no evidence behind it before the Middle Ages, and it turns the saying into advice that with less baggage you can just about manage, the opposite of the point. Reading rope for camel has only a few late manuscripts and would not help either. Jesus means what the disciples heard: humanly impossible (v. 27), and he does not correct them. He did not soften the impossible to make it bearable, because he intended to do the impossible himself.

Am I one of the rich Jesus means here? Almost certainly, by the measure that matters here. He says it looking round at his own disciples, men who had left their boats, as if no one is safe from the pull he has just watched win. Anyone with a home, a change of clothes, food that is not in question this week and medical care within reach is, by every standard the world has known and most it knows now, rich. This is not a passage about bankers. And wealth is dangerous not only for what it buys but for what it makes us feel: safe, competent, in control, without need. The question is not how much you have but whether it has you. Signs that it does: anxiety about money that crowds out trust, reluctance to give, envy of those with more, and a life arranged around keeping what you have. And the poor are not safe from it either: money can rule the man who longs for it as surely as the man who has it, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:9–10).
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then who can be saved? Exceedingly astonished, stronger than the amazement of verse 24: the second saying has hit harder than the first. And their question is exactly the right one: for once the disciples reason perfectly. If the man with every visible advantage, money, morality, eagerness, a clean record from boyhood, cannot get in, then no one can. They have understood that the difficulty is not a matter of degree. It is not that the rich have further to walk; it is that the door will not admit anyone under their own power. And this is personal for them. They have left everything, and if having wealth cannot buy entry, neither can giving it up.

Jesus looked at them. Mark’s third look in this passage (vv. 21, 23), because what is coming is the most important sentence in it.

With man it is impossible. Yes, they had understood. Not difficult; impossible. No one, rich or poor, has ever saved himself, met God halfway, or made himself easier to save: not the rich man with his clean record, not Peter with his abandoned boat, not you. This is the heart of the gospel’s bad news: we are unable.

But not with God. The impossibility is real and total, and it is God’s to solve, and he has solved it. It echoes the angel’s word to Sarah, laughing at the promise of a son: Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end: he gives the new heart, he grants repentance and faith, he draws us (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8–9). If God can save a rich man, and he can, as Zacchaeus and Joseph of Arimathea prove, he can save anyone. A camel through a needle is no harder for him than a world out of nothing.

God helps those who help themselves? This verse quietly demolishes one of the most popular religious sayings in the English language. It is not in the Bible, and it is the exact reverse of what Jesus says here. God saves those who cannot help themselves, which is everybody. And notice how it will be done, because it is not left in the air. The man saying it is on the road to Jerusalem, and in eighteen verses he will say why: to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45). The impossibility is not overcome by a change in the requirements. It is overcome by a death.

If salvation is God’s work, what do I do? Call on him. The God for whom all things are possible commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (1:15), and promises that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). His sovereignty is not a reason to wait passively; it is the reason to hope, because your salvation does not depend on a strength you do not have. If you want Christ, that wanting is already his work in you. Come to him and you will find that he has been drawing you all along. And keep praying for others, because nothing in them is beyond his reach.

In everyday life. If you have ever looked honestly at yourself and concluded that you have no business being in the kingdom of God, that is the correct assessment, and Jesus made it first, and then said the words that answer it: but not with God. And the person you think least likely ever to be saved is not beyond those words either.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have left everything. Peter began to say it: honest, blurted, and not quite what it should be. He has watched the rich man go, heard that it is impossible, and what comes out is: we did, though. It is true (1:18, 20), and it cost them something real. But two verses after with man it is impossible, he is doing arithmetic again. It is the oldest temptation of religious people: to serve God in order to put him in our debt, as though our sacrifices were deposits he must one day repay with interest.

There is no one who has left. Jesus does not rebuke Peter. He answers generously and promises reward, and the list is everything a man in that world had. In the early church many converts were disowned by their families or lost their property (Hebrews 10:34), and in many countries they still are.

For my sake and for the gospel. As in 8:35, only Mark adds and for the gospel. Loss for its own sake is not praised: Christians are not called to abandon families as a spiritual achievement. Jesus means what a person loses because he follows him.

A hundredfold now. Not only in heaven: now, the extravagant yield of the parable of the sower (4:8). He is not promising that a man who gives up a house will be given a hundred houses. He is promising the church. The one who loses his earthly family gains brothers, sisters and mothers in the church (3:34–35), homes opened to him, and a share in all that belongs to the people of God (Acts 2:44–46). Paul greets a woman in Rome as one who had been a mother to him as well (Romans 16:13). And notice that fathers is missing from the list of what is received: in God’s family there is one Father (Matthew 23:9). No one has ever out-given Christ. He left his Father’s house and his heavenly glory for us, and the reward of his sacrifice is a family beyond number, gathered in his name.

Can this be tested? It is one of the few promises of Christ that can be tested this month. The believer with no family who is never alone at Christmas. The convert cut off by his relatives who has more people praying for him than he can count. The student far from home given a key to a church family’s house. If your church is not that for somebody, this verse is an indictment before it is a comfort.

With persecutions. Only Mark adds this, in the middle of the blessings, as one of the things received. No recruiter was ever so honest: the hundredfold arrives with trouble attached, in the same parcel.

Is this a promise that God will make me wealthy if I give? No. The prosperity teaching that uses this verse to promise money in return for gifts has turned it upside down. The hundredfold is relational and spiritual, found in the family of God, and it comes with persecutions. Jesus had nowhere to lay his head, and Paul knew hunger and need while content in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13). God does provide for his children, and generosity is never a loss in the end. But the promise is that you will never lose by following Christ, not that following Christ is a financial investment.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the rich man’s question (v. 17). What he would not give up everything for, they will receive.

First will be last. A warning aimed at the man who said we have left everything. The rich man, first by every earthly measure, walked away, and the children were taken in; and those who think of themselves as first because of their sacrifices may find themselves last. The kingdom’s order is not a league table with the earliest and most sacrificial at the top. Reward is grace, not wages earned (Matthew 20:1–16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). On the road up to Jerusalem Jesus walks in front, the disciples are amazed and the crowd afraid, and he tells them for the third and fullest time what is waiting.

The request (vv. 35–45). James and John ask for the two best seats, the ten are furious, and Jesus lays down the rule of his kingdom: the great one is the servant, the first is the slave of all. He grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last healing before Jerusalem. A blind beggar will not be silenced, receives his sight and follows Jesus on the road.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom is the price paid to set a captive free, and Jesus says his own life is that price, paid in our place: the many go free because the One is handed over. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12).

The price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined; he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27). The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself. This is how the impossible of verse 27 is done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question, What do you want me to do for you?, is asked twice in fifteen verses: to James and John (v. 36) and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

Now: we often pray more like the brothers than the beggar: a decision already taken, brought to God to be signed. Bartimaeus asked for what he actually needed, from someone he had rightly named Son of David, on no ground but mercy. He had nothing in his hands, like the child of verse 15, and that is how anyone receives the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going up to Jerusalem. The first time Mark names the destination. The road from Jericho climbs about 3,500 feet (1,000 m) in 15 miles (25 km), but every Jew said up to Jerusalem whatever the road did, because the city of God was always up.

Walking ahead of them. Not carried along by events: he is setting the pace, going to his death on purpose (Luke 9:51). Isaiah had said it centuries earlier in the Servant’s voice: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:7). A shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

Those who followed were afraid. Two groups may be meant: the Twelve, amazed, and the pilgrims behind, afraid. One man striding ahead with a set face, and behind him people who sensed that something terrible lay ahead.

Amazed and afraid on the road. There are stretches of the Christian life where the honest description of your state is amazed and afraid. And the picture gives you the one thing that helps: he is in front, not sending instructions from a distance but on the road, going first, and there is nothing coming that he has not already walked into.

Is it wrong to be afraid as a Christian? No. The disciples were afraid on this road, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). Fear is a human response to real danger and loss. What Scripture forbids is fear that rules us and turns us back from obedience. The answer to fear is not pretending, but looking at the one who walks ahead: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). Follow him while you are still afraid. Courage is not the absence of fear but walking on with him through it.

Taking the twelve again. Privately, a third time and in more detail than ever: he will not let them arrive in Jerusalem without having been told.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, we are going up. The fullest of the three predictions (8:31; 9:31): eight steps, almost a summary of chapters 14 to 16.

Delivered over. Handed over, that word again (9:31): betrayed into the hands of the Jewish leaders (14:10, 43), who will pass sentence in the Sanhedrin (14:64).

To the Gentiles. This is new and shocking: the leaders of Israel will pass their own Messiah to the pagans, since they could not carry out executions under Roman rule (John 18:31). The Jewish penalty for blasphemy was stoning; crucifixion was Rome’s. When he says Gentiles, he is saying cross without using the word. God’s Messiah would be rejected by both Jews and Gentiles; the whole world is guilty (Acts 4:27).

Mock him and spit on him. Every verb was fulfilled (14:65; 15:15–20, 24). The mocking and the spitting are not necessary to an execution; the contempt is cruelty added for its own sake, and he names it in advance, walking toward it knowing he would be humiliated first. Isaiah had foretold it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6).

After three days. He has never once mentioned the death without the resurrection, and the disciples have never once shown that they took it in (9:10).

Hearing only what we want. Mark has arranged the contrast: after eight stages of humiliation and death, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats. They heard the word glory and nothing else. We do the same with Scripture: the promise received, the cost skipped over; a sermon about the cross followed by a conversation about lunch. The disciples are not a different species. They are us, with better excuses, because at least they had never seen a resurrection.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much, and not simply die? Because he was bearing the full weight of human sin, and sin is not only guilt but shame. We have despised God and treated his glory with contempt, and Christ received contempt in our place: the spitting, the mockery, the stripping, the curse of hanging on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), took our shame so that we might be clothed with his honour. And his suffering shows us what our sin deserves and how great his love is. Nothing was wasted, and nothing was accidental.

For worship. The face that shone on the mountain he gave to those who spat; the back that bore the cross he gave to those who struck. He hid not his face from shame, so that we would never have to hide ours from God. And on the third day he rose, exactly as he said.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Two of the inner three, and the Sons of Thunder (3:17). Matthew says their mother asked on their behalf (Matthew 20:20); she may have been Mary’s sister, which would make them Jesus’ cousins. Both accounts are true: she asked, they stood by, and Mark puts the responsibility where the ten put it (v. 41).

Whatever we ask of you. They ask him to agree to a question before they put it: a blank cheque, signed in advance, the way a child approaches a parent when he suspects the answer will be no.

Praying with a blank cheque. Hold this against our praying, because the same move is available in more respectable clothing. There is a way of praying that is not asking but informing: a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgment. Lord, bless what I have determined to do. The words are reverent; the transaction is a blank cheque.

What do you want me to do for you? He does not sign the blank cheque; he makes them say it out loud. He will ask Bartimaeus the same question (v. 51), and the two answers are the point of the chapter: they ask for glory, he asks for sight. (See Matthew 20:32 for the fuller answer.)

One at your right hand. The places of highest honour beside a king. They are asking for the top two positions in the government of the universe, which means they have already decided the other ten are not getting them. They want the glory without the cross, and they want it for themselves, above the others.

Something right in it. There is something almost admirable buried in it, and it should be said. They believe him. He has just told them he is going to be spat on and killed, and they are still asking about his glory, which means that somewhere in them is a genuine conviction that this man is going to reign. They have seen that glory on the mountain. That is more than the crowd had. But beside that faith is a deafness to what he has just said about dying, so complete it is hard to believe.

Who was at his right and left? Notice where he is standing while they ask: on a road, going up, walking ahead of them toward the day when there will in fact be a man on his right and a man on his left. They will be two criminals on crosses, and his glory will be the cross (15:27). His glory was not a seat above others but a death beneath them, and the thrones he gives at last are given freely to sinners who once asked for them for all the wrong reasons.

Is it wrong to ask God for things for myself? No. Jesus invites us to ask (Matthew 7:7), and he does not scold James and John for asking but for not knowing what they asked. Pray freely for your needs, your family, your work, your health. What is wrong is praying for position over others, and praying as though God existed to serve our plans. The best prayers have the shape of the Lord’s Prayer: his name, his kingdom, his will first, and then our daily bread, forgiveness and protection. Ask boldly, and let him correct the request.
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You do not know what you are asking. Not how dare you. He tells them, gently, that they have no idea what they have requested, and that is the first mercy in the passage. God does not grant our prayers according to our understanding of them. There is a great deal to be thankful for in the prayers he has declined.

The cup that I drink. In the Old Testament the cup is often God’s judgment, which the wicked must drink to the dregs (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17), and in Gethsemane Jesus will pray, Remove this cup from me (14:36). It is filled not by an outburst of divine irritation but by the steady, holy opposition of a pure God to everything evil, and Jesus drinks it in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty that sinners deserved. Penal, because it is a real penalty for real guilt; substitution, because he bears it in our place. He took the cup that was ours, foaming with the wrath we had stored up, and he drank it to the bottom.

The baptism with which I am baptized. Not water: being overwhelmed, as by a flood (Psalm 42:7; Luke 12:50). Can you be drowned in what is about to drown me?

We are able. Brave and ignorant, and Peter will say much the same at the last supper (14:31). But they mean it. Their loyalty at that moment is genuine, but it rests on their own strength, which will fail (14:50).

The cup that I drink you will drink. And the reply is not sarcasm. It is a prophecy, and it came true. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa in Jerusalem about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John was on Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 1:9), by early tradition as an exile, and is said to have lived to old age. They asked for thrones and were promised suffering, and they got the suffering, and they did not fall away when it came. But their cup will not be the same as his. Only he drinks the cup of God’s wrath for sin. Theirs is the cup of suffering for his sake (Paul can speak of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions, Colossians 1:24, but he means the sufferings of Christ’s people for the church, not any lack in the atonement).

Will I have to drink the cup of God’s wrath? Never, if you belong to Christ. That is the whole point of his drinking it. For those in Christ Jesus, condemnation is gone for good (Romans 8:1). He drained it to the dregs, and there is nothing left in it for his people. What you may be given is a different cup: suffering for his name, trials, losses, the ordinary weight of following him in a fallen world. That cup is real and sometimes bitter, but it is mixed by a Father’s hand for your good, and he drinks it with you. Never confuse the two.

Not mine to grant. Not that Jesus lacks authority. In the work of salvation the Father appoints and the Son carries out what the Father has planned, the same willing submission as in 13:32 and 14:36. The seats exist; they are not his to hand out on request.

For whom it has been prepared. By the Father, in his eternal purpose (Matthew 20:23), and not open to lobbying. You cannot secure a place in the kingdom of God by asking for it, deserving it, arriving early, or knowing the right person, and there is enormous relief in that for anyone who has ever felt they were losing a race they did not want to be running.

For worship. He went under the waves so that we would not drown. And the Father who prepared places in his kingdom prepared them for people who had asked for all the wrong things, because the Son had drunk the right cup.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indignant at James and John. They were furious, very likely not because the request was wrong but because the two had got in first. The ten had the same ambitions, and the lesson of chapter 9 had not taken. The ambition went underground and has now surfaced as outrage at somebody else’s ambition, which is the usual way it appears in religious company.

Jesus called them. All twelve: the disease is general, and so is the treatment.

Those who are considered rulers. Rome is the example: there authority means pressing down on those below, and greatness is measured by how many people must do what you say. And considered has a sting in it: they only seem to rule; the real ruler is God.

Lord it over them … exercise authority over them. Both verbs mean to domineer: power pressed down on people. The world’s pattern of leadership is power over others for the leader’s benefit.

Not so among you. Literally, it is not so among you: a statement of what his people are, and so a ban on bringing the world’s way of ruling into the church. Too much of church history is the story of ignoring it, in cathedrals and small congregations alike, wherever a man has discovered that a position in the things of God can be used to make other people smaller.

The one ruler who never lorded it. Jesus is not describing an authority he lacks: he is the ruler of kings on earth (Revelation 1:5). Of all who have ever held power, he alone had the right to press it down on everyone, and he never once did. He would not cry aloud or make his voice heard in the street (Isaiah 42:2); he used his power to heal, feed, forgive, and finally to die. There is no authority in heaven or earth like his, and none so gentle. The kingdom’s rule for leaders is a portrait of its King, and every true leader in his church holds a borrowed towel, the one with which he washed his disciples’ feet. On how this reshapes leadership in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Your servant. “Servant” (diakonos): one who waits at table. A servant has a role, and can, at the end of the day, go home.

Slave of all. Further still: one who has no time of his own and no choice about whom he serves. Once again the ambition is not forbidden; it is given a road, and the road runs downward. And slave of all removes the last escape, which is choosing whom to serve. All: including the ten who are furious with you, and the two who went behind your back.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no authority in the church. Elders are to lead and be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). But Christian authority is exercised as service, for the good of others, never for the leader’s benefit: shepherd the flock, not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples (1 Peter 5:1–3).

What about authority at home? The same rule holds. Scripture gives husbands headship and parents authority, and both are real (Ephesians 5:22–6:4). This commentary holds that complementarian reading, because Paul ties the husband’s role to Christ’s self-giving love for the church; other faithful Christians, often called egalitarians, read these passages as mutual submission without distinct roles, and they too love Christ and hate abuse. But Jesus defines all authority among his people by this verse: it is used for the good of those under it, and never to dominate, control or frighten. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); fathers are not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). A man who uses headship to demand, belittle or harm has not understood headship at all, and abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of authority. The test of all Christian leadership is the towel and the cross.

In everyday life. If you lead at work, home or church, you serve under a King who knelt to wash your feet. Name one person under your authority and, asking the Spirit to form your Master’s mind in you, do something this week that serves their good at a cost to your convenience.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The key verse of Mark. This one sentence sums up the whole purpose of Jesus’ coming. It explains the three passion predictions and everything that follows in chapters 11 to 16. And it comes as a reason: the verse begins with For. He has just told them to go to the bottom, and this is the reason: not a principle, but a Person, and what that Person is walking toward.

For even the Son of Man. That title is not a modest one. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him (Daniel 7:13–14). In Daniel the whole world serves him. If anyone had the right to be served, it was he.

Came not to be served but to serve. “Came” implies he came from somewhere, with a purpose. The one figure in Scripture entitled to universal service arrived and declined it. The King came as a servant. He took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7).

To give his life. The supreme service: his life itself. Not taken from him but given (John 10:18).

As a ransom. A “ransom” (lytron) is the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner, or someone condemned to death (Exodus 21:30). We are slaves of sin and under the sentence of death (Romans 6:23). Slavery here means more than that we sin now and then: it means that, left to ourselves, we cannot stop putting ourselves in God’s place: everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). And because God is just, that rebellion stands under his sentence. Jesus pays the price of our freedom, and the currency is his own life.

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to Satan, as some of the early fathers imagined, as though the devil held a rightful claim over us that God had to buy out. He holds no such claim; he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27), and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, whose law we have broken. And God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself. So there is no drama here of an angry Father and a reluctant Son. It is one God, Father, Son and Spirit, in perfect love, resolving in himself what could not be resolved any other way.

Is it fair for an innocent man to die in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if an unwilling victim were seized and punished for someone else. But that is not what happens here. The one who dies is the Judge himself, come in the flesh. He gives his life; it is not taken from him (John 10:18).
