And he gives it for people he has made his own, as a husband takes on his wife’s debts. The holy God does not ignore sin, and he does not punish the wrong party against his will. He bears in himself the cost of his own justice, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The moralist would rather pay his own way; the sceptic thinks no one should have to pay at all. The cross answers both: the debt is real, and only God could pay it.

For many. “For” (anti) means in place of. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, and the many go free because the One is handed over.

Who are the many? “Many” contrasts the one who dies with the great number of those for whom he dies. The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous. Reformed theology reads this as definite: Christ gave his life as a ransom for his people, those the Father had given him (John 10:11, 15; 17:9), and his death actually secures their freedom. A ransom that is paid frees the captive. Other traditions read many as all, a universal offer. The word alone does not settle it, since in Hebrew idiom many can mean the great multitude; the argument rests on what a ransom is and on Jesus laying down his life for the sheep. Many faithful Christians, Arminians among them (those who hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for all and that grace can be resisted), read it otherwise, and they love the same Saviour. This commentary’s view: the ransom is real and effective; it does not merely make freedom possible but actually purchases it for the many. This is definite atonement. And the gospel offer still goes freely to all, since no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37). His death is sufficient for all and is offered to all.

How do I know I am one of the many? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by coming to Christ. The invitation is to everyone: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you trust Jesus as your Saviour and Lord, you are one of the many he ransomed, because the faith that comes to him is itself the fruit of his ransom. Assurance grows as you look to his promises, as the Spirit testifies with your spirit that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and as you see the fruit of a changed life. The doctrine of definite atonement is not a wall to keep you out. It is a guarantee that, if you are his, nothing can undo what he paid for you.

The answer to the disciples’ question. The disciples asked, then who can be saved? (v. 26). This is how: not by a lowering of the requirement, but by a payment. And the sentence is not in a sermon on the atonement but closes a squabble about the best seats. He settles it by telling them that he is going to be sold for their freedom. Everything in the Christian life that is asked of you is asked on the basis of that. You are not told to serve because service is noble. You are told to serve because the one who owned everything went to the bottom and stayed there, until it killed him, and bought you on the way down.

For worship. The one who owed nothing paid everything (1 Peter 1:18–19). And the many he ransomed will stand before him at last and sing that he was slain, and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jericho. The last stop before the climb to the city, with Passover days away. This second healing of a blind man matches the one at Bethsaida (8:22–26); between them Jesus has taught about the cross while his disciples were blind to it.

As he was leaving Jericho. Luke says as he drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35), and Matthew mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30). There were two Jerichos in Jesus’ day, the ancient mound and the Herodian town, so he may have been leaving one and approaching the other; it cannot be proved. And Mark names the one blind man the church knew; he does not say there was only one.

Bartimaeus. The only person healed in Mark who is named (“Bar” is Aramaic for son of). The likeliest reason is that the church knew him, and a named man is a witness others could check.

Jesus of Nazareth. The crowd’s name for him. All Bartimaeus has is a name passed down the line, and he acts on it instantly.

Jesus, Son of David. Bartimaeus’ name for him, and a far greater one. Son of David is a messianic title: the promised king from David’s line, whose throne God would establish for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). And it is the first time in Mark anyone uses it. Everyone in this chapter who can see has misunderstood him, and the man who cannot see anything names him correctly at the first attempt. The Messiah was expected to give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1). And Jesus does not silence him: the time for keeping quiet about who he is has almost ended. He is about to enter Jerusalem as the Son of David (11:10).

Have mercy on me! The cry of one with no claim, only need: mercy is what you ask for when the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking (Luke 18:13). The beggar is the only one in the chapter who gets exactly what he came for. And every cry of Lord, have mercy, from Jericho to this morning, has reached the ears of a King who loves to answer it.

Many rebuked him. That word rebuked again, as with the parents of the children (v. 13). A beggar bawling at a distinguished rabbi on a pilgrimage road was a nuisance.

All the more. Persistent, unembarrassed faith. Jesus is passing by and will not come this way again, and being disapproved of by respectable people is not a price he is troubled by.

What if others discourage me from coming to Christ? Then do what Bartimaeus did: cry out all the more. Some are discouraged by a family that finds faith excessive, some by a church that made them feel they did not fit, some by an inner voice that says they are too much, too messy, too late. The crowd told this man to be quiet, and the crowd was wrong. Jesus stopped for the shouting. No one is turned away by him for being an embarrassment to others. And if you are part of the crowd, be careful whom you silence.

In everyday life. Pray the beggar’s prayer, Son of David, have mercy on me, on the way to work, before a hard conversation, when you have failed again.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stopped. He has been walking ahead with a set face (v. 32), and he stops because a blind man is shouting. The Son of God on his way to die halts the whole procession for one beggar whom everybody else was trying to silence. Nothing in his life was ever too urgent for a person.

Call him. He does not go to Bartimaeus. He tells the very people who had been telling the man to be quiet to call him, and Bartimaeus must answer the call and come. That is deliberate. The crowd that hindered is made to be the crowd that brings.

Take heart. Get up; he is calling you. Three short commands, and listen to the change in their voices. Thirty seconds ago they were telling him to be quiet. Now they are encouraging him. It is the same people. Nothing has changed except that Jesus stopped, and the moment he took an interest, so did they. There is a warning in that for anybody in a church: the person you find embarrassing, inconvenient, too loud or too needy may be the one Christ is calling. And these could be the words of every evangelist: take heart, get up, Jesus is calling you.

Throwing off his cloak. A beggar’s cloak was probably spread to catch coins, his bed at night and his shelter from the cold, a possession the law protected (Exodus 22:26–27): quite literally all he had. And he throws it aside, blind, with no idea whether he will find it again.

He sprang up. A blind man leaps to his feet toward a voice, not knowing what is in the way. He heard, he is calling you, and that was enough.

How does Jesus call people today? Through the gospel, spoken by ordinary people. Just as he used the crowd to call Bartimaeus, he uses preachers, parents, friends and colleagues to say: take heart, get up, he is calling you. When the Spirit takes that word and opens a heart, the call is effectual, and the sinner comes freely and gladly, as this man sprang up (Romans 8:30; 10:14–17). Effectual means that it does what it says: it does not merely invite, it actually brings the dead heart to life and the sinner to Christ, as surely as Jesus’ word brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43–44). So if you have heard the gospel and feel its pull, do not wait for a voice from heaven; this is his call. And if you know him, you are part of the crowd he sends. Tell someone.
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What do you want me to do for you? The same question he asked James and John (v. 36), and the answers could not differ more. It is obvious what a blind beggar wants, but Jesus will not do things to people over their heads, and gives the man a dignity nobody had shown him in years. (See Matthew 20:32 for the fuller answer.)

Rabbi. Literally Rabbouni, my master, a more personal and reverent form than the ordinary Rabbi. It appears elsewhere in the New Testament only on the lips of Mary Magdalene in the garden when she recognises the risen Christ (John 20:16).

Let me recover my sight. One clause, no preamble. Not money, which he had asked passers-by for all his life, but sight, which would end his livelihood. He asks for the thing that will cost him his old life.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) is literally has saved you, the same word Jesus spoke to the woman with the bleeding (5:34). Physical healing and spiritual salvation are both in it. Something more than eyesight has happened here: he has been put right with God, because the faith that received his sight received the Saviour himself. And note where the power lay: not in how much he understood, though he got the title right, and not in his persistence, though he had plenty. His faith was the empty hand that received what Jesus gave; the power was Jesus’. Faith saves because of whom it takes hold of, and this man took hold of the Son of David and would not be shouted down.

Immediately. No touch, no saliva, no clay, and no second stage, unlike the man at Bethsaida (8:22–25). Just the word.

Followed him on the way. The last words of the section, and the most important. Jesus told him to go his way, free to go home, find his cloak, start a life. And he does not go his way. He goes Christ’s. Given his freedom and his eyes in the same breath, the first thing he does with both is get on the road to Jerusalem behind the man who healed him. And on the way in this Gospel is never merely geography: it is the road to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32), the road the disciples have been walking amazed and afraid. He is the last person healed in Mark before the passion, and the picture of the true disciple, which the Twelve should be: his eyes opened, he follows Jesus to the cross.

How the chapter ends. It began with a wealthy, moral man who went home with everything he came with, and ends with a blind beggar who threw away the one cloak he had and followed. It is what Jesus said in verse 15: the ones who get in are the ones who come with nothing and simply receive.

Does Jesus still heal the blind? He can, and he sometimes heals in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence in his power and submission to his will (James 5:14–15). But Mark tells this story above all as a picture of salvation: we are all born blind to God, and only Christ’s word can open our eyes (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). The greater miracle, which he performs every day, is the opening of hearts to see his glory in the face of Jesus. And for those who are not healed in this life, the promise is sure: in the resurrection the eyes of the blind will be opened for ever (Isaiah 35:5).

For worship. He opened the eyes of the blind with a word, and the first thing the healed man saw was the face of Jesus. That is the gift he gives every one of his people: to behold the glory of God in the face of Christ, and then to follow him on the way.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology: Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew records an exception, except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9), and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. This is a difference of purpose, not a contradiction: Mark gives the principle from creation with its full weight, Matthew the qualification Jesus allowed, and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse, after which the believer is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So this commentary, with the Westminster Confession, recognises adultery and desertion as the grounds on which the innocent party may be freed. Mark simply refuses to lead with the exception: Jesus begins with the joining God performs.
10.examples:
Then: a blind beggar at Jericho is called to Jesus and throws off his cloak (v. 50). It was his bed at night and the one possession the law protected (Ex. 22:26–27).

Now: set him beside the man at the start of the chapter, who was asked to give up his possessions and went away sorrowful because he had a great many. What we hold on to when Christ calls shows what we trust. The beggar did not throw the cloak away to earn anything. He threw it away because the one calling him was worth more.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
After ten chapters of hushing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus makes a public claim to the throne, riding a borrowed colt as Zechariah said the king would come. The crowd spreads cloaks and branches and shouts the Passover psalm: Hosanna, save now. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do.

He goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves because it is late. Next morning he curses a fig tree in full leaf with no fruit and overturns the traders' tables, and on the third morning the tree is dead to its roots. Mark wraps the temple inside the fig tree so that each explains the other. Out of the dead tree comes teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness, and the chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking by what authority? and refusing the one question that would have led them home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The entry (vv. 1–11). Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt, the crowd sings the Passover psalm, and he looks around the temple and goes out to Bethany.

The tree (vv. 12–14). Next morning he finds a fig tree in full leaf with nothing on it, and curses it.

The temple (vv. 15–19). He overturns the tables, stops the traffic, and quotes two prophets against the leaders.

The lesson (vv. 20–26). The tree is dead to the roots, and Jesus teaches faith, prayer and forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves. A fig in that land puts out small edible knobs with or before its leaves, so a tree in full leaf was claiming to have something. Nobody was owed a crop; what the tree owed was consistency with its own appearance.

And look where Mark has put it. He splits the story and sets the temple in the gap: curse, temple, withered tree. The fig tree was a picture of Israel (Hos. 9:10). Israel's worship that week was in full leaf, and he came near and found no fruit. The sentence on the tree was carried out on the building forty years later (13:2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a temple full of activity, and worshippers who went home feeling delivered.

Now: does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you live the rest of the week, or less? If an hour on Sunday can settle a conscience without changing a grudge, a dishonest invoice or a cold marriage, the house of prayer has become a den. The way out is not to stay away but to come and confess, to the Lord who overturned the tables and welcomes every thief who comes to him empty-handed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 11 begins the last week of Jesus’ life. After ten chapters of hushing demons and the healed, Jesus makes a public claim as Zechariah’s humble King. The withered fig tree interprets the cleansing of the temple: splendid in leaf and barren, it stands under judgment. The King has come to his house, and the house has not known him.

The setting. Mark gives six of his sixteen chapters to this one week, which shows where the weight of the gospel lies. It is Passover, when pilgrims swelled Jerusalem several times over and the governor brought extra troops, because the feasts were when riots were most feared.

Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives. Two villages on the ridge east of Jerusalem; Bethany, about two miles (3 km) out, was where Jesus stayed this week (v. 11). From the Mount of Olives you look straight down onto the temple platform, and it is where Zechariah says the LORD will stand when he comes for his people: on that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4). He approaches from the one direction the prophets had marked.

Go into the village. For ten chapters this man has walked everywhere, and now he sends ahead for something to ride. The entry is staged, and that is the point: the secret is over, and he has decided the hour.

You will find a colt tied. A young donkey; Matthew mentions its mother as well (Matthew 21:2), and to mention more is not to contradict. Whether by foreknowledge (2:8) or prior arrangement, every step of this week is deliberate.

On which no one has ever sat. An animal for a sacred purpose had never been put to ordinary work (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for the King.

The Lord has need of it. “The Lord” (ho kyrios) could mean simply its master, Jesus as the one with the right to it, but Mark’s readers would hear the fuller meaning. The Lord of all creation borrows a donkey.

Will send it back. The King borrows; he does not seize, as Samuel warned that Israel’s kings would (1 Samuel 8:16–17). That is how he deals with what is yours: he has every right to take, and he asks. And no one has ever been the poorer for lending to him: whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed (Proverbs 19:17).

Does God really need anything from me? Not in the sense of lacking it. He is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). But he chooses to use what his people give, and he honours it by calling it a need. That is grace: the Lord who could ride on the clouds asks to borrow a donkey, so that an ordinary villager’s property becomes part of the coronation of the King. Your gifts, time and skills are not necessary to him, and they are wanted by him.

For worship. The King of glory rode into his city on a borrowed colt, as he would be laid in a borrowed tomb. Blessed is the Lord who has every right to command, and comes to us asking.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A colt tied at a door. Exactly as he said, in the flattest possible language: they went, they found, they untied. The door, the street, the bystanders: somebody remembered exactly where the animal was standing.

What are you doing, untying the colt? A natural question: two strangers taking someone’s donkey. Mark’s report is almost comic in its restraint, and entirely believable. Nobody in a village stands by while their livestock walks off.

They let them go. The objection evaporated. Perhaps the owners knew him, or had been asked in advance.

Two errands, one Lord. Mark tells a second errand in almost the same words: a man carrying a water jar and a furnished upper room, just as he said (14:13–16). The Lord who knew where the colt stood knew who would betray him and that Peter would deny him (14:30). He did not stumble into Jerusalem and get caught. He went up knowing every door and every street of the road to the cross, and walked it anyway, for us.

Going with nothing but the word. The disciples had no documents and no explanation that would satisfy anybody, only a sentence they had been told to say, and it held. That is a fair picture of much Christian obedience: you go with the word you were given, into a situation you cannot control, and you find that it holds. Not one of his words has ever fallen to the ground, and his people may lean their whole weight on them.

The people who lent. Mark does not name them. They handed over their property to two strangers on the strength of a sentence, and the King rode into his city on it. Like the man who lent the upper room, they are in the story because something they owned was asked for and they did not say no.

What if God asks for something and I do not know why? Then you are where these disciples were, and where the owners were. Obedience often comes before understanding. God does not always explain; he commands, and he shows himself faithful afterwards. Test any sense of calling by Scripture, and seek wise counsel, because not every impulse is his voice. But where his word is plain, to give, to forgive, to speak, to serve, do not wait until you see the whole picture. You will see it later, and you will be glad you said yes.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he sat on it. There is no saddle, so the disciples improvise with their cloaks. For the last two miles, he rides, and Zechariah had foretold it: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Mark does not quote it (Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 do), but the action speaks for itself. Jesus is publicly claiming to be the King.

An unbroken colt. An animal never ridden, in a noisy festival crowd. Anyone who has been near an unbroken young donkey knows what usually happens. Nothing happens. It carries him. The one creature in Jerusalem that week that did exactly what he wanted was a donkey.

A donkey, not a horse. Kings went to war on horses; Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). Zechariah goes on: God will cut off the chariot and the war horse, and the King shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The choice of animal is a sermon: a humble king of peace, not a warrior to overthrow Rome. They will get the first half and miss the second. The Lord of hosts rode into his city on the smallest of beasts, because he came not to crush his enemies but to die for them.

Cloaks on the road. Not mere enthusiasm but protocol: when Jehu was proclaimed king, the people put their garments under him (2 Kings 9:13). A cloak in the dirt says: this is my king, and I will spend something to say so.

Leafy branches. John specifies palms (John 12:13). Palms had been waved when Simon Maccabeus took the citadel of Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:51), so the crowd is doing something precise, and political: cloaks for a king, branches for a liberator.

Right about who, wrong about what. Here is the ache under the whole scene. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do. The man they are welcoming as the liberator of Israel is riding toward an execution, and within five days a crowd in this city will be shouting for it. And it is not only first-century enthusiasm. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled about Jesus, to sing loudly, to spend something on him, and to be expecting an entirely different Christ from the one who is actually coming: a Christ who will sort out your circumstances, vindicate your side, and deliver you from the things you want delivering from. The cloaks were sincere. Nobody was pretending. And by Friday the road was empty.

How do I avoid following a Jesus of my own making? Keep reading the whole of the Gospels, especially the parts that unsettle you, and let him define himself. The real Jesus came to save from sin before he saves from circumstances, calls us to a cross before he gives a crown, and is Lord over our politics, not a mascot for them. Ask what you expect him to do for you, and whether that expectation comes from his word or your wishes. When he disappoints your plans, do not leave the road; he is doing something greater than you asked.

For worship. He could have come on the clouds with ten thousand angels, and he came at walking pace, gentle with a crowd that would soon desert him. They laid down their cloaks for him; he laid down his life for them. And when he comes again, no one will mistake what kind of King he is.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosanna! Save, we pray (Psalm 118:25): a cry for help that had become a shout of praise, like God save the king. Both meanings fit: the crowd praises Jesus, and unknowingly prays for exactly what he has come to do. Psalm 118 was sung at Passover, and every pilgrim knew it by heart.

He who comes. Psalm 118:26, once a greeting to pilgrims at the temple gates, but also a title for the Messiah: it is what John the Baptist’s messengers asked, are you the one who is to come? (Matthew 11:3). The crowd sings it to Jesus. And the same psalm speaks of the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), which Jesus will quote against the leaders within a day or two (12:10). He is listening to what they are singing.

The kingdom of our father David. Only Mark records this line: the crowd says what the psalm means to them, David’s throne restored under Roman occupation, an enormously dangerous thing to shout. The kingdom is coming, but not as they imagine.

The right prayer, not recognised. That is the terrible irony of the scene. They were shouting the right word. Save now was exactly the right request, made to exactly the right person, at exactly the right hour. They simply had no idea what they were asking for. They wanted saving from Rome, and he had come to save them from something worse, and the salvation they were shouting for would be accomplished by Friday afternoon in a manner that would empty this road. He heard the prayer. He answered it. And almost nobody who prayed it recognised the answer when it came. But every hosanna ever sung is answered in him, and blessed is he who will come again, when the whole creation shouts it and understands it at last.

Are the crowds of Palm Sunday the same people who shouted crucify him? Probably not all of them, and we should not be too neat. Many of the Palm Sunday crowd were Galilean pilgrims who had followed Jesus; the crowd before Pilate was gathered in the city early in the morning and stirred up by the chief priests (15:11). But the point holds either way. Popular enthusiasm is fickle, and no one should build his faith on the mood of a crowd, including the crowd at church. And all of us, Jew and Gentile, have the same heart that can praise him one day and reject him the next. That is why we need a Saviour, not just a hero.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the temple. Not the palace or the fortress: the Messiah goes straight to the house of God. Malachi had promised exactly this: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire (Malachi 3:1–2).

The temple. Herod’s temple, under construction for more than forty years (John 2:20), was a wonder of the ancient world, on a platform of about 35 acres (14 hectares); the word means the whole complex with its courts.

Looked around at everything. An inspection, recorded only by Mark: the traders, the tables, the birds in cages, seen by the one person present who knew what the building was for, as God looks for fruit from his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). He did not say a word. The King has come, looked, and will judge. He sees everything, and he is never hasty and never unjust.

Out to Bethany. He lodged outside the city each night of this week (v. 19; 14:3; Luke 21:37). Jerusalem was overcrowded at Passover, and dangerous for him.

Judgment, not temper. Two things follow from the timing. First, what he does next day is not a loss of temper. He saw all of it the night before, slept on it, walked two miles back, and then overturned the tables: a considered act, which is what makes it judgment. Second, the inspection is itself the warning. Before God acts, God looks: he came down to see Babel (Genesis 11:5) and Sodom (Genesis 18:21), and the risen Christ walks among the lampstands saying to church after church, I know your works (Revelation 2–3).

Should I be afraid of Christ looking at my life? If you are not his, his gaze is a warning to flee to him while there is time. If you are his, it is the look of a Saviour who already knows the worst and has paid for it. Nothing he finds will surprise him, and nothing will make him cast you out (John 6:37). But his look is still searching, because he loves his house too much to leave it cluttered. Let it lead you to honest confession, not to hiding. The safest place for a sinner is under the eyes of the Lord who died for him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The structure. Mark sandwiches the cleansing of the temple between two halves of the fig tree story: the curse (vv. 12–14), the temple (vv. 15–19), the withered tree (vv. 20–21). He often does this (3:20–35; 5:21–43; 6:7–30), never by accident, and each story interprets the other.

He was hungry. The Son of God, walking two miles into the city before breakfast, wanting something to eat. Truly human. Mark keeps giving us this: asleep on a cushion in a storm, hungry on a road.

A fig tree in leaf. The likely answer to the obvious objection lies in how a fig tree works. With its spring leaves, or before them, it produced small edible early knobs (paggim); the main crop came in June. A tree in full leaf with no early fruit was probably barren that year, and its leaves were a false advertisement. Whatever the botany, Mark’s own note shows he knew no ripe figs were due, and he tells the story as a sign.

For it was not the season for figs. Not an embarrassment but the key: Mark puts it there so that no reader can mistake this for pique over a missed breakfast. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement. The cursing is not a fit of temper at an innocent tree. It is an acted parable, like the prophets’ symbolic actions (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13).

Did Jesus not know there would be no fruit? He went to the tree as a man looking for fruit, and that was the point of the acted parable: he came to Israel looking for fruit and found only leaves. It was a deliberate sign, not a mistake. In his human nature he did not display all he knew at every moment, but nothing here took him by surprise.

The fig tree in the prophets. The fig tree was a recognised picture of Israel (Hosea 9:10). When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered (Jeremiah 8:13). God came looking for fruit in his people and found none.

The curse. The only miracle of cursing in the Gospels, performed on a tree: a sentence pronounced on fruitless religion, said aloud to be remembered (v. 21).

The tree is the temple. Israel’s worship that week was in magnificent leaf, which is religious activity, and bare of fruit, which is true worship and righteousness. The courts were packed for Passover; the sacrifices ran from dawn; the money moved. From the road it looked like the healthiest religion on earth. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), and found nothing but leaves. The sentence the tree received would be carried out on the building about forty years later, when not one stone was left on another (13:2).

The owner comes for his fruit. Within a day Jesus tells the rulers the same story in words: a man planted a vineyard, sent servant after servant for his share of the fruit, and last of all sent his beloved son, whom they killed (12:1–8). The hungry man at the fig tree is that Son, the Lord of the harvest come in person. He is also what Israel was meant to be: the one Israelite whose life was all fruit and no mere leaves, loving God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself. The barren tree would wither, and the fruitful Son would be cut down for the barren, so that branches grafted into him might live and bear fruit for God.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever (Romans 11:1–2, 25–29). The judgment fell on the temple and the leadership that rejected their Messiah, and the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

Leaves and fruit in my life. The tree was not condemned for being fruitless in season. It was condemned for advertising. Leaves are what other people can see: the attendance, the vocabulary, the reputation for soundness, the Bible on the table. Fruit is what is actually there: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and lives changed by the gospel. He is not in the distance any more. He comes near, and looks.

What if I feel fruitless? A tender conscience that grieves over little fruit is itself a sign of life; the fig tree felt nothing. Fruit is not something you manufacture by effort but something the Spirit grows as you abide in Christ (John 15:4–5), through his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. It often grows slowly and is more visible to others than to yourself. Ask a mature Christian who knows you what they see. And bring your barrenness to the Lord who promised that the one who abides in him bears much fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What was happening in the temple. The trading was in the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the temple where non-Jews could pray; beyond it notices threatened death to any Gentile who went further. Pilgrims needed certified animals and paid the temple tax in Tyrian silver, changed at a profit, and the trade is thought to have enriched the high priestly family.

What he attacks and what he does not. He does not attack the sacrifices God commanded, or the changing of money as such. The offence is where all of it was happening, and what it had become. The one part of the house of God available to the nations of the world had been turned into a livestock market and a bureau de change. A God-fearing Greek who came to pray had to stand among the cattle pens and coin tables, in the noise.

The seats of those who sold pigeons. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8), as Jesus’ own parents had offered when they presented him in this very building (Luke 2:24). Profiting from the poor in the house of God was especially offensive, and those seats go over. The Lamb who overturned the tables would within days be the sacrifice himself, the offering no money could buy, so that rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, could come to God without a market in between.

Carry anything through the temple. Only Mark records this: the courts were used as a short cut, and Jesus stopped the traffic. For the first time in years a Gentile could have stood in that court and prayed. He has cleared the room for the people nobody thought about.

Cleansing or judgment? Both. It was a cleansing: the temple was restored, for a moment, to its purpose. But it was also an acted prophecy of judgment, like the fig tree. Jesus was not reforming the temple but announcing its end. He himself would be the new temple (John 2:19–21; 14:58), the place where God meets his people, and the court he cleared for the nations for one afternoon he would open for ever when the curtain of the temple was torn in two at his death (15:38).

One cleansing or two? John records a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22). Some think there was only one, placed differently for theological reasons. But it is quite possible that Jesus did it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry; the details and the words differ, and the abuse was the kind that would have returned. We cannot be certain, and nothing in the meaning hangs on it.

Was Jesus’ anger sinful, and may I copy it? His anger was holy: zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17), aimed at the abuse of God’s worship and of the poor, controlled, considered overnight, and without any personal grudge. Ours is rarely so pure. Scripture allows righteous anger, be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), but most of our anger is about our own rights and comfort, and the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). This passage gives no licence for violence or for taking the law into our own hands. It does call us to care about what God cares about: his worship, his glory, and the outsider and the poor.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is it not written. The tables are on the floor and the birds are loose, and Mark calls it teaching, grounded in two prophets.

A house of prayer for all the nations. Isaiah 56:7 is God’s promise to the outsider, the foreigner and the eunuch once excluded from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1–8). Only Mark keeps for all the nations: the market stood in the one court where the nations could pray, and had evicted precisely the people the verse was about.

A den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, from his sermon at the temple gate before Babylon destroyed it. A robbers’ den is not where the robbery happens but where the thieves retreat afterwards to feel safe: the people would steal and swear falsely, then stand in God’s house and say, We are delivered (Jeremiah 7:9–10). The quotation carries its threat with it: as before, the temple will fall.

Using the den. The test still works. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you conduct the rest of your week, or less? A man who can hold a grudge for years, sharpen his invoices, be cold to his wife, and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without altering any of it, has not been worshipping. He has been using the den. And the way out is not to stop coming but to come differently: the den is where sin is hidden, and the house of prayer is where it is confessed and forgiven (1 John 1:9). The same Lord who overturned the tables welcomes every thief who comes to him empty-handed.

The eunuch and the foreigner come home. Within a few years an Ethiopian eunuch, reading Isaiah 53 on the road home from Jerusalem, was baptised into Christ (Acts 8:26–39). Jesus did not merely clear a court; he became the house. In him, crucified for all nations, God’s house of prayer stands open to every people, and the outsider Isaiah promised to make joyful is made joyful at last.

Seeking a way to destroy him. The first time the chief priests act against Jesus in Mark (8:31; 10:33). The temple authorities, whose institution and income he had challenged, join the plot (14:1).

They feared him. They could not arrest him openly; they will have to do it at night, with somebody on the inside. He will not sleep inside the walls this week, until the night he spends there as a prisoner.

Is my church a house of prayer for all nations? Ask what an outsider meets when he comes in. Can a stranger, an immigrant, a person of another class or background, find a welcome and room to pray, or does he meet a closed circle, insider language and a busy programme with no space for him? Do we pray for the nations, support mission, and welcome those from other cultures as family? The temple courts were cluttered with good things put in the wrong place. Our clutter is usually good things too. Clear room for the people Jesus cleared room for.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Withered away to its roots. The third day of this chapter and the second morning on this road, and the tree is dead. Not wilted, not dropping leaves: completely dead, killed from the roots up, from the part nobody can see, within a day. Complete judgment: their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit (Hosea 9:16; Job 18:16). Matthew, compressing, says it withered at once (Matthew 21:19). Mark, following the days as they came, gives us the two mornings, which means the disciples walked past this tree twice, and the second time it was a dead stick.

Rabbi, look! If Peter’s preaching lies behind Mark, he tells it against himself: I saw a dead tree and got excited about the tree. The withering is not the point. The temple is the point, and he has walked past that twice as well.

The curse he would carry. The disciples stand in front of a tree under a curse. Within three days the Lord who spoke that curse would himself be hanged on a tree, and Paul draws the line plainly: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). The sentence on fruitless religion is real, and it falls; but the only fruitful Israelite who ever lived went under it in the place of the fruitless. That is why Have faith in God is good news and not a threat.

Have faith in God. A surprising response. Jesus does not explain the fig tree, though he will spell out the temple’s end soon enough (13:2). He turns to faith, because the temple, the centre of Israel’s worship, is under judgment. Where will God’s people meet with him now? Not in a building, but through faith in God, and prayer. They have watched a word spoken to a tree, and the tree obeyed, and they are about to be sent into a world of things far more immovable than a fig.

Faith in God, not faith in faith. Faith whose object is God: not faith in the power of your own believing, a modern superstition and a cruel one, but in a Person, who hears, and decides, and is good. That distinction governs the promises that follow.

Where do I meet God now that there is no temple? In Christ. He is the true temple, the place where God dwells with men (John 2:19–21). Through him every believer may draw near to God at any time and in any place, by the Spirit (Hebrews 10:19–22; John 4:21–24). The church, the gathered people of God, is now his temple too (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22), which is why meeting with God’s people on the Lord’s Day matters. You do not need a holy building, a priest or a pilgrimage. You need Christ, and faith in God through him.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says to this mountain. Moving a mountain was proverbial for doing the impossible (1 Corinthians 13:2). But they were on the Mount of Olives, within sight of the temple mount, and this mountain may be pointed: the great obstacle he had just pronounced fruitless can be removed by God in answer to prayer (compare Zechariah 4:7).

Thrown into the sea. Does not doubt: is not divided, wavering like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind (James 1:6–8), as opposed to faith that rests entirely on God and believes that what he says will come to pass.

Believe that you have received it. “Have received” (elabete) is a past tense: believe it as already given. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read receive; the earliest have the past tense, which most modern Bibles follow. Faith counts God’s answer as certain before it is seen (Hebrews 11:1). That does not mean pretending you already hold the thing. It means trusting that God has heard you and will give what is truly good, so that you can stop pleading anxiously and leave the request with him (Philippians 4:6–7).

What it plainly does say. Do not soften it first. Jesus means his people to pray with enormous boldness, to ask for things far beyond their resources, and to expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption; we are in danger of praying for nothing much, in case nothing happens. The whole point of the mountain is that it is too big, and he tells them to say so out loud. Nothing is too hard for the God we pray to. He moves mountains, raises the dead and turns hearts of stone to flesh, and he invites the weakest of his children to ask him for great things.

What it does not mean. Not a technique for making God do our will by believing hard enough, which turns God into a force. Prayer in faith is prayer according to God’s will (1 John 5:14–15), in Jesus’ name (John 14:13–14), from a heart that seeks his kingdom (Matthew 6:10, 33). The promise is about the power of God, not the power of positive thinking.

The prayer that was not granted. The boldness of this promise rests on a garden on the same hill, where within days the one man who never doubted in his heart asked his Father to remove the cup, and the cup did not pass: not what I will, but what you will (14:36). The Father did not take the cup from his Son, so that he could say yes to us. The mountain of our guilt, which no faith of ours could shift, was cast into the depths of the sea when Christ drank that cup (Micah 7:19). We ask for mountains to move because the greatest one has already been moved.

I prayed in faith and did not receive. Was it my fault? Very likely not, and this is written for you, because you are the person this passage most often wounds. Heaping blame on your faith only adds a second grief to the first. It is prayer offered to a Father, not an incantation aimed at a force. A good Father sometimes gives what we did not ask because it is better than what we did, and sometimes withholds what we begged for, because his love can see the whole of a story we can see only the middle of. His no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you were hoping for. Keep praying, keep trusting, and bring him the grief as well.

What mountains should I pray about? The ones that are truly beyond you and plainly on God’s heart. The conversion of a hardened friend or child. Your own besetting sin. The spread of the gospel among an unreached people. The unity of a divided church. Courage in persecution. Provision in real need. These are mountains he has promised to move in his time, because they concern his kingdom. Pray about them specifically, persistently and expectantly, and watch for his answers, which often come in ways you did not foresee.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you stand praying. Jews commonly prayed standing (1 Samuel 1:26; Luke 18:11, 13), with hands lifted. So this is not a special occasion but the daily one: every time you pray. And we stand to pray as people whose ten thousand talents have been written off.

Anything against anyone. Having said that a believing man can move a mountain, he names the thing that will stop him. Faith is the first condition of answered prayer (v. 24); forgiveness is the second. You cannot come to God holding a grudge. Every word widens the scope. Anything: not only the large injuries, but the slight, the exclusion, the remark, the thing said about you at work. Against anyone: no exceptions for family, for the person who has never apologised, for the one who does not know they did it, for the dead. And notice that the initiative is yours. You stand up to pray; you find something in your hand; you put it down.

Your Father also who is in heaven. The only time Mark has your Father in heaven, close to the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). “Trespasses”: false steps off the path.

The one who forgave first. Within the week he would be betrayed, deserted, mocked and nailed up, and his prayer there was for his executioners: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though many scholars judge it genuine. More than that, his death is why the Father can forgive at all. When a Christian puts down a grudge, he is not achieving a moral feat. He is letting the cross of Christ, by Christ’s own Spirit in him, have its way in one more relationship. In practice that means saying to God: what this person did to me was real and it was wrong, and I will not make them pay for it, because you did not make me pay.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others; God forgives freely, because a ransom was paid (10:45). But a person who has truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32). A man who has grasped what he has been let off does not seize a fellow servant by the throat over a few coins, and if he does, the question is not whether he has forfeited his forgiveness but whether he ever understood it.

Must I forgive someone who has not repented? Letting go of the grudge before God is commanded here, repentance or not; the restored relationship waits for repentance (Luke 17:3). Someone wronged by an unrepentant person, even an abuser, need not trust where trust has not been earned or return to danger, and seeking justice is not unforgiveness. (See Matthew 18:21 for the fuller answer.)

What if I cannot feel forgiving? Jesus’ instruction is not that you should feel differently about them. It is that you should let it go, in prayer, deliberately, now, and go on doing it whenever it comes back, because it will. Forgiveness is first a decision before it is a feeling. Tell God honestly how much it hurts, hand the person and the wrong to him as the righteous Judge, ask him to bless them, and refuse to rehearse the injury. Feelings often follow slowly. Remember how much you have been forgiven; that is the fuel. And if the wound is deep, seek a wise pastor’s help. There is a name you thought of while reading this. Start there.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add verse 26: But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses. The numbers here run 25, then 27. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts, and was probably added from Matthew 6:15, perhaps written in a margin and later taken into the text. The ESV puts it in a footnote. Nothing has been lost: the truth stands plainly in verse 25, and Jesus does teach it in Matthew, where it belongs.

In everyday life. Your Father has let go of everything against you; let this go before him, then pray. You will forgive unevenly, and the grudge will return; the Son forgave perfectly in your place, and for his sake your halting forgiveness is accepted.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The challenge (vv. 27–28). Back in the temple, Jesus is met by chief priests, scribes and elders, a delegation of the Sanhedrin, asking who gave him authority to do these things.

The counter-question (vv. 29–30). He asks whether John's baptism was from heaven or from man. John's commission came straight from God, as his own does.

The calculation (vv. 31–33). They weigh each answer by what it will cost them, never by whether it is true, and say they do not know.
verseByVerse.theology: Why does Jesus refuse to answer? He never withholds truth from honest enquiry in this Gospel: he explained the parables to those who stayed and asked (4:10, 34) and told a scribe he was not far from the kingdom (12:34). What he refuses is to give an answer to men who will not deal honestly with one. The withdrawal of light is itself a judgment, and a merciful one, because more truth given to a man determined to reject it only deepens his guilt. And we do not know cost them their standing: having declared themselves unable to judge John, they had no ground left from which to judge Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the most religiously trained men in the nation weighed two answers about a prophet, and nobody asked which was true.

Now: the same temptation comes to any church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine not preached because of who would leave, the question about your own life never brought to God because you already guess what the answer would cost. A shrug of not knowing can feel like humility and be a decision. The one who asks the question is the one who died for those who have dodged it, and it is not too late to answer him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking in the temple. Back in the building he has just judged, in the colonnades where teachers gathered (John 10:23), entirely at home, as though the place belonged to him. Which it does: my house (v. 17).

The chief priests and the scribes and the elders. The three groups of the Sanhedrin, the supreme council, which Jesus had named in his first prediction of his death (8:31): an official delegation. This question opens the long day of debate that runs to 12:37, and every round comes back to it.

By what authority are you doing these things? “These things”: above all the clearing of the temple, but also the entry, the teaching, everything. The temple was under the authority of the high priest; who gave this Galilean the right to interfere? It is a legitimate question for the guardians of the temple. If a stranger did the same in any church today, the elders would be right to ask. But it is also a trap. If Jesus claimed his authority came from God directly, they could charge him with blasphemy. If he claimed human authority, they could dismiss him; he had no rabbinic ordination and no official position.

Or who gave you this authority to do them? That is the real question, and it reveals how they think. In their world, authority came through channels. A man was trained, appointed, licensed. The question assumes there must be a name: a school, a rabbi, a body that stands behind him. And the answer is that nobody gave it to him, or rather, the Father did (1:11; 9:7). That has been the issue since the first chapter, when the crowd at Capernaum said he taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes (1:22). Their authority was derived, cited, borrowed. His is not derived from anyone. There is no name to give them but one, and if he says it plainly here, days before Passover, the week ends at once.

Why should I accept his authority over my life rather than my own? Because no one lives without a master. If it is not Christ, it is our own desires, the approval of others, money, or the pressure of the age, and none of those has ever died for anyone. The question is not whether you will be ruled but by whom. This King used his authority to cleanse a house of prayer for outsiders, and within the week he would use it to lay down his life as a ransom for many (10:45). Freedom is not having no Lord; it is having the right one.

Do church leaders have authority? Yes, a real but derived authority, given by Christ to serve his people through his word (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Elders rightly ask who sent a teacher, and churches rightly test those who claim to speak for God (1 John 4:1). But all church authority is under Christ and under Scripture. It must never be used, as the Sanhedrin used theirs, to shield an institution from the truth or to silence a just rebuke. When leaders and Christ conflict, Christ wins.

For worship. He needs no one’s licence. After the cross he would say, All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matthew 28:18). The council that questioned him sat in his house by his leave, and every throne and every pulpit still answers to him.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will ask you one question. A recognised rabbinic method, not an evasion: a fair bargain. If they answer honestly, they will have answered their own question, which is exactly why they will not. Only Mark records Answer me: Jesus is now examining them.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? “The baptism of John” stands for his whole ministry: his preaching of repentance and his baptism. “From heaven” is a reverent Jewish way of saying from God, avoiding the divine name. Did John’s ministry come from God, or was it a merely human movement? There is no third option.

A genuine parallel. The question is not a trick. John had no institutional standing whatever. He held no office, belonged to no school, had no ordination and was not attached to the temple, though as a priest’s son he could have been (Luke 1:5). He appeared in the wilderness, preached, baptised, and was recognised by the nation as a prophet. His authority came directly from God, without a single human channel, which is precisely the kind of authority Jesus has. So the question is: you have already had one case exactly like mine; what did you conclude about it? If they cannot assess John, a man dead perhaps a year or two whose ministry the whole country witnessed, they have disqualified themselves as judges of anybody’s commission.

Why this question? Because John had pointed to Jesus. He had announced the coming of one mightier than himself (1:7), and at Jesus’ baptism by John the Spirit descended and the Father spoke (1:10–11). If John was from God, then his testimony about Jesus was true, and Jesus’ authority came from God. The two are bound together. To accept John is to accept Jesus. And there is mercy in it. Anyone who honestly settled the question of John would have been carried straight to the answer about Christ. Jesus has handed them the one question in the world that would have led them home.

In everyday life. Before you ask God for more light, obey the light you have.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it. Mark lets us listen inside the huddle of the supreme court of Israel. They ask only what each answer will cost them.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? They see it instantly. They had not believed John. Luke records that the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptised by him (Luke 7:30). They know perfectly well that if they concede he was sent by God, they are condemned out of their own mouths. They had already made a decision about John and knew it was indefensible. They are not weighing evidence; they are managing an exposure.

Afraid of the people. The sentence breaks off, and Mark finishes it for them. John was revered as a martyr prophet, and to deny him in the temple at Passover could provoke a riot; Luke says they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6). One road costs them their credibility; the other costs them their safety.

The question never asked. Two options are weighed for consequences, and no one in that circle asks which is true. The most religiously trained men in the nation, in the house of God, discuss whether a prophet was sent by God, and truth is not a factor. That is what institutional self-preservation does to a mind, and it is the standing temptation of any church, board or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine not preached because of who would leave, the sin not named because of whose family it is in, the question about your own life never put to God because you already know roughly what the answer would cost.

We do not know. A lie, and the perfect lie, because it sounds like humility. The men whose job was to judge true and false prophets (Deuteronomy 18:20–22) declared themselves unable to judge John, and so disqualified themselves from judging Jesus.

Is it wrong to say I do not know? Not when it is true. Honest uncertainty is not a sin, and God is patient with those who are genuinely seeking. Many questions in Scripture are hard, and humility often says, I do not yet know. But we do not know can also be a position taken because it is the cheapest one available: a way of never having to say yes and never having to say no, and of keeping every door open by walking through none of them. The test is whether you want the answer. If you are really seeking, keep reading, asking and praying, and God will meet you (Jeremiah 29:13). If you are avoiding, admit it.

Neither will I tell you. The bargain was one question for one; they refused, and so does he, withholding truth from those who would not receive it (Matthew 7:6). It is judgment, because the withdrawal of light from a man who has decided against it is itself a mercy of a terrible kind. More truth given to someone determined to reject it would only deepen the guilt of the rejecting.

He would tell them soon enough. And yet in the parable that follows he tells them, in a form they cannot miss: he is the beloved Son (12:1–12). Asked again at night in the high priest’s house, he will answer in full, and they will condemn him for it (14:61–64). He was never unwilling to tell them. He was waiting for the hour when the answer could not be turned into anything else, and that hour was a cross.

For worship. The Truth stood in the temple, and the supreme court of Israel would not ask what was true. He walked on into the trap they were setting; on the cross he gave his answer in blood, and at the empty tomb the Father gave his.

11.theology:
A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave the robbers retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe. The charge is not mainly about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house.

For all the nations. Matthew and Luke quote Isaiah 56:7 without its last phrase; Mark keeps it. Isaiah 56 is God's promise to the foreigner and the eunuch, and the trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew could pray. The market had pushed out the very people the verse was about.
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours (v. 24).

Now: it calls us to pray boldly for what is far beyond us and to expect God to act. It does not say that enough certainty compels God: within days, on the same hill, Jesus asked his Father to remove the cup, and it did not pass (14:36). If you asked and did not receive, your faith was very likely not the problem. Ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own.

And with no pause he adds: whenever you stand praying, forgive (v. 25). The instruction is not to feel differently but to let the grudge go, deliberately, and again whenever it comes back, as one who has been forgiven far more.

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
This is Jesus’ last day of teaching in the temple, and it is one long interrogation. He answers the challenge to his authority with a story: tenants who beat and kill the owner’s servants and finally kill a beloved son, a phrase that has twice come out of heaven in this Gospel. The leaders understood it and went away to arrange the arrest.

Then come the traps: a coin with Caesar’s face on it, and a riddle about a woman with seven husbands. He answers the first by asking whose image the coin bears, and the second from a present-tense verb at the burning bush. One honest scribe is told he is not far from the kingdom of God, and after that nobody dares ask him anything more. The chapter ends with Jesus watching a widow put in two of the smallest coins in the empire, everything she had, days before he gave his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable (vv. 1–12). Asked by what authority he acts, Jesus tells the least veiled parable he ever told, and the leaders understand it perfectly.

The coin (vv. 13–17). Pharisees and Herodians set a trap with two jaws: endorse the tax and lose the crowd, oppose it and be reported for sedition. He asks whose face is on the coin.
