The riddle (vv. 18–27). The Sadducees bring a puzzle meant to make resurrection look absurd, and he answers them from the books of Moses, the Scriptures they prized most.
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts two ways, and both must be held.

A real obligation. The coin is Caesar’s; give it to him. The governing authority is God’s servant for the ordering of society, so pay taxes, keep the law and honour the office (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17).

A bounded obligation. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul, which bears God’s image. When the state demands what belongs to God alone, the Christian renders to God: We must obey God rather than men, the apostles told the council that plotted this trap (Acts 5:29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, the priestly party who ran the temple, held the five books of Moses above all other Scripture, and say that there is no resurrection (Acts 23:8). So Jesus goes to the burning bush, which every priest knew by heart, and finds the resurrection in I am the God of Abraham, spoken of a man long dead.

Now: note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are still the two ways to go wrong. Some err because they do not know the text; some because they know it and have quietly decided what God is not able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 12 is Jesus’ last day of public teaching in the temple, and every scene asks who he is and what is owed to God: from tenants who kill the beloved son, through three traps and an honest question, to a widow who gives everything she has, days before he gives his life.

The setting. The same scene as 11:27–33: in the temple, to the chief priests, scribes and elders, who had just asked by what authority he acted. Now he answers in a parable, one of the least veiled he ever told, and they understand it perfectly (v. 12).

A man planted a vineyard. The first sentence is a quotation, and every man listening would have known it. Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard uses almost the same words: my beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill; he dug it and cleared it of stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower and hewed out a wine vat (Isaiah 5:1–2). And Isaiah says what it means: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:7). God looked for good grapes and found only wild ones; he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed. Before a single character has acted, the delegation knows the story is about them.

Everything the owner did. Every detail is an investment: the fence against animals, the winepress cut in rock where grapes were trodden, the tower for a watchman and for storage. He has spent years and money on the land before anyone else touches it. So God chose a people, planted them in a good land, fenced them with his law, and watched over them.

And leased it to tenants. This is the change from Isaiah. There the vineyard is at fault; here the tenants are, the leaders to whom God had entrusted his people. Tenants worked the land and paid rent with a share of the harvest; they owned nothing. That is the position of everyone who has been given anything by God: a church, a family, a gift, a life. None of it is freehold, and the parable turns on what happens to a man who forgets he is a tenant.

He sent a servant. The owner went into another country: God had entrusted Israel to its leaders and given them time. A new planting gave no fruit to eat for years (Leviticus 19:23–25). Then the owner sent for his share, and note the modesty of the request: some of the fruit, the agreed share, in the season it was due. He has every right, and he asks. The servants are the prophets (Jeremiah 7:25).

The teller is the Son. Isaiah sang his song for my beloved, the owner of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1). When Jesus retells it, the word beloved returns at the climax, attached to the owner’s son (v. 6). The man telling the story in the temple courts is the one it is moving toward. He stands among the tenants as the Son who has come for the fruit, and as the one Israelite who has rendered it, every season of his life given back to his Father whole. What the vineyard owed and never paid, he is about to pay with his life.

What fruit does God want from me? The same fruit he wanted from Israel: justice, mercy and faithfulness (Micah 6:8), love for him and for neighbour (vv. 30–31), and the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). It is not a percentage of your achievements but a life given back to the one who gave it. He has planted you in a family, a church, a workplace, and supplied everything you need. He asks for the fruit of trust, obedience, worship and love, in the season he has given you, which is now.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The history of Israel’s prophets. The parable summarises centuries, with the violence escalating each time. God sent prophet after prophet to call his people to repentance and fruitfulness, and they were rejected, persecuted and killed (2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Hebrews 11:36–38).

Empty-handed. The first servant’s return with nothing is a message as much as an assault: there will be no rent.

Struck on the head. Worse; some think Mark’s readers would hear an echo of John the Baptist (6:27), the latest of the servants. Treated him shamefully means he was publicly humiliated as well as hurt.

And him they killed. Now the line is crossed. With many others Jesus stops counting, because the pattern never changed. The record is exact. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the temple’s chief officer (Jeremiah 20:2) and left in the mud of a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). And Stephen will put the same charge to the same council within a few years, and it will cost him his life: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52).

An owner who keeps sending. After the first beating, any landlord in that room would have gone to law or come with force. This one sends another man, and another, and after a murder, more still. The astonishing thing is not human wickedness, which anyone could predict. It is that after the beating, the humiliation and the killing, there is still somebody else at the gate. He has borne with us as he bore with them, and every fresh call to repent is one more servant at our gate, sent by a Lord who will not give us up easily.

Every bruised servant points ahead. Every prophet who was struck, mocked or killed suffered a small share of what the last messenger would suffer in full, a dotted line toward a hill outside the city. And the one telling the story would weep over Jerusalem as the one who had longed to gather her children (Matthew 23:37). The patience of the owner has a face, and it is his.

Why does God put up with so much? Because he is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and because he is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). His patience is not weakness or indifference; it is mercy giving time to turn. But patience has an end, as the parable goes on to show: the owner will come and destroy the tenants (v. 9), and the time to respond is while he is still sending. If you have been resisting God’s word for years, his patience is not a sign that the matter is closed. It is the reason you are still being called.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had still one other, a beloved son. The servants are exhausted; what remains is not another employee. And here the parable stops being a story about someone else, because that phrase has twice come out of heaven in this Gospel. At the Jordan: You are my beloved Son (1:11). On the mountain: This is my beloved Son; listen to him (9:7). So he answers the leaders’ question about his authority (11:28): he is not one more prophet but the Son, beloved perhaps in the sense of only, as Isaac was (Genesis 22:2). He is telling them who he is and what they are about to do, days before they do it.

Finally. The word (eschaton) means last of all. There is no one after the Son. He is God’s final word: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

They will respect my son. A servant can be brushed aside; the heir is the owner in person. And a first-century listener would feel the cost at once: this man has already lost servants to these tenants, knows what they do to the people he sends, and sends his son. So the Father sent his Son to his rebellious people: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

Did God not know what would happen to his Son? He knew perfectly. The parable speaks as a human landlord would, to show the depth of the tenants’ guilt and the patience of the owner. But Jesus himself is telling the story, and he knows its ending. The Father sent the Son knowing he would be killed, and the Son came knowing it, because it was the plan of God from before the foundation of the world that the Son should die for sinners (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). That is not less love but more. They did not surprise God. He sent his Son into their hands on purpose.

This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. They recognise him. That is the horror of the parable and of Good Friday: they kill him because they know who he is. It is often suggested that, under the law of the day, land without an heir might pass to those who had occupied and worked it. Their rejection is not ignorance but rebellion: they want the vineyard, God’s people, for themselves, without God. And “Come, let us kill him” is what Joseph’s brothers said about the favoured son (Genesis 37:20).

The logic of all sin. Their reasoning is the reasoning of every human rebellion against God, stated with unusual honesty: the inheritance will be ours. Get rid of the heir, and the estate is ours to keep. It is the serpent’s offer in a garden, you will be like God, and it is the whole logic of sin, which is never finally about pleasure but about ownership. We want our lives without their Lord.

Threw him out of the vineyard. Matthew and Luke say they threw him out and then killed him (Matthew 21:39; Luke 20:15), which matches Jesus’ crucifixion outside the city wall: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). He is standing in the temple describing his own murder, in the third person, to the men who will commit it, and they are listening.

In everyday life. Ask where you are still saying, in small ways, the inheritance will be mine: your time, your body, your money, your future, kept back from the Son who did not keep back his life for you. Hand one of them back to him today.

For worship. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10), the sacrifice that bears God’s just wrath and so puts it away. The Heir was thrown out of the vineyard so that the tenants who killed him could be brought in as sons and share his inheritance.
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He asks the question and answers it himself. Matthew records that the listeners themselves answered (Matthew 21:41), and so condemned themselves, as David did when Nathan told him the parable of the lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7). There is no ambiguity left, and none intended.

He will come and destroy the tenants. Judgment on the leaders who rejected the Son. Fulfilled within forty years, in AD 70, when Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and the priestly aristocracy and the Sanhedrin came to an end. Jesus will soon foretell it stone by stone (13:2).

And give the vineyard to others. New tenants: the apostles and the leaders of the church, Jewish and Gentile, who would care for God’s people under Christ; Matthew says to a people producing its fruits (Matthew 21:43). The vineyard itself is not destroyed. God’s people continue; the wicked tenants are replaced. And the others turn out to include Gentiles from every nation, gathered in by apostles who would soon stand before this very council and tell it that the rejected stone had become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11).

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No. The parable is aimed at the tenants, the leaders standing in front of him, not at a nation, and Paul insists that God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew (Romans 11:2). (See Luke 20:16 for the fuller answer.)

A warning to every church. Tenancy is not freehold for any congregation either. A lampstand can be removed (Revelation 2:5), as churches that once preached the gospel and now deny it have learned.

The cornerstone. Psalm 118:22–23 comes from the psalm the crowds had sung at his entry two days earlier (11:9); they sang verse 26 at him, and now he reads them verse 22. The picture changes from vineyard to building, perhaps with a Hebrew play on son (ben) and stone (eben). The builders, the professionals whose job is to know which stones are usable, examined this one and threw it away. But God picked it up and made it the cornerstone, which sets the line of every wall. So the parable ends not with the son’s death but with resurrection, told in the language of masonry: the rejected stone is holding up the house.

The Lord’s doing. The rejection and the vindication are both God’s work. What they meant as rejection was the very thing God was doing. Human evil and divine purpose meet at the cross (Acts 2:23). The Father raised the Son the builders rejected and set him at the head of the corner, and on him he is building a living temple from every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They perceived. Unlike the parables of chapter 4, which outsiders did not understand (4:11–12), this one was plain. They knew they were the tenants, they knew who the beloved son was, and they knew what was being said about their future. Their problem was not information.

And they were seeking to arrest him. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. That is what a hardened heart does with the truth: it does not soften; it uses the light to see by while it does the thing the light exposed.

But feared the people. Not conscience: crowd management (11:18, 32). The city is full for Passover, and a public arrest would start a riot with the governor in town. They will need to take him secretly, at night, through a traitor (14:1–2, 10–11).

Held back until his hour. Mark gives the human reason, the crowd; the deeper reason is that the Son was keeping his own appointment. He would let them act out the story he had just told only when he chose: at Passover, on the night he took bread and said, This is my body. The tenants thought they were deciding when the heir would die. The heir had decided, and for the sake of men like these.

So they left him. The Son of God had just told them who he was, what they were about to do, and what it would cost them, and they simply turned round and walked. Yet the Son told his murderers the truth to their faces, and the truth was still an offer: even this parable held out the stone they could have built on. It is possible to understand the gospel completely and walk away because it costs too much, the most ordinary way in the world of being lost. But if a passage has found you out and you are still here, troubled, listening and wanting to be put right, you have not done what they did. They walked away from the light; you are standing in it, and that is the Spirit’s work in you.

What should I do when a sermon or a passage exposes me? Do not leave and go away. Stay under it. Admit to God what it has shown you, plainly, without excuses. Ask him what repentance looks like here, and take the first step today, while the word is still sharp. If it involves someone you have wronged, go to them. And do not resent the preacher or the friend God used. The leaders hated Jesus for telling them the truth. A softened heart thanks God for the wound that leads to healing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A series of tests. Three groups now put questions to Jesus (vv. 13–34), and then he puts one to them (vv. 35–37). The first two are traps; the third comes from an honest man. Many have seen here the Passover lamb, chosen days before the feast and required to be without blemish (Exodus 12:3–6): the Messiah is examined in the temple and found without fault.

Pharisees and Herodians. An unlikely alliance, as in Galilee (3:6): the Herodians backed Herod’s family and the Roman rule that kept it in power; the Pharisees resented that rule as an insult to God’s people. Nothing unites opposites like a shared hatred of the light. They were sent by the Sanhedrin to trap him in his talk, a hunting word (agreusōsin) for snaring wild animals.

Teacher, we know that you are true. Flattery, to set him up. They praise him for independence, fearlessness and indifference to what people think, precisely the quality they need him to display in the next thirty seconds. And every word was true: they described him accurately for the purpose of destroying him.

How flattery works. It is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by somebody who wants something, and the tell is not the content but the timing: it arrives immediately before the request. Anyone with responsibility should learn to feel a cold draught when a conversation opens like this one.

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? They ask it twice, to shut off any escape into generality: yes or no. The tax was a poll tax, a head tax paid by every adult directly to the Roman treasury. It had been imposed when Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, and provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), who taught that paying it was treason to God, the only king. It was a symbol of subjection. The trap had two jaws. If Jesus said yes, he would lose the crowd, who hated the tax and hoped he would liberate them. If he said no, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel. Either answer would destroy him. And Luke records that at his trial they accused him of exactly that: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

But, knowing their hypocrisy. He names the trap before he answers, and does not pretend the flattery was sincere. No trap held him, no flattery moved him, no fear bent him.

A denarius. A silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer, and the coin in which the tax was paid. Jesus apparently did not carry one. They did, even in the temple. Somebody in that group of scrupulous men has one in his pocket and hands it over, and the trap is already sprung on them.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whose likeness and inscription is this? Take the coin in your hand for a moment, because the whole answer is stamped on it. The coin was most likely a denarius of Tiberius, emperor at the time, which carried his head in profile and, round the edge, Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus. On the other side, high priest. So it is not merely a coin with a portrait. It is a small metal blasphemy: a claim that a living man is the son of a god and the chief priest of Rome’s religion. To devout Jews it was doubly offensive: a graven image (Exodus 20:4), and a claim to divinity.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Caesar’s, they answer, because there is only one answer, and by producing the coin they have shown that they use Caesar’s money and enjoy his roads and protection. Render (apodote) means give back, repay a debt. The coin bears Caesar’s image; it is his; give it back. The state has a legitimate, God-given authority in its own sphere (Romans 13:1–7).

And to God the things that are God’s. What bears God’s image? Human beings: God created man in his own image (Genesis 1:26–27). The coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image; you belong to God because you bear his. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, all of you, because there is no part of a human being that is not stamped. Put into daily terms: your body, your time, your money, your loves and your thinking are his to direct, so that you live for his praise at work and at home as much as in church (Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 10:31). And Caesar’s claims are limited by God’s: his inscription claimed divinity, but Caesar is owed taxes, not worship.

The fault line of the martyrs. He does not say how much belongs to Caesar; that will vary with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit: when Caesar demands what belongs to God, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). That is the line the early martyrs died on. They paid every tax Rome levied and prayed for the emperor, and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

Son of the divine, high priest. The coin called Tiberius son of a god and high priest. The man holding it, in the temple, is the true Son of God, days from offering himself as the great high priest who brings his own blood. And likeness, eikōn, is Paul’s word for Christ: he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). We were made in God’s image and defaced it; the Son, who is that image perfectly, came to renew it in us, making us like himself again, truthful, loving and holy (Colossians 3:10).

And they marveled at him. The trap had failed: he had neither endorsed Roman rule unconditionally nor called for revolt.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Christians have understood this saying in many ways: as dividing life into two separate spheres, secular and sacred; as subordinating the church to the state; or as subordinating the state to the church. This commentary’s view: Jesus does not make Caesar and God equal partners. Everything belongs to God, including Caesar (Romans 13:1). The state has real but limited authority under God, and Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers. But their final loyalty is to God, and they may not give the state what belongs to God alone.

Must I pay taxes to a government I think is unjust? Yes, in ordinary circumstances. Tiberius was a pagan emperor whose government occupied Israel, and Jesus still said render. Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. Paying taxes, obeying laws, praying for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honouring them is part of rendering to Caesar, even when we disagree with how the money is spent. Christians may work by lawful means to change unjust laws and should speak for justice. But disobedience is right only when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, such as worship, the gospel or the protection of life. Then we obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost.

For worship. The emperor’s coin has long been melted down, but every human face still carries the stamp of its Maker. Caesar was given back his coin. God, who has every claim on us, first gave himself for us, and so we are his twice over, by making and by buying.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sadducees. Their only appearance in Mark: the aristocratic priestly party, including the high priestly families who controlled the temple Jesus had just disrupted: wealthy, politically conservative, cooperating with Rome. They rejected the Pharisees’ oral tradition, gave the five books of Moses the highest authority, and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8), arguing that Moses never taught life after death.

Moses wrote for us. They begin with Moses, the authority they prized above all: Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law of levirate marriage (from Latin levir, brother-in-law). If a man died childless, his brother married the widow, and the first son carried on the dead man’s name and inheritance. In a world with no pensions, where a widow rarely inherited her husband’s land, a childless widow could easily be destitute, and the law provided for her. It is a mercy, and the Sadducees are about to turn it into a weapon.

There were seven brothers. Not a real case but probably a stock argument against the Pharisees, with seven chosen for maximum absurdity: if Moses commanded levirate marriage, and the resurrection would make it absurd, then Moses could not have believed in the resurrection.

The woman nobody noticed. She is the object of every sentence and the subject of none, until she is disposed of at the end: last of all the woman also died. There is no suggestion anywhere in their story that she is a person. Seven times widowed, childless and passed along. Jesus, who noticed the wife in chapter 10 and will notice the widow at the end of this chapter, is about to answer men who use a suffering woman as a debating prop.

In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? The trap is meant to make Jesus look foolish. It is not really a question but a joke. And notice the assumption underneath it, which Jesus goes straight for: they picture life after the resurrection as this life continued, with the same arrangements, institutions and property law running on for ever. That is exactly the mistake made by a great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee.

Asking the Resurrection about the resurrection. The clever men brought their joke to the Lord of life, and he was not embarrassed. Within the week the man they were mocking would be laid in a tomb and walk out of it, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The Sadducees were not debating a theory with a rabbi; they were asking the Resurrection whether there would be one. And the widow they passed from brother to brother has a better hope than any levirate law could give: not a name kept alive by a son, but life itself, kept by the Son.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are wrong. The word (planasthe) means to wander, to go astray. A blunt diagnosis, delivered to the custodians of Scripture and temple.

Neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two causes of error, still the two causes of most theological error. They had the Scriptures largely by memory but did not see what they teach, and they could not imagine that God can raise the dead. They had shrunk God to the size of their own imagination.

The quiet unbelief of realism. That second failure is common among religious people, and it does not announce itself as unbelief. It sounds like realism. It is the settled assumption that God will not act, that this marriage will not change, that this person will not be converted, that nothing much is going to happen: an assumption formed not from Scripture but from experience, and then read back into Scripture. Weariness is not the same thing. A believer worn down by long waiting who still brings the matter to God is not a Sadducee; the psalmists cried how long, O LORD, and were heard (Psalm 13:1–5).

Neither marry nor are given in marriage. The age to come is not this age with the same furniture. Marriage belongs to this age; its purposes, companionship, the bringing of children into the world, and the picture of Christ and the church, will be fulfilled. In the new creation there will be no death, so no need for children to carry on the family line, and the whole basis of their story falls apart.

But are like angels in heaven. Not that we become angels, or lose our bodies or our identities. But like angels, we will not die (Luke 20:36), and will not marry. The Sadducees did not believe in angels either; Jesus corrects them on that too.

I have buried my husband or wife. What does this mean for us? Jesus does not say love ends, or that you will not know one another. The fear that the resurrection means less, thinner relationships and a vague eternity, is the Sadducees’ mistake in reverse. Paul expected to know the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Marriage as an institution ends not because it was too small but because it was a signpost to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), and you take the signpost down when you arrive. Nothing good will be lost: not the years, not your knowledge of each other, not the love. It will be taken up into something so much larger that what you fear losing will look, when you are standing in it, like the smaller version of what you have.

In everyday life. Name one situation you have quietly decided God will not change, and pray about it this week as one who knows the power of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the book of Moses. Now he goes on the attack, on well-chosen ground. He could have quoted Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19, but the Sadducees did not give the Prophets the authority of Moses, so he answers from the books they prized most. Have you not read is a pointed question to put to men whose profession is reading, and he asks it twice in this chapter (v. 10).

In the passage about the bush. This is how passages were located before chapter and verse numbers: Exodus 3, which every priest in that delegation knew by heart.

The God of Abraham. Exodus 3:6, said to Moses centuries after the patriarchs’ bones were laid in the cave of Machpelah. Mark’s Greek reads I am; the Hebrew has no verb at all, simply I the God of Abraham.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. The argument is not a play on grammar but rests on what a covenant is. God had bound himself to Abraham personally, to be God to you and to your offspring after you (Genesis 17:7). If Abraham had simply ceased to exist, God would be describing himself by a relationship with nobody, the God of a memory. If God is still their God, they are still alive to him; Luke adds, for all live to him (Luke 20:38). And his promises to them concerned not only their souls but their bodies, the land, an inheritance. The living God will not leave his friends in the grave.

A deep argument. Jesus grounds the resurrection not in a proof text but in God’s covenant faithfulness: God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city (Hebrews 11:16). He put their names into his own title, and he is not the God of dust. Mark alone records the final sentence: You are quite wrong.

The voice from the bush. Jesus speaks here not as one more rabbi but as the one who would say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). The promise to Abraham, to be God to you and to your offspring, comes to rest on Abraham’s one true offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The patriarchs live to God because God keeps covenant, and he keeps it in his Son, who within the week would go down into death and come up again as the pledge that the God of the living keeps every one of his own.

Do believers who die now go to sleep until the resurrection? No. This passage is one of the clearest answers. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were alive to God centuries before the resurrection of the body. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), conscious and at rest in his presence, as the thief on the cross was promised: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Scripture calls death sleep because the body rests and will be woken, not because the soul is unconscious. And there is no purgatory between: the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received at once into glory, waiting for the redemption of the body at Christ’s return.

More in your Bible than you have found. The resurrection is not a late addition invented between the Testaments. It was lying in the most familiar passage of the books of Moses, in a present-tense verb, and the men who read it every year had never seen it. Remember that the next time you read a chapter you think you know.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks which commandment is most important, agrees warmly with the answer, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God.

Jesus’ question (vv. 35–37). If the Christ is David’s son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning and the widow (vv. 38–44). He warns against scribes who love the best seats and devour widows’ houses, and then, in his last act in the temple, points out a widow putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.
verseByVerse.theology:
David’s son and David’s Lord. Everyone agreed the Christ would be David’s son, but in Psalm 110:1 David calls him my Lord, and honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. Mark records no answer.

The New Testament gives it: concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Romans 1:3–4). David’s son by birth; David’s Lord from eternity.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God. The scribe says aloud, as a temple professional, that love outweighs the whole sacrificial system. Jesus does not say he is in. He says not far.

Now: not far is still outside, and it describes many people who have been in church all their lives. The gap is not knowledge but a Person standing three feet away, about to keep the law for him. And if you have come to Christ and still fear you are only near, your safety rests on his welcome (John 6:37), not on your feelings.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the scribes came up. A different kind of questioner: he has been listening, he is impressed, not hostile, and he asks because he wants to know. Matthew’s version has a harder edge and suggests it was still a test (Matthew 22:35), but Mark shows his sincerity (v. 34).

Which commandment is the most important of all? A live question, not an idle one. Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the law, 248 positive and 365 negative, and the teachers of Jesus’ day already debated which were heavy and which light, and whether one could summarise the whole. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, had said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law, the rest is commentary.

Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema (Hebrew for hear), recited twice daily by devout Jews and written on the doorposts of the house. Only Mark includes it: asked for a commandment, Jesus begins not with what you must do but with who God is. There is one God, and only one, not a department of life alongside others; and so he alone is to be loved with everything. A rival would deserve a share. He has none. Christians confess the same one God, as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:6).

And you shall love the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 6:5. Love here (agapēseis) is not mainly a feeling but a commitment of the whole person, shown in loyalty and obedience: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

With all your heart. Deuteronomy has heart, soul and might; Jesus adds mind. The four are not separate parts but the whole person, with nothing left out. Heart: in Hebrew thought, the control room, what you decide, want and are committed to. Soul: the life itself. Mind: lazy thinking about God is not humility. Strength: the body, the energy, the money, the hours, so that loving God is a question about your diary and your bank statement.

The second is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus was asked for one commandment and gave two, and the second flows from the first: whoever says I love God and hates his brother is a liar (1 John 4:20–21). He lifts it from a chapter about wages, harvests, the deaf, the blind and honest scales. As yourself is not a command to love yourself first but an assumption that you already do. You know how attentively you consider your own comfort, reputation and future: that much, to him. There is no other commandment greater than these: all the others hang on them (Matthew 22:40), and love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10).

How can love be commanded? Because in Scripture love is first a direction of the whole self, not a mood. You cannot order a feeling, but you can turn toward someone, give to him, keep faith with him and seek his good, and feelings tend to follow what we give ourselves to. Yet the command also unmasks us. We find we cannot love God like this by trying harder, and that is the point: the law shows us the shape of the life we were made for and drives us to the one who lived it for us and gives his Spirit to make it ours (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Heart, soul, mind and strength, on a cross. Within three days the man who recited this would fulfil it in a single act. With all his heart he said in the garden, not what I will, but what you will. With all his soul he poured it out to death. With all his mind he held to Scripture to the last, praying a psalm on the cross. With all his strength he carried the beam, as John records, until Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it for him (John 19:17; Mark 15:21). And in the same act he loved his neighbour, not merely as himself but above himself, bearing the sins of the people who put him there. The greatest commandment has the shape of the cross, and that whole-hearted obedience, kept where we fail, is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19).

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37): anyone in need whom God puts in your path, beginning with those nearest and reaching to the stranger and the enemy. (See Matthew 22:39 for the fuller answer.)

What it does not mean. Not that we can be saved by loving God and neighbour. No one has ever kept these two commandments fully, except Jesus; nobody has kept the first for a single hour. They expose our need (Romans 3:20). In Christ, forgiven, we begin to keep them by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are right, Teacher. Only Mark records the scribe’s response. A scribe agrees with Jesus, warmly, and repeats the answer back in his own words, adding there is no other besides him from Deuteronomy 4:35. He is not parroting; he is thinking.

More than all burnt offerings. Consider who is speaking: a scribe, in the temple courts, during Passover week, with the smoke of the altar going up near by and the whole machinery of sacrifice running around him, and he says that loving God and neighbour matters more than all of it. He echoes the prophets: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6). The temple’s sacrifices, without love, were empty, like the leaves of the fig tree (11:13). He is honest enough to say so in the one place where it costs something.

Does this mean sacrifice did not matter? No. God commanded the sacrifices, and they pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, which does what love alone could not: it takes away sin (Hebrews 10:1–14). What the prophets and this scribe condemned was sacrifice without love, ritual offered by people who did not love God or their neighbour. The same is true of our worship. Attendance, singing, giving and the Lord’s Supper are good gifts, but God is not pleased by them from a heart that is cold toward him and hard toward others.

Not far from the kingdom. Wisely (nounechōs) means thoughtfully, and the praise is genuine. But not far is still outside, and there is no other category: the man closest to the kingdom in this chapter is on the wrong side of a line.

What did he lack? Not information; he probably knew the law better than most of the Twelve. He needed to see that he could not keep these commandments, and to recognise and follow the one who was speaking to him, the King. The gap is a Person, and he is three feet away. The King has come close, close enough to be spoken to in the temple, close enough to be nailed to a cross. The whole chapter has been asking who Jesus is: the beloved son in the vineyard, the rejected stone, David’s Lord. Understanding the law is not the same as entering the kingdom. A person can be very close and still outside. Mark never tells us what he did. The account simply stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Could I be not far but not in? Yes, and the question should be asked plainly. A person can hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith competently, grow up in a Christian home, and be near. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it. The test is not what you know but whether you have come to Christ: turned from your sin, trusted him alone for forgiveness, and given yourself to follow him. If you are not sure, do not stay in the doorway. Come to him today; he has promised not to cast out anyone who comes. And if you have come to him and still fear you are only near, take heart: your safety rests on his welcome, not on the strength of your feelings, and a heart that grieves at the thought of being outside is already being drawn by him (John 6:37, 44).

No one dared to ask him any more questions. Priests, Pharisees with Herodians and Sadducees have tried to trap him and failed; the silence is the verdict.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? Nobody dares ask him anything more, so now he asks the decisive question. The scribes were right to say it (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and it is not an attack on the doctrine. Bartimaeus had called Jesus Son of David and been commended (10:47–48), and the crowds had hailed the kingdom of David (11:10). But is that all the Messiah is: a human descendant of David, a new king like David? Jesus is asking whether it is the whole of it.

David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared. The phrase packs in a doctrine of Scripture. David himself: so the psalm is his. In the Holy Spirit: so it is also God’s. Two authors, one text, and no tension between them. Scripture is God’s word through human authors (2 Peter 1:21). That is how Jesus read his Bible.

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New. In Hebrew the first Lord is the divine name, printed LORD in small capitals; the second is adoni, my master, a title of superior rank. God speaks to someone David calls his master, and seats him at his right hand, the place of supreme honour, sharing God’s throne.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. Conquered kings had the victor’s foot placed on their necks (Joshua 10:24). And he chose this line standing in the temple, surrounded by men who have already resolved to kill him, and he quotes to their faces a promise about what God will do with the enemies of his Christ.

David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? The puzzle, and in that culture the difficulty is total. Honour flowed upward: a son honoured his father, a descendant his ancestor, never the reverse. Abraham does not call Isaac my lord. Yet the greatest king Israel ever had looks down the centuries at his own descendant and calls him Master. Mark records no answer. Nobody had one.

In the flow. This answers the rulers’ question earlier that same day: by what authority are you doing these things? (11:28). His authority is that of David’s Lord, seated at God’s right hand, as the parable said in story (v. 6) and the trial will say in plain words (14:62).

The answer Jesus leaves them to find. He is the Son of David by human birth, and the Son of God, David’s Lord, by nature: concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:3–4). The one who came from David’s line existed before David did. It may be the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in this Gospel, and he does it as a riddle, days before the cross, because a claim like that stated flatly in the temple would end the week early.

Why must the Saviour be both David’s son and David’s Lord? Because only such a Saviour could save us. As David’s son, a real man, he could stand in our place, obey the law we broke, and die the death we deserved. As David’s Lord, God the Son, his obedience and death have infinite worth, enough to pay for the sins of a multitude, and death could not hold him. A merely human Messiah could be admired but not trusted with our souls; a God who never became man could not die for us. The Lord who is David’s son is the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he reigns now at the Father’s right hand.

And the great throng heard him gladly. The ordinary people are delighted to see the experts outmatched. It is the last note of his public debates in this Gospel, and within days the same city will be shouting for his execution.

For worship. The child laid in a manger in David’s town is the Lord to whom David bowed a thousand years before he was born. The head crowned with thorns now wears the crown at the Father’s right hand. The last enemy to be destroyed is death, and the Lord of David has already walked out of its house.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware of the scribes. Not every scribe; one had just been commended (v. 34). It is a warning about what religious office does to a man who lets it, spoken publicly, to ordinary people, about the most respected class in the community.

Who like to walk around in long robes. Long, white linen robes, sometimes reaching to the ground, marked out men of learning and rank. Note the verb: they like to walk around in them. It is not the robe that is condemned but the strolling, the enjoyment of being seen in a garment that says what you are.

Greetings and the best seats. Public greetings with titles, Rabbi, master. In the synagogue, the bench at the front facing the congregation, where everyone could see them; at feasts, the seats nearest the host.

The appetite for honour. Read the four together and the portrait is not at first of a wicked man, but of one who has come to need the deference. None of these things is a sin in itself; a robe is a robe and a seat is a seat. What is described is an appetite, the quiet, constant, unadmitted pleasure of being thought well of, which grows so slowly that nobody notices it arriving. And it is entirely available now, without a robe: in whose name gets mentioned, who is asked to pray, who is consulted, who is thanked from the front.

Who devour widows’ houses. Now the charge turns from vanity to something far worse. Widows were the most vulnerable people in Israel, and God commanded special care for them (Exodus 22:22–24; Isaiah 1:17). Scribes relied on gifts, and some apparently exploited widows’ generosity or managed their estates as trustees and ate up their property. A religious profession was being used to strip the assets of the most defenceless people in the land.

And for a pretense make long prayers. Long, public prayers that make them look holy while they cheat the vulnerable: the hypocrisy of Isaiah 29:13 again (7:6). The long prayer is not incidental to the exploitation; it is the instrument of it. It is what persuades the widow that her money is safe with such a man. But the Lord sees through every long prayer to the heart that prays it, and he does not forget the poor.

They will receive the greater condemnation. Greater because they knew the law better than anyone (James 3:1; Luke 12:47–48), and because they used religion to cover their sins. To use the name of God as the tool of a fraud is worse than the fraud, and judgment is weighed by knowledge and privilege.

Robes, greetings and seats, reversed. Every mark of honour the scribes loved, Jesus would receive in mockery within the week. They loved long robes; soldiers would dress him in purple, then strip him and gamble for his clothes (15:17, 20, 24). They loved greetings in the marketplace; he would be greeted with Hail, King of the Jews, and spat on (15:18–19). And where they devoured widows’ houses, he, dying, provided for his own mother, by then apparently a widow, as John records (John 19:26–27). The true Teacher took the lowest seat.

How should a church protect the vulnerable from its own leaders? By taking this warning seriously rather than assuming it applies only to others. Leaders should be accountable to other elders, with no one beyond question. Money should be handled openly, by more than one person, with proper records. No one should be pressed to give, sign over property or trust a leader with their affairs under spiritual pressure. Widows, the elderly, the disabled and the lonely should be cared for by the whole church, not left to one person’s influence. And when a leader is found exploiting or abusing anyone, it must be dealt with openly and firmly, reported where the law requires, and never covered to protect a ministry.

In everyday life. The Lord who took the lowest seat has already given you the honour that lasts, so watch your heart for the love of being seen, especially if you lead in church. Ask yourself honestly what you enjoy most about any role you hold, and whether you would serve as gladly if no one noticed.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast. Straight after the scribes who devour widows’ houses comes a widow, perhaps one of their victims, laid alongside them on purpose in Jesus’ last scene in the temple. He is finished with the arguments.

And he sat down opposite the treasury. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, so called because women could go that far and no further. Jewish tradition describes thirteen trumpet-shaped collection chests there, and a great many coins made a great deal of noise.

And watched. Deliberately, for some time, on his last day in that building. Not the accounts, not the total: he watched the people, their faces and hands. He still does. The Lord of heaven sat in the temple court and watched a poor widow drop two coins into a box, and he cared. Nothing done for him escapes his eyes, and nothing small is small to him. There is no anonymous giving; there is only giving that other people cannot see.

Many rich people put in large sums. Jesus does not condemn them, and neither should we. These were large gifts, genuinely given, and nothing says they were hypocrites. But they were heard.

Two small copper coins. She is a poor widow (ptōchē, a beggar’s poverty). The lepton (literally thin one) was the smallest coin in circulation, about 1/128 of a denarius, a day’s wage. Mark translates it for his Roman readers: two lepta made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. Into a bronze trumpet, it would have made almost no sound at all.

She gave both. There were two, and the detail matters. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known, nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Does Jesus really see what I give? Yes. He sees the amount, and he sees what it costs, and he sees the heart. That should humble anyone who gives for show, and it should comfort anyone who gives quietly and little. Many Christians keep their giving secret, rightly (Matthew 6:3–4). It is not secret from him. He knows the gift you made when you could barely afford it, and the one you held back when you could easily have given. Give to him, not to the people who might notice.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called his disciples to him. He gathers them round, which he does when something matters. Within minutes one of them will say, look, Teacher, what wonderful stones (13:1); he calls them over to look at a woman with two of the smallest coins in the empire.

More than all. Truly, I say to you marks something not to be missed, and then comes a statement that is false by every measure the treasury could apply. She put in a fraction of a penny; they put in large sums. God measures gifts not by the amount but by the cost, and by the heart. They all contributed out of their abundance: real gifts, honestly given, and probably nothing in their lives changed on the way home.

All she had to live on. Literally her whole life (holon ton bion autēs): she put her life in the box, trusting God to provide her next meal. And the kingdom’s arithmetic cuts both ways. The largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing, and the gift you are embarrassed by, the small amount from a pension, the hour given by someone with almost no hours, is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

The wider meaning. She stands in contrast to the rich man who would not give up his possessions (10:22), and to the scribes who devour widows’ houses (v. 40). She has done in small what the first commandment requires (v. 30). And she pictures what Jesus is about to do: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? Some hear Jesus lamenting a temple system that took the last coins of the poor. This commentary’s view: the context of corruption is real (v. 40; 13:2), but his words are commendation: she put in more than all, and she gave to God, not to a system. (See Luke 21:3 for the fuller answer.)

Should the poor give everything they have? Jesus commends her heart; he does not command the poor to give away their living. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Corinthians 8:12), and that a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). And this passage stands immediately after Jesus’ warning against those who devour widows’ houses (v. 40): no church or ministry may press the poor to give beyond their means. A church should be giving to its widows, not taking their last coins.

If she gave everything, how much should I give? The widow shows that Jesus measures a gift not by its size but by what is left behind after it. The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it sets a pattern: give regularly, in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2), generously, cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:6–7), and sacrificially, so that it costs you something. Many Christians take the Old Testament tithe as a sensible starting place and go beyond it as God prospers them. Give first to your local church, which feeds you with the word, and then to the poor and the spread of the gospel. Ask not how little you can give, but what it would look like to trust God with more.

For worship. She put in her whole life, and three days later he put in his. The widow gave all she had to live on into the hands of God, and the Son gave all he was into the hands of sinners, to ransom them. He was rich and became poor for us. Then he walked out of the temple and never went back, because the true offering was about to be made, once for all, outside the city wall.

12.theology:
What is owed to God. Every scene in this chapter asks it. The tenants owe the owner his fruit. The coin is Caesar’s, but the person who bears God’s image is God’s (Genesis 1:27). The whole law is summed up as loving God with everything and your neighbour as yourself. And a widow gives God all she has.

The chapter also shows who is owed it: the beloved Son of the parable, the rejected stone made the cornerstone, and David’s Lord seated at God’s right hand. The one who has every right to ask for everything is about to give everything for those who have withheld it.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, dropped into a bronze chest that made almost no sound. She could have kept one. She gave both.

Now: Christ measures a gift by what is left afterwards. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift, and the small gift from a pension is registered by him as larger than the endowment.

Is he commending her or lamenting her? He does not commend the machinery that took her coins, but he commends her: she gave to God in the only way open to her. And she does in small what he is about to do on Friday, when he gives his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
As they leave the temple a disciple points at the stonework, and he had reason to: Herod’s platform covers some thirty-five acres, and the work was not finished until AD 63. Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone.

On the Mount of Olives, facing the building, four disciples ask when. His answer is most striking for what it withholds. He describes signs and says they do not mean what people will claim: the end is not yet. He describes the fall of Jerusalem and sets it inside a generation. Then, at verse 32, the discourse turns: of his own coming there is no sign and no timetable, and no one knows the day, not even the Son.

What is left is a command, repeated: stay awake, which the closing parable defines as being found at your post, doing the work you were given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stones (vv. 1–4). A disciple admires the temple; Jesus says it will be thrown down, and four disciples ask him privately when.

The age (vv. 5–13). Deceivers, wars, earthquakes and famines will come, and none of them means the end has come. The church will be put on trial and betrayed by its own families. In the middle of the list stands one line that is not a disaster: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

The crisis (vv. 14–23). Then a specific sign, the abomination of desolation, and instructions so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go down for his belongings. A generation later Roman legions came up the valleys.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two questions, two answers. Everything down to verse 30 carries signs and a timeframe: false messiahs, wars, the abomination, the flight from Judea, and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. All of it happened in AD 70. Then verse 32 turns a corner: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. From there on there is no sign and no timetable.

So the discourse keeps two events apart, the fall of the temple and his own return, and Jesus was not mistaken: the temple fell in their lifetime, as he said, and his coming remains unknown, as he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10), one bright line in a catalogue of disasters, and the only item to be done rather than endured. The word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people.

Now: Paul reached Caesar’s household because he was arrested. So a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 13 is Jesus’ longest speech in this Gospel. Its warnings, deceivers, wars, persecution while the gospel goes to all nations, the abomination and the flight from Judea, came upon Jerusalem within that generation, in AD 70. Then he lifts their eyes to the Son of Man coming in clouds to gather his elect. At its centre stands its comfort: his words will not pass away.

The setting. The Olivet Discourse, given on the Mount of Olives (v. 3), stands between Jesus’ last day of public teaching and the account of his death. He has just watched a widow put her last two coins into the treasury (12:41–44), and now he walks out of the temple for the last time.

And as he came out of the temple. A solemn departure. In Ezekiel’s vision the glory of God left a defiled temple, paused at the threshold, and went out to the mountain east of the city, the Mount of Olives, before Babylon destroyed it (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Now the Lord of the temple walks out of it and climbs that same mountain (v. 3). He had come suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1), taught in it, cleansed it and been rejected in it, and now he leaves it to its fate. The glory that left that house came to rest in a crucified and risen man, and in him we have a temple no army can take: one whose foundation is laid in heaven, whose stones are living, and whose light is the Lamb.

What wonderful stones! You cannot blame the man. The disciples were Galileans from the country, and Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Its retaining walls were dressed limestone cut so precisely that they needed no mortar, and the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons. Josephus says that from a distance its white stone made the whole building look like a mountain covered with snow, and the rabbis said that whoever had not seen Herod’s temple had never seen a beautiful building.

Do you see these great buildings? Not a dismissal. He grants the premise: yes, look at them. Jesus never pretends that human achievement is small. He simply measures it against eternity.

Not one stone upon another. The Greek doubles its negative (ou mē): this will surely happen. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus took Jerusalem after a terrible siege. Josephus, who was there, describes the sanctuary burning, and says the city was so levelled that visitors could hardly believe it had ever been inhabited. The fig tree had withered (11:20), and now the temple it pictured follows it.

Why does the Western Wall still stand? Because it is part of the retaining wall Herod built around the temple platform, not part of the temple itself. Jesus spoke of these great buildings, the sanctuary and its courts, and of them not one stone was left on another. The platform survived as a ruin; the house of God on it did not.

Heard as blasphemy. We hear this sentence as history; they heard it as something close to blasphemy. This was the house of God, the place where atonement was made, the guarantee of the covenant. Jeremiah nearly died for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–9), and a twisted version of this very saying will be produced at Jesus’ trial in two days’ time (14:58). And something had happened in their hearts. The house God gave as a place to meet him had become a guarantee people held over him, as if the building would keep them safe whatever they did. Jeremiah had warned against exactly that trust (Jeremiah 7:4), and every religious heart is tempted to lean on the place or the practice instead of on the Lord.

Why did the temple have to fall? Because its work was finished. The temple was the place where a holy God dwelt among a sinful people, and where sacrifice was offered day after day so that they could draw near. All of that pointed to Jesus. He is the true temple, God dwelling with us in the flesh (John 1:14; 2:19–21), and within days his body will be torn down and raised again in three days. When he died, the curtain of the temple was torn from top to bottom (15:38). Once the one sacrifice for sins had been offered for all time (Hebrews 10:12), a building where lambs were slain could only be a denial that he had come. Its destruction was judgment on a city that rejected him, and it was also God taking away the picture once the reality it pointed to had come.

Was this prediction written after the event? It is a fair question. Some scholars date Mark after AD 70 for exactly that reason, but the argument often assumes the very thing in question: that Jesus could not know the future. Even on purely historical grounds the prediction is not strange: Jeremiah had foretold the first temple’s fall, and Josephus tells of another Jesus, son of Ananias, who cried woe on the temple for years before the war. The text itself does not read like hindsight. Mark describes no fire and none of the details of the siege that a writer looking back would naturally include, only warnings and a command to run, and many scholars date the Gospel to the late 60s, before the end came. Jesus staked everything on his word holding (v. 31), and in AD 70 it held, stone by stone.

Does this mean church buildings do not matter? No. A place set aside for worship is a good gift, and it is right to build it well and care for it. But it is never the house of God in the sense the temple was. The church is the people, the living stones built on Christ (1 Peter 2:4–5), and the Spirit dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16). A congregation that loses its building has lost a roof, not God. And a congregation that would rather keep its building than keep the gospel has already lost the thing that mattered.

In everyday life. That disciple was admiring the most permanent-looking thing in his world, and it had only a few decades left; what survived that generation was twelve men and a message. Everything you can point at and call impressive is on a clock: the company, the reputation, the house, the body. Build on the kingdom that cannot be shaken, already given you in Christ (Hebrews 12:27–28): his word, his people, and treasure laid up where nothing is thrown down.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opposite the temple. From this ridge across the Kidron valley you look straight down onto the temple platform, so the whole discourse is delivered with the building in view. He sits, the posture of a teacher and of a judge, facing the house he has just condemned. And the place carries prophecy of its own: Zechariah says that on the day of the LORD his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4). On the mountain of the prophets he spent his last free hours not defending himself but preparing four frightened men for a future he would face first.

Peter and James and John and Andrew. The first four disciples called from their nets (1:16–20). Privately: the crowd that heard him gladly (12:37) is gone, and this last extended teaching before the passion is given to four men who will lead the church through everything it describes.

Tell us, when will these things be? Two questions, and everything about how you read this chapter depends on noticing them. The first asks for a date. And notice what it asks about. Not the end of the world; Mark’s version has no such phrase. These things are the stones. He said the temple would be flattened, and they want to know when.

And what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished? The second asks for a warning, a marker visible in advance. The verb (synteleisthai) means brought to completion, and it suggests that in their minds the fall of the temple and the end of all things belonged together. Matthew makes that explicit: what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age? (Matthew 24:3). Jesus’ answer will gently separate the two. The temple will fall within their generation, with signs (v. 30). The end of the age will come at a time no one knows, with no signs to announce it (v. 32).

A question refused in the form it was put. It is what any of us would ask, and the discourse declines to answer it as asked. He gives signs, then says they do not mean what people will think; a timeframe for the temple, then no day or hour for his coming; and he ends with the one thing they need: stay awake. A man who knows the date will prepare on the last afternoon. A man who does not must live ready every day. By refusing them a date, Jesus is caring for them.

Where Christians differ: how to read this chapter. Some (preterists, from the Latin for past) take the whole discourse as fulfilled in AD 70. Some (futurists, especially dispensationalists, who see distinct stages in God’s plan, with separate futures for Israel and the church) take most of it as describing a future tribulation before a millennium. Others see it as speaking of both, with the near event foreshadowing the far.
