This commentary’s view: the best reading, held widely in Reformed and amillennial interpretation, is that verses 5–23 speak mainly of the period leading to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which also serves as a pattern of the troubles of the whole church age; verses 24–27 speak of the second coming of Christ at the end of the age; verses 28–31 return to the destruction of the temple within that generation; and verses 32–37 speak of the unknown day of the end. There is no secret rapture here; the gathering of the elect is at Christ’s visible return (v. 27). The reason is the text’s own seams: the disciples asked about the stones, and Jesus answers with signs inside a generation, then speaks of a day no one knows. Faithful Christians read the chapter in other ways too, and deserve to be heard charitably.

What does amillennial mean? It is the view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 pictures the present age, in which Christ reigns from heaven while the gospel goes to the nations, with one future return of Christ followed at once by the resurrection, the judgment and the new creation. That is how this chapter reads too: one public coming, one gathering of the elect. (See Acts 1:6 for the fuller answer.)

Is it wrong to be curious about the future? No. The disciples asked, and Jesus answered them at length; he did not rebuke the question. God has told us a great deal about the end, and it is meant to be read and treasured. What goes wrong is curiosity that wants control, that treats prophecy as a puzzle for the clever and the end as a date to be extracted. Notice that almost everything Jesus says here is an instruction: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, be on your guard, flee, do not believe it, learn, stay awake. Ask about the future, and expect to be told how to live today.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus began to say to them, "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he!' and they will lead many astray. And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one leads you astray. They asked when; his first word is watch out. Before a single sign is described, the danger is named, and it is not the wars or the earthquakes. It is being deceived. The verb (blepete, see, watch) runs through the chapter like a bell (vv. 5, 9, 23, 33). Jesus’ first concern is not information but protection.

I am he! Not claiming to be Jesus of Nazareth, but claiming the role he holds: I am the Messiah (Matthew 24:5), perhaps even taking the divine name, I am (egō eimi, see 6:50). Such men kept coming: Theudas, who promised to part the Jordan, and the Egyptian who led thousands out to this very Mount of Olives (Acts 5:36; 21:38). And note the exact shape: they come in my name. Not opposing Christ but claiming him, which is why the danger is to the church and not to the world.

Do not be alarmed. The word (throeisthe) means shaken, thrown into alarm. He does not say the wars will be small; he tells his people how to receive the reports, and two clauses undo the whole business of predicting the end. This must take place: the little word dei, must, means that God has decided it, and it is the word used of his own suffering (8:31). History is not out of hand. But the end is not yet: these things are not the countdown. He is deliberately disconnecting the calamities from the calendar.

Wars, earthquakes and famines. None of them is rare. In the decades before AD 70 there were wars on the Roman frontiers, a severe famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28), and great earthquakes, one destroying Laodicea around AD 60 and another striking Pompeii in 62. The wars that fill the headlines are not news to the one who said this must take place, and the earth that shakes beneath us is the footstool of the one who stilled the sea with a word. Behind every rumour of war stands the Lamb who holds the scroll of history, and he has never once lost his place in it.

The beginning of the birth pains. The prophets used labour as a picture of the sufferings before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9; Micah 4:9–10). Labour pains are real agony, they mean that something is coming, and the early ones tell you almost nothing about how long it will be. Paul uses the same picture: the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Romans 8:22). The world is not simply decaying. It is in labour, and its pains are leading to a birth (Romans 8:21).

The one who really is he. The title the deceivers claim already has an owner. Jesus alone can say I am truly: he said it on the water to frightened men (6:50), and he will say it before the high priest, I am, and you will see the Son of Man (14:62). Every false messiah is a forgery of him, which is why his people are not finally fooled: the sheep know the voice. And the birth pains are bound up with him too. The new age they labour toward was born on the morning he rose, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and every groan since is creation straining toward the day his risen life fills the world.

Are the wars and disasters in the news signs that the end is near? Not in the sense people usually mean. Jesus lists exactly these things and then says the end is not yet. They are the normal weather of the whole age between his first and second coming, not a countdown that lets you work out a date. In another sense they are signs of something: that this world is broken, that it is groaning for redemption, and that Christ’s words are true. So every disaster should send you to prayer, to compassion and to the gospel, and none of them should send you to a chart.

How should I read the news? As a man who has been told in advance what the age would look like. When the next catastrophe arrives, and it will, two responses are available and both are wrong. One is panic, the anxious scanning of events for the pattern. The other is the calculating excitement that treats disaster as a timetable, which has produced a long line of confident predictions and an equally long line of quiet retractions. Jesus forbids both in one sentence: do not be alarmed, the end is not yet. Then get on with the work he actually gave you: pray for those suffering, give where you can, and tell people about the only kingdom that will not be shaken.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

verseByVerse.quote: But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be on your guard. Literally, see to yourselves: what is coming is coming to you. Deliver over (paradōsousin) is the word used of John the Baptist (1:14) and of Jesus himself (9:31; 14:10; 15:1): the disciples will walk their master’s road. Councils (synedria) were the local Jewish courts as well as the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.

Before governors and kings. Read Acts with this verse open and it is a table of contents. Councils: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). Beaten in synagogues: Paul received forty lashes less one five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Governors: Felix and Festus (Acts 24–25). Kings: Agrippa (Acts 26), and finally an appeal to Caesar himself (Acts 25:11). Note also where the first blows land: in synagogues. The persecution begins at home, among their own people. It usually does.

To bear witness before them. The purpose Jesus names is not suffering but witness: the dock becomes a pulpit. Every one of those trials put the gospel in front of an audience it would never otherwise have reached, which is exactly what Paul says from prison: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12).

The gospel must first be proclaimed. One bright line in a catalogue of disasters, and the only item to be done rather than endured. The same dei, must, as verse 7, and the word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people. This is the real sign of the age between the comings: not wars, but mission. Persecution is not an interruption of the mission but one of its engines; the gospel travelled furthest along the roads that arrested men were dragged down.

Has this already happened? In one sense, yes: Paul could say before AD 70 that the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Colossians 1:23; see Romans 1:8; Colossians 1:6). In its fullest sense it goes on until the end (Matthew 24:14; 28:19–20). But Christ’s return is not triggered by our success, as though the church could finish a list and bring him back. The day is fixed by the Father (v. 32). Our part is to be faithful in the task, and to know that it cannot fail, because the Lord of the harvest has said it must be done.

Do not be anxious beforehand. A promise for the dock: before a hostile court, God undertakes to supply the words in the moment. Stephen’s face and speech are its fulfilment (Acts 6:10, 15). It is not a licence for the preacher who has not opened his Bible all week. Paul told Timothy to do his best to present himself as a worker rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). To preach unprepared and call it trusting the Spirit is not faith but presumption. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit: the Spirit sent by the risen Christ stands beside the accused as his advocate.

Should I prepare to speak about my faith, then? Yes, in ordinary life. Peter tells every believer to be always prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Know the gospel well enough to say it simply; think about the questions your friends actually ask. What this verse removes is not preparation but fear: the sleepless rehearsal of what you will say if you are ever questioned, arrested or mocked for Christ. When that hour comes, you will not be left to your own resources.

What if I am never persecuted? Does that mean my faith is weak? No. The fact that you live in a place of relative freedom is a mercy to be thanked for, not a failure to be ashamed of (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Jesus does not promise every believer the same measure of suffering. But all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will meet opposition in some form (2 Timothy 3:12), even if only quiet contempt. And you belong to a body that is suffering right now in many countries. If one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26). Your part may be to pray, to give, and to speak up for them.

In everyday life. The courtroom in your life may only be a lunch table, but it is still a place to bear witness. Think of where you are most likely to be asked about Christ this week, at work, at the school gate, in the family, and ask the Spirit for courage there.
verseByVerse.note: The councils were local Jewish courts; synagogues had the authority to flog.

parallels.desc: Peter and John before the council

verseByVerse.quote: And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brother will deliver brother. What he said would be done to him (10:33) is now done to his people, by their own. It names the closest bonds human beings have: a brother, and even a father handing over his child.

Children against parents. It is Micah’s picture of a society in total moral collapse, where a man’s enemies are the men of his own house (Micah 7:6), and Jesus echoes it because it is precisely what following him will cost some of his people. He had already said he came not to bring peace but a sword, dividing families over him (Matthew 10:34–36). Under Nero, Tacitus records, a great multitude of Christians was convicted on the information of those first arrested, and there are believers today, especially converts from other religions, whose own families reported them.

Hated by all. By every kind of person, Jew and Gentile. The reason Jesus gives is my name. They are hated because they belong to him. Not for being difficult or rude; Christians sometimes attract dislike for other reasons entirely and then claim this verse. And the verse searches the heart. For many of us the need to be liked is a quiet idol, and nothing exposes it like the prospect of being disliked for Christ. If approval is what you cannot live without, this verse will feel unbearable. If his approval is enough (Galatians 1:10), it becomes bearable, and even, as the apostles found, an honour (Acts 5:41).

Hated for his name. If your own family regards your faith as a betrayal, if you have lost a brother’s respect or a father’s welcome over it, hear that your Lord said this would happen, said it in advance, and knew it from the inside. His own family came to take him away by force, believing he was out of his mind (3:21). His brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). You are not on a road he has not walked.

The one who endures to the end. The sentence that has kept anxious believers awake. Endures (hypomeinas) means remains under the weight, does not give up. Will be saved means saved eternally, not rescued from death. It is not salvation by stamina; we are saved by grace through faith. Endurance is not the price of salvation; it is the evidence of it. In the parable of the sower, the rocky ground also received the word with joy, but had no root, and fell away when trouble came (4:16–17). The falling away did not cancel a genuine faith; it revealed a shallow one.

Where Christians differ: endurance and perseverance. Some Christians, among them Arminians (who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted and finally lost), take this to mean that a true believer can lose salvation if he does not endure, and they rightly take the warning with great seriousness. This commentary’s view: endurance is required, and it is real; those who fall away permanently show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). But God himself keeps his elect so that they will endure (v. 20; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The saints persevere because God preserves them: that is what the perseverance of the saints means. The warning is one of the means God uses to keep them.

The guarantee in the same chapter. If you are asking, will I hold on?, which is a healthy question, read on. For the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days (v. 20), and at the end the Son of Man gathers his elect from the four winds (v. 27). He does not lose them: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). You are told to endure. You will, because the God who shortened the days for his elect keeps them.

Should I cut off family members who oppose my faith? No, not on your side. Jesus warns that they may turn against you; he never tells you to turn against them. Keep honouring your parents, keep loving your brothers and sisters, keep the door open, and keep praying for them. Christ must come first, so when they demand that you deny him, stop worshipping, or give up your church, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But that is a refusal, not a rejection. Wise distance may be necessary if there is real danger or abuse, and you should seek help from your church if there is. Even then, the aim is that they would one day see Christ in the way you bore it.

I have doubted and stumbled. Have I failed to endure? Enduring is not the same as never wavering. Peter denied Christ three times in one night and was restored (14:72; John 21:15–19). The one who endures is the one who keeps coming back to Christ, however weakly, and does not finally walk away from him. If you are troubled by your stumbling and still clinging to him, that is what endurance looks like from the inside. Falling away is a settled turning from Christ, not the struggle of a weak believer who hates his sin and keeps running back to the cross.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The abomination of desolation. This is the sign they asked for in verse 4. The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11); some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add spoken of by Daniel the prophet, as Matthew has it (Matthew 24:15), but the earliest copies of Mark do not. An abomination is something detestable to God, and the word is the standard Old Testament term for an idol. Of desolation means that causes desolation, a desecration so vile that it drives God’s worship out and leaves his sanctuary empty. Daniel’s words had already seen one fulfilment. In 167 BC the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus on the altar of burnt offering and sacrificed pigs there; the book of 1 Maccabees calls it a desolating sacrilege (1 Maccabees 1:54). To every Jew who heard it, the phrase meant the worst thing that had ever happened, happening again.

Standing where he ought not to be. Let the reader understand. Mark’s Greek is deliberately odd: the word for standing is masculine, as for a person, though abomination is neuter, as for a thing. So this is not merely a thing set up in the holy place; it is somebody. And let the reader understand is probably spoken to whoever reads the Gospel aloud in a congregation, a nudge: be alert, and when it happens do not stand about discussing it.

What was the abomination? Luke gives Jesus’ words in a form his Gentile readers could not miss: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). A generation later Roman legions came up the valleys carrying their standards, which bore the emperor’s image and were treated as objects of worship. When the temple fell, Josephus records, the soldiers brought those standards into the temple court and offered sacrifice to them there. Earlier, in AD 67–68, Zealot factions had occupied the temple, committed murders in its courts and installed a false high priest, and some see that defilement as part of the fulfilment. The masculine he most likely points to the Roman commander and his army. A sign seen only when the temple was already burning would come too late to flee, which is why many take the warning to begin with the defilement and the approach of the armies, before the siege closed.

Is this fulfilled in AD 70, or by a future Antichrist? Many Christians, especially dispensationalists, expect a future ruler to set himself up in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Revelation 13). But Luke’s version and the instruction itself point to AD 70: the remedy is to flee from Judea to the mountains, which only makes sense of a crisis in that land in that century. The more likely reading is that this is the Roman desecration and destruction. Paul’s man of lawlessness shows that a final rebellion against God is still to come before Christ returns, and Antiochus and Titus are both foreshadowings of it. But that is not what Jesus warns of here.

Run, do not fight. Those in Judea are to flee to the mountains, not defend the holy city. Every nationalist instinct said the opposite, and it destroyed the Zealots. The church historian Eusebius, writing in the fourth century, records that it worked: the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophecy, left the city before the war, crossed the Jordan to Pella, and survived. If the report is right, a church took its Lord’s word literally and lived.

The desolation he went into. The disciples are told to run from a desolated holy place; their Lord was about to walk into a desolation of his own. Within days, on a hill outside these walls, he would cry, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (15:34), abandoned in the place of sinners so that sinners would never be abandoned. The temple Rome would profane was already finished as the place of meeting with God, because the true holy place was the crucified and risen Christ. That is why his people could leave the building behind without leaving God: they ran with him, not from him.

On the housetop. Houses had flat roofs with an outside stair. When you see it, go down the steps and keep going; do not step inside for anything.

Not turn back for his cloak. A man working in a field left his outer cloak at the edge. It was his blanket at night, and the Law protected it from creditors precisely because a poor man could not do without it (Exodus 22:26–27). Leave it. And behind it is Genesis: another family was told to get out of a doomed city and not look back, and one of them turned round (Genesis 19:17, 26). Jesus makes the connection himself in Luke: remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:32). Lot’s wife looked back at a city she loved more than her deliverer. Christ’s people looked forward at a Lord they loved more than their city, and he brought them through.

Is it right for a Christian to flee persecution? Yes, when fleeing is possible without denying Christ. Jesus commands it here, and elsewhere tells his disciples that when they are persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). Fleeing is not cowardice, and staying is not always faith. What is never allowed is to save your life by disowning him. Sometimes a believer is called to stay, as shepherds stay with their flocks, and many have died faithfully doing so. Seek wisdom, take counsel, and trust that the Lord who told the Jerusalem church to run is the Lord of both choices.

In everyday life. This is tactical advice for a crisis in AD 70, and also a permanent picture of what judgment does to the value of possessions: there comes a moment when the cloak is not worth the four seconds. Your inheritance is kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4), so when Scripture tells you to flee sexual immorality, idolatry or the love of money (1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Timothy 6:10–11), take it as literally as the Jerusalem church did, and run in the strength of the Spirit who lives in you. Do not go back inside for one last thing.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple; it was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alas for women who are pregnant! He has just told them to run without stopping for a coat, and now he thinks about who cannot run. The Son of God, describing the fall of a city a generation away, pauses over the women who will be nine months pregnant that week and the mothers with a baby at the breast. He is imagining particular people, and it costs him something. The word is not a curse but a cry of grief.

Pray that it may not happen in winter. Then he tells them to pray about the timing. Winter in Judea means rains, swollen wadis, impassable tracks, the Jordan in flood and cold nights in the open. So: ask God to arrange the date of a judgment he has already determined, so that the flight will be survivable. That settles something about prayer. A thing can be fixed in the purpose of God and still be a proper subject of prayer, and God’s sovereignty over an event is not a reason to stop asking about its details. God ordains the means as well as the end, and our prayers are among the means. He told Elijah he would send rain, and Elijah still prayed for it on Carmel until the cloud came (1 Kings 18:1, 42–45).

Such tribulation as has not been. The prophets’ language for a catastrophe beyond comparison (Daniel 12:1). Josephus, an eyewitness, describes famine so complete that people ate leather, a mother who ate her own child, crucifixions outside the walls at up to five hundred a day until there was no room left for the crosses, and at the end the city burned and its people killed or enslaved. The words and never will be show that Jesus is speaking of an event inside history, not the very end, for there will be time after it.

If the Lord had not cut short the days. Saved here means survived. The siege lasted about five months; had it gone on, no one would have come out.

For the sake of the elect. The pastoral heart of the whole discourse. The tribulation has a limit. It does not stop because evil runs out of strength or because the church is strong enough: God shortens it, and for the sake of the elect (eklektous), whom he chose, and Mark says it twice. To be elect is to have been chosen by God, before the foundation of the world, as his own, out of love and not for anything found in us (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). God’s choice of his people governs even the length of a war. It does not promise that they are exempt; it promises that they are the reason it stops. Behind the worst of history there is a hand on the clock, set by love for particular, named people (Romans 8:28).

Was the fall of Jerusalem God’s judgment on the Jewish people as a race? It was a judgment on that generation’s rejection of the Messiah, as Jesus wept over the city and said (Luke 19:41–44), and as the parable of the tenants had warned (12:9). But it was never a licence for hatred of Jewish people. Jesus himself, his mother, every apostle and the whole first church were Jews, and those who fled to Pella were Jewish believers. The guilt for the death of Christ is shared by Jew and Gentile alike (Acts 4:27), and his blood was shed for both. The church’s long history of contempt for the Jews is a sin, not an application of this passage. Paul speaks of them with great sorrow, and still prays for their salvation (Romans 9:2–3; 10:1).

If God has decreed what will happen, why should I pray? Because he has decreed our prayers too, and works through them. Jesus held both truths in one sentence: the days are fixed by God, and his people should pray about them. Prayer is not an attempt to change God’s mind from outside his plan; it is one of the ways his plan unfolds. We do not know the decree, but we do know the command, and we are told to ask (James 4:2). So pray about the timing of the operation, the weather on the journey, the length of the trial. The God who shortened the days for the elect still listens.

In everyday life. When you cannot see how a thing can go on and anyone survive it, the persecution in that country, the sickness in this house, the years that have been taken, the promise is not that you will be lifted out. It is that there is a limit, that the limit was fixed before it started, and that it was fixed for your sake (1 Corinthians 10:13). Say that to yourself this week about the hardest thing you are carrying.

For worship. No suffering of his people runs a minute longer than he has decided, and he has decided in love. And the one who shortened their days did not shorten his own. He did not cut short his own suffering but drank the cup to the dregs, so that our troubles would have a limit and his love would have none.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: And then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not believe it. He returns to the danger he opened with (v. 5): the worst thing in this passage is not the siege but deception. In times of crisis people look for a deliverer and will follow anyone who claims to be one. Josephus records that on the day the temple fell a false prophet told the people to go up into its courts to receive signs of their deliverance, and some six thousand died when the colonnade where they waited was set on fire.

Here and there. Note the specific form it takes: here and there, a location. Somebody has him, somewhere, and you must go and see. That is the mark of the counterfeit: the real coming will be like lightning from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and nobody will need to be told where to look (v. 26).

Signs and wonders. The signs will impress; Jesus does not say they will all be obvious tricks. Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues (Exodus 7:22). Deuteronomy legislates for exactly this case: if a prophet gives a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, you shall not listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul warns of false signs and wonders to come (2 Thessalonians 2:9). Whether such wonders are real or skilful deception, the point is the same: a miracle does not prove that the one who does it comes from God. A thing can be genuinely inexplicable and not be from God, so the fact that something works is never, by itself, a reason to follow anybody.

The test is truth, not power. The test is the doctrine underneath it: does this lead people to the Christ who came in the flesh, died on a cross and rose, or away from him? Deuteronomy’s test is John’s (1 John 4:2–3). Miracles, crowds and visible success prove nothing either way.

To lead astray, if possible, the elect. The elect are the target. Not the world, which needs no deceiving; the deception is aimed at the church, by people using Christ’s name. If possible: the phrase implies that it is not possible. The attempt will be formidable, and God’s people will not finally be lost, because he keeps them (John 10:27–29). But the way they are kept is not by magic. It is by remembering what they were told: I have told you all things beforehand (v. 23).

I have told you all things beforehand. The third of the chapter’s four calls to watch, and the reason given is a mercy. God protects his people from deception not by making them incapable of being fooled, but by telling them in advance and expecting them to remember. Forewarned is forearmed, but only for somebody who has read the warning: know your Bible well enough that a false thing sounds wrong when you hear it. He told us everything beforehand because he loves us, and he guards his elect because he bought them.

How do I recognise a false teacher today? Ask three questions. First, what does he say about Jesus: is Christ fully God and fully man, crucified for sinners and risen, the only way to the Father? Second, what does he say about the gospel: is salvation by grace through faith, or is it something you earn, buy or unlock with a technique? Third, where does he point you: to Scripture and to Christ, or to himself, his new revelation, his special experiences, his secret knowledge of the date? Watch the fruit of his life as well (Matthew 7:15–20), but begin with his doctrine. A teacher who is warm, gifted and successful can still be wrong, and one who is plain and unknown can be right.

Can a true Christian be deceived at all? Yes, for a time and in part. Believers can be misled on many things, and the Galatians were led a long way before Paul wrote to them (Galatians 3:1). What this verse promises is that the elect will not be finally carried away from Christ. God uses his word, his church and his Spirit to bring his people back. So do not be proud, as if you could never be fooled, and do not despair, as if one error has ruined you. Stay close to the Scriptures and to a faithful church, and test what you hear (1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The coming (vv. 24–27). The heavens are shaken, and the Son of Man comes in clouds with great power and glory to gather his people from the four winds.

The fig tree (vv. 28–31). A lesson in reading signs, the much-argued this generation, and a claim no creature could make: his words will outlast heaven and earth.

The hinge (v. 32). No one knows the day, not the angels, not the Son. Everything before this verse had signs; nothing after it does.

The command (vv. 33–37). A householder leaves each servant a job and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake, for he may come in any watch of the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against the deity of Christ, from Arius in the fourth century onwards: if Jesus did not know the day, the argument runs, he cannot be God.

The church’s answer is the heart of who Christ is: two natures in the one Lord. As God he knows all things; as man he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52). And in verse 31 the same speaker sets his own words above heaven and earth, a claim no creature could make. The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart: that is God become man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a householder goes away and leaves his servants each with his work, and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake. Watching, in this parable, is not scanning the road but doing what you were left to do.

Now: that corrects both anxiously working out dates and living as if he were never coming. The one who is ready is found at his post when the door opens: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes (Matthew 24:46). So the question is not when, but what he left you to do; and since the servants were his household before he left, they work because they belong.

verseByVerse.quote: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After that tribulation. After the distress of the siege (v. 19) and the whole church age that it represents; Jesus does not say how long after. He now looks past AD 70 to the far horizon, his own return.

Sun and moon darkened. Every phrase echoes the prophets. The sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light: Isaiah 13:10, against Babylon. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining: Joel 2:10. It is the prophets’ settled language for the day God acts in judgment. They used it for events inside history, the fall of Babylon and the ruin of Edom, as well as for the last day: the world turned upside down, the powers falling, God acting.

The powers in the heavens. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). The powers (dynameis) may be the heavenly bodies, or the spiritual powers people worshipped through them (Ephesians 6:12). Either way, the whole created order is shaken by the coming of its maker (Hebrews 12:26–27).

What the imagery says. The sun, moon and stars were the fixed points, what you steer by, plant by and set your calendar by. To say the lights go out is to say that the last reliable things are not reliable. The building was going to fall (v. 2); now the sky. Only one thing in the chapter will be called unshakeable, and it is his words (v. 31).

Darkness at noon. Three days later, as Jesus hung on the cross, darkness came over the whole land from the sixth hour until the ninth (15:33). The sign of the day of the LORD fell first on one man outside the city, as he bore the judgment the prophets had described. That is why the shaking of the heavens is not a terror for his people. The darkness that will cover the old creation at his coming has already covered him, and those who are in him have nothing left to fear from the day the lights go out.

Where Christians differ: AD 70 or the end? Some (preterists, who hold that much of this prophecy was fulfilled in the past, and some others such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright) take verses 24–27 as prophetic imagery for the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s vindication in AD 70, since the prophets used such language for historical judgments. Others take it as the end of the world and the second coming. This commentary’s view: after that tribulation marks a new stage, and the gathering of the elect from the whole earth (v. 27) and the coming of the Son of Man in glory (8:38; 14:62) describe the visible return of Christ at the end of the age, as the New Testament elsewhere teaches (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The cosmic imagery may be partly symbolic, but it points to a real event that ends history.

Will the universe literally be destroyed? Scripture speaks of the present heavens and earth passing away and being dissolved by fire (2 Peter 3:10–12), and also of creation being set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:19–21). The best way to hold these together is that God will not throw his creation away but purge and renew it, as a refiner purifies gold. What passes away is the old order, marred by sin and curse. What comes is a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–5). So the shaking of the heavens is not the end of God’s world. It is the end of the world as we have known it, and the beginning of the world as he always meant it to be.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man coming in clouds. This is Daniel 7:13–14, and Jesus draws on it directly: with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him. In Daniel he comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom. Here, having received it, he comes in glory to the earth.

The clouds. In the Old Testament, cloud is where God is: the pillar in the wilderness, Sinai, the mountain of transfiguration (9:7). To come with the clouds is a claim to deity, and the high priest will understand it perfectly when Jesus says it under oath at his trial, and will tear his robes (14:62–63). The cloud also hid God’s glory, because sinful people cannot see his face and live (Exodus 33:20). When the Son of Man comes with the clouds, the holiness that Sinai fenced off will be unveiled before the whole world, and the glory that is terror to the proud will be home to those he has washed.

They will see. This Gospel has been full of people not seeing (8:18, 24). That ends here, and they means all people. His return will be visible and public, not secret: every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7).

With great power and glory. He says it, probably, on the Tuesday of the last week. On Friday he will be nailed up naked outside the city with a mocking placard over his head, and the men who arranged it will stand underneath telling him to come down. His first coming was in weakness; his second will be in power, and it will prove that the crucified one was God’s King.

Is this the second coming or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some, reading Daniel 7 carefully, note that there the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom, and take these verses as Christ being proved right by the temple’s fall. The more likely reading is that here the far horizon breaks through. People will see him; the elect are gathered from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven; and Jesus speaks of his final coming in the same terms elsewhere (8:38; 14:62). As in the prophets, the near judgment and the final one appear in one view, and these verses are where the final one shows.

He will gather his elect. After twenty verses of warnings, the end of the story is not a courtroom scene, though the rest of Scripture makes clear that judgment will follow. The one thing the Son of Man is shown doing when he comes is collecting his people. The angels are his angels (8:38); the elect are his elect, the Father’s chosen and Christ’s own. The language is the old promise of regathering: if your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD will gather you (Deuteronomy 30:4). And now it includes believers from every nation, since the gospel will have been preached to all nations (v. 10).

From the ends of the earth. The reach of it is total. Christians have been scattered by exile, slavery, war, famine, prison and the sea. They have died in places nobody recorded and been buried where nobody knows. He does not leave one of them behind.

No secret rapture. Some (dispensationalists) teach that believers will be secretly taken from the earth before a seven-year tribulation, and that this passage describes a later stage. This commentary’s view: the gathering of the elect happens at Christ’s visible coming in glory, after the tribulation (v. 24), just as Paul describes the gathering of believers to meet the Lord at his public return with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 2:1). There is one return of Christ, public and glorious, at which his people are gathered to him. The church is not promised escape from trouble, but keeping through it (v. 13). Many who were taught a pre-tribulation rapture love Christ and long for his coming; the difference is over the order of events, not over the hope itself.

What happens to believers who have already died? They are with Christ now, consciously, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware, and they are not in a place of purging; their souls are made perfect in holiness and wait for the redemption of their bodies. When Christ comes, God will bring them with him, their bodies will be raised imperishable, and the living will be changed and caught up together with them (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). The gathering from the four winds includes every grave. No believer who has died is behind, and none will miss that day.

What will happen to those who are not gathered? Mark’s verse speaks only of the elect, but Jesus says plainly elsewhere that when the Son of Man comes in his glory he will sit on his throne and separate the nations, and those who do not know him will go away into eternal punishment (Matthew 25:31–46; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). That is why the gospel must first be preached to all nations (v. 10). The same coming that is the hope of the church is the terror of the unbelieving world, and the time to be reconciled to the King is before he appears, while he is still calling.

For worship. The one who was lifted up in shame will be seen in glory. He died alone, deserted by his friends, and because he was abandoned, his people never will be. He will send his angels to the four winds, to the deserts and the seabed and the graves no one tends, and gather every one the Father gave him.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the fig tree learn its lesson. The last time a fig tree appeared in this Gospel it was in full leaf with nothing on it, and he cursed it, and it was an acted parable of the temple (11:13–21). They are on the same mountain, and now a fig tree teaches something positive. He curses barren religion and he makes dead branches bud.

Summer is near. Why the fig? Many of the commonest trees in that country are evergreen, the olive, the carob, the pine, so they tell you nothing about the season. The fig is bare all winter and one of the last to bud. When the sap rises and the fig breaks into leaf in late spring, the hot season is coming. A child could read it. The sign is unmistakable, and it gives you not a date but a season.

When you see these things. Everything turns on how much these things covers. The phrase points back to the events leading up to the destruction of the temple (vv. 5–23). Those are the buds on the branch. The disciples had asked for a sign (v. 4); this is it.

At the very gates. The Greek can mean he is near or it is near, meaning either the Son of Man or the destruction of the temple they asked about. Either way, when the signs appear the event is as near as someone standing at the city gate.

The one at the gates. The last time Jesus leaves the city in this Gospel, he is led out to be crucified, to suffer outside the gate (15:20–22; Hebrews 13:12). The one who is near, at the very gates, whether in judgment on the city or at his final coming, is the same Lord who was thrown out of them. And his people read every budding branch as the nearness of a Friend, because the one standing at the door has already gone through death for them.

The right response to a budding tree. It is not to calculate the date of midsummer but to get ready for hot weather. The signs were given so that when the world goes dark his people would not panic, would recognise the season, and would keep working. A man who ignores the tree entirely is caught out by the summer just as surely as the man who publishes a date for it and is wrong.

Should I be looking for signs today, then? Not to fix a date, but to stay awake. The particular signs Jesus gave here belonged to the fall of Jerusalem, and that generation saw them. For us the lesson of the fig tree still holds in its broader sense: the whole age since the resurrection is the last days (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18), and everything that happens in it should remind us that summer is coming. So when you see false teachers, persecution, wars and the gospel spreading, do not reach for a calculator. Reach for your work, your Bible and your prayers, because the season you are living in is the season before his coming.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation. The verse sceptics reach for first: here, they say, Jesus promised his return within his hearers’ lifetime, and he did not come. It is a fair question, and C. S. Lewis once called this the most embarrassing verse in the Bible. But the discourse itself shows why it is not a failure. This generation (hē genea hautē) everywhere else in Mark means the people then living (8:12, 38; 9:19). All these things refers to the events of verses 5–23, leading to the destruction of the temple, the thing the disciples asked about (v. 4).

Two comings held apart. The false messiahs, the wars, the abomination, the flight from Judea: every one took place within that generation, in AD 70, and the temple fell down to the last stone. Then the discourse turns (v. 32) and says the opposite about his own return: no countdown, no timetable, nobody knows the day. Paul does name a final rebellion that must come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but that gives no timetable, and the return is always near for those who watch.

Where Christians differ: this generation. Some take this generation to mean the Jewish race, or the human race, or the generation alive at the end, which sees the signs. Some critics conclude that Jesus expected the end of the world within a generation and was mistaken. This commentary’s view: the plain meaning is Jesus’ contemporaries. All these things refers to the events leading to the destruction of the temple, which did take place within that generation. Jesus then carefully distinguishes that day (v. 32), the day of his coming, whose timing no one knows. He was not mistaken.

But what of verses 24–27? Do they not come before this verse? They do, but these things in verse 29 are what you see before he is near, the signs and not the event they point to. These things are the false messiahs, wars, persecution, the desolation and the flight (vv. 5–23). The coming of verses 26–27 is the event those signs foreshadow, and of its day no one knows (v. 32). Read this way, and it is the reading the text’s own turning points ask for, Jesus was not mistaken in either promise. Faithful interpreters draw the line in slightly different places, but each of their readings keeps his words true. He told them the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He told them his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.

Words that outlast the universe. Over both comings stands a sentence easy to skate over. He has spent the chapter showing that nothing we count on as permanent will last: the temple, the nation, the family, the possessions, the sun and moon and stars. Now he adds heaven and earth, the whole created order, and sets his own words above it.

Who is speaking. A Galilean carpenter with four fishermen, two days from arrest, with no writings, no institution and no army, says that when the universe has gone, the sentences he has spoken this afternoon will still be standing. The prophets said, thus says the LORD, and put the permanence where it belonged: the word of our God will stand forever (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 119:89). Jesus says my words. Only God’s word can outlast creation, because only God was there before it (Psalm 90:2), so by putting his own words where Isaiah put the word of our God, Jesus puts himself where the LORD stands. No promise of his has ever lapsed. The temple fell on his word; the elect will be gathered on his word; and the sinner who trusts him is forgiven on his word, with a security more lasting than the universe.

Why has he not come after two thousand years? Peter answers this directly. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day; the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is not forgetfulness or failure. It is mercy, the time in which the gospel goes to all nations and the last of his elect are gathered in. Every year he waits, more people are saved. And Jesus never said he would come soon in the sense of a date. He said no one knows, and stay awake.

In everyday life. Choose one sentence of Jesus this week, perhaps this one, and learn it by heart, so that it is in you when other things are taken. And when someone tells you that Jesus got the end wrong, show them this chapter, the two questions and the hinge, and tell them that he got the temple right to the last stone.

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day or that hour. The hinge of the whole discourse: from these things (v. 30) to that day. That day is the Old Testament’s own phrase for the day of the LORD, the day of final judgment and salvation (Amos 8:9; Zechariah 14:4–9), and here it is the day of the Son of Man’s coming (v. 26).

No one knows. No marker fixes the day and no calculation reaches it, a fact that ought to have retired the date-setting business and never has; the very claim to know is a mark of a false teacher. And note the ascending scale: not men, not angels who stand in God’s presence, not the Son. He goes as high as it is possible to go before stopping at the Father. The Father has fixed the time by his own authority (Acts 1:7).

Nor the Son. No verse in Mark is wielded more often against the deity of Christ, and it is a statement the church would never have invented. Arius built on it in the fourth century: if Jesus did not know the day, he cannot be God. The church’s answer is the heart of who Christ is. The eternal Son took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that there are two natures in the one Lord. As God he knows all things; as man he learned to speak, grew tired, and increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52). In becoming man, the Son willingly accepted the limits of a human mind, and did not draw on his divine knowledge in his human mind except as the Father willed. This is part of his humbling (Philippians 2:6–8), and of his perfect obedience. The Son who knows the end from the beginning chose to stand on a hillside with a human mind and say, I do not know. He emptied himself so far that he would not reach for what his Father had not given him, and he says so honestly to four men who would have given anything for a date.

The same structure as the storm. His not knowing is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat because he was exhausted, and then stand up and silence a hurricane with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus is less than fully God: he places himself above the angels, alongside the Father, as the Son. And Mark has set the proof one verse back: the same speaker who says he does not know the day has just said that heaven and earth will pass away but his words will not, a claim no creature could dare to make. The starkest claim to deity in the Gospel and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true: that is what God become man looks like.

Does the risen Christ know the day now? Scripture does not say directly, and we should be modest. But many theologians have thought that the limitation belonged to the days of his humiliation. The risen and exalted Christ has received all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), and in Revelation it is he who is given the revelation of what must soon take place to show to his servants (Revelation 1:1). What is certain is that he is no longer in the state of humbling, and that the day is safe in the hands of the Father who has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). Either way, it is not ours to know.

So what am I to do with not knowing? Treat it as a gift rather than a gap. If you knew the day, you would be tempted to put off repentance, obedience and kindness until the last moment, and to live the rest of the time for yourself. Not knowing means every day is a day to be ready. It also frees you: you are not responsible for working out God’s calendar, only for being faithful in yours. Plan for the future, as wise servants do, and hold your plans in open hands: if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15).

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be on guard, keep awake. The practical point of the whole discourse, and the reason he gives is that they do not know when the time will come. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and pray; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. The time (kairos) is the appointed moment.

A man going on a journey. The man is Jesus, about to leave by his death, resurrection and ascension, and to return. The master is genuinely absent for an indefinite period, which is exactly the situation of the church between the ascension and the return, and he hands the running of the house to the people who work in it: real authority, real responsibility, real trust.

Each with his work. This phrase defines watchfulness in this chapter. Every servant has a job, specific, assigned, different from the next man’s, and the servants are not at the window scanning the road. Watching is doing the thing you were left to do. Waiting for Christ is not passive; every believer has work prepared for him (Ephesians 2:10), and it is never in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Nor do they work to earn a place in the house. The servants are already his household before he leaves; they work because they belong, not in order to belong (Ephesians 2:8–9).

And commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. One man has a post at the door, ready to open the moment the master knocks, at any hour. His job is the watching, which produces nothing visible and is still work. The doorkeeper may picture church leaders, who keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17), or every believer. Either way, someone is meant to be listening for the knock. He is coming back to the house he bought with his blood, and the one who knocks will be the one who once stood outside and was rejected, and who now comes home in glory to share his joy with his servants.

How do I know what my work is? Start with what is already in front of you, because the master assigned it. Your calling in the home: a husband loving his wife, parents raising children in the Lord, children honouring parents. Your calling in the world: the job you are paid for, done honestly and well as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23). Your calling in the church: the gifts the Spirit has given you, used for others (1 Peter 4:10). And the calling of every believer: to pray, to love your neighbour, and to make Christ known. You do not need a dramatic sense of destiny. You need to be faithful in what he has put in your hands.

Does watching mean I should not plan for the future? No. Servants left in charge of a house for an indefinite period must plan: repair the roof, sow the field, save for the winter. Paul rebuked those who stopped working because they thought the end was near (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Plan your career, save for your children, build things that will take years. Watchfulness is not idleness and it is not panic. It is doing everything as someone who will give an account to the master, and holding it all ready to be handed back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore stay awake. The four watches of the Roman night: evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning, from about six in the evening to six in the morning.

The four watches. Look at what Mark does with those four watches in the next two chapters. In the evening: when it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17), and they sat down to the supper. At midnight: Mark does not name the hour, but deep in the night they are in Gethsemane, where he asks them to watch with him, and comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says to Peter, could you not watch one hour? (14:37). When the rooster crows: the courtyard, and Peter’s third denial, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). In the morning: as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation and delivered him to Pilate (15:1). All four watches, in order, in a single night: Mark seems to have told the story of Jesus’ last night so that it follows the parable, watch by watch.

Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. That is exactly what happens in the garden, and stay awake is the same verb, three times in Gethsemane (14:34, 37, 38). The disciples were told this on Tuesday and failed it on Thursday. Sleep pictures spiritual unreadiness (Romans 13:11–14).

A mercy, not merely an indictment. The men who failed the test in the garden are the men Christ went to the cross for, restored on a beach and sent to the ends of the earth. Failing to watch is not the end of a disciple: Christ kept the watch they broke, and his faithfulness is counted as theirs. But do not imagine, reading this comfortably, that you would have stayed awake. They loved him and they were exhausted and they meant it, and they could not manage an hour.

And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake. The last words of Jesus’ teaching before the passion, addressed past the four men on the hillside to everyone who would ever read this. The chapter that began with a question about dates ends with a command instead. Not calculate. Not be afraid. Stay awake: at your post, doing your work, in a house whose master is coming back.

What does spiritual sleep look like? It rarely looks like open rebellion. It looks like prayer slowly crowded out by busyness, Scripture read without expecting to meet God, sin tolerated because it has become familiar, and a heart more excited about the next holiday than about the return of Christ. It is the condition of the five foolish virgins, who were not wicked, only unprepared (Matthew 25:1–13). Its great symptom is that you do not notice it, because sleepers rarely know they are asleep. That is why the command is repeated so often, and why we need one another to say it: wake up.

I know I am spiritually drowsy. What do I actually do? First, admit it to God plainly, and do not wait to feel awake before you come to him. Then return to the simple means he has given: his word read daily and slowly, prayer at a set time, the Lord’s Day with his people, and the Supper. Cut out what dulls you, whether it is a habit of the screen, a hidden sin or a constant noise. Find a believer who will ask you honestly how you are doing. And remember Gethsemane: the remedy for sleepy disciples was not their resolve but his intercession. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for you.

For worship. And then he gets up off that hillside and walks down into the four watches of his own night, the evening, the midnight, the cockcrow and the morning, awake through every one of them, while everybody who loved him slept. He stayed awake through the darkest night in history, so that his sleeping, failing, forgiven disciples would be found ready when he comes. The master of the house never slumbers nor sleeps, and when he comes suddenly, he will come for those he has kept awake by his grace.
verseByVerse.note: These are the four Roman watches of the night, roughly from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

13.theology: The signs will work (v. 22). Jesus does not say the wonders of false christs will be faked; Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes to pass and who then leads you after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). A miracle does not prove that the one who does it comes from God, and the fact that something works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody. The test is always the doctrine underneath: does this lead to the Christ who came in the flesh, died and rose (1 John 4:2–3)?
13.examples:
Then: the four watches of the Roman night, evening, midnight, cockcrow and morning, named as the hours the master might come home. Mark writes all four into the next two chapters, in order, from the supper to the morning trial (14:17–15:1).

Now: the men who slept in the garden loved him, meant it, and could not manage an hour; the one who kept watch that night kept it for them.

14.title: The Cup, the Kiss, and the Fire
14.text: <sup>1</sup>It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, <sup>2</sup>for they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.” <sup>3</sup>And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. <sup>4</sup>There were some who said to themselves indignantly, “Why was the ointment wasted like that? <sup>5</sup>For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they scolded her. <sup>6</sup>But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>7</sup>For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. <sup>8</sup>She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. <sup>9</sup>And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” <sup>10</sup>Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. <sup>11</sup>And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>12</sup>And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>13</sup>And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him, <sup>14</sup>and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>15</sup>And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.” <sup>16</sup>And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>17</sup>And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. <sup>18</sup>And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.” <sup>19</sup>They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. <sup>21</sup>For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>22</sup>And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” <sup>23</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. <sup>25</sup>Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>27</sup>And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ <sup>28</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>29</sup>Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” <sup>30</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” <sup>31</sup>But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same. <sup>32</sup>And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” <sup>33</sup>And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. <sup>34</sup>And he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” <sup>35</sup>And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <sup>36</sup>And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” <sup>37</sup>And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? <sup>38</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>39</sup>And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. <sup>40</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. <sup>41</sup>And he came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>42</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>43</sup>And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <sup>44</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.” <sup>45</sup>And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>46</sup>And they laid hands on him and seized him. <sup>47</sup>But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>48</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? <sup>49</sup>Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” <sup>50</sup>And they all left him and fled. <sup>51</sup>And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, <sup>52</sup>but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. <sup>53</sup>And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. <sup>54</sup>And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. <sup>55</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. <sup>56</sup>For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. <sup>57</sup>And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, <sup>58</sup>“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’” <sup>59</sup>Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. <sup>60</sup>And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>61</sup>But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” <sup>62</sup>And Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” <sup>63</sup>And the high priest tore his garments and said, “What further witnesses do we need? <sup>64</sup>You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?” And they all condemned him as deserving death. <sup>65</sup>And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, “Prophesy!” And the guards received him with blows. <sup>66</sup>And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, <sup>67</sup>and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” <sup>68</sup>But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you mean.” And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. <sup>69</sup>And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, “This man is one of them.” <sup>70</sup>But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, “Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.” <sup>71</sup>But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” <sup>72</sup>And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
14.overview:
The longest chapter in Mark, and the clock runs in hours. Two days before Passover the chief priests decide to take Jesus quietly, not during the feast, and are overruled by their own accomplice, so that the Lamb dies at Passover after all.

A woman in Bethany breaks a flask of nard worth a year's wages over his head; the room calls it waste, and he calls it beautiful. Judas sells him for less than the perfume cost. In a borrowed upper room he gives the Passover bread and cup a new meaning: his body, and his blood of the covenant, poured out for many.

In Gethsemane he asks his Father to take away the cup of wrath, and then submits, while his friends sleep. He is betrayed with a kiss and deserted by all. Upstairs in the high priest's house he answers the direct question at last, I am, and is condemned for it. Downstairs, at a charcoal fire, Peter denies him three times, and a rooster crows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Anointing, Betrayal, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The plot and the perfume (vv. 1–11). The chief priests look for a way to take him quietly. Mark sets inside their plot a woman in Bethany who breaks a flask of nard over his head, and closes it with Judas going to the priests for money.

The upper room (vv. 12–21). Two disciples find the room just as he said, and at the table he tells the twelve that one of them will hand him over.

The Supper (vv. 22–26). He takes the Passover bread and cup and gives them as his body and his blood of the covenant. Then they sing, and go out into the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
He is not attending the Passover. He is the Passover. Every element of that meal pointed backwards to Egypt. Jesus turns it round. The bread is his body. The cup is my blood of the covenant, Moses's phrase at Sinai (behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you, Exodus 24:8), and the fulfilment of Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant with sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). There is a new exodus, and he is its lamb.

And poured out for many is Isaiah 53, the Servant who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many. Not a tragedy that overtook him, but a ransom deliberately paid for the people he came to save.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the room objects that the nard could have been sold for the poor. Jesus answers, you always have the poor with you, echoing Deuteronomy 15:11, which commands open-handedness. He is not excusing anyone from generosity. He is saying that this week will not come again.

Now: and for everyone who has felt they had nothing worth giving: she has done what she could. The measure is not the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, for they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. After its opening verses Mark 14 covers less than a day, from a plot to kill Jesus quietly to his leading disciple weeping in a courtyard before dawn. It is sin at its worst, in friends and rulers, and a Saviour who walks into it with open eyes, for those who fail him.

The setting. The passion narrative, the account of Jesus’ suffering and death, begins. Most of chapters 14–15 covers about a day, told in great detail; the early church told this story more than any other, and Mark’s account was probably shaped by years of preaching it.

Two days before the Passover. Mark starts the clock. From here to the end of the chapter, time is measured in hours. Passover (Hebrew Pesach) was the feast of deliverance, the night the angel of death passed over the houses marked with a lamb’s blood (Exodus 12). The lamb was sacrificed on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten that evening, the start of 15 Nisan by Jewish reckoning, and the week of Unleavened Bread followed (Exodus 12:15–20). Jesus will die as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

By stealth. They have wanted this since chapter 3 (3:6; 11:18; 12:12). What has changed is the question: no longer whether to kill him, but how. They need him away from the crowd, in the dark, with no witnesses.

Not during the feast. Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims, many from Galilee who supported Jesus; Passover, the feast of liberation, ran high with nationalist feeling, and the Roman governor brought extra troops to the city. A public arrest could start a riot. So the highest religious authority in Israel decided: not this week. And he died on the Friday of that very feast, because an opportunity arrived they had not counted on: one of his own disciples, offering to hand him over quietly, at night. The timetable of the crucifixion was set not by the council’s plan but against it. The plot to kill Jesus quietly became the most public act of love the world has ever seen, at exactly the moment God had appointed.

The date was not negotiable. The lamb had to die at Passover, as fixed since Exodus 12. Judas thinks he is arranging a transaction. The priests think they are managing a problem of public order. Pilate will think he is settling a provincial dispute. Every one of them is a free agent doing exactly what he wants, and every one of them is running to a schedule set before the world was made: this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23).

If God planned it, were the plotters really guilty? Yes, entirely. They did what they wanted to do, for their own reasons, and God did not put one evil desire into their hearts. What God did was rule over their evil, so that it accomplished the very thing they never intended: the salvation of the world. They meant to dispose of a troublemaker before the pilgrims noticed; God meant to offer his Lamb at the feast, in front of the whole nation. It is the story of Joseph’s brothers written large, whose evil God turned to the saving of many lives (Genesis 50:20). Scripture never explains how both are true together, but it never lets go of either. That is a comfort, not a puzzle, for anyone who has been wronged: the people who hurt you are answerable, and they are not in charge.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt; Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that followed it. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims.
