parallels.desc: the council resolves to kill him

verseByVerse.quote: And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly, "Why was the ointment wasted like that?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The structure. Another of Mark’s sandwiches: one story set inside another, so that each sheds light on the other. The plot of the leaders (vv. 1–2) and the betrayal by Judas (vv. 10–11) are the bread; the woman’s devotion is the filling.

Simon the leper. Bethany is the village over the ridge where he has been sleeping all week (11:11). The house belongs to Simon the leper, plainly not a leper any longer, since he is hosting a dinner; a leper lived outside the town and shouted unclean at anyone who came near (Leviticus 13:45–46). So presumably somebody healed him, the nickname stuck, and the man who used to warn strangers away has the Son of God at his table two days before the cross. John places this dinner six days before Passover, and Mark may have placed it here for its meaning rather than its date (John 12:1–8).

A woman came. Guests reclined on couches around a low table, so a woman could come up behind him. Mark does not name her. John tells us she was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus (John 12:3).

Pure nard. Alabaster flasks often had a long sealed neck that had to be snapped off. Nard was an oil from the root of a Himalayan plant, carried overland from India, and priced accordingly; pure (pistikēs) may mean unmixed, not thinned with cheaper oil. Verse 5 gives the cost: about a year of a working man’s income in a bottle. Perfume was a way of storing wealth, and for a woman with few property rights a sealed flask of nard might be everything she had against old age.

She broke the flask. Once the neck is snapped it cannot be resealed; there is no using half and keeping half. The breaking is a decision that all of it is going somewhere. And this is not a drop on the wrist but the whole flask, running down his hair and beard and onto the floor, until the house could smell nothing else. John mentions only his feet (John 12:3); she may well have anointed both.

A King anointed in a leper’s house. Messiah means anointed one, and in Israel kings were made with oil poured on the head (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). Jesus, the Christ, receives his royal anointing from a nameless woman, in the house of a man who once had to cry unclean, days before he is lifted up under a notice that names him King of the Jews (15:26). Nobody in the room says the word. The oil running down his hair says it for them: this is the Anointed One, and his throne is waiting at Golgotha.

There were some who said to themselves indignantly, Why was the ointment wasted like that? And the room turns on her. Matthew says the disciples said it (Matthew 26:8); John, that Judas led them (John 12:4–5). Wasted: that is their verdict. Something valuable has been destroyed and there is nothing to show for it. Love always looks like waste to those who only count the cost.

Was this the same woman as the sinful woman in Luke? Almost certainly not. Luke’s anointing happens in Galilee, much earlier, in the house of a Pharisee also named Simon, and the woman is known in the town as a sinner who weeps over Jesus’ feet (Luke 7:36–50). This one is in Bethany, in the last week, and John names her as Mary of Bethany. Simon was a common name, and anointing an honoured guest was a known custom. The two stories teach different things: Luke’s, the love of the forgiven; this one, the love that sees what is coming and gives everything before it is too late.

In everyday life. Ask what in your life is sealed in an alabaster flask: the thing you have kept back because it is too precious to spend on him, though he spent himself for you. Your time on a Sunday afternoon, a career plan, a sum of money, a child you have never really handed over, a reputation. If the word that rises when you think of giving it is waste, you have probably found the flask.

For worship. She broke the flask because he was about to be broken: he loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). She poured out a year’s wages; he poured out his soul to death. Nothing given to him is wasted, because he gave himself without measure, and there is no flask in any house on earth worth as much as the head she anointed.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three hundred denarii. This is a good objection. Three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages, and it would have fed a great many families in a city where the only safety net was almsgiving, and it was customary to give to the poor at Passover. Jesus himself had told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor (10:21).

And they scolded her. The word (enebrimōnto) is strong: they rebuked her harshly, with indignation. She has just done the most extravagant thing she will ever do, in a room full of men, and the room rounds on her. Mark records not one word from her.

Who started it. It was Judas, John tells us, who said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). So the objection about the poor came first from a man stealing from the fund for the poor, and the rest agreed because it was a reasonable thing to say. So a sound principle can be used as cover for a bad motive, and sincere people can end up repeating it.

The poor man at the table. Within two days Judas will have his silver and this woman will have nothing left: one person in this chapter turns Jesus into money, and one turns money into worship. And the man they are arguing over is himself the poorest person in the room, about to be stripped of his clothes and laid in a borrowed tomb. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The disciples want the perfume turned into alms. They do not see that the greatest gift ever made to the poor is reclining at the table, about to give away everything he has.

How do I balance generosity to the poor with gifts for worship? Not by choosing one. Jesus does not say the poor do not matter; in the next verse he reminds them of the command to open wide your hand. The same Lord who received the perfume told the rich man to sell everything for the poor. The real contrast in this passage is not between worship and charity but between love and calculation. A heart that has given everything to Christ will be generous to the poor, because he loves them. So give regularly to the needy, give gladly to the work of the gospel, and when someone else gives extravagantly to Christ, do not appoint yourself auditor of their gift.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave her alone. He protects her first, and only then explains what she has done. Why do you trouble her is tender. He has seen what the room is doing to a woman who cannot answer back.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. The word is kalos: good, fine, lovely, and it is the whole answer to waste. The disciples had only one measure, usefulness. Jesus brings in another, beauty, which a purely practical religion has no room for. Worship is like that: nobody is fed by it and nothing is produced, and God calls it lovely.

You always have the poor with you. This sentence has been misused for centuries as a shrug, but it is a quotation and the original settles it. He is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11: there will never cease to be poor in the land; therefore I command you, you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor. The permanence of poverty is the reason for open-handedness, not an excuse from it. And note his own clause, found only in Mark: whenever you want, you can do good for them. It assumes they will, and should.

But you will not always have me. This is not a general principle about extravagance against charity but a statement about a week that will not come again. The opportunity to do anything at all for the physical body of Jesus of Nazareth is closing, and this woman is the only person in Jerusalem who appears to have noticed.

She has done what she could. Only Mark has this. Not what a more capable person would have managed, but what she could: one thing, done once, with everything she had, and he called it beautiful. Two small coins from a widow outweighed the treasury (12:44); a flask from a woman with nothing else outweighed the criticism of the whole room.

She has anointed my body beforehand for burial. Now he tells them what she has done, more than she knew. Bodies were anointed with spices and perfumes for burial. Jesus would die as a criminal, there would be no time to anoint his body properly, and the women who came to do it on Sunday morning would find the tomb empty (16:1). This woman is the only person who managed it, and she managed it while he was still alive. Whatever she understood, Jesus gives her act its meaning. She came to honour him; he tells her she has prepared his body for the grave. The one anointed for burial in Bethany is the one who rose, and the fragrance of what he did has filled the whole world.

In memory of her. A remarkable prediction, two days before his death (see 13:10), and it has come true on every continent. The disciples criticised her; Jesus made her remembered, though Mark does not give her name. The one who noticed it and made sure it was written down is the same one who watched a widow put in two coins nobody heard. He receives what we bring, small and clumsy as it is, and calls it beautiful, and writes it down for ever.

Is it right to spend money on beautiful buildings, music and worship? It can be, within limits this passage itself sets. God cares about beauty; he commanded it for the tabernacle and he called this woman’s act beautiful. Worship offered with care, skill and cost honours him. But the gift was love poured on Christ himself, not display. Beauty that serves pride, or that is bought while the church neglects its poor, or that replaces the preaching of the gospel, has lost the point. The test is the one Jesus applies: is this done to me? A plain room where Christ is adored is more beautiful to him than a cathedral where he is ignored.

What if what I can do for Christ is very small? Then you are exactly the person this verse was written for. Perhaps you are ill, elderly, poor, housebound, caring for small children, or simply ordinary. He does not ask what a gifted or wealthy person could do; he asks what you can. A prayer offered faithfully every day, a meal taken to a neighbour, a note to a missionary, a hard conversation had in love: he sees it, and he calls it beautiful. No one will be asked on the last day why they did not do what someone else could. The only question is whether you gave him what was yours.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas Iscariot. The sandwich closes: a woman pours out a year’s wages on him, and a man goes out to sell him. Iscariot may mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea. He went to them; they did not come to him.

Who was one of the twelve. Mark says it here, and Jesus will say it at the table (v. 20), and Mark will say it again when the mob arrives (v. 43). Three times in one chapter. One of the twelve: appointed on the mountain (3:19), sent out two by two with authority over unclean spirits, present at every private explanation, a man who had shared his life for some three years.

They were glad. The word is chilling in its ordinariness: the problem they could not solve has walked through the door and offered to solve itself. An insider could tell them where to find Jesus at night, away from the crowds.

Money. Mark does not give the figure; Matthew does: thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). That is the compensation the Law fixed for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the wage thrown to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah with the LORD’s own dry comment, the lordly price at which I was priced by them (Zechariah 11:12–13). Set the two halves of this passage against each other and the arithmetic is unbearable. The perfume was three hundred denarii. Thirty pieces of silver was perhaps a hundred and twenty. A woman spent more on his head than the priests paid for his life. The silver bought a potter’s field for burying strangers; his blood bought a people from every nation.

An opportunity. Mark’s word is eukairōs: a convenient time. Judas goes back to the group and waits, and eats with them, and watches for a gap. He sat through the supper knowing. He heard one of you will betray me and, Matthew tells us, said is it I? with the rest (Matthew 26:25).

Why did he do it? The Gospels give several reasons, and it is worth resisting the urge to supply more. Greed: he was a thief (John 12:6) and asked what they would give him (Matthew 26:15). Satan: Satan entered into him (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Perhaps also disillusionment: Jesus was not the political Messiah he expected, and kept talking about dying, and the waste of a year’s wages may have been the last straw. What Mark gives us is not why Judas did it but how, and that is more useful. Betrayal waits for an opportune time, a convenient moment: privately, quietly, when nobody is watching and the cost of loyalty has suddenly become visible and a reasonable-looking alternative has appeared. That is how it always works. Almost nobody decides to abandon Christ. A moment simply arrives in which it is very much easier not to be associated with him, and there is a way out that can be explained to yourself, and it is taken. Judas found his gap in a garden after dark. Peter will find his beside a fire within hours. The difference between them is not the failure. It is that Peter wept and came back.

Handed over. The word for betray (paradidōmi) simply means to hand over, and Mark uses it like a relay. Judas hands Jesus over to the priests; the priests hand him over to Pilate (15:1); Pilate hands him over to be crucified (15:15). But the chain does not begin with Judas. Paul uses the same verb of the Father, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and of the Son, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Judas handed him over for silver. The Father handed him over for sinners, and the Son handed himself over in love. The darkest word in the chapter turns out to name the brightest thing God ever did.

Was Judas ever a true believer? No. Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), and Judas, though called and gifted, never belonged to Christ in the heart. Gifts, office and experience are not the same as faith. (See Matthew 26:14 for the fuller answer.)

Could I turn out to be a Judas, one of the twelve? Mark repeats that phrase to unsettle the comfortable, not to terrify the trembling. If you are asking with fear, that is already a good sign, because Judas never asked it with fear. The question to ask is not whether you have ever failed, since every disciple in that room failed that night, but whether you are still coming to Christ as your Saviour and treasure. Judas’s heart was set on money and he hid it. If you bring your sins into the light, grieve over them and run to Christ, you are on Peter’s road, not his. Examine yourself, as Scripture says (2 Corinthians 13:5), and then look away from yourself to the one who keeps all who come to him.

In everyday life. Ask where your opportune time is likely to come: the meeting where saying nothing would be easier, the deal where no one would know, the friendship where Christ is never mentioned. Decide now, in the light, what you will do then, and ask the Son who handed himself over for you to keep you. If you handle money for others, be scrupulously open about it: Judas began with the moneybag.

For worship. The Son of God was sold for the price of a slave so that slaves could be bought back for God. No traitor’s bargain could stop the plan of grace. It only fixed the price, and he paid it.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they sacrificed the Passover lamb. The Thursday, 14 Nisan. That afternoon in the temple the slaughter went on for hours: each household brought a lamb, the priests caught the blood in basins to be poured at the base of the altar, and the carcass was taken home to be roasted whole and eaten that night. And while that was happening, the Lamb of God was arranging where he would eat. He was not hunted into the cross; he went to it by appointment, keeping every promise of the old Passover and arranging every detail of the new.

The date of the Last Supper. Mark, Matthew and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the afternoon when the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (John 18:28; 19:14), which would make the supper a day earlier. Of the explanations offered, the likeliest is that John’s phrases refer to the whole week of the feast, with Preparation meaning the day before the Sabbath of Passover week, though the question is not fully settled. However it is resolved, both accounts present Jesus’ death as the fulfilment of Passover.

Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? A practical question and a real problem. The Passover had to be eaten inside the walls, and the city was heaving; every room was spoken for. Preparation involved buying and sacrificing the lamb, and preparing the unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and sauce.

A man carrying a jar of water. No address, no name, in a city of hundreds of thousands, and it works. Carrying water in a jar was usually women’s work; men more often carried water in skins. Either Jesus foreknew it, as with the colt (11:2), or he had arranged it secretly. Mark does not say which.

Why the secrecy? Judas has already been to the priests and is waiting for his opportunity. If the place of the meal had been announced in the morning, the arrest could have happened in the middle of it, and the Last Supper might never have taken place. So Jesus arranges a meeting place that even his own disciples cannot give away, because they do not know it. Two men are sent, and they cannot tell anybody where they are going until they get there. He is buying an evening. He has something to say and to give to those men that has to be done before the arrest, and he takes precise practical measures to make sure he gets the time. Nothing in this chapter happens to him by accident. He knows what Judas has done and what the priests want, and he plans around them, which is a very different thing from being caught.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, The Teacher says, Where is my guest room? The password again, as with the colt (11:3). The Teacher says, and apparently that is enough. So there is a man in Jerusalem who knows exactly who the Teacher is, has a room ready and asks no questions: another of the anonymous people in this Gospel whose property was requested and who did not say no. Perhaps he was a disciple. Note also the confidence of my guest room. Not a room; he speaks as a man with an arrangement. Guest room (katalyma) is the very word used for the inn in Bethlehem where there was no room (Luke 2:7). At his birth there was no room. At his last meal, a room is ready.

A large upper room. Large enough for thirteen men to recline, as free men did at Passover, unlike the first Passover eaten standing; furnished and ready with couches and cushions.

A room that may turn up again. Many think this was the house of Mark’s mother, Mary, where the church later met (Acts 12:12), and perhaps the upper room of Acts 1:13. This cannot be proved, but the church’s first address in Jerusalem was an upstairs room lent by somebody nobody bothered to name.

Just as he had told them. It is the pattern of the colt (11:4–6): what Jesus predicts keeps turning out exactly right. And in a few hours he will say one of you will betray me, you will all fall away, and before the rooster crows twice you will deny me three times, and those will turn out exactly right too.

They prepared the Passover. That meant work: taking a lamb to the temple, waiting in the queue, holding it while its throat was cut, carrying it back, roasting it whole, and setting out the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs, the sauce and the wine. Two disciples spent that afternoon preparing a lamb for the man who was about to become one.

Does Jesus still guide his people in such specific ways? He guides us as surely, but not usually in this way. These detailed instructions belonged to his unique hour, and to the apostolic age when new revelation was being given. Today he guides us through his finished word, which is sufficient for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17), through wisdom, counsel and the ordinary providence that arranges the details of our lives without announcing them. Christians differ over whether God still gives specific guidance by prophecy or inner impressions, and this commentary holds that such revelation ceased with the apostles, whose foundation was laid once (Ephesians 2:20); but those who expect it agree that nothing received that way may add to Scripture or overrule it. You should not expect a man with a water jar, or wait for a sign before obeying what Scripture already says. But you can be sure that the rooms of your life are prepared before you arrive in them.

For worship. The Lord who had nowhere to lay his head had a room ready on the night he was betrayed, because his Father provides for his Son and his Son provides for his friends. And he has gone ahead of us to prepare another: in my Father’s house are many rooms (John 14:2). We will find it just as he told us.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was evening. The Passover was eaten at night, after sunset (Exodus 12:8). And evening is the first of the four night watches he named in the parable on the Mount of Olives: evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and morning (13:35). This night will pass through them all.

One who is eating with me. The words do not narrow the field, since all twelve are eating with him. They are there for their weight. In that culture sharing a meal created a bond of loyalty; to eat a man’s bread and then harm him was the deepest treachery available. And the phrase is a quotation: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Psalm 41:9), a psalm Jesus quotes in John’s account of this evening (John 13:18).

They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, Is it I? This moment goes by in a line, and it teaches a great deal. Nobody looks at Judas. Eleven men have spent about three years with him, walked hundreds of miles with him, slept in the same fields. He held the money bag, which means they trusted him with it. And when the Lord says one of them is a traitor, not one of them turns his head. So Judas was not obviously a Judas. Nothing about him gave him away. And it tells you something about them too. The Greek expects the answer no, surely not I?, so it is not a confession but a fearful hope. Still, every one of them, hearing that a betrayer was in the room, looked first at himself. That instinct is the healthiest thing in the chapter, and the exact opposite of Peter’s boast ten verses later. To suspect yourself is not morbid; it is sanity, and Paul later told the overconfident at Corinth the same: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12). Jesus has seen every treachery, and no failure can surprise him, and he goes to the cross for people who say, is it I?, and mean it.

Dipping bread into the dish. They dipped bread and bitter herbs into a common bowl of sauce. He does not name him. Matthew and John record a further exchange that identified him to those close enough to hear; Mark leaves it as a description that fits everyone at the table. So Judas is given every chance, up to the last minute, to stop. He could have got up.

As it is written. Goes means goes to his death, as foretold in Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22. The cross is not the failure of the plan; it is the plan.

Woe to that man. Yet God’s plan does not excuse Judas by an inch. Woe is a cry of lament and of judgment together, and the betrayer is fully answerable.

Better if he had not been born. Few sentences Jesus spoke are more terrible, and it should not be softened. It means that non-existence would have been preferable to what Judas has coming, a plain statement that there is something worse than never having lived. That implies conscious, everlasting loss, not annihilation (simply ceasing to exist), and shows that Judas was not saved in the end (John 17:12). And it is said in his hearing, while he could still have moved: a last warning delivered to a man’s face, which is what makes it mercy as well as judgment.

Is it fair that Judas was lost if his betrayal was written beforehand? Yes. God foretold what Judas would do; he did not make Judas want it. Judas acted from his own greed and unbelief, after some three years of seeing Christ’s goodness and receiving his warnings. Nobody will be condemned for what God planned, but for what they themselves chose and loved. That God can rule over a sinner’s free choice to bring about salvation for others is a mystery beyond us, but it is not injustice. And notice how Jesus spoke of it: not with satisfaction, but with woe.

Should I live in fear that I might betray him? Live in humility, not in terror. The disciples’ question is a good one to ask yourself, because it keeps you from trusting your own strength. But the answer to it is not found by staring inward. It is found at the table, where Christ gives himself to sinners who know they are weak. The twelve all failed that night, and all but one were restored, because their hope was in him and not in themselves. Ask is it I?, and then take the bread.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover meal. The meal followed a set order, as later Jewish sources describe it. The head of the household explained the meaning of each element, retelling the story of the exodus: the lamb (God passed over our houses), the unleavened bread (we left Egypt in haste), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). Four cups of wine were drunk at fixed points, and every man at that table had heard the script all his life. Jesus now takes the bread and the cup at their appointed moments and says something else, about himself.

He took bread. Four verbs, and by now the reader of this Gospel knows them: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave. He did the same on a hillside with five loaves (6:41) and again with seven (8:6). What he did for the hungry crowds he now does for the twelve, and this time the bread is himself. Blessing means thanking God over it.

Take; this is my body. Not the bread of affliction from Egypt, but his own body, about to be given in death for them. And take: they must receive it. Whatever else the Supper is, it is Christ given, and given to be received: not looked at, not admired, not discussed. Taken.

He took a cup. Given thanks translates eucharistēsas, from which we get Eucharist, an old name for the Lord’s Supper. Probably the third cup of the Passover meal, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the meal (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). They all drank of it: all, including Judas it seems (Luke 22:21), though John may mean that he had already gone out (John 13:30); either way this is a sober warning that to take the bread and the cup is not the same as to have the Christ they point to.

This is my blood of the covenant. My blood of the covenant is Moses’ sentence at Sinai, when he threw the blood of the sacrifices over the people and said: behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exodus 24:8). A covenant is a binding bond that God makes with his people, with promises on his side and loyalty asked on theirs, ratified by sacrifice and blood. And it is new, as Luke and Paul both record (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25); the KJV has new testament in Mark as well, but the earliest manuscripts of Mark lack the word new, so most modern Bibles omit it here. That takes us to Jeremiah: a new covenant, in which God writes his law on hearts and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8–9). At Sinai the blood was thrown over the people from outside. Here it is put into a cup and handed round to be drunk. At Sinai the law stood outside the people, on stone; in the new covenant God changes the person inside, so that you begin to want what he commands and to love the one who gave it (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Poured out. The image is the blood of sacrifice poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7), a death poured out deliberately, for people. For many is Isaiah 53 again, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and his own word from 10:45, the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. His blood is shed in the place of many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28). This is the heart of the gospel: the substitutionary, atoning death of Christ. Substitutionary means in our place: he died the death our sins deserved, so that we do not have to. Atoning means that his death deals with sin and brings sinners back to God, at one with him again (Romans 5:10–11).

For many. Not a limitation grudgingly admitted but a promise gladly made. There is a great multitude no one can number whose sins were actually and effectively dealt with that Friday, not made able to be dealt with but dealt with, and if you are trusting him tonight, you are one of the many he had in mind while he was holding that cup. Many Christians read for many as a Hebrew way of saying all, the multitude set against the one (see Romans 5:15–19), and so as a death for every person, and they are brothers who love the same cross. The reading given here is the Reformed one: Christ’s blood was poured out for his people, and actually secured their forgiveness, because the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11, 15) and a ransom actually paid sets its captives free. But both readings agree that his death is sufficient for all, offered to all, and that no one who comes is turned away.

In the flow. These verses tell the reader what the rest of the chapter means. Jesus has explained his death before anyone lays a hand on him, so that the arrest, the trial and the cross read as the ransom promised in 10:45, paid on purpose.

Where Christians differ: the Lord’s Supper. Four main views. Roman Catholic teaching holds transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine becomes the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance remains, and the Mass is a sacrifice. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Zwingli taught that the Supper is chiefly a memorial, reading the words this is my body as this represents my body. Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that Christ is truly and spiritually present, and that believers, by faith and through the Holy Spirit, truly feed on Christ, though his body is in heaven. This commentary’s view: Calvin’s view is the best reading. When Jesus said this is my body, his body was sitting at the table, and the disciples would not have thought they were eating his flesh; he speaks as he did in I am the door. But the Supper is more than a reminder. It is a real communion with Christ by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 10:16), in which believers are nourished by him. And it is not a repeated sacrifice; Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

What all Christians agree on. Do not let the argument cost you the thing itself. Nearly every tradition agrees that this meal is commanded, central, more than a bare memory exercise, and that Christ is truly given to faith in it. The first point of Jesus’ sentence is not to explain how he is present. It is that he gave it to them and told them to take it.

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? More than thinking about him, and less than chewing his flesh: as you eat the bread trusting his promise, the Holy Spirit unites you to the risen Christ, so that you truly receive him and his benefits. (See Luke 22:19 for the fuller answer.)

Who should come to the Lord’s Supper? Those who belong to Christ and have publicly confessed him. In the New Testament the Supper is for the church, those who have repented, believed and been baptised (Acts 2:41–42). Each one is to examine himself and so eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), not to prove he is worthy, but to come as a sinner trusting Christ and at peace with his brothers. This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for believers and comes before the table, because in the New Testament those baptised are those who have heard, repented and believed; paedobaptist brothers who baptise their children also generally require a credible profession of faith before admitting them to the Supper. Those who do not yet trust Christ should not take it, but should take him, and then come.

What if I feel unworthy to take it? Then you understand what the table is for. It was given on the night of betrayal to men who would all run away within hours. Nobody comes because he is worthy; the Supper is medicine for the sick, not a reward for the healthy. Paul’s warning about eating in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27) is about coming carelessly, despising the body of Christ or one’s brothers, not about coming while feeling weak. If you are holding on to a known sin with no intention of leaving it, or refusing to be reconciled to someone, deal with that first. Otherwise, come. The bread is for the hungry.

In everyday life. Before the next Lord’s Supper, prepare during the week: confess the sins you know, put right anything between you and another believer, and ask the Spirit to feed you. At the table, do not only remember; receive. Hold the bread and say in your heart: this is for me.

For worship. On the night he was betrayed, with Gethsemane an hour away, he took into his hands the sign of his own broken body and thanked God for it. He handed men who would run within the hour a covenant sealed in his blood, with their forgiveness written into its terms. The Lamb of the Passover became the host of the feast and its food, and he still comes by his Spirit to his people at his table, and gives them himself, until he comes.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit of the vine. The last thing he says at the table is not about his death but about a party. I will not drink again: this is the last meal on this side of the cross, and he is truly giving something up. Some think he did not drink the fourth Passover cup, the cup of completion, and would finish it only in the kingdom.

Until that day. On the last night of his life he looks past the arrest, the nails and the grave, and speaks with complete confidence about a future meal at which he will be present. There is no if in the sentence. The prophets had promised it: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, and he will swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:6–8; see Matthew 8:11). Revelation names it: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). So every time the church takes this cup it is doing two things at once: looking back to a death and forward to a dinner. He said he would be there.

When they had sung a hymn. By the custom later recorded in the Mishnah, the Passover meal ended with the second half of the Hallel, the psalms of praise, Psalms 115 to 118. If so, the last thing Jesus of Nazareth sang before Gethsemane included these lines. The snares of death encompassed me; then I called on the name of the LORD (Psalm 116:3–4). I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD (Psalm 116:13), sung an hour after he had lifted the cup of the covenant. And the last line of the last psalm, very probably the final words he sang before he walked out into the dark: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever (Psalm 118:29). In a voice that would be praying in agony within the hour, he sang that God is good and his love does not stop.

They went out to the Mount of Olives. Across the Kidron valley, east of the city, to Gethsemane. Luke says this was his custom (Luke 22:39), so Judas knew where to find him. He did not change his habits to avoid arrest.

Will there really be eating and drinking in the kingdom? Scripture speaks of it plainly and often, and we should not thin it out into mere symbol. The risen Jesus ate fish in front of his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), and the resurrection body is a real body. The new creation will be a world, not a cloud, and the feast is a picture of what it will be: fellowship, joy, abundance, and the presence of the King at the head of the table. Exactly what we will eat we do not know. That we will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and with Christ himself, we do.

How can I sing when my heart is breaking? By singing what he sang. The psalms were not written by people whose lives were going well. They hold grief and praise together, as he did on the way to Gethsemane, and they give you words when you have none. You need not feel cheerful to sing that God is good and his love endures; you need only believe it, and sometimes singing it is how you come to believe it again. Paul and Silas sang in prison with their backs bleeding (Acts 16:25). Your song may be quiet and full of tears. It is still a song he has sung before you.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning (vv. 27–31). On the walk out he tells them they will all fall away, and in the same breath tells them where to meet him afterwards. Peter insists he will not, and the rest say the same.

The garden (vv. 32–42). He takes three men further in, tells them his soul is sorrowful even to death, falls on the ground and asks his Father to take the cup away, and then submits. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.

The arrest (vv. 43–52). Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies him with a kiss. A sword is drawn, and then everybody runs, including a young man who escapes leaving his linen cloth behind.
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and it is not the general dread of dying.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image for the wrath of God: all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8). That is what is set in front of him, and it is why a man who slept through a storm is on the ground shaking.

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). There is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him, and that is why a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ faced it in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27), and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28). The order is the gospel: he announces the restoration before the failure has happened, on no condition, to eleven men who are about to abandon him.

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7). If you have failed him badly and wonder whether there is a road back, the road was mapped and announced before you took the wrong turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will all fall away. Not some: all of them, and he says it on the road with them in the dark. The verb (skandalisthēsesthe) means to be tripped up, to stumble over something. It is the word used of the seed on rocky ground that falls away when the heat comes (4:17), and of the offence Nazareth took at him (6:3).

I will strike the shepherd. He quotes Zechariah 13:7, and the striking thing is who does the striking. In Zechariah God says: awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me; strike the shepherd. Jesus gives it as God’s own words: I will strike the shepherd. So the hand behind tomorrow is not finally Judas’s, or Caiaphas’s, or Pilate’s, but the settled purpose of the Father: it was the will of the LORD to crush him (Isaiah 53:10). The Father strikes the Son, in judgment for the sins of his people. This is penal substitution in the words of the prophet. The penalty is the punishment God’s law demands for sin; the substitution is that someone else bears it. Christ took the penalty his people owed, so that God’s justice is satisfied and they go free (Isaiah 53:5). And the shepherd is the man who stands next to God: no ordinary man is struck here. He was struck so that we would be spared, scattered so that we would be gathered, forsaken so that we would be found.

After I am raised up. The whole force of the sentence is in where it stands: before the failure, not after it. Peter has not yet boasted; nobody has run. Having just told eleven men that every one of them will abandon him within hours, he tells them where he will meet them afterwards. There is no condition attached. He does not say if you repent, or if you prove yourselves.

Go before you. A shepherd’s word: to walk ahead of the flock so they can follow (John 10:4). The scattered sheep will be gathered. And Galilee, of all places: not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong, but home, where they were called off their boats. The promise is repeated by an angel in an empty tomb on Sunday morning (16:7).

If the Father struck the Son, was God angry with Jesus? The Father never stopped loving his Son; Jesus was never more pleasing to him than when he obeyed to the death (John 10:17). But on the cross the Son stood in the place of sinners and bore the wrath their sins deserved. God was not angry with Jesus for anything Jesus had done. He poured out on him the judgment due to us, and Jesus willingly drank it. That is what Scripture means when it says the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6) and made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a Father punishing an unwilling victim. It is the Father and the Son together, in one love, saving the guilty.

In everyday life. Christ knows your failures before you commit them, and he has already planned your restoration. If you have failed him badly enough to wonder whether there is any road back, notice the order: the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it. Go to him today, where he said he would be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even though they all. It is just like Peter: meant well, and wrong. In four words he has accepted the prophecy for the other ten and made himself the exception, in front of them. That is not merely presumption about himself; it is a low estimate of his brothers said aloud in their hearing. The man who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anybody.

Before the rooster crows twice. Jesus does not rebuke him. He gives him the details, more exactly than in any other Gospel: this very night, twice, three times. That exactness fits the early tradition that this Gospel carries Peter’s preaching: this is the sentence that broke him, as he himself remembered it.

Why does only Mark say twice? Matthew, Luke and John say before the rooster crows; only Mark says twice. The others give the general warning, before the cockcrow at dawn; Mark, from Peter’s own memory, gives the precise form, with a first crowing that Peter ignored and a second that broke him. There is no contradiction; one account is simply more detailed. A few early manuscripts lack twice here and the first crowing at verse 68, probably because copyists brought Mark into line with the other Gospels; most modern Bibles keep them.

Emphatically. Over and over. And he means it, which is what makes this passage useful rather than merely a story about a boastful man. Peter was not lying. He loved him. In a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd (v. 47; John 18:10), which is more than the other ten manage. He was not a coward. But courage in a fight is different from courage alone in a courtyard. He simply did not know himself.

They all said the same. Mark will not let Peter carry it alone. Every one of them said it, and every one of them ran (v. 50).

The danger of untested confidence. The danger is confidence in a strength that has never been tested: the quiet assumption that you would hold, that you would speak up, that you would not do what those people did. And Jesus does not say, then you were never mine, or withdraw the promise of Galilee. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, then takes him into the garden anyway, dies for him on the Friday, and has him named by an angel on the Sunday. The boast was hollow. The love behind it was not, and Christ knew the difference.

Die with you, or die for you. Peter offers to die with Jesus, and the offer is upside down. Before the weekend is over it will be plain that Peter cannot die with him, and that Jesus must die for Peter. The one who is faithful to the death in this chapter is not the disciple but the Master, who goes to the cross alone for the man who swore he would go too. And then grace turns it round once more. Restored and filled with the Spirit, Peter did at last glorify God by his death, as the risen Lord told him he would (John 21:18–19). He kept his promise in the end, because Christ had first kept his.

Is it wrong to promise loyalty to Christ? No. Christians rightly make promises: at baptism, in membership, in marriage, in hymns that say I will follow thee. What went wrong with Peter was not the promise but the ground of it. He put his confidence in his own heart, contradicted his Lord, and compared himself favourably with his brothers. Promise, then, but promise leaning on Christ: by your grace, I will. Pray that he will keep you. And when you hear a warning in Scripture, do not argue with it as Peter did; let it send you to your knees.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gethsemane. The name means oil press: an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, where olives were crushed for their oil. Here, Jesus will be pressed. Sit here while I pray, he tells eight of them, and as at the beginning of his ministry (1:35) and at every turning point (6:46), he prays.

Peter and James and John. The same three who were taken into Jairus’s house to see a dead girl raised (5:37), and up the mountain to see him transfigured (9:2). They have seen him at his most glorious; now they see him at his lowest. James and John had said they could drink his cup (10:39); Peter had said he would die with him (v. 31). Now they will see what that cup is.

Greatly distressed and troubled. Mark reaches for two of the strongest words available. Greatly distressed (ekthambeisthai): overwhelmed with horror, shuddering. Troubled (adēmonein): in anguish, the sort of distress that has no bottom to it. And he began: this is not a settled sorrow he has carried all week. It falls on him in that garden.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, turns to three friends and says how bad it is. The phrase echoes the Psalms, where the sufferer says why are you cast down, O my soul? (Psalms 42:5, 11; 43:5), and the word Mark uses is the one the Greek Old Testament uses there. Even to death means a sorrow of a weight that could kill a man. Luke the physician records what it did to his body: his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke 22:44). Those verses (Luke 22:43–44) are missing from some early manuscripts, and Luke says like drops of blood, not that he bled.

Why such anguish? Many martyrs have faced death calmly, even joyfully. Was Jesus less brave than them? No. Jesus faced something no martyr has faced: the cup of God’s wrath against sin (v. 36), separation from the Father (15:34), being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). It was not death itself but what death meant for him: bearing the judgment of God in the place of sinners. The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love from eternity, was about to bear his wrath. This is the measure of what our sin deserved, and of his love. God’s wrath has nothing of human spite in it. It is perfect holiness set against every evil, and the purer the one who sees it coming, the more terrible it looks. Jesus, who alone was without sin, saw it more clearly than anyone ever has.

How can the Son of God be so distressed? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so. But his will was never set against the Father’s; he asked, and then submitted: not what I will, but what you will (v. 36). This is not a crack in the Trinity. It is the obedience of the Son, learned with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7–8).

Remain here and watch. The word from the parable, grēgoreite, stay awake (13:35, 37). He is not asking them to fix anything. He is asking them to stay awake near him. He wants their company, and their prayer.

Is it sinful for a Christian to be overwhelmed with sorrow? No. Jesus was sinless, and he was overwhelmed. Grief, dread and anguish are not in themselves failures of faith; they are what a true human heart feels in a fallen world. The Psalms are full of them, and so was Gethsemane. What matters is where you take them. Jesus took his to his friends and to his Father. So do not pretend to a calm you do not have, and do not let anyone tell you that a Christian should never be cast down. Tell God the truth about your state, and tell a friend.

How can I keep watch with someone who is suffering? Stay. Most of the time you will not be able to explain the suffering or end it, and you are not asked to. Be present, be quiet more than you speak, pray with them and for them, and keep coming back. Do not hurry them to feel better or quote verses at them as a way of closing the conversation. Jesus asked for exactly this, and his friends could not give it to him. You can give it to his people, and in doing so you give it to him (Matthew 25:40).

For worship. The olive press closed on the Son of God, and he let it. He went down into the anguish our sin deserved, all of it, and came out the other side still saying Father. Our high priest can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because on that night he was weaker than any of us, and loved us through it.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fell on the ground. Not knelt: fell, and Jews normally prayed standing (11:25). The man who slept through a storm and faced down a legion is on the ground in the dirt among the olive roots, prostrate in anguish and submission.

That the hour might pass. The hour is the appointed time of his suffering and death (v. 41; John 12:27). And note the if: if it were possible. He is not demanding. He is asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

Abba, Father. Mark keeps the Aramaic, the actual sound of Jesus praying. Abba is the ordinary family word a child used for his father in the home. It is not Daddy, since grown men used it of their fathers all their lives, but it is unmistakably intimate and domestic. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. Jesus did, because he was the Son. And in the deepest agony of his life, that is the word he reaches for.

The name he handed over. It did not stay his alone. Twice the New Testament says that the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he gave away. We pray as sons and daughters because of the Son, and because he was willing on this night to be treated as though he were not.

All things are possible for you. Before he asks, he says what he believes about God, as he had taught (10:27). He states that God is able, and then asks, which is the right order, and the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

Remove this cup from me. Everything depends on what the cup is, and it is not simply death. It is a fixed Old Testament image for the wrath of God (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). That is what is standing in front of him in the dark: not the nails, but the undiluted anger of God against every sin of everyone he came to save, and he is to drink it to the dregs. It is a true request, from a true human will, shrinking from the horror of what lay ahead: if there were any other way to save sinners, let it be found. He drained the wrath of God to the last drop, and handed us instead the cup of blessing.

Yet not what I will, but what you will. He does not withdraw the request. He asks honestly for the thing he wants, and then submits, and both are prayer. The asking is not unbelief and the submitting is not resignation. This is the obedience that undid Adam’s disobedience (Romans 5:19), and it is counted to every disciple whose own obedience still falters. In the garden of Eden a man was told what the Father’s will was and said, in effect, my will, and the world broke. In this garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended. And this is the model for all Christian prayer: honest about our desires, and submitted to God’s will (Matthew 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that there was conflict or sin in Jesus, or that his will was against the Father’s. His human will naturally shrank from suffering, as it should; to desire suffering for its own sake would be unhealthy. But he willingly submitted it. The early church taught from this passage that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in perfect harmony. Behind the technical language lies something tender: Jesus is one person, truly God and truly man, and a true man has a human will: real desires, and a real recoil from pain and horror. As man he wanted the cup to pass; as the obedient Son he wanted his Father’s will more, and chose it (Hebrews 5:8).

Was there really no other way? Gethsemane is the answer. The Son asked the Father, who can do all things, whether the cup could pass, and the answer was no. If sinners could have been saved by teaching, by example, or by God simply overlooking sin, the Father would not have handed his beloved Son that cup. Sin is so serious, and God so just, that nothing but the death of a perfect substitute could pay for it (Hebrews 9:22; Romans 3:25–26). That should silence every suggestion that there are many roads to God. If there had been another road, the Father would have opened it in that garden.

If the plan was already fixed, why did Jesus ask at all? Because prayer is not a way of informing God or bending his mind; it is a child speaking honestly to his Father. Jesus knew the Son of Man must suffer (8:31), and still he told his Father what his human heart desired, and then laid it down. God’s plan does not make prayer pointless. It is what makes prayer safe: we can pour out our real wishes to a Father who will never give us anything less wise than his will. And God has appointed prayer as one of the very means by which he carries out his purposes (James 5:16).

Is it a lack of faith to pray if it is your will? Not when it means what it meant on Jesus’ lips. Some teach that adding if it be your will undermines faith. But the Son of God prayed it, at the moment of greatest need, and he did not lack faith. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess, pray with confidence. Where he has not told you his will, such as whether a sick friend will recover, ask boldly for what you want, and then entrust it to him. That is not a hedge against disappointment. It is the trust of a child who knows the Father is wiser than he is.

In everyday life. Take the hardest thing you are praying about this week and pray it in two halves, aloud if you can: first the plain request, with nothing held back, then the handing over. And when the answer is no, remember that the cup did not pass from him, and he drank it, and that is why there is nothing left in it for you.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found them sleeping. Two days before, on this hillside, he told them of a master who might come suddenly and find you asleep (13:36). He came. They were asleep.

And he said to Peter, Simon, are you asleep? It is the only time in Mark that Jesus is recorded calling him by name, and he uses the old name. Simon: not Peter, the rock, but the name he had when he was pulling nets out of the lake, before any of this. It is gently said, and it must have cut deep. The man who earlier that night said even though they all fall away, I will not, cannot stay awake.

Could you not watch one hour? One hour. Not the night; an hour. It is the smallest possible request, made by a man dying of grief thirty yards away, and it was too much. A gentle reproach, more sad than angry. And before it is used against them, be honest about the circumstances. It was late, they had eaten a heavy festal meal with its cups of wine, they had walked, and Luke kindly records that they were sleeping for sorrow (Luke 22:45). Grief exhausts people. They were not indifferent; they were shattered. That does not remove the failure, but it does explain it, and Jesus explains it too.

Watch and pray. Temptation (peirasmon) is a test, a trial, the testing that could make them fall, and it is coming within the hour. He is not scolding them; he is telling them that this hour is the preparation for a test, and their only defence is watchful prayer. They slept through the preparation, and failed the test.

Where the battle is decided. The battle is lost or won before the moment of temptation arrives. The man who has not prayed does not fall in the moment; he fell in the hours before it, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Peter’s denial in the courtyard was decided here in Gethsemane, while he slept.

The spirit indeed is willing. Having named their failure, he explains it, with a sympathy that is almost unbearable. Spirit here means the human spirit, the inner person with its good intentions; flesh means human nature in its frailty, not wickedness but weakness. Their intentions were real. But the flesh is weak. He is not saying they are hypocrites. He is saying they are men (see Romans 7:18–25). And the one diagnosing it has just been on the ground under a weight none of them can imagine. He has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than we have ever been, and he stayed awake for us.

Why does prayer help against temptation? Because temptation is a lie that looks true in the moment, and prayer puts you in the presence of the truth before the moment comes. In prayer you confess your weakness, so you stop trusting your own strength. You ask for help, and God has promised to give it (1 Corinthians 10:13). You set your mind on Christ, so that other loves look smaller. And you are reminded that you are not alone. That is why Jesus said watch and pray, not merely try harder. Willpower is the spirit being willing. Prayer is how weak flesh is held up.

In everyday life. Think of the hour of the day when you are most likely to fall, late at night, after a bad meeting, alone with a screen, and pray before it arrives, not during it. Name the temptation to God in the morning. And if you have failed again, hear him call you by your old name, gently, and then hear him say the spirit is willing. He has not given up on you.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same words. Some treat repetition as a failure of faith. Jesus prayed the same words again that night, and Matthew says a third time (Matthew 26:44). Matthew records the second prayer, and its wording has moved on: my Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done (Matthew 26:42). He now speaks of drinking the cup: the submission deepens.

Not vain repetition. Jesus warned against heaping up empty phrases (Matthew 6:7), mechanical repetition to wear God down. This is different: the same cry from the same heart, because the need has not changed. Paul did the same about his thorn: three times I pleaded with the Lord about this (2 Corinthians 12:8). And when there are no words left, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). So if all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you are not praying badly. You are praying in Gethsemane.

They did not know what to answer. A sad clause, very possibly Peter’s own memory: their eyes were heavy, they had failed twice, and there was nothing to say. Mark has recorded this before. At the transfiguration Peter blurted out a suggestion about tents, for he did not know what to say (9:6). The same three men, on the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, both times with nothing to say.

Honest reporting. A community inventing a founding story would hardly write down that its leaders slept through the crisis and had no answer when they were caught. The only one in that grove who did not fail was the one on his face, praying.

What if God says no to my prayer? Then you are in good company. The Father said no to his own beloved Son in this garden, and it was not because he loved him less, but because the no was the way to the greatest yes in history: the salvation of the world and the Son’s exaltation. God’s no to a believer is never indifference. It is the refusal of a Father who sees what you cannot, and who has promised that all things work together for good to those who love him (Romans 8:28). Keep praying, as Jesus did, until your will is shaped to his, and trust him with what you do not understand.

For worship. Three times he prayed in the dark, and three times his friends failed him, and he never once failed them. The prayer did not end among the olive trees. The one who knelt there now lives for ever at the Father’s right hand, pleading for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While we sleep he watches; when we do not know what to answer, he answers for us. The Son who prayed your will be done in Gethsemane now asks for what the Father has already willed: that not one of his people will be lost.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came the third time and said to them, Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? Three times he prayed; three times he came back; three times they were asleep. And within hours Peter will deny him three times. Mark’s numbers are not accidental. The sentence can be read as a question or as a resigned statement, sleep on now and take your rest, and the Greek allows either. Either way the tone has changed. He is no longer asking them for anything.

Settled in prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out of it settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness in it. He rose from his knees and went, with his face set like flint.

It is enough; the hour has come. It is enough (apechei) is hard to translate: it may mean it is settled, or even the account is paid, for it was used on receipts. The hour he prayed might pass (v. 35) has not passed. It has arrived, and he announces it.

Into the hands of sinners. He has said this before (8:31; 9:31; 10:33). Now it is no longer will be. It is happening. And sinners: the leaders, who considered themselves righteous and the Gentiles sinners, are themselves the sinners into whose hands he is given.

Rise, let us be going. It sounds for half a second like an escape. It is the opposite. Torches are probably already coming up the path from the Kidron valley (John 18:3), and he is walking towards them. Nobody takes him. He goes as the good shepherd goes, laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). And notice the pronoun: my betrayer. Not the betrayer. He does not disown him even now; the man is still, in some terrible sense, his.

How did Jesus go from anguish to such calm? Through prayer, and through submission. He did not talk himself into courage or stop feeling the weight. He laid the whole matter before the Father three times, until his human will rested in the Father’s will. The cup was no smaller, but he had accepted it. That is the peace Paul describes: by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God will guard your hearts (Philippians 4:6–7). It is not the peace of having your way. It is the peace of having given it up to someone you trust.

In everyday life. If there is something you have been dreading, the appointment, the confession, the conversation, the operation, take it to God until you can say rise, let us be going, and then go and meet it. You will not go alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas came. Mark says it again: one of the twelve, the third time in the chapter.

Swords and clubs. An armed party sent by the Sanhedrin: the temple police probably, with servants, and John adds a detachment of Roman soldiers and their commander with lanterns and torches (John 18:3, 12). All this for one unarmed teacher and eleven tired men.

A sign. The men sent to arrest him could not reliably pick him out, at night, by torchlight, among a dozen Galileans dressed alike. Nothing distinguished the Son of God from the fishermen standing next to him.

Under guard. Perhaps Judas remembers that Jesus had passed through hostile crowds before (Luke 4:30). Judas is taking no chances.

Rabbi! And he kissed him. The kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher: respect, affection, belonging. Mark’s verb (katephilēsen) may mean he kissed him warmly. So the sign chosen to identify him for execution was the sign of love, and it was not done by halves. The Bible knows this wickedness: Joab took Amasa by the beard to kiss him and killed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). And Rabbi, not Lord, is the last word Judas speaks in this Gospel. Matthew records the answer: friend, do what you came to do (Matthew 26:50). Luke records another: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48). He did not turn his face away. He received the kiss.

They laid hands on him. Here the Gospel turns: from now until the resurrection, everything is done to him. The one who could not be bound by a legion of demons, or a storm, or a fever, or death itself, lets a temple guard put its hands on him in the dark and take him away.

How can someone so close to Jesus betray him? Because closeness of position is not the same as love. Judas had the same sermons, the same miracles, the same meals as Peter. What he did not have was a heart that treasured Christ above everything else, and years of nearness without love hardened him rather than softened him. That is the danger of familiarity with holy things. The cure is not to stay away from Christ, but to keep asking whether you love him, and to be honest when you find something else on the throne. If your love feels cold, that is a reason to come nearer to him, not to despair: he receives the weak and warms them.

In everyday life. Ask whether any outward sign of devotion in your life, the songs, the words, the church, has become a kiss without a heart.

For worship. The Lord of glory offered his cheek to the traitor, and then held out his hands to be bound. He did not need to be identified; he was going to give himself up. He was handed over by a kiss so that we could be welcomed with one, like the son who came home and was embraced by his father before he could finish his confession.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of those who stood by. Mark does not name him. John, writing much later, says it was Peter, and that the servant’s name was Malchus (John 18:10); perhaps Mark, writing while Peter was alive or, as tradition holds, recently martyred, protected him. And be fair to Peter. Eleven men are about to run, and one of them draws a weapon against an armed party sent by the Sanhedrin. He was keeping his promise (v. 31), and whatever else he got wrong tonight, he got it wrong bravely.

The wrong kind of loyalty. He also got it entirely wrong. Taking only an ear suggests a wild swing in the dark, at a servant, not even a soldier. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). And Luke the physician records the last healing miracle of Jesus’ ministry before the cross: he touched the ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). The last thing he did with his hands free was to repair the damage his own disciple had done to a man who came to arrest him, a healing done for an enemy.

Does this forbid Christians to use force? Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke, all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52), and John his reason, my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). Jesus forbids the sword to defend his kingdom or to stop the cross. He does not abolish the state’s sword (Romans 13:4), nor the defence of life (Exodus 22:2). Christians may protect themselves and others; they may never advance Christ’s cause by force.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? He addresses the arresting party, and the question is a rebuke about their method. Robber (lēstēs) is not a pickpocket but a bandit, an armed insurrectionist. It is the word Josephus uses for the armed rebels against Rome, the word John uses of Barabbas (John 18:40), and the word Mark uses of the two men crucified beside him (15:27). So: you have turned out in force, at night, armed, as though I were a terrorist.

Day after day. He has been standing in their own building, in public, all week, and they did not arrest him because of the crowd (12:12; 14:2). So the whole apparatus of swords and torches and a midnight raid is not a security precaution. It is a confession: men who take a prisoner in the dark know their case would not stand in daylight.

Let the Scriptures be fulfilled. And with that he stops arguing and submits, perhaps thinking of Isaiah 53:12, he was numbered with the transgressors, and Zechariah 13:7, the struck shepherd (v. 27).

They all left him. Mark does not soften it by a syllable. All: the eleven who had said an hour ago that they would die with him; the three who could not stay awake; Peter, who had just drawn a sword. Left him: it is the same verb Mark used in chapter 1 when they left their nets and followed him (1:18). They left everything to follow him; now they leave him. The Shepherd is struck, and the sheep are scattered (v. 27). From here he is alone. The Shepherd stood alone in the torchlight so that the sheep could run, and then he went to gather them again. There is no loneliness like his that night, and because of it, no believer will ever be truly alone.

How should I defend Christ when he is attacked? With truth, love and courage, never with the world’s weapons. Peter’s sword is the model of what not to do: anger, force, a wild swing in the dark. The modern versions are online abuse, mockery of opponents, manipulation, and political power used to coerce faith. The apostles learned the right way after Pentecost: they spoke boldly, suffered patiently, and blessed those who cursed them (Acts 4:29; 1 Peter 3:15–16). Christ does not need protecting. He needs witnesses.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only Mark records this. A strange, brief episode: a person nobody has heard of loses his clothes and runs. Who was he, and why is it here?

A young man followed him. Many have suggested he was Mark himself, which would explain why the story is included at all. It may be the signature of an eyewitness, like an artist painting himself into the corner of a picture. If the supper was eaten in the house of Mark’s mother in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12), a young man in that household might well have heard where they had gone, got up in the night with a sheet round him, and followed at a distance. It cannot be proved. He had nothing but a linen cloth about his body: linen was expensive, suggesting a family of some wealth, and he had perhaps been asleep and thrown on a sheet.

He ran away naked.
