They all left him and fled (v. 50), and now the desertion is given a face, one person caught in the torchlight who would rather lose everything he was wearing than be taken with Jesus. He did not decide to run; he bolted. Amos spoke of the day of judgment: he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day (Amos 2:16).

The contrast. The disciples had left everything to follow Jesus (10:28). Now this young man leaves everything to escape him. And watch the linen. In the next chapter Joseph of Arimathea bought a linen shroud, took the body down and wrapped him in it (15:46), and Mark uses the same word, sindōn, for both. The young man leaves his linen behind to save himself; within a day his Lord lies wrapped in linen, the one who saved others and would not save himself (15:31). And the word for young man, neaniskos, occurs only once more in Mark: they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe (16:5). So Mark has framed the story of Jesus’ suffering with two young men: one who fled from Christ stripped and ashamed, and one seated in an empty tomb, clothed in white, announcing that he has risen. That is the gospel in two pictures, and if the young man is Mark himself, the man who wrote it put himself in the first one.

Why would Mark tell such an embarrassing story about himself? We cannot be sure the young man was Mark, but if he was, the reason is plain. It is the same reason Peter told the story of his denial: because the gospel is not about how faithful we were, but about how faithful Christ is. A Gospel writer who painted himself as a hero would be pointing at himself. One who shows himself running away naked is pointing away from himself, to the one who did not run. It also tells every reader who has fled from Christ in shame that the story does not end there. Mark, who once deserted Paul as well (Acts 15:37–38), later became useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11), and wrote this Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council (vv. 53–65). The Sanhedrin meets at night in the high priest's house, looking for evidence to justify a verdict already reached, and finds none that holds. Jesus says nothing until the high priest puts the direct question, and then answers it plainly for the first time in this Gospel: I am. He is condemned, and they begin to spit on him.

The courtyard (vv. 66–72). In the same building, a servant girl looks at Peter across a fire, and three challenges bring three denials, the last with oaths and a curse. Then the rooster crows, he remembers, and he breaks down. Upstairs, Christ confesses and is condemned; downstairs, Peter denies and is safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
A court with its verdict already made. Mark's own sentence is enough: the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death (v. 55). A court seeks the truth and then decides the penalty; this one had the penalty and went looking for grounds.

I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Under oath and with nothing left to protect, he answers plainly, and adds seated at the right hand of Power (Psalm 110:1) and coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13). The man in the dock tells the court that he will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the blindfolded prisoner is struck and told, Prophesy! (v. 65). He had prophesied that very night: betrayal, desertion, and Peter's three denials.

Now: while they were demanding a prophecy, the last of those predictions was coming true below them, in the courtyard. Every word Jesus spoke about his friends' failure came true, and so did every word about his rising and their restoration. His word can be trusted at the worst moment as well as the best.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the high priest. Caiaphas, high priest from AD 18 to 36 (Matthew 26:57). John records a first hearing before Annas, his father-in-law and the power behind the office (John 18:13). And Caiaphas was the man who had already said it was better that one man should die for the people (John 11:50).

The High Priest before the high priest. John adds that in saying it Caiaphas unknowingly prophesied (John 11:51–52). So tonight the high priest of the old covenant sits in judgment on the great high priest of the new (Hebrews 4:14). Caiaphas’s office was to offer the blood of animals, year after year (Hebrews 9:25). The prisoner in front of him is about to offer himself, holy, innocent, unstained (Hebrews 7:26–27), once for all. The man in the robes is condemning the only priest who could take his own sins away.

They came together. The Sanhedrin, the council of seventy-one, or at least a quorum of it, assembled in the middle of the night. A night trial was irregular by any standard, and they were in a hurry to finish before the crowds could react.

The structure. Another Mark sandwich. Peter in the courtyard (v. 54), Jesus before the council (vv. 55–65), Peter in the courtyard (vv. 66–72). Inside, Jesus confesses who he is, and is condemned. Outside, Peter denies who he is, and saves himself.

At a distance. Among the saddest descriptions of discipleship in the New Testament. Yet do not despise Peter too quickly: the others have fled, and he followed. But at a distance: close enough to see, far enough not to be associated. Near enough to keep your conscience quiet, far enough to keep your safety: nobody stays there long. He followed right into the courtyard of the high priest, the open yard at the centre of a wealthy house; John says another disciple, known to the high priest, got him through the gate (John 18:15–16).

Warming himself at the fire. Sitting with the guards, not standing at the edge: he has sat down among the men who arrested his Lord an hour ago. Spring nights in Jerusalem can be cold, and Peter is at the charcoal fire with his hands out. He has not denied anything yet. He has simply taken a place at the enemy’s fire because it was cold and he wanted to see what would happen, and the next thing that happens is that the firelight falls on his face (v. 67). While his friend warmed his hands below, Jesus stood upstairs in the cold of their hatred and did not flinch.

Is it wrong to keep quiet about Christ among people who have no time for him? Not always. There are times when silence is wise, and you are not obliged to preach at every lunch table. But there is a version of Peter’s fire in every Christian’s life: the place where you can be near Christ and comfortable at the same time, sitting with people who mock him and saying nothing, because it is warm and leaving would cost something. The question is not whether you speak every time, but whether you have settled in. If the company you keep regularly requires you to hide that you belong to Jesus, it is time either to speak or to move away from the fire.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking testimony against Jesus. Mark convicts the court in one line: they are seeking testimony against him, to put him to death. The verdict is fixed, and they are hunting for evidence to fit it.

The irregularities. The later Mishnah required capital cases to be heard in daylight, in the temple’s own hall, and a condemnation to wait overnight, though how much of it was in force in AD 30 is uncertain. This trial is held at night, in a private residence, at Passover, and the sentence is passed within the hour. But Mark does not lean on any of that.

But they found none. The supreme court of Israel, with every motive and the whole night, could not assemble a credible case against him from three years of public ministry watched by hostile professionals. That does not by itself prove he was sinless, but it is striking testimony: a hostile prosecution had every reason to produce something and could not. He was innocent, the spotless lamb (1 Peter 1:19). Every word he had spoken was true, every deed holy, every thought pure.

Their testimony did not agree. They had witnesses; the witnesses were lying; and the lies did not match. They broke the ninth commandment to convict the Son of God (Exodus 20:16), and the psalmist had foretold it: false witnesses have risen against me (Psalm 27:12; 35:11). The Law required at least two agreeing witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the penalty for a false witness in a capital case was the death he had sought to inflict (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). Yet none of the false witnesses in that room is charged with anything.

Why did God let an innocent man be convicted? Because only an innocent man could save the guilty. If Jesus had been condemned for real sins of his own, his death would have paid for nothing but those sins. The fact that his enemies could find nothing is the very thing that makes his death a substitution: the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). God did not approve of the injustice; the men who committed it were guilty. But he wove their injustice into the greatest act of justice in history, in which sin was truly punished and sinners truly pardoned.

In everyday life. If you are falsely accused, remember that Jesus was, and commit your cause to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Do not pay back slander with slander; the Spirit of the Lamb who was silent before his accusers lives in you. Tell the truth plainly, accept help, and leave the outcome with him.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will destroy this temple. A lie built out of something true, which is how the most effective lies are made. John records what he did say: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. And John adds the explanation the witnesses have conveniently lost: he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). He had predicted the temple’s destruction (13:2), but not that he would do it.

Count the alterations. He said destroy this temple, a challenge to them; they report I will destroy this temple, turning a saying about his own death into a plot against the national sanctuary. Jeremiah nearly lost his life for prophesying against the temple of his day (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and Stephen will lose his for the same accusation (Acts 6:13–14). Nothing is invented. Everything is turned. That is still the commonest way Christ and his people are misrepresented: not by inventing things, but by quoting part and leaving out what explains it.

Not made with hands. Made with hands was used of idols and man-made temples (Acts 7:48). The witnesses may have been twisting Jesus’ teaching that a new temple was coming, not a building but a people built around himself (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Even about this. Even the best lie in the room could not survive two men telling it. The charge failed on the Law’s own safeguard, the demand for witnesses who agree (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Not convicted on this. The whole trial turns on this: the temple charge fails, and the charge that finally kills him comes out of his own mouth. They could not find a crime. So they asked him who he was, and he told them, and that was enough.

The irony. The false testimony was, in a deeper sense, true. By putting Jesus to death they would destroy the temple of his body; in three days he would rise; and his resurrection would bring into being the true temple, not made with hands, the church, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:21). The false witnesses were accidentally right. The lie they told at his trial became the truth of Easter.

How should I respond when my words, or my faith, are twisted? Calmly, and with the truth. Clarify what you actually said, once, without bitterness. Do not be surprised: if they twisted the words of Jesus, they will twist yours. Do not twist theirs in return. And when Christianity itself is misrepresented, by a quotation torn from context or a caricature of what Christians believe, be ready to restore the missing context gently, as John restores it for us in his Gospel. The truth usually needs only to be stated fully to defend itself.

In everyday life. Before you repeat a report about someone this week, especially a Christian leader or a person you dislike, ask whether you have the whole of what was said, or only a sentence with the key removed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, Have you no answer to make? The case has collapsed, and Caiaphas stands up, physically moves into the middle of the room, because the trial is failing and he has to rescue it. His first move is to try to get the prisoner talking. What is it that these men testify against you?

He remained silent. Mark says it twice over, because the silence is the point. He does not point out that the witnesses contradict each other, or explain what he actually said about the temple, which would have taken thirty seconds. And it is a quotation: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Every instinct in a wronged man is to explain. He will not say a word in his own defence, because a defence would have worked, and he had not come to be acquitted.

Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? Now the direct question, the question the whole Gospel has been asking since 1:1. The Blessed is a reverent Jewish substitute for the divine name; Caiaphas will not say God aloud. So he is asking: are you the Messiah, the Son of God? Matthew adds that he put him under oath (Matthew 26:63).

I am. Two words, the plainest claim in Mark. All through this Gospel he has told people to keep quiet about who he is, because the title would have been misunderstood and a crowd would have tried to crown him. Now he is bound, and at the moment when it can only cost him his life, he says it plainly. The words are egō eimi, I am, the words he spoke on the water in the dark (6:50), and they may echo the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Seated at the right hand of Power. He adds a sentence that joins two Old Testament texts. Seated at the right hand of Power is Psalm 110:1, the psalm he had put to these very men as an unanswerable riddle two days ago (12:36). Power is another reverent way of saying God. Coming with the clouds of heaven is Daniel 7:13, the one like a son of man given dominion and glory and a kingdom, whom all peoples serve. A bound prisoner tells the court about to sentence him that he will be on the throne and come as their judge. The dock and the bench are about to change places, and that is why the high priest tore his robes.

When would they see this? Some take it as the vindication of Christ after his death, in his resurrection, ascension and the judgment on Jerusalem, since in Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. Others take it as the final coming, when every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7). The more likely reading holds both together. From his resurrection Jesus is enthroned at God’s right hand, and those who condemned him saw the signs of it; the coming with the clouds will be seen by all at his return, when these judges stand before their Judge.

Why was he silent before, and then answer? Because the two questions were different. The first invited him to defend himself against lies, and he would not; his silence was the silence of the Lamb, who had come to be condemned, not to escape condemnation. The second asked who he was, under oath, and to stay silent then would have been to deny the truth. So he spoke. That is a pattern for his people. We need not always defend our own reputations, and often should not. But when we are asked whether we belong to Christ and who he is, we must answer, whatever it costs.

For worship. A prisoner with bound hands spoke two words, and they were the truth about the universe. Caiaphas sat on the bench that night; one day he will stand before the man he judged. And until that day the same throne is a throne of grace, and the Judge on it pleads for all who come to him.
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tore his garments. The formal gesture on hearing blasphemy. The Law forbade the high priest to tear his clothes: the priest who is chief among his brothers shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Leviticus 21:10). This probably referred to mourning, and later practice allowed the gesture at blasphemy, so Caiaphas was likely within the rules of his day. The deeper irony is elsewhere: in a room full of experts on the letter of the law, the only person wholly keeping it was the one they were about to kill for breaking it.

What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. Relief: the problem of the witnesses is solved. And this is the one honest sentence any of his judges speaks all night, though not in the way Caiaphas intends. He is right that no further witnesses are needed; the case is settled out of the prisoner’s own mouth. And he is right about the logic too. Blasphemy under the Law was punishable by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Strictly it meant using the divine name irreverently, and claiming to be the Messiah was not in itself blasphemy; others had done it. But claiming to sit at God’s right hand and come on the clouds, sharing God’s throne and his role as judge, was claiming to be equal with God. If it was false, it was blasphemy. If it was true, they were condemning God.

Only two options. There were never more than two options in that room, and there are never more than two now. Either the man in the dock is God’s Son, or he said the most blasphemous thing a human being has ever said. Caiaphas at least sees what is at stake, and the trial leaves no room to call Jesus merely a fine moral teacher.

Did Jesus really claim this, or did the church put it in his mouth later? The trial itself is the best answer. Nobody crucifies a man for telling people to love their neighbours. Jesus was condemned by his own nation’s court for blasphemy and handed to Rome on a charge of claiming to be king (15:2, 26), and those charges make sense only if he said something like this. And within about twenty-five years of his death, Paul, a strict Jew who confessed that God is one, was writing that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6). The claim is not a later decoration. It is why he died.

They all condemned him. All: the verdict was unanimous among those who voted. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, had not consented (Luke 23:51); perhaps he was absent.

Spit on him. Spitting in the face was the deepest contempt in that culture (Deuteronomy 25:9), and Isaiah said the Servant would receive it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6).

Prophesy! A cruel game. They blindfold him, hit him and demand that he name who did it; Luke spells it out (Luke 22:64). Then the guards take him over with blows. And prophesy! is the most ironic word in the chapter: his prophecy of Peter’s denials was at that moment coming true below them, in the courtyard.

Who was responsible for the death of Jesus? Scripture answers: the Jewish leaders who condemned him, the Roman governor who sentenced him, the soldiers who crucified him, and the crowd who called for it, Jew and Gentile together (Acts 4:27). Behind them all stood the purpose of God, who delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32). And in the deepest sense, every sinner, for it was for our sins that he died (Isaiah 53:5). That rules out forever the wicked charge that the Jews as a people are uniquely guilty, which has caused so much suffering. It also rules out every comfortable view of the cross in which someone else did it. The hymn is right to say: it was my sin that held him there.

In everyday life. Let the picture of his spat-on face cure you of self-pity the next time you are mocked or treated with contempt for his sake, and refuse to join, even with a laugh, in the mockery of Christ that passes for wit in your office, your family or your feed.

For worship. The face that angels cannot look upon was covered with a rag and slapped by servants, so that God would never turn his face from us. The blindfold was on his eyes, and still he saw everything: the servants, the council, the friend at the fire below.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Below in the courtyard. Mark gives us the architecture. Upstairs, Christ on trial, confessing who he is and being struck for it. Downstairs, in the same house, in the open yard, Peter at the fire, about to be asked the same question. One says I am, and it costs him his life. The other says, in effect, I am not, and it costs him everything else.

One of the servant girls. Not a soldier or the temple police who had seen him draw a sword: a servant girl, one of the lowest-status people in the household (John calls her the girl at the door, John 18:17), whose opinion could not have hurt him and who had no power over him whatsoever.

She looked at him. She stared across the fire, with the light on his face. It is precisely because he sat down at that fire that she can see him at all. In the shadows at the edge of the yard, nobody asks you anything.

You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. Not you are a disciple, but you were with him: association, that is all, and being with him was the very purpose for which Peter was chosen (3:14). The Nazarene is faintly contemptuous.

He denied it. The first denial is not a flat lie so much as a fog, the answer of a man buying time. We imagine Peter’s denial as dramatic and unlike us. It begins as an evasion at a fire. Not I renounce Christ; just a vague sentence said to somebody unimportant, to make a moment go away.

The rooster crowed. He moves out to the entrance passage, further from the light. Some manuscripts omit the rooster’s crowing here, but it matches Jesus’ twice (v. 30) and the second crowing in verse 72. There is mercy in that detail: the first crow was a warning, and there was still time. Even while Jesus was being struck, he was still caring for the friend who was letting him down. Peter heard it and it meant nothing to him.

Why do the small denials matter so much? Because they are where the large ones begin, and because they are the ones we commit most. Very few of us will be asked under threat of death whether we follow Jesus. Many of us will be asked, lightly, at work or at a party, whether we are religious, or what we did on Sunday, or what we think of something Christ forbids, and the temptation will be to answer with fog. That is the first step of Peter’s road. The remedy is to decide in advance what you will say, simply and kindly, so that when the servant girl asks, you are not deciding in the firelight. Underneath the fog there is usually an idol: the approval of the people at the fire. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25), and the cure for craving their approval is to remember that in Christ you already have his.

In everyday life. Listen for the roosters in your life: the conscience that stings, the verse that comes to mind, the friend’s question. They are mercies, sent while there is still time.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man is one of them. The pressure is widening, from private to public, and the wording has hardened. Not you were with him but he is one of them: a category, a group, a party.

Again he denied it. Mark does not even record the words, and the tense means he kept on denying. The first denial makes the second one cheap. Having said I neither know nor understand, he now has to defend the first statement as well as himself, and the only way to defend it is to say it again with more force. A man who tells one lie has taken out a loan. Every later lie is interest.

You are a Galilean. Now it is a group, and they have evidence: his accent. Galilean Aramaic was noticeably different from the speech of Jerusalem; later rabbinic stories joke about Galileans swallowing their consonants and confusing their gutturals. Matthew makes it explicit: your accent betrays you (Matthew 26:73). He can deny knowing Jesus; he cannot deny the sound of his own mouth.

Peter’s accent was more faithful than Peter was. He was recognisable by what he could not help. And upstairs another Galilean, from a village Jerusalem despised, was on trial. He did not hide where he came from or whose Son he was. The Galilean in the dock owned his Father; the Galilean at the fire disowned his friend. And Peter carried deeper marks than an accent, put there by Jesus himself. He had been seen with Jesus, and had come to resemble the company he kept. That is what following Christ does to a person, and it is a mercy even when it is inconvenient. His Spirit writes his likeness into ordinary lives until it cannot be hidden.

What should give a Christian away? Not a special vocabulary or a religious manner, but the marks of having been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). The way you speak: without cruelty, gossip or filth, and with grace (Colossians 4:6). The way you handle money: honestly and generously. The way you treat people with no power to help you. The way you face loss, with grief but with hope. The way you refuse certain things without making a show of it. None of these makes you a Christian. But if you are one, they will grow, and people will notice before anything is said. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16).

In everyday life. If you have told one small lie this week to avoid being identified with him, go back and correct it now, before the interest grows.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To invoke a curse. This is the lowest point. It is not bad language but something formal and terrible. He invokes a curse: in the standard oath formula of that world, may God do so to me and more also if I am lying. And he swears: he takes an oath, calling God to witness. Some think the Greek could mean he cursed Jesus, since the verb has no object. Either way, Peter calls God as his witness, and calls down God’s curse on his own head, to guarantee a lie about God’s Son.

This man. He will not say the name, and puts as much distance into the sentence as the grammar allows. He knew him better than almost anyone alive, and had said at Caesarea Philippi, you are the Christ. At that very moment, upstairs, this man was confessing that he is the Son of God.

A second time. Exactly as Jesus had said. God used the most ordinary sound in the world, and timed it to the second.

Peter remembered. Remembering is where he begins to turn back. And Luke adds the detail that finishes a man: the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61). If the prisoner was being moved across the courtyard at that moment, the two men’s eyes met at the instant the bird called.

He broke down and wept. Mark’s phrase is unusual (epibalōn eklaien) and hard to translate: perhaps he thought about it and wept, or he threw himself down and wept, or he began to weep. The tense means he went on weeping: bitter tears of repentance (Luke 22:62).

Peter and Judas. Two men betrayed Jesus that night, both of the twelve, both warned to their faces. Judas betrayed him and despaired, and died by his own hand (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied him and wept, and was restored (16:7; John 21:15–19). The difference was not in the size of the sin; denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. The difference was in what each did with the wreckage. Judas felt remorse, and it drove him away from Christ. Peter felt grief, and it drove him back. That is the difference between remorse and repentance. Repentance is more than feeling bad about a sin; it is a change of heart that turns from the sin and back to God, trusting his mercy. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). And on the third morning an angel in an empty tomb will say: go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). Named, specifically. The one who denied him is the one singled out to be told.

But did Jesus not say he would deny those who deny him? He did: whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father (Matthew 10:33), and Paul writes, if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Timothy 2:12). Those words describe a final, settled denial, the denial of someone who will not come back. Peter’s was a terrible fall, but not a final one. Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and it did not. A believer can fall badly; Christ keeps him from falling away for good. If you have denied him and your heart is breaking over it, that grief is the proof that you are not the person those verses describe.

Why record this? The early church did not hide the failure of its greatest leader. Mark, probably writing from Peter’s own preaching, records it in detail. Peter told this story against himself, again and again, as a testimony to the grace that restored him. No Christian is too great to fall, and no fallen Christian is beyond restoration.

I keep failing in the same way. Is there still a way back? Yes, as many times as you come. Peter did not fall only once; years later he drew back from Gentile believers out of fear and had to be rebuked to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Restoration is not a single event but the pattern of the Christian life: fall, grieve, return, be received. Do not let the size or the repetition of your failure persuade you that Christ is tired of you. He told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (older versions say seventy times seven); he will not do less himself. Come back today, confess it plainly, and get up.

In everyday life. If you have denied Christ, in word or deed, don’t despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back: tell him exactly what you did, without excuse, and let him restore you among his people. And if someone you know has fallen, be the angel at the tomb for them: go and tell them, by name, that he is waiting.

For worship. The tears in that courtyard are the beginning of the man who preached at Pentecost, so that everyone who has warmed their hands at the wrong fire would know there is a way back. The Lord who turned and looked at Peter is the Lord who was at that moment being condemned for Peter. He bore the curse Peter called down on himself, so that Peter would never have to bear it. That is our Saviour: he looks at us at our worst, with eyes that break our hearts and then heal them.

14.theology:
Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man was told the Father's will and said, in effect, my will, and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended. The cup he accepted there was the cup of God's wrath against sin, and he drank it so that there is nothing left in it for anyone who is in him.

Abba (v. 36), the family word a child used at home, did not stay his: the Spirit puts it into the mouths of ordinary Christians (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).
14.examples:
Then: the chapter ends with two men who failed him. One went out and hanged himself; one went out and wept. The difference is not the size of the sin but what each did with the wreckage: remorse drove Judas away from Christ; grief drove Peter back.

Now: if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter's fall began: at a distance (v. 54), and then at the enemy's fire, near enough to keep his conscience quiet and far enough to keep his safety.

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Fifteen hours from the garden to the grave, and Mark tells it almost without adjectives.

At first light the council hands Jesus to Rome, because it could pass a religious sentence but could not carry one out. Before Pilate he says almost nothing, and the governor is amazed. Pilate knows the case is malicious (v. 10), but the crowd, worked by the chief priests, asks for Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, guilty of the very crime Jesus is falsely charged with, rebellion against Rome. And Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, hands Jesus over.

Soldiers mock him as a king and, without knowing it, get every detail right. Simon of Cyrene carries the beam. At noon the light goes out; at three Jesus cries the first line of Psalm 22, cries out again and dies. The temple curtain tears from top to bottom, a Roman officer confesses him the Son of God, and Joseph of Arimathea lays him in a rock tomb while the women watch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transfer (vv. 1–5). At first light the council hands him to Rome. Pilate asks one question, gets a guarded answer and then silence, and is amazed.

Barabbas (vv. 6–15). Pilate sees that the charge comes from envy and tries to release him through a festival custom. The chief priests work the crowd, the crowd asks for a murderer, and Pilate, after asking what evil he has done and getting no answer, hands him over anyway.

The mockery (vv. 16–20). The soldiers dress him in purple, crown him with thorns and salute him as king, and without knowing it they are telling the truth: he is the King.
verseByVerse.theology: Barabbas is the atonement acted out in a Jerusalem courtyard. A rebel guilty in fact of the crime Jesus is falsely charged with walks free, and the innocent one dies on the cross prepared for the guilty. That is the gospel. Barabbas was spared a cross because Jesus hung on it; everyone who trusts Christ is spared God’s judgment because Jesus bore it: Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: what evil has he done? (v. 14) is the right question, asked by the one man with the authority to act on it, who then signed the order anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Now: that is the commonest failure of people in authority: the doctrine not defended because of who would leave, the wrong not named because of whose son it was, the decision made by counting who is for it rather than weighing what is right. Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular. That is a different sin, and one far easier for any of us to commit.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 15 is one day, dawn to dusk on the Friday, and everything turns on it. Pilate knows Jesus is innocent and frees a murderer instead; soldiers crown him in jest; his mockers preach without meaning to: he saved others; he cannot save himself. This is the day the Son of God bore the wrath of God for sinners and opened the way to God for all who come through him.

The setting. The night hearing before the council (14:53–65) is over, Peter has wept in the courtyard (14:72), and the sun is coming up over the Mount of Olives. Jesus has had no sleep. Within nine hours he will be dead.

As soon as it was morning. Jesus had told them to stay awake, because the master might come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning (13:35). This night has had all four: evening at the supper, midnight in the garden, cockcrow in the courtyard, and now morning. The disciples have slept or run through every one of them.

A consultation. They meet again at first light, probably because a capital verdict reached at night was irregular (by the rules later written down in the Mishnah), and a daylight session could be recorded as the proper trial. It was a formality to make an irregular trial look proper, held by men who had fixed the sentence before they looked for evidence (14:55). They also agreed how to present the case. Blasphemy would mean nothing to a Roman governor, so they turned it into a political charge: Jesus claims to be a king, a rival to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

They bound Jesus. Isaac was bound on the altar (Genesis 22:9); the true sacrifice is bound now. Delivered over is the word Mark has used for Judas’s betrayal (14:10) and for what the Son of Man must undergo (9:31; 10:33), and it will be used of Pilate (v. 15). Everyone in this chapter is handing him on to somebody else. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands.

Why Pilate at all? Because under Roman rule the council could pass a religious sentence but could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome as prefect for ten years, AD 26 to 36. He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem at festivals with extra troops to keep order. Ancient writers describe him as harsh, stubborn and contemptuous of the Jews; Luke mentions Galileans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1). A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 still bears his name.

And Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews? The political form of the charge, and the first thing out of his mouth, before any evidence is heard, which tells you what he had been told in advance. King of the Jews is a Gentile phrase; Jews said King of Israel (v. 32). The title runs through this chapter (vv. 2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32). Judea was a difficult province with a history of messianic risings, and Rome tolerated no king without Caesar’s permission. Pilate is not asking about theology. His question is practical: is this man a threat? In Greek his you may be emphatic: you, a bound and beaten Galilean, are a king?

You have said so. A guarded yes. He is not dodging the question; he is refusing the meaning Pilate gives the word king. King of the Jews is Pilate’s phrase, loaded with everything Rome feared: insurrection, a rival throne, tax revolt. Jesus will not deny the kingship, because he is the King. He will not affirm it in Pilate’s terms, because in those terms it means something he has never claimed. John gives the fuller exchange: my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36–37). He is not the rebel Pilate fears. And this is his last recorded answer to a question in this Gospel. From here, almost nothing, until a cry at three in the afternoon.

Should Christians seek political power for Christ’s kingdom? Christians may serve in government, vote, campaign for justice and hold office; Joseph and Daniel did, and the state is God’s servant for good (Romans 13:1–4). But Christ’s kingdom does not come by political power, legislation or force. It comes by the word and the Spirit, through the new birth (John 3:3–5), and it is not of this world. When the church confuses the two, it either tries to make people Christian by law or makes the gospel a political badge, and both betray the King who answered Pilate as he did. Seek the good of your city; do not mistake any party or nation for the kingdom of God.

In everyday life. Most of us have a king we consult on Sundays and a small kingdom of our own that runs the rest of the week: the money, the evenings, the way we speak at home. He does not storm that kingdom. He waits to be asked in, and he rules it far more kindly than we do.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many things. Luke itemises them: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). Every one is false or twisted; he had told them to pay the tax (12:17), and men sent by these same leaders heard him. The strategy is volume: if no single charge will hold, pile them up.

And Pilate again asked him, Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you. Roman law gave the accused the right to defend himself, and a man who did not was normally convicted. And Pilate, it seems, is trying to help. A governor who wanted a conviction would let the accusations stand and move to sentence. Pilate is prompting the prisoner, say something, they are burying you, because he can see the case is thin and he would rather not do this. Matthew adds that his wife sent word about a dream and told him to have nothing to do with this righteous man (Matthew 27:19). Pilate is not acting on any conviction. He is looking for a way out.

No further answer. He will not take the way out he is offered, just as he stayed silent before the high priest (14:61). A single sentence would have collapsed the case: I told them to pay the tax; ask them. He says nothing (Isaiah 53:7). The Word of God, through whom the worlds were spoken into being, stood silent before liars, because his silence was the price of our acquittal. His silence is not weakness but dignity, and submission to the Father’s will.

Pilate was amazed. He had seen every kind of defendant, the pleaders, the bribers, the weepers, and every one of them fought. He had rarely seen a man decline to save himself. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him (Isaiah 52:15).

Why would an innocent man refuse to defend himself? Because he had not come to be acquitted. If Jesus had talked his way out, he would have walked free and we would have stayed condemned. He was not on trial to clear his name but to bear our sentence. The silence was not resignation and it was not despair. It was the most deliberate act in the room. That is also why it is not a rule for every Christian in every courtroom. Paul defended himself and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:10–11). Jesus’ silence belonged to his unique work as the Lamb.

For worship. He kept his mouth shut so that ours could be opened. Because he was silent then, he speaks for us now, as our advocate with the Father, and his defence of his people has never once been refused.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover release. A goodwill custom at the feast of liberation. It is attested nowhere outside the Gospels, but Roman governors did grant such amnesties elsewhere, and a local custom in one province would not be expected to leave much record. And the Lord of the feast of liberation was not released, so that every prisoner of sin could be.

Barabbas. Not a common criminal but a political prisoner: one of the rebels who had committed murder in the insurrection, perhaps one of the armed nationalists later called Zealots. He is guilty of exactly what Jesus is falsely accused of, sedition against Rome, and he is exactly the kind of king many wanted.

Son of the father. Then there is his name. Bar-abbas is Aramaic for son of the father. Some manuscripts of Matthew give his first name as Jesus: Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17). So the choice put to the crowd is between two men called son of the father. One is a murderer. The other is the Son of the Father, who prayed Abba a few hours before (14:36).

The crowd came up. The crowd initiates it, and they have somebody in mind. It is not necessarily the crowd from Sunday: early on a Friday, the people present are those men with influence could assemble at short notice (v. 11).

Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? Pilate makes his move, and it is shrewd. He offers the amnesty in a way that puts his preferred outcome first, thinking he can free Jesus this way. And the title needles the priests: this is your king? It is his title for Jesus throughout; he uses it here, again in verse 12, and will have it nailed to the cross and refuse to change it (John 19:22).

Out of envy. Mark tells us what Pilate had worked out, and it settles his guilt. Not concern for public order, not theological outrage: they wanted him dead because the crowds hung on his teaching (11:18; 12:37), because his real authority showed how hollow theirs was, and because he had turned their tables over. So Pilate knows the charge is malicious and the man innocent. Envy, one of the sins Jesus listed as coming from the heart (7:22), sent him to the cross.

How do I recognise envy in myself? Envy is sorrow at another’s good and quiet pleasure at his harm. It rarely calls itself envy. It calls itself concern, or justice, or high standards. Watch for these signs: you find it hard to rejoice when a colleague, sibling or fellow Christian is praised; you look for flaws in people who succeed; you feel a small lift when someone you resent stumbles; you speak of another’s gifts with a qualification attached. The cure is not to pretend, but to confess it to God, thank him specifically for the other person’s gifts, pray for their good, and remember that in Christ you already have more than you could ever envy (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. And Pilate again said to them, "Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?" And they cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stirred up the crowd. The key to the next hour: the crowd is being worked. They did not arrive with a view about Barabbas; somebody moved among them and gave them one (Matthew 27:20).

How crowds are made. Nobody in Jerusalem had changed his mind about Jesus on the evidence; there was no new fact. People with authority told them what to think, and within minutes they were shouting for a man’s execution. A crowd does not think; it makes louder whatever it is given, and whoever gets to it first decides what that is (Exodus 23:2).

Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? Mark writes again because he is keeping count. This is Pilate’s second attempt, and there will be a third. And look at the question he has just made public. What shall I do with him? He puts it to a crowd, out loud, as though it were theirs to answer. It is the question of every person who hears of Jesus, and the tragedy of Pilate is that he asked it in the one way that guaranteed the wrong answer. He asked the room instead of deciding himself.

Crucify him. Two words, no charge, no reasoning: a demand for a Roman method of execution, the most shameful death Rome knew, reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. And the Law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). They wanted not only his death, but his disgrace. The Lord who could have silenced the crowd with a word let their cry stand, because the curse they demanded for him was the curse he had come to bear for them. The crowd that shouted Hosanna (11:9), or a crowd like it, now shouts for this.

Why? What evil has he done? The third attempt, and the only honest question of the morning. The judge declares him innocent. Luke records that Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). It is a fair question, and it has an answer: nothing. Mark records no reply, because there was none. Nobody in that courtyard could name a crime, and that silence shows the whole trial for what it was. The judge’s own words testify that Jesus died not for his own sins, but as the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

All the more. Louder: that is the reply. The mob does not reason. When a case cannot be made, volume does the work, and it worked.

How do I stand firm when a crowd has been worked up? Notice when you are agreeing with something mainly because everyone around you does, or because it was said loudly and often. Ask the question Pilate asked and the crowd ignored: why? what is the evidence? Be especially careful online, where crowds form in minutes and outrage is rewarded. Slow down before you share, sign or join. Test what you hear by Scripture rather than by its popularity. And be willing to be the one person in the room who says, quietly, I do not think that is true. The crowd that shouted crucify him was sure it was right.

Is there a neutral answer to Pilate’s question? No. Pilate tried to find one, by handing the question to others, and it did not save him. Every person who hears of Jesus does something with him: bows to him, rejects him, or postpones him, and postponing is a decision too. Jesus himself said whoever is not with me is against me (Matthew 12:30). That is not a threat; it is the plain logic of who he is. If he is the King, the only right answer is to receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wishing to satisfy the crowd. Mark gives the motive in one phrase, and it is not a legal judgment. He knows the man is innocent, and he gives way, because his position could not survive a riot at Passover or a complaint to the emperor: if you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12). His record with Rome was already poor, and Philo records a rebuke from Tiberius himself. He was recalled a few years later anyway. So a man weighed an innocent life against his career, chose the career, and lost it in any case.

Washing his hands. Matthew records that he washed his hands to declare himself innocent (Matthew 27:24). But a judge who condemns a man he knows is innocent is not innocent, and his name is fixed in the creed, suffered under Pontius Pilate, as a witness that this happened in real history and that the governor was guilty.

He released Barabbas. Before nine that morning a convicted murderer walked into the street a free man and did not know why. Barabbas is the first person in history who could say, literally: Jesus died instead of me. He had not repented, or asked, or understood; somebody else’s name was called instead of his. This is a picture of substitution: one man dying in another’s place.

Having scourged Jesus. Roman scourging was the normal preliminary to crucifixion: the prisoner stripped, tied to a post and beaten with leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, with no fixed number of strokes. It tore the flesh, sometimes to the bone, and men died under it; this is why Simon must carry the beam (v. 21). He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5).

He delivered him to be crucified. The final handing over, from Pilate to the soldiers. And behind every human hand in the chain stands the Father, who gave up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32).

Was Pilate really guilty if he did not want to do it? Yes. Not wanting to do evil is not the same as refusing to do it. Pilate had the authority, the knowledge and the duty to release an innocent man, and he chose his own safety instead. Scripture names him among those who gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:27). His reluctance makes him more instructive, not less guilty. Most evil in the world is done not by monsters but by people who know better and give way. That is a warning to every Christian who holds any kind of authority, from a boardroom to a classroom to a home. Pilate’s real master that morning was the approval of the crowd and the favour of Caesar, and every heart has its own version: the good opinion of people we feel we cannot live without. Only a heart already accepted by God in Christ can afford to disappoint the crowd (Galatians 1:10).

Did Jesus die for Barabbas? We do not know whether Barabbas ever believed, and Scripture does not say. What his release gives us is a picture, not a guarantee about him. The picture is exact: a guilty man goes free because an innocent man takes his place, and he contributes nothing to it. That is what happens to every sinner who trusts Christ. The picture becomes your story not by being near the cross, as Barabbas was, but by faith, as you stop pleading your own case and rest on the one who took your place.

In everyday life. Ask where you are most tempted this week to do what you know is wrong because the pressure is rising: to sign off something dishonest, to stay silent while someone innocent is blamed. Decide now, before the noise, what you will do; the one who stood under that noise for you will stand with you in yours.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor's headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. And they began to salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor’s headquarters. The praetorium, the governor’s residence in Jerusalem, either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city or the Antonia fortress next to the temple.

The whole battalion. A cohort, nominally six hundred men, though probably only those on hand: not Italians but auxiliaries recruited from the Gentile cities of the region, garrisoned in a province they despised, on riot duty at a festival they did not understand. A Jew handed to them as a king is entertainment.

A purple cloak. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from an expensive dye and restricted to the powerful. What they had to hand was probably a faded red soldier’s cloak (Matthew 27:28 says scarlet), passed off as a king’s robe.

A crown of thorns. A wreath, a parody of the emperor’s laurel, perhaps woven from long palm thorns sticking out like the rays of a crown on coins. And thorns arrive in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:17–18). The first visible mark of a world under judgment is pressed onto the head of the man who came to lift it.

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of the imperial greeting, Ave, Caesar, with the name changed. They are acting out the crowning of an emperor, and the joke is that a bleeding provincial is given the honours of an emperor.

Kneeling down in homage. The reed was his mock sceptre (Matthew 27:29), and then they beat him on the head with it, driving the thorns in. Kneeling down in homage is the language of worship (5:6; Matthew 2:11). They are bowing the knee to the Son of God as a joke.

Every element is true. He is the King of the Jews; Pilate will nail the words over his head within the hour. At the name of Jesus every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), including, one day, every knee in that room. The soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right. They were the only people in Jerusalem that morning conducting the correct ceremony. They simply thought it was funny.

They led him out. The game ends. The robe comes off, because it belongs to somebody and will be wanted back, and in a few verses they will gamble for the clothes he is standing in. Out of the city, for Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12).

Why did God allow his Son to be so humiliated? Because shame is part of what sin deserves, and he came to bear all of it. Adam and Eve’s first experience of sin was shame, and they hid (Genesis 3:7–10). Jesus was stripped, mocked, spat on and paraded so that sinners covered in shame could be clothed and honoured before God. Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). If you carry shame, for what you have done or what was done to you, he has carried it too, and he can lift your head.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. Purple was the colour of royalty.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The road and the cross (vv. 21–27). A man coming in from the country is pressed into carrying the beam. At Golgotha Jesus refuses the drugged wine, the soldiers gamble for his clothes, and Mark records the crucifixion itself in a few words: and they crucified him.

The mockery (vv. 29–32). Passers-by, the chief priests and the two men dying beside him take their turn, and the taunt is always the same: come down; save yourself.

The darkness and the death (vv. 33–41). At noon the light goes out for three hours. At three he cries the opening line of Psalm 22, then gives a loud cry and dies. The temple curtain tears, a Roman officer confesses him, and the women who have been there all along are named.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cry of dereliction, the cry of one forsaken (v. 34), must be kept from two errors. The first would soften it, as though Jesus were merely reciting a psalm and was not truly forsaken. He was: he was bearing sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). The second would break God in two, as though the Father ceased to love the Son. What he lost was not his Father’s love but every sense of it, the comfort of his Father’s presence, and he lost it in our place.

And he still says my God, my God, twice claiming as his own the One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still holding on. For the believer who has prayed and heard nothing back, this is the word: the real forsakenness has already been borne by the Son, so that it will never fall on you, and you may pray my God in the dark, as he did, knowing you do not pray it alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31). The chief priests, jeering at the foot of the cross, state the gospel accurately without believing a word of it. He did save others, and his enemies concede it. And he could not save himself, not for lack of power, but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done.

Now: their demand, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe (v. 32), is still the common one: show me and I will trust you. But it was by staying on the cross, not by coming down, that he saved anyone, and the gospel still asks us to trust him there.

verseByVerse.quote: And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon of Cyrene. The condemned man normally carried his own crossbeam (patibulum), perhaps 75–100 pounds (35–45 kg), to the place of execution, where the upright post was already standing. John tells us he set out carrying it himself (John 19:17); the likeliest reason it was taken from him is that he could no longer carry it. After a night of interrogation, a scourging and a battalion’s mockery, he is physically finished, and the soldiers needed the prisoner alive at Golgotha. Compelled is the word for a soldier’s right to force a civilian to carry a load, the word behind if anyone forces you to go one mile (Matthew 5:41). Simon does not volunteer.

Who was coming in from the country. Into the city, as Jesus was being led out. Cyrene, in modern Libya, had a large Jewish community (Acts 2:10; 11:20), and Simon was probably a pilgrim who had travelled a very long way to keep the Passover. A soldier picks him out of the crowd, and the day is not his any more.

The father of Alexander and Rufus. Only Mark has this. He names two men, and the likeliest reason is that his readers knew them, probably as fellow Christians. This Gospel was probably written for the church at Rome, and Paul’s letter to that church greets Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Romans 16:13). It cannot be proved, but Mark expects his readers to nod at those names, which strongly suggests that the family of the man pressed into carrying the cross ended up in the church.

What that morning did. A pilgrim is dragged out of a crowd against his will and made to carry a condemned criminal’s cross, and it turns out to be the best thing that ever happened to his family. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), the very picture of a disciple (8:34). Nobody pressed into carrying something for Christ is the poorer for it in the end, though it very rarely feels like that at the time.

The wood and the Lamb. Simon bears the beam a few hundred yards; Jesus will bear on it the sins of his people, a weight nobody could carry for him. Long before, Isaac carried the wood up Moriah and asked where the lamb was (Genesis 22:6–8). Now the wood goes up another hill, and the Lamb God provided walks in front of it, too spent to lift it, not too weak to finish what it was for.

Golgotha. Aramaic for skull; Calvary comes from the Latin calvaria. Perhaps a rocky outcrop, or simply what an execution ground was called. It was outside the wall but beside a road, because passers-by were meant to see (v. 29). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre has a strong claim to be the site.

What does it mean to take up my cross today? It means accepting whatever it costs to follow Jesus, rather than choosing the parts that are convenient. For Simon it was a crossbeam he did not ask for. For you it may be the loss of approval at work, a hard obedience in your marriage, a temptation refused every day, a costly forgiveness, or a call to serve somewhere unglamorous. It is not every hardship of life, such as illness or traffic, but the hardships that come because you belong to him. And notice that Simon carried it behind Jesus. You never carry your cross ahead of him or alone; he has carried the heavier one first.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” Rufus may be the man Paul greets in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wine mixed with myrrh. A rough anaesthetic. Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it as a mercy to the condemned, on the strength of Proverbs 31:6: give strong drink to the one who is perishing. He did not take it, and it was a decision. He had said he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom (14:25), and the cup he had been given in Gethsemane was to be drunk to the bottom, with a clear mind (14:36). Everything that follows, the mockery, the darkness, the cry, he goes through fully conscious. He would not be half-present at his own crucifixion. He would not dull what he had come to bear.

They crucified him. Three words in Greek, and that is all. None of the four Gospels describes the physical process; the nails are mentioned only after the resurrection (John 20:25). The victim was nailed or tied to the beam, hoisted onto the upright, and hung there, sometimes for days, struggling to push himself up to breathe, until he died of exhaustion and suffocation. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty. The Gospels are not trying to move you by the horror, but to show you its meaning: a reader overwhelmed by the physical agony can miss the darkness at noon and the cry at three, which are the heart of what he bore.

Divided his garments. The clothing of the executed belonged to the soldiers, and the Romans normally crucified men naked; the shame was total and public. The soldiers, four of them (John 19:23), sat in the dirt a few feet away and gambled. What makes the detail terrible is its ordinariness: the Son of God is dying above their heads, and the men closest to him are playing for a coat, because it is a working day.

Psalm 22. Mark does not point out the quotation; anyone who knew the Psalms would have recognised it with a shiver: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (Psalm 22:18). It is the first echo of the psalm of the righteous sufferer, laid in quietly until the man on the cross says its first line aloud. And there is an older background still, in Eden: Adam and Eve were clothed by God after the first sin (Genesis 3:21). Christ was stripped to clothe us in his righteousness.

Is it wrong for a Christian to take painkillers or sedation, since Jesus refused? No. His refusal belonged to his unique work. He had a cup to drink that no one else could drink, and he had to drink it with full awareness as our substitute. You are not bearing God’s wrath, and you are not asked to suffer more than you must. Scripture approves of medicine and relief: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. Receive pain relief with thanks as a gift of God’s kindness. What we learn from Jesus here is not to refuse medicine but to marvel at what he chose to endure for us.

In everyday life. Notice what you reach for to dull the edge of a hard day: the screen, the drink, the noise, the shopping. Not all of it is wrong, but some of it keeps you from facing God with what is actually happening. Choose one evening this week to sit with the hard thing in prayer, clear-headed, instead of numbing it.

For worship. The Lord who clothes the lilies of the field hung without a thread, while four soldiers diced for all he owned. They won a tunic. He won a people, and dressed them in garments of salvation that no one can gamble away (Isaiah 61:10).
verseByVerse.note: Wine mixed with myrrh was a drugged drink to dull pain; Jesus refused it. The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And it was the third hour when they crucified him. And the inscription of the charge against him read, "The King of the Jews." And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third hour. About 9 a.m., counting from sunrise, as Mark does throughout: the sixth hour is noon (v. 33) and the ninth three in the afternoon (v. 34). Arrested around midnight, before Pilate at first light, crucified at nine, dark at noon, dead by three.

The hour in John. John says it was about the sixth hour when Pilate handed him over (John 19:14), which on Mark’s reckoning would be noon. Some hold that John counts from midnight, which would put the judgment at about six in the morning, though it is not certain anyone counted that way; others note that without clocks both writers work in rough three-hour blocks, and John himself says only about. Believers who hold Scripture true can leave this open. Mark’s own account is consistent to the hour, and all four Gospels agree on the day, the place, the manner and the outcome.

The inscription of the charge. A placard stating the crime was fixed to the cross, as mockery and warning: this is what happens to rebel kings. But this charge, posted by the state as a sneer, was the plain truth. John adds that it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, and that when the chief priests asked Pilate to change it, he refused: what I have written I have written (John 19:19–22). The one decisive thing Pilate did all day was to leave a true sentence standing.

Two robbers. Robbers is the word Jesus used at his arrest (14:48), probably meaning rebels like Barabbas, perhaps his companions; Jesus may well hang on the cross meant for Barabbas. One on his right and one on his left: James and John had asked for those places in his glory, and were told they did not know what they were asking (10:37–40). The cross was his glory, and the places at his right and left went to two condemned men.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 28: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37). It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from Luke. The KJV and NKJV print it; the ESV puts it in a footnote. It is true, though not original to Mark. That is why the numbers in your Bible run 27, then 29.

Does a verse in the footnotes make the Bible unreliable? No. It shows how carefully the text has been preserved and studied. We have thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, far more than for any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can see where a scribe added something, as here, where someone probably wrote the reference in the margin and a later copyist took it into the text. Modern Bibles tell you openly. The words themselves are true Scripture, from Isaiah and Luke, and nothing of doctrine depends on this verse. The God who inspired the Scriptures has kept them, and their message has come to us intact.

What does it mean that he reigns from the cross? It means the cross was not the interruption of his kingship but the way he exercised it. A king fights for his people and defeats their enemies, and on the cross Jesus defeated sin, death and the devil, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). He gave his life for his subjects rather than taking theirs. So the placard was truer than Pilate knew. The Lord we worship is a crucified King, and his crown was won at Golgotha before it was shown on Easter morning.

In everyday life. When you wish for a place of honour, at work, in the church, in the family, remember who sat at his right and left in his glory, and ask whether you want the places beside him on his terms.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 28: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’”

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wagging their heads. The first of three groups to mock: the public on the road. Derided him is literally blasphemed him: he was condemned for blasphemy, and the real blasphemers are those who mock the Son of God.
