Wagging their heads is another quotation: all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Psalm 22:7).

Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. They throw back the false witness from last night (14:58), which even the court could not get two men to agree on. Of all the things they might have mocked, they chose the one about to come true: the temple of his body was being destroyed, and in three days he would raise it.

Come down from the cross! Recognise the voice. In the wilderness Satan offered him the kingdoms of the world without a cross (Matthew 4:8–9). At Caesarea Philippi Peter rebuked him, and was told get behind me, Satan (8:32–33). In Gethsemane he felt the full dread of the cup and prayed that, if possible, it might pass, and then yielded to his Father’s will (14:36). And now, from the foot of the cross: come down. The same offer in different voices, an enemy, a friend, a crowd: be the Christ without the cross. He could have come down (Matthew 26:53). But if he saved himself, he could not save us, and the only way he could save the men jeering at him was to stay where he was and let them go on jeering. It is still the constant temptation of every Christian: the crown without the cross, a faith that costs nothing. It always sounds reasonable, and it is always the voice from the wilderness.

Could he have stepped down if he had chosen to? Yes. He was not held there by the nails or the soldiers but by his own will and his love for his Father and his people. He had said that nobody would take his life from him; he would lay it down himself, and take it up again (John 10:18). If he had been unable to come down, his staying would not have been obedience. That is what makes his endurance so astonishing. Every minute of those six hours was chosen, and every taunt was an invitation he declined, for us.

In everyday life. Listen this week for the voice that says come down: you have suffered enough, you deserve this, nobody will know, protect yourself first. Recognise it, and answer it in the strength his Spirit gives, the strength of the one who stayed on the cross for you (8:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe." Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked him to one another. The second group, and the worst: the religious leadership of Israel, sharing the joke among themselves with the satisfaction of people whose problem has been solved. They speak to one another, not to him. That should frighten religious people more than it does. People who use religion to earn their own place with God can hate grace more fiercely than open unbelievers do, because grace says that place can never be earned.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. They state the gospel more accurately than anyone else in Mark, and do not believe a syllable of it. He saved others: a concession made in mockery by his enemies, and all the stronger as evidence because it comes from enemies; they never disputed the miracles (3:22). He cannot save himself: true too, not because the power was gone, but because saving himself and saving others could not both be done. If he comes down, he is safe and we are lost; if he stays, we are saved and he is not. Love bound him to the cross more firmly than nails. The priests thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the heart of the atonement, the Saviour not sparing himself so that God can spare us (Romans 8:32).

That we may see and believe. They call him the Christ, the King of Israel, the Jewish form of the title on the placard (v. 26). They are mocking his claim before the council (14:61–62), and making an offer of belief on their terms: show us and we will trust you (8:11–12). It is a lie, and they had already proved it. They had seen a withered hand restored and gone out to plan a murder (3:5–6), and within days they will pay soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). He would do something greater than coming down from the cross: he would come up from the grave. And still they would not believe (Luke 16:31).

Why he did not come down. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a wonder and gone home exactly as they came: impressed, and unforgiven. He stayed up, and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

Also reviled him. The third group. Two men in the same agony a few feet away join in; even shared suffering wins him no sympathy. Mark, focusing on Jesus’ total abandonment, records only the reviling. But Luke tells us that one of them, before the afternoon was out, said Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom, and was told today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:39–43).

Why does God not give unbelievers the sign they ask for? Because the problem is not a lack of evidence but a refusal to submit. These men had seen miracle after miracle and had already decided. A sign on demand would have made them spectators, not believers. God has given the greatest sign of all, the resurrection (Matthew 12:39–40; Romans 1:4), and he gives his Spirit to open blind eyes through the preaching of Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:22–24). So when a friend says, I would believe if God showed himself, do not despair of them, and do not try to manufacture wonders. Point them to the cross and the empty tomb, and pray for the Spirit to do what signs cannot.

In everyday life. Is there someone you have written off? A family member hostile to Christ, a colleague who mocks, perhaps your own heart on a bad day. Both robbers reviled him, and one was in paradise by evening; pray for that person again today.

For worship. The priests meant it as the final insult, and God has made it the song of his people for ever: he saved others. He saved a reviling robber before the afternoon was out, and Peter after his denials and Paul after his persecutions, every one because he would not save himself. The two halves of their sneer are the two halves of his glory: power enough to save anyone, and love enough to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darkness over the whole land. Noon until three, the brightest hours of a spring day, and the light goes out. It is not an eclipse; Passover falls at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible, and none lasts three hours. The ninth hour was the hour of prayer at the evening sacrifice (Acts 3:1).

Darkness in Scripture. On that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight; I will turn your feasts into mourning; I will make it like the mourning for an only son (Amos 8:9–10). Darkness at noon, at a feast, mourning for an only son: Amos said it eight hundred years earlier. And on the eve of the first Passover there was a darkness to be felt, and then the night the firstborn died (Exodus 10:21–23). At the first Passover the darkness came before the firstborn was struck, and it does so again. In the Bible darkness at midday is never mere scenery. It is a sign of God’s judgment, the day of the LORD, and here that judgment falls on Jesus. The mockers demanded to see (v. 32); God’s answer is darkness, and Mark records no voice at all in it. Whatever passed between the Father and the Son in those hours happened where nobody could watch.

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? Out of the dark comes the loudest sound of the day. Not the faint whisper of a dying man but a cry. A crucified man probably died by slow suffocation, and every word would have cost an agonising push upwards. This is shouted. Mark keeps the Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, as he did with Talitha cumi to a dead girl, Ephphatha to a deaf man, and Abba in the garden (5:41; 7:34; 14:36). All of them are moments of extremity, and all are the actual sound of his voice. These are the only words of Jesus from the cross that Mark records.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? There are no darker words in Scripture. It is Psalm 22:1, and the psalm that has been surfacing all chapter is now named aloud by the one it was written about. Jesus, who always called God Father, Abba (14:36), now says my God. It is the only place in the Gospels (Matthew 27:46 records the same cry) where he addresses his Father as anything other than Father. He is not doubting or losing faith; he still says my God, twice, claiming as his own the very One he can no longer feel. But he experiences what no one else ever has: being forsaken by God. Why? Because he was bearing our sin. For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The holy God turns away from sin, and Jesus, bearing it, experienced the abandonment that sinners deserve. This is the essence of hell: separation from the favour of God. Jesus endured it in the place of his people, so that they would never be forsaken. This is what is meant by penal substitution: Jesus bore the penalty our sins deserved, in our place, so that it is not left for us to bear (Isaiah 53:5–6).

Psalm 22. Quoting the first line of a psalm brought the whole psalm to mind. Psalm 22 moves from abandonment (vv. 1–21) through mockery (vv. 7–8), pierced hands and feet (v. 16, where the standard Hebrew text reads like a lion and the ancient Greek translation reads pierced) and the dividing of garments (v. 18), to victory and praise: all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD (vv. 22–31). Its last words are: he has done it. Jesus’ cry is real abandonment; but it is also the cry of one who knows the end of the psalm.

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son. The Father was never more pleased with the Son than in this act of obedience (John 10:17; Ephesians 5:2). The Son, in his human nature, bore the Father’s wrath against sin and lost all sense of his favour, yet he remained the beloved Son, and God, through every moment of the dark. What he lost was the comfort of his Father’s presence, not his Father’s love or his own deity. The mystery is beyond us; the fact is clear: he was forsaken so that we would be accepted.

Is it fair to punish the innocent for the guilty? It would be unjust if God seized an unwilling third party and punished him for someone else’s crime. That is not the cross. The one who bears the sin is God the Son, the Judge himself, who came willingly (John 10:18) and who stands as the head of the people he dies for, as Adam stood for the human race (Romans 5:18–19). God did not punish a stranger. In his own Son he bore the cost of his own justice, so that he is both just and the one who justifies the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). At the cross justice and love do not compete; they meet.

Did Jesus descend into hell? The Apostles’ Creed says he descended into hell, and Christians have understood the phrase in different ways. Scripture does not teach that he went to a place of torment after death; he told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46). Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) take the phrase to mean the hellish agony he suffered in soul on the cross, above all in this cry. Others understand it simply as his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 50). Either way, the hell he entered was the forsakenness of these hours, and he entered it so that we never will.

What if I feel forsaken by God? Then pray as he did: my God, to the God you cannot feel. The blackest hour a soul can know, real God-forsakenness with its full weight, has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. A believer may feel abandoned, as the psalmists often did, but he is never actually forsaken; I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5) was bought with this cry. Keep praying, even if all you can say is why. Keep going to his people and his word. The darkness is not proof that he has let go; the cross is proof that he never will.

In everyday life. Read Psalm 22 through slowly this week, all thirty-one verses, and notice how much of this chapter is in it, and how it ends. Then, when you next sin, do not tell yourself it is small. Look at the darkness at noon and hear the cry, and know what it cost, and that it is paid.

For worship. From before the foundation of the world the Son had known nothing but the Father’s delight, and at three in the afternoon he cried my God into a darkness that gave no answer. That silence was the silence our sins deserved, and he took the whole of it. The Father hid his face from the Son; and because he hid it there, he will never hide it from us, and has made the word Abba safe in the mouth of every sinner who trusts him.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is calling Elijah. They mishear, or deliberately misunderstand: Eloi sounds like Eliyahu, and popular belief seems to have held that Elijah came to help the righteous in trouble. The cry of the Son bearing our sin is taken for a superstitious call for help, as all through this Gospel the crowd hears the words and gets the meaning wrong (8:28).

Sour wine. Cheap vinegary wine, the standard drink of soldiers and labourers, kept at the site for the squad standing there all day. It is not the drugged wine of verse 23, which he refused, but a mouthful for a man dying of thirst, and somebody ran. John records that Jesus said I thirst and received it (John 19:28–30). It is also Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

Let us see whether Elijah will come. Then the reason is given, and it turns the kindness into something else: keep him going a little longer, so we can see whether anything happens. Mockery to the end. The whole crowd has become an audience waiting for an ending.

The irony. Elijah had already come. Jesus had said so: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased (9:13), meaning John the Baptist, beheaded for telling a king the truth, and nobody rescued him either. There was never going to be a rescue, because rescue was never the plan: he had come to die.

Was the man with the sponge being kind or cruel? Perhaps both, as people often are. He ran, which suggests pity; the words that follow sound like curiosity and mockery, and in Mark they may come from him or from those around him. We need not decide. What matters is that even this small act fulfilled Scripture, and that Jesus, who refused the anaesthetic, accepted the drink. He thirsted truly, as a man, so that he could give living water to all who thirst (John 7:37). No kindness done to him, however mixed, went unnoticed.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A loud cry. This is not how crucified men die, and the centurion in the next verse knows it. Death came when a man had no strength left to push himself up for another breath, and near the end even speech was a struggle. He shouted. John tells us what: it is finished (John 19:30), tetelestai, it is complete; the debt he came to pay is settled. Luke gives the words that came with it, from Psalm 31:5: the Son committing his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). That is not a man dying of exhaustion. It is a man finishing something.

He breathed his last. A real death, of a real man: the Son of God died. He had come to give his life as a ransom (10:45), and nobody took it.

Six hours. Crucified men often took days to die, and Pilate was surprised he had died so soon (v. 44). He had suffered terribly before the cross, but his early death also shows that he laid down his life when the work was finished. So the death of Jesus is not the moment the Romans finally overcame him. It is the last act of his freedom, at three o’clock in Passover week, a few hundred yards from the temple where the lambs had been killed. And in that same instant, in that temple, a curtain tore.

What does his finished work mean for me? It means there is nothing left to pay. Everything required to forgive your sins and bring you to God was completed on the cross: the law fully obeyed, the penalty fully borne, the wrath fully satisfied. Satisfied means that God’s holy anger against sin has been fully met, not ignored or softened, so that none of it remains for those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1). You cannot add to it by good works, sacraments, suffering or religious effort, and you do not need to. That is why the gospel calls you not to achieve but to receive. When your conscience accuses you, do not answer it with your record; answer it with his receipt.

Where did Jesus go when he died? His body lay in the tomb; his human soul went to the Father, as he said: into your hands I commit my spirit, and today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43, 46). He did not cease to exist, sleep unconsciously or pass through a place of purging. That is also what happens to every believer who dies: absent from the body, at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), consciously with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), waiting for the resurrection of the body. The death of Jesus has turned the death of his people into a homecoming.

In everyday life. If you have been trying to finish what Christ finished, adding your efforts to make sure God accepts you, you can stop. Over the sins that trouble you most stand three words from John’s account of this moment: it is finished. A forgiven person is not on probation. Your obedience will stay patchy to the end; his was finished, and it is counted as yours (2 Corinthians 5:21), so your faltering work is accepted for his sake. And if you fear death, for yourself or someone you love, hear his last words: Father, into your hands. They can be yours too.

For worship. He did not die as Rome’s victims died, with the last strength drained out of him; he died with a shout, like a conqueror ending a battle, and the debt written against us was cancelled with him (Colossians 2:14). Nothing he finished that afternoon has ever needed finishing again.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curtain of the temple. There were two: one at the entrance of the Holy Place, and an inner one separating it from the Most Holy Place, the inner sanctuary that represented God’s throne room. Most interpreters take this to be the inner curtain, which Jewish tradition says was about 60 feet (18 m) high and as thick as a man’s hand.

What the curtain was for. It was a locked door made of cloth. Behind it no one went, except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Leviticus 16:2; Hebrews 9:7). For well over a thousand years it said one thing: sin has separated a holy God from unholy people, and you cannot come in on your own terms. And it was a mercy as well as a barrier, because God’s holiness is a pure and burning majesty that sin cannot survive. So the tearing does not mean that God became less holy that afternoon. It means a sacrifice had been offered that makes sinners fit to come in.

Was torn in two. In the same breath as the death: not three days later at the resurrection, but the instant he died. And the verb is the one Mark used when the heavens were torn open at Jesus’ baptism (1:10). He uses it exactly twice: heaven ripped open at the start, the veil at the finish, and between them the whole ministry.

From top to bottom. Men would have started at the bottom, where hands reach. This one opened from the top, and it is Mark’s way of telling you whose hands did it. The way into the presence of God was not forced open from our side. It was torn open from his. The most exclusive room in the world was opened to everybody at three o’clock on a Friday afternoon, and the man who opened it did it by dying. The God who once said keep out now says come in, and the hand that tore the veil from top to bottom is the hand of a Father running to meet his children.

Its meaning. Two things together. First, access: we may enter the holy places with confidence by his blood, along the new and living way he opened through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). His body was torn so the veil could be. Second, judgment: the temple and its sacrifices are finished, as Jesus foretold (13:2). The place where God meets sinners is now Christ himself, and God dwells among his people.

Do we still need priests to come to God? No. Every believer has direct access to the Father through Christ, our one great high priest (Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Timothy 2:5). Pastors and elders are given to teach, shepherd and pray for the church, and we should honour them, but they are not mediators who go into God’s presence on our behalf, and no sacrifice is offered by them. The whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and service. You do not need anyone’s permission to pray, confess or draw near.

Does the torn curtain mean anyone can come to God any way they like? No, and that would turn its meaning upside down. The curtain was torn at the moment of Christ’s death, because his death is the way through it. The access is real and open to all, but it is through his flesh, by his blood, and in no other way. Jesus said I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). The door is wide open, and it has one name on it.

In everyday life. When you pray tonight, an ordinary person with an ordinary week’s failures behind you, there is no queue, no annual appointment, no priest to send in on your behalf, because the blood has been shed and the door is off its hinges. Pray boldly, about large things and small, and do not hang back as if the curtain were still there.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion. Here is the sentence the whole Gospel has been travelling towards. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, and this one was in charge of the execution: a professional, a Gentile and a pagan, who had very likely supervised many crucifixions. And he is standing facing him, directly in front of the cross, close enough to see a man’s face, for six hours.

In this way. What convinced him was not a miracle but the way this man died: the refused wine, the silence under mockery, the absence of cursing, the prayer in the dark, and a shout from a man who should not have had breath for a whisper. He had watched men die before and had never seen anything like it.

Truly this man was the Son of God! The climax of Mark’s Gospel, and Mark has built his whole book to reach it. He opened his book with these words: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1). (A few early manuscripts lack the Son of God there, but most, including some of the oldest, have it.) Since then the title has been spoken by the Father (1:11; 9:7) and shrieked by demons (3:11; 5:7), and no human being in fifteen chapters has said it. Peter got as far as you are the Christ and then argued about the cross. The first person in this Gospel to call Jesus of Nazareth the Son of God is not a disciple, not a Jew, but a Roman execution officer, at the cross.

What did he mean? Some translate a son of God, since the Greek has no word for the here, and a Roman might mean only a divine man, a hero. And was, past tense, as of a dead man. The centurion may have understood less than he said. But Mark records the words as the confession his whole book has been building towards (1:1). Whatever the centurion understood, Mark wants us to hear the full confession. And the emperor was called son of god (divi filius) on coins. A Roman soldier gives the title to a crucified Jew instead.

The secret revealed. All through Mark, Jesus silenced those who would announce him. Now, at the cross, the secret is out. He can be proclaimed as Son of God, because the cross shows what that means: not a conqueror who takes life, but one who gives his life as a ransom for many. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. Not by the healings; the crowds saw those and stayed baffled. Not by the teaching; the scribes heard it and planned a murder. At the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a human being finally sees it. The Son of God reveals his glory most clearly where it is most hidden, in weakness, shame and death.

The wall has been leapt. The confession comes from a foreigner, an occupier, a man outside God’s covenant people and without the Scriptures, at the very hour the chief priests stand in the same place jeering. The nations are coming in, and the first of them is standing in front of a cross with blood on his boots.

Did the centurion become a Christian? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. Luke records that he praised God and said, certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). What Mark wants us to see is not his later history but his words, which are the truth about Jesus spoken at the foot of the cross. The question for the reader is not whether the centurion was saved, but whether we will make his confession our own, with all that it means.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women looking on. Mark has said little about them for fifteen chapters, and now, when everyone else has gone, he tells you they were there. The men had fled; the women stayed. From a distance is the phrase used of Peter (14:54), but Peter kept his distance for safety; theirs was probably as near as the soldiers allowed, and at one point some stood by the cross itself (John 19:25). There was nothing they could do, and they stayed to the end.

Mary Magdalene, Mary and Salome. Named witnesses, who could be found and questioned by anyone in the early church who wanted to check the story. Mary Magdalene, from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, had seven demons cast out of her (Luke 8:2), and she will be the first person on earth to see him alive (John 20:11–18; also 16:9, in the longer ending of Mark, which the earliest manuscripts lack). She was not the sinful woman of Luke 7, as later Western tradition assumed without evidence. Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses is identified by her sons, presumably because the church knew them; she was perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25). Salome was probably the mother of James and John (Matthew 27:56); if so, the woman who once asked for the best two seats in the kingdom for her sons (Matthew 20:20–21) is watching what those seats actually cost, with two rebels occupying them.

They followed him and ministered to him. Followed is the word for discipleship in this Gospel (1:18), applied to women without comment in a world where a rabbi did not normally have female disciples. Ministered is the word of the angels in the wilderness (1:13) and of the sentence that defines his mission: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45). They provided for him out of their means (Luke 8:3), and nobody wrote down what it cost them.

The Servant served. They gave him bread and money; he gives them his life. They can do nothing at the cross but look, and looking is what the cross asks of sinners: turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22; John 3:14–15).

Many other women. A company, and Mark has arranged the contrast. The twelve men are not in this chapter: one sold him, one denied him with oaths, and the rest, who had sworn they would die with him (14:31), are probably hiding in the city. The women watched him die, watched where he was buried, and will be at the tomb at dawn on Sunday with spices they had no idea they would not need. The witnesses who link the cross, the burial and the empty tomb are women, in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight in court: a writer making the story up would hardly have built it this way.

What does this teach about women in the church? That women are full and honoured disciples of Jesus, followers and servants, faithful when men failed, and chosen by God as the first witnesses of the resurrection. The church that forgets this has forgotten its own foundation. Scripture also assigns the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), a pattern this commentary holds, with Jesus himself, who chose twelve men as apostles. Paul grounds it in creation (1 Timothy 2:13), not in the customs of his day. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and they are to be respected as brothers and sisters in Christ. The pattern itself is a difference of calling, not of worth or of devotion, and it is never a licence for men to belittle women. Some of the most faithful service in every church is done by women whose names only Christ records.

In everyday life. Thank God for the faithful women in your church, and tell one of them this week, specifically, what her quiet service has meant. Faithful service that no one notices is noticed by Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The request (vv. 42–43). Evening and the Sabbath are coming, and Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council that condemned Jesus, took courage and asked Pilate for the body, on the day when association with Jesus could only cost him.

The verification (vv. 44–45). Pilate is surprised he is already dead and has the centurion confirm it before releasing the body.

The tomb (vv. 46–47). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across, and two women watching where he is laid.
verseByVerse.theology: The burial is evidence, not a postscript. In six verses Mark establishes four facts. He was really dead: Pilate was surprised, and the centurion who had stood facing him confirmed the death before the body was released. He was buried in a known place: not a common grave but the rock tomb of a named member of the council. The tomb was closed with a stone. And the place was witnessed: the women saw where he was laid, so on Sunday morning they went to the right tomb. There is no room in this account for a faint mistaken for death, a visit to the wrong tomb or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John tells us Joseph had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). Of all the moments to come out, he chose the Friday afternoon, when Jesus was an executed criminal and the twelve had vanished, and he asked a Roman governor for the body of the man his own colleagues had just condemned.

Now: if you have been quiet about Christ for a long time and are waiting for an easier moment, it does not come, and it is not supposed to. Joseph's courage came on the worst possible day. The cross that made him brave is the same cross you look to, and the Spirit who made frightened disciples bold is given to you.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of Preparation. Late afternoon; the Sabbath would begin at sunset, and no burial could be done on it. The Law also required that an executed man’s body not remain all night on the tree, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), the verse Paul quotes of this event (Galatians 3:13). Roman practice was often to leave corpses hanging, or throw them into a common pit, and no one has come to claim this one.

How can Friday afternoon to Sunday morning be three days? Jews counted any part of a day as a day, so after three days and on the third day name the same span (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1). Even Jesus’ three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40) is a way of saying three days, not a count of seventy-two hours. Some have argued for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, but Mark is plain that Jesus died on the day before the Sabbath. And when John calls this Friday the day of Preparation of the Passover (John 19:14), that most likely means the Friday of Passover week, the preparation for that week’s Sabbath, which is exactly how Mark explains the term here (see 14:12).

Joseph of Arimathea. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of Jerusalem. He appears in all four Gospels, and only here, at the burial. Matthew says he was rich, a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57); John says secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).

A respected member of the council. The Sanhedrin, the same body that condemned Jesus at midnight. Luke tells us he was a good and righteous man who had not consented to their decision and action (Luke 23:50–51). He has a position, colleagues, a reputation and a rock-cut tomb, which was an expensive thing to own.

Looking for the kingdom of God. A believer’s description, like Simeon and Anna watching for God to act (Luke 2:25, 38). What had kept him silent was fear of his colleagues on the council.

Took courage. To ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself with him, before both Pilate and the council, and Jesus’ family was not there to ask. And the timing is what is remarkable about him. He does not come out on Sunday, when the tomb is empty, or on the day of the entry, when it would have cost nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a dead criminal, the twelve have vanished, and association means ruin. The disciples had fled; Joseph came out of hiding. Jesus had openly borne shame for Joseph, and that broke Joseph’s fear of bearing shame for Jesus.

Is a secret believer a real Christian? He may be, for a time, as Joseph and Nicodemus were. Faith can be real and still timid, and Jesus does not break a bruised reed. But faith is not meant to stay hidden. Jesus says whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (8:38), and Paul says that with the mouth one confesses and is saved (Romans 10:10). The normal way to confess him is baptism and joining his church. If you have believed quietly for a long time, Joseph’s story is not permission to stay hidden but a summons to come out, and a promise that the cross will give you courage.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate was surprised. A professional’s surprise. Crucifixion was designed to be slow, and victims could last a day or more; soldiers sometimes broke the legs to hasten it, as they did to the two men beside him (John 19:32). Six hours was fast enough to be worth checking.

Summoning the centurion. Pilate does not take Joseph’s word for it. He sends for the officer commanding the detail, very probably the man who has just said truly this man was the Son of God.

He learned from the centurion. The body is not released until a professional soldier has confirmed the death to the governor’s face. That closes the door on the claim, made since the eighteenth century, that he only fainted and revived in the tomb (the swoon theory); John adds that a soldier pierced his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). Any such theory has to get past a Roman officer’s report, and then explain how a man scourged, crucified and sealed in a rock tomb rolled away a stone from the inside and convinced terrified men that he was the risen Lord of life.

He granted the corpse to Joseph. Everywhere else the body is called a body. Here Mark uses ptōma, a corpse, the blunt word he used once before, of John the Baptist (6:29). He is being exact, because everything depends on it: what Joseph carried down was a dead man, with a Roman officer’s word on it and a governor’s release.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus really died? Because a Saviour who did not die could not pay the penalty of death, and a resurrection without a death is no resurrection at all. The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and he had to receive those wages in full in our place. And because death is the enemy every one of us will face, we need a Lord who has been there and come back. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4): every link matters. If he only fainted, your grave is as final as it looks. Because he truly died and truly rose, it is not.

For worship. The Author of life became a corpse. He did not look into death from the doorway; he went all the way in, the cold, still, certified way every one of us will go. And because death had him completely, his rising is complete: not a recovery but a conquest, death beaten on its own ground.
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A linen shroud. Fine linen, bought quickly before the shops closed for the Sabbath. And the word is sindōn: a chapter ago a young man fled the garden leaving his linen cloth behind (14:51–52). One man abandoned his linen cloth to get away from Christ. Another bought one to wrap him in.

Taking him down. Somebody had to draw the nails, take the weight of the body and wrap it, and it was a member of the Sanhedrin, on the eve of the Sabbath, making himself unclean for a week by handling a corpse (Numbers 19:11). John adds that Nicodemus, another member of the council, came with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Two members of the council that condemned him are the only men in Jerusalem attending to his body. It was done in haste; the women would come to complete the anointing (16:1).

A tomb cut out of the rock. Wealthy families had chambers carved into the limestone hillsides around Jerusalem. It was Joseph’s own new tomb (Matthew 27:60), where no one had yet been laid, in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41–42), so there could be no confusion about which body was there. Joseph gives away his own grave. Executed among criminals, buried in a rich man’s tomb: both halves of Isaiah 53:9 happened on the same afternoon.

He rolled a stone. Heavy work to move, which is why the women will worry about it on Sunday (16:3–4); Matthew adds a seal and a guard (Matthew 27:62–66). And that is the last thing anybody does for Jesus of Nazareth: a stone across a door, and then everyone goes home because the sun is going down.

Saw where he was laid. Everyone else has gone; two women stay in the fading light and watch which tomb it is, so on Sunday morning they would not go to the wrong one. Mark records the same women as witnesses of the death (v. 40), the burial (v. 47) and the empty tomb (16:1): crucified, dead and buried, as the creed has it.

The silence of Friday night. The King of the Jews is dead, the body in a borrowed grave, the disciples hiding, the women walking home in the dark. Every person who loved him believed that night that it was finished. They were right, but not as they thought: his saving work was finished, not his life. He had told them three times that he would rise again after three days, and not one of them acted as if they remembered it.

Why does the burial matter? It confirms the death, and it makes the resurrection unmistakable: a known body in a known tomb, sealed and watched, and found empty. It also means that Jesus has gone where all his people go. He lay in the grave and sanctified it. The Westminster Shorter Catechism says the bodies of believers, being still united to Christ, rest in their graves till the resurrection (Q. 37). When you stand at the grave of a believer, you stand where the Lord himself lay, and it is not the end of the story any more than this tomb was.

How should I live on the Fridays of life? As people who know that Sunday is coming, even when we cannot feel it. The women did the next faithful thing: they watched, they went home, they kept the Sabbath, they prepared spices. They did not understand, but they did not leave. When God seems silent and his cause looks buried, keep to the ordinary means of faithfulness, worship, prayer, service, and wait. The darkest Friday in history was followed by the brightest morning, and the God who did that has not changed.

For worship. He who rested on the seventh day when the world was made rested that Sabbath in the rock, the work of redemption finished. He went down into the place of our deepest fear and made it a bed: since that night, a believer’s grave is only a room where the body rests until its Lord calls it. The stone across his door was already waiting for the morning.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology: The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. For centuries it said that sinners could not come into God's presence on their own terms. It was torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top, beyond human reach: the way in was not forced from our side but opened from his. It is the second thing in Mark torn from above, after the heavens being torn open at the baptism (1:10), the same word at the beginning and the end. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20).
15.examples:
Then: what convinced the centurion was not a wonder. Mark says he saw that in this way he breathed his last: he saw how Jesus died. At the cross, where Jesus looks least like the Son of God, a pagan officer sees it, the first human being in this Gospel to say the words Mark opened his book with (1:1).

Now: that is still where people learn who Jesus is. If you want a friend to see him, do not first reach for wonders or arguments; take them to the cross, and let them watch him die.

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Three women buy spices when the shops reopen on Saturday evening, and set out at first light to finish a burial. Not one of them expects a resurrection: he had told them three times and they had not taken it in. Their only worry is a stone they cannot move.

They find it moved, and a young man in white sitting inside, who says the most important sentence in the book: He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. The resurrection happened at a place that can be pointed to, and the women are invited to look for themselves. Then comes a message with two extra words in it, and Peter, and the women run away and say nothing, because they are afraid. That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop.

The twelve verses that follow are printed in brackets in the ESV, and the question they raise is answered plainly in the notes. They summarise appearances recorded elsewhere, give the commission, and end with Jesus taken up and seated at the right hand of God, as he had told the high priest he would be. And the last sentence of Mark reverses verse 8: the people who said nothing went out and preached everywhere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The errand (vv. 1–4). When the Sabbath ends, three women buy spices and set out at first light on Sunday to finish a burial, worrying about a stone they cannot move. They find the problem solved.

The announcement (vv. 5–7). Inside the tomb a young man in white tells them that Jesus has risen, and sends a message to the disciples with one name added to it.

The silence (v. 8). They run, and say nothing to anybody, because they are afraid. That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop, and the question it raises is dealt with plainly below.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? Before verse 9 the ESV notes in square brackets that some of the earliest manuscripts do not include these verses. The two oldest complete manuscripts, both fourth century, end Mark at verse 8; Eusebius and Jerome say the accurate copies known to them ended there; and the Greek of verses 9–20 does not read like Mark. So Mark very probably did not write these twelve verses, which were added early enough to be widely read in churches by the second century.

What that does not mean. Nothing has been smuggled into your Bible. Everything in these verses that matters is taught plainly elsewhere, and no doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the differences openly at the bottom of the page, and that openness is a reason to trust the rest of the text.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7). Peter had denied him three times with oaths and a curse, and as far as he knew he was no longer one of them. The first message from the other side of the grave names him, in case he thought the word disciples no longer meant him, and it keeps a promise made before the failure happened (14:27–28).

Now: if you have failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in those two words. The way back was promised before you ever went wrong, and when the message came, the one who had failed worst was named.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Mark 16 opens on the morning after the longest Sabbath in history. The women who watched Jesus die and saw where he was buried find the tomb open and hear that the crucified one is risen, with a message for his disciples, and Peter by name. They flee and say nothing, and there the earliest manuscripts end. The crucified one is alive, failures are called back by name, and the gospel Mark called a beginning runs on to the ends of the earth.

The setting. Jesus died at about three on Friday and was buried in haste before sunset (15:42–47). Then came the Sabbath, twenty-four hours in which nothing could be done, the longest day of his friends’ lives, and Mark says nothing about it at all.

When the Sabbath was past. Saturday evening, after sunset, when the shops could open again.

Bought spices. The same names as at the cross (15:40) and, for two of them, at the burial (15:47): named witnesses, who saw him die, saw where he was laid, and now go to the same tomb. And they spend money on the last thing they expected to be able to do for him.

To anoint him. Fragrant oils to pour over the body, an act of love and honour. The burial on Friday had been done racing the sunset, and they are going to finish it. Which means that not one of them expected a resurrection, though he had told them three times (8:31; 9:31; 10:34). So the resurrection was not something they wanted so much that they imagined it. The story begins with his friends buying ointment for a dead man.

Anointed already. Their spices will never touch him. He had been anointed for burial days before, by a woman at Bethany (14:3–8). The women are carrying gifts for a funeral to the one person in history who will never need one again.

The first day of the week. Very early, and yet with the sun up: most likely they set out in the dark (John 20:1) and arrived as the sun came up. All four Gospels use the phrase, and within a generation Christians were meeting on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and John was very probably calling it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). The Sabbath commemorated God’s rest after the first creation; the Lord’s Day celebrates the beginning of the new creation. The Sabbath had rested over a sealed tomb; the first day broke over an empty one.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Christians differ: many, following the Westminster and 1689 London Baptist Confessions, hold that the Sabbath command still stands and has moved to the first day; others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10). This commentary’s view: the second fits the New Testament best: the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship and rest, and no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5), though gathering with God’s people each week is not optional. (See 1 Corinthians 16:2 for the fuller answer.)

Why did no one remember that he had said he would rise? Because grief and unbelief are deafening, and because what he said did not fit what they expected of a Messiah. Each time he predicted his death and resurrection, the disciples either argued, misunderstood or were afraid to ask (8:32; 9:32). They heard the death and could not hear the rising. We are not so different. Many of us know the promises of God and forget them the moment trouble comes. That is why Scripture keeps saying remember, and why the angel will soon say: just as he told you.

In everyday life. Every Lord’s Day is the risen Lord’s gift, a celebration of what he has already done, so plan your week around it rather than fitting it into the gaps. Prepare on Saturday night as these women prepared their spices: go to bed in good time, pray for the preaching, decide whom you will welcome. And when you wake on Sunday, say first: he is risen.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were saying to one another, Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb? The tense is continuous: they kept saying it, all the way there. It is entirely reasonable. They had watched Joseph roll it across on Friday (15:46). The stone was too heavy for three women, and Matthew says it was sealed and guarded as well (Matthew 27:66). Yet they set out anyway, to do what love required, without knowing how. A more calculating person stays at home until the problem is solved.

Looking up. The tomb was perhaps up a slope, or they had been walking with their heads down in grief. Had been rolled back names nobody who did it: it was God’s doing. Matthew says an angel rolled it away and sat on it (Matthew 28:2).

It was very large. Mark puts the size at the end, as somebody tells a story afterwards: and it had been moved, and it was enormous. Mark’s verb, rolled, suggests the rarer kind of stone found at the tombs of the wealthy: a disc set in a channel, perhaps a ton or more, far easier to roll into place than out again. It could not have been moved by accident, or by the women. The stone was very large, and it was nothing to him.

Moved so the world could look in. The stone was not moved to let Jesus out; he would come through locked doors that same evening (John 20:19). It was moved so the witnesses could look in. And here is the plainest comfort in the chapter: they spent the walk on a difficulty that had already been settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still certain nothing had changed.

Does God always remove the obstacles I worry about? Not always in the way we hope, and we should not promise ourselves that he will. Sometimes the stone stays, and he gives strength to live beside it. But the empty tomb tells you that the greatest obstacle of all, death itself, has already been rolled away, and that nothing you face is beyond his power or outside his care. Very often, the thing you are rehearsing at four in the morning is dealt with before you reach it. When it is not, he walks with you through it. Either way, it is still right to set out in faithful love without having the solution.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And entering the tomb. A rock-cut tomb of this kind had a low doorway and an outer chamber, with a shelf cut into the rock where the body was laid. So they stoop through and stand up inside a room built for the dead.

A young man in a white robe. An angel in human form, as angels often appear (Genesis 18:2; Daniel 9:21); Matthew says so plainly (Matthew 28:2–5). White is the colour of heaven and glory, like Jesus’ clothes on the mountain (9:3).

Sitting on the right side. Sitting, the posture of somebody whose work is finished, on the side of honour, where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19). The messenger sits because the Son has finished: after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3).

The two young men. The phrase a young man (neaniskos) occurs exactly twice in Mark. The first was in the garden: a young man left his linen cloth and ran away naked (14:51–52), perhaps Mark himself, putting his own worst moment into his own book. The second is here: a young man, dressed in white, inside an empty grave, telling women that Christ is risen. One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark. One sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news. Whether or not Mark intended every echo, the picture is the gospel: that is the change Christ’s death and resurrection make in people.

And they were alarmed. Utterly astonished, overwhelmed with awe, the strong word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:33). They came expecting a corpse and found a living stranger where it should have been.

Why do the Gospels differ about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Luke two men in dazzling clothes (Luke 24:4), John two angels; the women and the times vary too. Each Gospel tells the story selectively, and none says there was only one. If there were two, there was certainly one, and a writer may mention only the one who spoke. The women evidently came in more than one group, at slightly different times. Such differences are what you expect from independent witnesses, not from a story agreed in advance. The core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen. Not every detail can be fitted together with certainty, and careful believers propose different orders of events; but the differences lie at the edges of the story, not at its centre.

For worship. Heaven sat down in the grave. The angel had nothing to guard and nothing to fight, only news to give, because death had nothing left to hold. The room built for an ending has become the doorway of the world’s beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be alarmed. He takes up the very word used of them in the last verse. He deals with their terror before he gives them the news, which is how heaven habitually speaks to frightened people: do not be afraid is what Zechariah, Mary, the shepherds and John on Patmos all heard (Luke 1:13, 30; 2:10; Revelation 1:17).

Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. The personal name, the village that made people take offence (6:3), and a Greek form (estaurōmenon) that describes a past event with lasting effect: the one who has been crucified and remains the crucified one. When he appears to Thomas he will still have the wounds (John 20:27). Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got past the cross, but a man who went through it and is known by it for ever: a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6). The resurrection does not erase the cross; it declares that the cross achieved what he died for.

He has risen. The Greek (ēgerthē) is literally he has been raised: God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9). The resurrection is the Father’s public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark; the court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas (12:10). It proves that he is who he claimed to be (Romans 1:4), that death has been defeated (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and that his sacrifice was accepted, for he was raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). To be justified is to be acquitted in God’s court and counted righteous for Christ’s sake: if God had refused his sacrifice, he would still be lying dead.

He is not here. A bodily resurrection. Not merely that his spirit lived on, or that his disciples felt his presence, or that his cause continues. It is a claim about a physical location on a spring morning. The body was not in the room, and the room was one the women had personally watched him carried into (15:47).

See the place where they laid him. The angel does something legends rarely bother to do: he invites inspection. Come and look at the shelf. John records that the grave clothes were still lying in place (John 20:5–7), and Paul says that without the resurrection our faith is worthless (1 Corinthians 15:17). The location was known, and the authorities had soldiers: had the body still been there, they had only to produce it to end the whole movement.

Evidence for the resurrection. The empty tomb, which, Matthew reports, the authorities did not dispute but explained by claiming the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11–15). The appearances to many witnesses, including over five hundred at once, most of them still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The transformation of frightened, scattered disciples into bold witnesses ready to die. The conversion of sceptics like James and Paul. And Jewish believers, raised to keep the seventh day, gathering for worship on the first. Sceptics explain each in turn, but it is hard to find one explanation that accounts for them all.

Could the appearances have been grief visions? Grief can give a mourner a vivid sense of someone’s presence, but it does not empty a tomb. Nor does it come to five hundred people at once, to a sceptical brother like James, or to an enemy like Saul (1 Corinthians 15:6–8). And first-century Jews who had seen a vision would have said they had seen his spirit or his angel (Acts 12:15), not that he had been raised bodily, which none of them expected before the end of the world. The women in this verse were not imagining a presence. They were shown an empty place.

Will my risen body be like his? Yes. Paul says Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). It will be truly your body, recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, scars and all; he ate, he could be touched, he was not a ghost (Luke 24:39–43). But it will be changed: raised imperishable, in glory and in power, a body fully suited to life in the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). No more sickness, ageing, disability or death. The empty tomb is God’s pledge that he does not throw away what he made. He redeems it.

In everyday life. When you are tempted to despair, about your sin, your health, the state of the world, go back in your mind to the empty shelf: your greatest enemy is already beaten. And if someone asks why you believe, do not begin with your feelings. Begin where the angel began: with Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified, and a tomb that was empty.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, tell his disciples. The first commission of the new age is given to three women in a graveyard, in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight: someone inventing the story to persuade would hardly have done that. And they are still his disciples, though they deserted him.

And Peter. Two extra words that have comforted failing Christians ever since. Only Mark has them. Peter was one of the disciples; the word covered him. There was no need to add anything, unless heaven knew that one man in Jerusalem was certain the word no longer included him. Peter had denied him three times, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, with oaths and a curse on his own head, and had broken down and wept (14:71–72). He had probably spent Saturday somewhere in that city with nothing to think about but that. As far as he knew he was not merely ashamed; he was no longer a disciple at all. And the first message sent from the other side of the grave has his name attached to the end of it, in case he thought the word disciples no longer meant him. Before Peter could find his way back, Christ had sent a message to find him. Mark probably heard the story from Peter himself, who never forgot those two words. The risen Lord appeared to Peter personally (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5), and restored him publicly (John 21:15–19).

Going before you to Galilee. Not new information but a quotation: before anybody had failed, Jesus had said, after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The restoration was promised before the betrayal, the meeting place fixed while they were still swearing they would never fall away. Go before is a shepherd’s picture: the struck shepherd is out in front of the scattered flock again. And Galilee, not Jerusalem where it all went wrong, but home, the boats, the place they were called in chapter 1. He takes them back to the beginning to start again.

But did he not appear in Jerusalem first? Yes. Luke and John record appearances in Jerusalem that Sunday and the week after, and Luke has Jesus tell them to stay in the city (Luke 24:49). The Jerusalem appearances came first; the meeting in Galilee followed (Matthew 28:16; John 21); and they returned to Jerusalem to wait for the Spirit. Luke’s command to stay belongs to the end of the forty days. Mark points to Galilee because it was the promised meeting and the place of their calling, not because nothing happened before it.

Just as he told you. The angel’s own comment, gentle and slightly pointed. Every element of this weekend had been announced in advance, and not one of them had held on to it. The message on Easter morning is a reminder that he keeps his word even when nobody believed it.

Have I failed too badly to be called back? If Peter was not beyond it, you are not. His failure was public, repeated, sworn and at the worst possible moment, and the first message of the risen Christ named him. Christ does not restore only those whose failures were small. He restores those who come back. Your feelings may tell you that you have used up his patience; his word says that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Put your own name after the words and Peter, and go to meet him where he has promised to be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

In everyday life. Somewhere in your church is a believer who has gone quiet: someone who failed badly and now stays away out of shame, sure that the general welcome cannot mean them. The angel’s two extra words are for them too. Be the messenger. Send them a message this week that says, in your own words, he is asking for you.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named: the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trembling and astonishment. They run, not from unbelief but from overwhelming awe: trembling (tromos), and ekstasis, being beside oneself. It closes a Gospel in which awe has followed his power from the first storm to the last morning (4:41; 5:42).

And they said nothing to anyone. Matthew and Luke tell us they went and told the disciples (Matthew 28:8; Luke 24:9), so this was most likely a stunned silence on the road, not lasting disobedience. And there is a superb irony in it: all through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet (1:45; 7:36). Here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

For they were afraid. In Greek the sentence ends with the small word gar, for: they were afraid, for. An extraordinarily abrupt ending, a little like ending a book with the word because.

Textual note: the ending of Mark. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century) end Mark’s Gospel here, at verse 8. Early church writers, Eusebius and Jerome, said that most of the Greek manuscripts they knew ended here. Other manuscripts have a short ending of a sentence or two; most later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, have the longer ending (vv. 9–20), which differs from Mark’s style and vocabulary and appears to be a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts. The ESV prints verses 9–20 in brackets.

Where Christians differ: did Mark end here? Some think Mark meant to end at verse 8. Others think the original ending was lost, perhaps from the end of a scroll or the last leaf of a codex, or that Mark could not finish; early tradition places him in Rome under Nero, around the time the early church remembered as Peter’s death there. This commentary’s view: the evidence is strong that verses 9–20 were not written by Mark, but were added early, probably in the second century. Whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 is less certain. But if he did, it is a powerful ending. The resurrection has been announced; Jesus has been seen to be who he said; and the story leaves the reader with the question: what will you do? The women were silent for fear; will you be? Mark’s Gospel began with the beginning of the gospel (1:1). It ends where the church’s preaching begins.

What an ending at verse 8 does. The last human beings in the book fail, for a time, to pass the message on. His people’s obedience is never complete; his was, and the empty tomb is God’s verdict that it counts for them (Romans 4:25). The women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 started, so the end of the book sends the reader back to its beginning.

Nothing is lost. Whatever the ending, the resurrection is stated as fact in verse 6, and the appearances are recorded by Matthew, Luke, John and Paul, whose list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8) was written within about twenty-five years. Mark ends with three frightened women running from an empty grave, not with any doubt about whether the grave was empty.

Why were they afraid, if the news was good? Because it was too good and too great to take in at once. They had come to anoint a corpse and had met an angel, an empty tomb and a message that turned the universe upside down. This is not the fear of punishment but the holy fear of creatures who have seen God act. Matthew says they ran with fear and great joy (Matthew 28:8): both at once. A faith that has never trembled at the resurrection may not have understood it. But such fear is meant to give way to witness, as theirs did.

In everyday life. The women were silent at first, and the risen Lord did not give up on them; the power is his Spirit’s, not yours. Ask what keeps you quiet: fear of ridicule, of not having answers. Then tell one person this week, simply, that you believe Jesus rose from the dead, and why.

For worship. God did not wait for brave messengers. He used frightened women, then deserting men, then a persecutor, then us. The power of the resurrection does not depend on the courage of those who carry it; it is the power of God, who still sends the news out of the mouths of the weak to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What this passage is. Before verse 9 your Bible notes in square brackets that some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. The notes on these verses answer the question plainly.

What it contains. Appearances to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples walking into the country, and to the eleven at table, each report disbelieved until Jesus rebukes them in person. Then the commission to the whole creation, a promise of accompanying signs (including the sentence about serpents and poison that a few churches have built a deadly practice on), and the ascension: he sits down at the right hand of God, as he told the high priest he would (14:62). The last verse of Mark is the disciples doing what the women in verse 8 could not.
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves. Believing and being baptised belong together, but the second half settles the matter: the condemnation falls on whoever does not believe, not on whoever is not baptised. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign of that faith, not its ground. That is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands (v. 18). On the strength of that sentence a handful of churches have handled snakes and drunk poison in their services to prove their faith, and people have died.

Now: these are among the most doubtful words in Mark, and even at face value they describe what may happen to Christ’s servants, as when a viper fastened on Paul’s hand on Malta (Acts 28:3–6), not what they are to seek out. Reaching for danger to prove that one believes is what Jesus refused in the wilderness (Luke 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About verses 9–20. These verses are not found in the earliest manuscripts and were very probably not written by Mark. They were added early and have been read in the church for centuries, so they are printed in our Bibles, in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded elsewhere; where they agree with the rest of Scripture they are true and useful, but no doctrine should rest on them alone.

The facts, laid out plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end Mark at verse 8, and so do some of the oldest versions in other languages. Eusebius, in the early fourth century, says the accurate copies known to him ended there; Jerome says the same a century later. Some manuscripts have a much shorter ending instead, and a few have both, which is what copyists do when they know of two and cannot decide. And the Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book. Most tellingly, verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, although she was named a few verses earlier (v. 1). That is not how a writer refers to a character he has been following all morning. It is how a different writer begins.

The other view. Some Christians defend the longer ending as Mark’s own: it is in the great majority of manuscripts, Irenaeus quotes verse 19 around AD 180, and it seems unlikely Mark meant to end with for they were afraid. Their concern is honourable: they do not want to lose any of God’s word. But the oldest manuscripts and the early writers who knew the evidence point the other way.

Should this unsettle my confidence in the Bible? No, and here is why. First, nothing has been smuggled in. Every substantial thing in this passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary in John 20, the two on the road in Luke 24, the commission in Matthew 28 and Acts 1, the ascension in Luke 24, Acts 1 and Hebrews 1:3. No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here. Second, this is what a reliable text looks like. We possess thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, vastly more and vastly earlier than for any other ancient document, and so we can see exactly where copyists differed. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one shows the copyists’ variations openly, in the margin and the footnotes. Third, be clear what is not in doubt: the empty tomb, the announcement of the resurrection and the promise of the appearances are all in verses 1–8, in every manuscript there is.

Appeared first to Mary Magdalene. As John 20:11–18 records. The first person on earth to see the risen Christ was not Peter, not his mother, not a priest, but a woman whose past was so wrecked that seven demons had to be cast out of her (Luke 8:2). Grace does not choose the impressive; it chooses the rescued. And it is hardly a detail anyone would invent to impress the ancient world.

In the flow. Verses 9–14 move in three steps, Mary, then the two on the road, then the eleven, and each time the news is refused until the Lord himself confronts the unbelief. Then verses 15–20 send those same doubters out with the gospel. The writer is answering the abrupt fear of verse 8: the silence was not the end, because the risen Lord overcame his disciples’ unbelief himself.

As they mourned and wept. On Easter Sunday the disciples are mourning, not waiting hopefully. They thought it was over.

They would not believe it. The first of three refusals in four verses: these words seemed to them an idle tale (Luke 24:11). They had to be convinced, against their will, by the man himself. The disciples refused the news, and he did not refuse them.

Why would God allow words not written by Mark into most Bibles? God has preserved his word not by making copyists infallible, but by giving his church so many copies that errors can be seen and corrected. The longer ending was added very early, it teaches nothing contrary to Scripture, and for centuries most readers had no easy means of telling it apart. Now that the earlier manuscripts are known, translations mark it honestly. That is not a failure of God’s care but an example of it: he has kept the text so fully that we can see even the additions. The canon of Scripture is closed, and its message has reached us intact.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
