In another form. Luke 24 in one sentence: the road to Emmaus, where two disciples walked with him for hours and knew him at last when he broke the bread (Luke 24:13–35). Luke explains the failure to recognise him differently: their eyes were kept from recognising him (Luke 24:16). His risen body was the same, but changed and glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and Mary too took him for the gardener (John 20:15).

They did not believe them. The second refusal, and harder to fit with Luke, where the two are greeted with the Lord has risen indeed (Luke 24:34). The likeliest answer is that faith and doubt were mixed in that room, as they still disbelieved for joy minutes later (Luke 24:41), and this summary stresses the doubt. It is a real difficulty, and not every question about it can be settled.

Reclining at table. The Twelve minus Judas (Luke 24:36–43; John 20:19–29), at a meal, which is where the risen Christ keeps turning up: at Emmaus, in the upper room asking for fish, on a beach in Galilee cooking breakfast.

Hardness of heart. The phrase used of the men who watched a withered hand restored and planned a murder (3:5), and of the disciples who had carried the baskets and understood nothing (6:52; 8:17). Unbelief in the face of credible testimony is not a mere intellectual difficulty, and the risen Christ rebukes it, lovingly, before he commissions them. He rebuked his friends because he loved them, and then trusted them with the world.

Not easily convinced, and sent anyway. The apostles are often accused of having wanted a resurrection so badly that they talked themselves into it. Every account says the opposite: they dismissed the women and the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person, and even then some doubted (Matthew 28:17). And he sends them anyway. Men who had run away in a garden, denied him in a courtyard and refused two reports are handed the gospel for the whole creation. He does not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.

Is it a sin to doubt as the eleven did? Doubt as a struggle is not the same as unbelief as a refusal. Many true believers wrestle with questions and seasons of uncertainty, and Scripture is full of them: Thomas, John the Baptist in prison (Matthew 11:2–3), the father who cried I believe; help my unbelief (9:24). Jesus met those doubts with patience and evidence. What he rebukes here is the hardness that will not believe credible testimony because it does not want to. So bring your doubts to him honestly, as the father did. Do not nurse them as a badge of sophistication, and do not hide them in shame. He has given you the testimony of the eyewitnesses, and he is able to strengthen weak faith. The eleven were rebuked not for having questions but for refusing two sets of witnesses, and the same men, once they had seen him, became his witnesses (Acts 1:8).

In everyday life. Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing (John 20:29). This week, read 1 Corinthians 15:1–20 and watch Paul pile up the witnesses. Then ask whether your own unbelief, in some area of your life, is a question that wants answers or a hardness that does not want to change, and bring either one to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into all the world. The commission, in the form found also in Matthew 28:18–20, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, and every phrase widens it. Go: the movement is outward. The Old Testament pattern was largely that the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3); now the direction reverses and the people of God are sent out. Into all the world: said to eleven men, most of them from one lakeside district of one small province, with no money, no organisation and no standing. Proclaim: the herald’s word (kēryssō), to announce publicly what a king has decreed. A herald does not improve the message; he carries it. The King who was crucified as a rebel now sends his heralds to the whole creation with a royal decree of pardon. To the whole creation: all people everywhere, and more than that, for the rescue is not merely of souls out of a doomed world but the beginning of the repair of everything (Romans 8:21–22; Ephesians 1:10). The gospel that Jesus said must first be preached to all nations (13:10) is now the church’s task.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. Faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament: those who believed were baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12; 16:31–33), and nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines the water. A believer who refuses baptism is refusing his Lord’s plain command.

Whoever does not believe. It does not say whoever is not baptised. If baptism were part of what saves, its absence would be part of what condemns, and the sentence carefully does not say so. We are saved by grace through faith, not by any work, not even a good and commanded one (Ephesians 2:8–9).

What it does not mean. Not that baptism itself saves, or that a believer who dies unbaptised is lost; nor is this verse, from the longer ending, a foundation for any doctrine of baptism on its own. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read Acts 2:38 and 22:16 as teaching that baptism is a means by which God gives forgiveness. But there, as here, baptism is joined to repentance and faith as their outward sign; forgiveness is given to faith (Acts 10:43).

Why should not believing be enough to condemn someone? Because unbelief is not an innocent lack of information but the refusal of God’s own remedy. Everyone already stands guilty for sins against the light he has (Romans 1:20; 3:23); the gospel comes as the rescue, and to turn it away is to stay where one already was. Jesus put it plainly: whoever does not believe is condemned already (John 3:18). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), which is why the same verse that warns of condemnation comes wrapped in a command to go and tell everyone.

Where Christians differ: the order of believing and baptism. Paedobaptists (those who baptise infants) baptise the children of believers before faith, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise to believers and their children, as circumcision was (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Credobaptists (believer-baptists) baptise on a credible profession of faith. Faithful Christians who love the Bible have differed here for five centuries. This commentary’s view: this verse, like the New Testament pattern generally, places believing before baptism, which fits the credobaptist position: every baptism the New Testament describes in detail follows a profession of faith (the household baptisms are read differently by each side), and baptism pictures a union with Christ received by faith (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12). Because this verse belongs to the longer ending, the case rests on that wider pattern, not on this verse alone. It is held charitably toward brothers who differ.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? On the view this commentary holds, yes: ask to be baptised as a believer, without contempt for your parents’ love or for the many godly Christians who regard infant baptism as true baptism. (See Galatians 3:27 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. The commission is yours too. Write down three people who need to hear the gospel, pray for them by name every day this week, and look for one opportunity to speak, leaning on the Spirit he promised his witnesses (Acts 1:8). And do not despise baptism, nor lean your weight on it: a confidence resting on something done to you with water rests on the sign and not on Christ, to whom the sign points.

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These signs will accompany. The signs are not the point; they follow the message and confirm it (v. 20). Those listed are found in Acts: casting out demons (Acts 16:18), tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:46), surviving a snake bite (Acts 28:3–6), healing by laying on of hands (Acts 28:8). Drinking poison unharmed is not in the New Testament. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message in the founding of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and every one pointed away from the apostles to the risen Lord whose name they carried.

In my name. The authority is borrowed, never possessed, which the disciples forgot when they failed to cast out a demon at the foot of the mountain (9:18, 28–29). In Acts 2, at least, the new tongues were real languages, understood by those from many nations.

Serpents and poison. This sentence has done real harm, and it needs a plain word. On the strength of it a handful of churches, mostly in the Appalachian mountains of the United States, and rejected by almost all Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, have handled venomous snakes in their services and drunk poison to demonstrate their faith. People have been bitten, and some have died, including pastors, some refusing medical treatment on principle. Two things must be said. First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all, and to build a dangerous practice on a text the oldest copies do not contain is unwise twice over. Second, even taken at face value, the verse describes what may happen to Christ’s servants, not what they are to go looking for. Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, was gathering firewood when a viper fastened on his hand, and he shook it into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6). He did not seek it, was not proving anything, and was engaged in the humble business of collecting sticks to warm shipwrecked strangers. It happened to him while he was serving others; he did not stage it.

What it does not mean. Not a command to handle snakes or drink poison. Inviting danger to prove one believes is what Satan urged in the wilderness, quoting a promise of protection (Psalm 91:11–12), and Jesus answered: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12). Engineering a crisis to see whether he will come through, refusing the doctor to prove one has faith, is not trust. Faith trusts God; it does not dare him.

Where Christians differ: do the signs continue? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians (often called continuationists) hold that the miraculous gifts, tongues and healing continue in the church today as normal, pointing to Peter’s word that the Spirit is poured out in the last days (Acts 2:17–18) and to Paul’s teaching on the gifts (1 Corinthians 12–14). Cessationists hold that the sign gifts were given to confirm the apostles and their message while the New Testament was being written, and ceased with the apostolic age. This commentary’s view: the cessationist position fits Scripture best. The signs authenticated the apostles as the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). God still answers prayer, and still heals according to his will (James 5:14–15), but not through the apostolic sign gifts. This is held charitably toward brothers and sisters who differ, many of whom love Christ deeply; the question is how God works today, not whether he is at work.

Does God still heal today? Yes, as he wills, in answer to the prayers of his people (James 5:14–15) and through doctors and medicine, though he has not promised that every sickness will be healed in this life; every believer’s final healing is certain at the resurrection. (See John 9:6 for the fuller answer.)

What about Christians I know who say they speak in tongues or prophesy? Receive them as brothers and sisters in Christ, not as suspects to be watched. Many of them love Christ deeply and are more zealous than we are. You can hold your conviction that the apostolic sign gifts have ceased, and still learn from their prayerfulness and expectancy. Where you differ, test everything by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and be clear that no experience adds to the closed canon of God’s word. Speak about it gently, with your Bible open, and do not let it break fellowship over what is not the gospel.

For worship. The Lord who crushed the serpent’s head let a viper fall harmless from his servant’s hand, because the sting of death had already been drawn. The signs have done their work and the foundation is laid, but the greater wonder goes on in every new birth, as dead sinners are raised by the same power that emptied the tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taken up into heaven. The ascension in one sentence, forty days after the resurrection (Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–11), and it is the last thing this book says about Jesus. Was taken up: the Father receives him, as Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:11).

At the right hand of God. Psalm 110:1, the verse Jesus quoted in the temple (12:36) and before the high priest (14:62). Bound, with the case against him in ruins, he had said: you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and they condemned him for it. Here, in one flat sentence, it has come true, within weeks of his execution for saying it. He is enthroned, interceding for his people (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25), until all his enemies are under his feet.

He sat down because it was done. The sitting itself teaches something. Priests in the temple never sat down; there were no chairs in the holy place, because the work of sacrifice was never finished. Hebrews makes the point directly: every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Hebrews 10:11–12).

Preached everywhere. The book of Acts in a sentence, and the exact reversal of verse 8. The same terrified company goes out and preaches everywhere, and it was not a change of temperament: the risen Christ stood in the room, and he poured out his Spirit. Early tradition says most of them died for it and none recanted.

The Lord worked with them. He has just sat down in heaven, and he is working alongside them on earth in the same sentence: that is how things stand for the whole age of the church. He worked with them by his Spirit: behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). The mission was never the disciples carrying on alone after Jesus had left. It was, and is, his work, done through people who had recently proved themselves entirely unreliable.

The end of Mark. Whether one reads to verse 8 or 20, Mark’s Gospel ends at a beginning. Its first line was the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1): sixteen chapters, from the baptism to the empty grave, are the beginning. It was carried along the roads of an empire, and it has reached you.

Where is Jesus now, and what is he doing? He is in heaven, bodily, at the right hand of the Father, the same Jesus with the same scars, now glorified. He is reigning over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is praying for his people, and his intercession never fails (Hebrews 7:25). To intercede is to plead on someone’s behalf: he presents his finished sacrifice before the Father for his people, so that their acceptance never hangs on the strength of their own prayers (1 John 2:1). He is building his church by his word and Spirit, working with every faithful preacher and witness. And he is waiting for the day when he will come again, visibly, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. He is not absent. He is enthroned, and he is busy, and he is with you.

What does this mean for my witness? It means you never speak for Christ alone. When you share the gospel, pray for someone, explain your hope, or serve your neighbour in his name, the Lord works with you. Results are his responsibility; faithfulness is yours. You do not need to be eloquent, brave by nature or theologically trained. The disciples were none of those. You need to go, to tell, and to trust that the King at the Father’s right hand is confirming his own word.

For worship. The man who was appalled and shaking in a garden, who shouted into the darkness, who lay as a corpse behind a stone, is seated at the right hand of God, and will never again need to offer himself. The prisoner who stood before Caiaphas is the King before whom Caiaphas will stand. The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has no end.

16.theology:
Does Mark end at verse 8? The last word is gar, for: an extraordinarily abrupt way to end a book, rather like ending a book with the word because. Three explanations are offered, and we do not know which is right: the last leaf of an early copy was lost; the author was interrupted (tradition places him in Rome under Nero); or he meant to stop there. An ending at verse 8 leaves the resurrection announced and not described, the appearances promised and not narrated, and the reader left to decide how to respond. Mark called his book the beginning of the gospel (1:1), and the women are sent back to Galilee, where chapter 1 began.

Whatever is decided about verses 9–20, nothing in the question touches verses 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8). All through this Gospel, people told to be silent could not keep quiet (1:45; 7:36). Here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Now: the last verse of the chapter is the reversal: the same frightened company went out and preached everywhere. What changed them was not their temperament but the risen Christ, who confronted their unbelief in person and then sent them anyway. His Spirit still makes frightened people into witnesses.
